title: Yearly Notes
text:
This page documents the eddy covariance setup periods and the flux versions calculated for each year, including the software versions used and notes on specific periods.

The fluxes of FP2026.1 (2016 to September 2026) come from a Level-1 re-run of the whole IRGA72 record in September and October 2026, one EddyPro run per setup period. Release details are in Dataset versions. The per-year sections below record the earlier flux versions.
The numbered notes in the setup table, (1) to (24), are defined in the setup table on the Swiss FluxNet site page. They describe corrections, unusable periods and time-lag settings; read a setup period together with its notes.
The flux levels are defined in the Swiss FluxNet Flux Processing Chain.
Periods are given as the names of the raw eddy covariance files, e.g. 2013070615.b02. The name gives the start time of the file; a file typically holds 6 hours of 20 Hz data.




Model (from the GIN fieldbook): a Gill HS-100 (serial 000027) until 19 December 2019, then a Gill HS-50 (serial 000063). The electronics unit of the HS-100 stayed in use until 10 January 2020. The fieldbook has no sonic record before 2016, so the HS50-B in the earlier rows of the setup table is not confirmed by it. Where the fieldbook and the table disagree, the fieldbook is correct.
Height and orientation: 47 m and 209°, unchanged across all years. Histograms of wind direction for 2004 to 2019 give very similar results across years with an orientation of 209° from north. One of the oldest setup files (locations.table) gives orientations between 183° and 209° and is not used. Note 5 records a possible change to 206° from 2005_2; this has not been resolved.

IRGA75: open-path LI-7500; IRGA72: enclosed-path LI-7200

Notes on the table:

The raw-file ranges of 2025_1 and 2026_1, and their sonic model, height, orientation and analyser separation, are taken from the Level-1 EddyPro output (file names of the first and last raw files processed, and the instrument metadata of each run). 2026_1 is processed up to the raw file that starts on 30 September 2026 at 19:00. The BICO and FR configuration letters have no published legend and are still to be checked for these two periods.
The end of 2022_4 was previously given as 2023123119.L00. The Level-1 run of 2022_4 ends with the raw file that starts on 31 December 2022 at 19:00, so the table now reads 2022123119.L00.
(a) The fieldbook records a freshly calibrated LI-7200RS head (72H0577) with analyser unit AIU2485 installed at 47 m on 2 December 2025, within 2025_1. Whether this is a setup boundary is still to be checked; the Level-1 run of 2025_1 covers the whole year as one run.

Affected raw files: from 2013070615.b02 to 2013071214.b00 (inclusive).
The start times in the names of these raw files are wrong by about 6 hours. The fieldbook entry of 12 July 2013 records that the clock of the data acquisition (MOXA) was wrong and was changed at 16:44 from 22:43:50 to 15:44.
The original raw files still carry the wrong names (checked July 2025). The files are therefore renamed after the conversion to ASCII with bico, by subtracting 6 hours (for example, 2013070802.b00 becomes 2013070720.b00), and the fluxes are calculated from the renamed files. This has to be repeated for every new flux calculation of this period.
In FP2021 the shift was still present in the IRGA75 Level-1 fluxes and was corrected after the flux calculation: between 2013-07-06 15:45 and 2013-07-12 23:45 the timestamps were shifted by about 14.5 hours (data at 2013-07-06 15:45 belong to 2013-07-06 08:15). The Level-1 data were shifted accordingly and the transition day, 12 July 2013, was set to missing.

text:
Model (from the GIN fieldbook): a Gill HS-100 (serial 000027) until 19 December 2019, then a Gill HS-50 (serial 000063). The electronics unit of the HS-100 stayed in use until 10 January 2020. The fieldbook has no sonic record before 2016, so the HS50-B in the earlier rows of the setup table is not confirmed by it. Where the fieldbook and the table disagree, the fieldbook is correct.
Height and orientation: 47 m and 209°, unchanged across all years. Histograms of wind direction for 2004 to 2019 give very similar results across years with an orientation of 209° from north. One of the oldest setup files (locations.table) gives orientations between 183° and 209° and is not used. Note 5 records a possible change to 206° from 2005_2; this has not been resolved.

title: Yearly Notes
text:
Affected raw files: from 2013070615.b02 to 2013071214.b00 (inclusive).
The start times in the names of these raw files are wrong by about 6 hours. The fieldbook entry of 12 July 2013 records that the clock of the data acquisition (MOXA) was wrong and was changed at 16:44 from 22:43:50 to 15:44.
The original raw files still carry the wrong names (checked July 2025). The files are therefore renamed after the conversion to ASCII with bico, by subtracting 6 hours (for example, 2013070802.b00 becomes 2013070720.b00), and the fluxes are calculated from the renamed files. This has to be repeated for every new flux calculation of this period.
In FP2021 the shift was still present in the IRGA75 Level-1 fluxes and was corrected after the flux calculation: between 2013-07-06 15:45 and 2013-07-12 23:45 the timestamps were shifted by about 14.5 hours (data at 2013-07-06 15:45 belong to 2013-07-06 08:15). The Level-1 data were shifted accordingly and the transition day, 12 July 2013, was set to missing.

title: Site information
text:
CH-LAE (Lägeren) is a managed mixed deciduous mountain forest on the south-facing slope of the Lägern, in the Jura mountain range that marks the northern boundary of the Swiss Plateau, north-west of Zurich (Etzold et al. 2011). The stand is diverse in species, diameter class and tree age, and has a complex canopy structure (Etzold et al. 2011; Shekhar et al. 2024). Eddy covariance measurements started in April 2004 and are ongoing.
This page draws on the Swiss FluxNet site page for CH-LAE and on two published site descriptions, Etzold et al. (2011) and Shekhar et al. (2024). Every value below names its source; where sources disagree, both are given. The eddy covariance setup (sonic anemometer, gas analysers, sensor separations and the setup periods of the flux runs) is listed per year in Yearly Notes. The dataset itself is described in Overview.






Figure 1: The CH-LAE tower in December 2019. The instrument platform carrying the eddy covariance system and the meteorological sensors stands clear of a leafless deciduous canopy with scattered conifers; the Swiss Plateau below is under fog. Photo: Markus Staudinger, Grassland Sciences Group, ETH Zurich

Reported slopes differ in value and in unit. Etzold et al. (2011) give 27° for the flux site, while the LWF plot page gives a mean slope of 37 %, which is about 20°. The two describe different areas, the flux footprint and a 1.34 ha inventory plot, so they do not conflict. Do not read 37 % as 37°.
The slope is the property of this site that most affects the flux measurement. Advection on the slope contributes measurably to the carbon budget, and the site has been used as a study case for that term (Etzold et al. 2010). That work is also the origin of the constant friction-velocity threshold of 0.3 m s-1 that later studies of this site have applied (Shekhar et al. 2024). The thresholds used in the present dataset are documented under Level 3.3.






NotePublished positions differ from the values above



The position in Table 1 is the correct one. Some published descriptions of the site give slightly different values: 682 m a.s.l. instead of 689 m (Etzold et al. 2011; Shekhar et al. 2024), and coordinates about 50 m away, 47°28’40.8” N, 8°21’55.2” E (Etzold et al. 2011). The prose of the Swiss FluxNet page separately describes the site as being at 800 m a.s.l., which describes the mountain rather than the tower. Use the values in the table.


The tower position on a map: OpenStreetMap · Swiss national map (swisstopo) · Google Maps. The swisstopo map shows the relief and the forest cover, and with them the slope and the extent of the stand.






Figure 2: The view from the top of the tower on 17 April 2014, over the canopy and onto the Swiss Plateau, with snow-covered mountains on the horizon. The stand is in early leaf flush, the broadleaves light green against the dark conifers. In the foreground are the tower’s own instrument booms, among them a cup anemometer and a shielded temperature and humidity sensor.





The tower is 47 m tall and belongs to WSL, which describes it on its Zindlen measurement tower page. It is not the original structure. The first tower was built under the Swiss National Research Programme NFP 14+ and was replaced after being damaged by storm Lothar in December 1999. The eddy covariance measurements of this dataset began in 2004 on the replacement tower, so no part of the record spans the rebuild.
The tower carries instruments of several groups, which is why more than one measurement of the same quantity exists at this site (see Monitoring programmes and networks). Physical access requires authorisation from the WSL safety officer.
The instruments of this dataset are at the 47 m level. The NABEL sensors used as co-located references in the meteorological products are recorded at 49 m.




Published long-term means for the site differ, because they cover different periods and rest on different measurements. All of them are given here.

The temperature means are consistent with a warming record: the Swiss FluxNet page reports 7.8 °C over 2005-2012 and 9.4 °C over 2013-2020, a difference of 1.6 °C between the two halves of that period. The two precipitation figures are not directly comparable, because they cover different years and come from different gauges. When quoting either as the site value, state which one it is.






WarningTo do: recompute the climate figures from this dataset



Every climate value on this page (the means above, the extremes below and the growing-season conditions) comes from an external source or a published study, and each covers a period that ends before this dataset does. They are to be recomputed over the full period of the products documented here: air temperature from 02_METEO_TA, precipitation from 08_METEO_PREC, vapour pressure deficit from 07_METEO_VPD and soil water content from 09_METEO_SWC. Recomputed values will be cited as this dataset and will state their own period.
The tables will then hold only this dataset’s numbers, and the published values will be dropped. The papers remain cited on this page, so a figure quoted from one of them can still be traced to its source.

The site air temperature record is affected by a sensor and acquisition change in January 2016; see Air temperature for what this means when early and late years are compared. Measured precipitation at the tower is documented under Precipitation.
Three MeteoSwiss stations lie close enough to serve as references: Lägern (845 m a.s.l., 2.5 km), Ehrendingen (428 m a.s.l., 3.8 km) and Zürich/Kloten (426 m a.s.l.). They do not all measure the same variables: Lägern measures no precipitation and no longwave radiation, and Ehrendingen measures precipitation only. The reference used for each product is named on that product’s page under Meteorological data.


Shekhar et al. (2024) characterise the growing season and the water-related conditions of the site over 2005-2022. These values help to identify the years in the record that were climatically unusual.



Table 4: Growing-season conditions over 2005-2022, after Shekhar et al. (2024). The growing season is day of year 115-275, approximately 25 April to 2 October.

Days below the soil-moisture percentile occurred mainly in 2006, 2009, 2015 and 2018, and days that were both soil-dry and air-dry fell largely in 2015, 2018 and 2022. 2015 had the most extreme-dryness days of any year in that period (Shekhar et al. 2024). Soil moisture and vapour pressure deficit at the site are negatively correlated (r = -0.36), more strongly than at the subalpine site the same study compares against.




The stand is dominated by European beech (Fagus sylvatica L.), with ash (Fraxinus excelsior L.) and Norway spruce (Picea abies (L.) Karst.) the other abundant species (Etzold et al. 2011). Canopy composition has been quantified as beech 40 %, ash 19 %, sycamore maple (Acer pseudoplatanus L.) 13 %, European silver fir (Abies alba Mill.) 8 % and Norway spruce 4 % (Paul-Limoges et al. 2017; Shekhar et al. 2024). The Swiss FluxNet site page additionally lists Tilia cordata Mill., Quercus robur L. and Ulmus glabra Huds. as present. In spring, bear’s garlic (Allium ursinum L.) forms a dense understorey, growing from about March to June (Etzold et al. 2011; Shekhar et al. 2024).

NoteThe stand numbers describe a 1.34 ha plot, not the footprint



Four of the rows above (top-height diameter, stem density and the two maximum ages) appear identically on the Swiss FluxNet site page and on the LWF plot page, and the LWF plot is where they were measured. That plot is 1.34 ha, was installed on 1 May 2012 and spans 643-718 m elevation. The flux footprint is much larger and spans two management regimes (see Management and footprint). The plot statistics describe the forest, but they are not an inventory of the area the fluxes come from.


The LWF plot classifies the woodland association, after Ellenberg and Klötzli (1972), as Galio odorati-Fagetum typicum to Pulmonario-Fagetum typicum.
The eddy covariance system and the meteorological sensors of this dataset are mounted at 47 m, well above the mean canopy height of about 30 m (Etzold et al. 2011; Shekhar et al. 2024).



The bedrock is limestone, marl and sandstone, with transition zones between them (Swiss FluxNet site page). Soils are rendzic leptosols (rendzinas) and haplic cambisols in the World Reference Base classification (Etzold et al. 2011). The litter layer is thin: leaf litter decomposes nearly completely within one year (Swiss FluxNet site page).



Table 6: Soil properties reported by Etzold et al. (2011).





property
value

The LWF plot page classifies the same soils in the WSL scheme as calcareous brown soil, chromic luvisol and mixed rendzina. The luvisol is not named in the World Reference Base pair above.
The pH range is wide because the two soil types differ: rendzinas over limestone are near-neutral to alkaline, the cambisols acidic. Soil moisture and soil temperature measured at the forest floor are documented under Soil water content and Soil temperature.



The forest is a high forest, and the two halves of the flux footprint are managed differently. The southern part has been managed under Forest Stewardship Council certification since 1998. The northern part is a nature reserve in which tree harvesting stopped around the late 1990s. Footprint modelling indicates that the eddy covariance fluxes come from both parts in roughly equal proportion (Etzold et al. 2011).
The fluxes therefore describe an approximately even mixture of a managed and an unmanaged stand, not a single management regime. The dataset holds no record of management events.



The site belongs to several programmes besides Swiss FluxNet, which is why more than one measurement record exists at the same location:

Swiss FluxNet, operated by the Grassland Sciences Group, ETH Zurich, which runs the eddy covariance system this dataset is built from (Shekhar et al. 2024).
NABEL, the Swiss national air pollution monitoring network, operated by EMPA, which runs its own meteorological sensors on the same tower (Etzold et al. 2011). The NABEL air temperature and radiation measurements at 49 m are used as co-located references in the meteorological products. WSL gives the NABEL presence as running through 2017. In the data used here, the NABEL series ceases to be independent in mid-2018; the meteorological products use this date, because it is taken from the measurements rather than from a report.
LWF, the long-term forest ecosystem research programme of WSL (Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research), which runs the 1.34 ha inventory plot described above.
The University of Zurich (Soil Science and Biogeochemistry) and a second ETH Zurich group (Land-Climate Dynamics) also measure at the plot (LWF).
CarboEurope IP, the European carbon flux network the site joined at the start of the measurements (Swiss FluxNet site page).

The site is not an ICOS station. Shekhar et al. (2024) name ICOS Class 1 status for the subalpine site CH-Dav, which they treat alongside CH-LAE, not for CH-LAE itself.




Swiss FluxNet site page for CH-LAE: the site description, and the definitions of the numbered notes referenced by the setup table in Yearly Notes.
EC raw binary format for CH-LAE: the setup periods, their raw file ranges and the notes that document corrections and unusable periods.
CH-LAE FP2022 (2004-2022): an earlier published dataset of ecosystem fluxes and meteorological data from this site, in the ETH Research Collection (Hörtnagl et al. 2023).
WSL: Zindlen measurement tower: the tower, its history and the conditions of access.
WSL LWF: Lägeren plot: the long-term forest ecosystem research plot, its inventory statistics and its deposition and foliar data.
Instrumentation: the instruments deployed at the site and their measurement periods.

Hörtnagl, Lukas, Ankit Shekhar, Mana Gharun, and Nina Buchmann. 2023. CH-LAE FP2022 (2004-2022) Ecosystem Fluxes and Meteorological Data from Lägeren (Switzerland). ETH Zurich Research Collection. https://doi.org/10.3929/ethz-b-000582198.

In the foreground are the tower’s own instrument booms, among them a cup anemometer and a shielded temperature and humidity sensor.





The tower is 47 m tall and belongs to WSL, which describes it on its Zindlen measurement tower page. It is not the original structure. The first tower was built under the Swiss National Research Programme NFP 14+ and was replaced after being damaged by storm Lothar in December 1999. The eddy covariance measurements of this dataset began in 2004 on the replacement tower, so no part of the record spans the rebuild.
The tower carries instruments of several groups, which is why more than one measurement of the same quantity exists at this site (see Monitoring programmes and networks). Physical access requires authorisation from the WSL safety officer.
The instruments of this dataset are at the 47 m level. The NABEL sensors used as co-located references in the meteorological products are recorded at 49 m.

The temperature means are consistent with a warming record: the Swiss FluxNet page reports 7.8 °C over 2005-2012 and 9.4 °C over 2013-2020, a difference of 1.6 °C between the two halves of that period. The two precipitation figures are not directly comparable, because they cover different years and come from different gauges. When quoting either as the site value, state which one it is.






WarningTo do: recompute the climate figures from this dataset



Every climate value on this page (the means above, the extremes below and the growing-season conditions) comes from an external source or a published study, and each covers a period that ends before this dataset does. They are to be recomputed over the full period of the products documented here: air temperature from 02_METEO_TA, precipitation from 08_METEO_PREC, vapour pressure deficit from 07_METEO_VPD and soil water content from 09_METEO_SWC. Recomputed values will be cited as this dataset and will state their own period.
The tables will then hold only this dataset’s numbers, and the published values will be dropped. The papers remain cited on this page, so a figure quoted from one of them can still be traced to its source.

Three MeteoSwiss stations lie close enough to serve as references: Lägern (845 m a.s.l., 2.5 km), Ehrendingen (428 m a.s.l., 3.8 km) and Zürich/Kloten (426 m a.s.l.). They do not all measure the same variables: Lägern measures no precipitation and no longwave radiation, and Ehrendingen measures precipitation only. The reference used for each product is named on that product’s page under Meteorological data.

Days below the soil-moisture percentile occurred mainly in 2006, 2009, 2015 and 2018, and days that were both soil-dry and air-dry fell largely in 2015, 2018 and 2022. 2015 had the most extreme-dryness days of any year in that period (Shekhar et al. 2024). Soil moisture and vapour pressure deficit at the site are negatively correlated (r = -0.36), more strongly than at the subalpine site the same study compares against.

title: Site information
text:
The stand is dominated by European beech (Fagus sylvatica L.), with ash (Fraxinus excelsior L.) and Norway spruce (Picea abies (L.) Karst.) the other abundant species (Etzold et al. 2011). Canopy composition has been quantified as beech 40 %, ash 19 %, sycamore maple (Acer pseudoplatanus L.) 13 %, European silver fir (Abies alba Mill.) 8 % and Norway spruce 4 % (Paul-Limoges et al. 2017; Shekhar et al. 2024). The Swiss FluxNet site page additionally lists Tilia cordata Mill., Quercus robur L. and Ulmus glabra Huds. as present. In spring, bear’s garlic (Allium ursinum L.) forms a dense understorey, growing from about March to June (Etzold et al. 2011; Shekhar et al. 2024).

Four of the rows above (top-height diameter, stem density and the two maximum ages) appear identically on the Swiss FluxNet site page and on the LWF plot page, and the LWF plot is where they were measured. That plot is 1.34 ha, was installed on 1 May 2012 and spans 643-718 m elevation. The flux footprint is much larger and spans two management regimes (see Management and footprint). The plot statistics describe the forest, but they are not an inventory of the area the fluxes come from.


The LWF plot classifies the woodland association, after Ellenberg and Klötzli (1972), as Galio odorati-Fagetum typicum to Pulmonario-Fagetum typicum.
The eddy covariance system and the meteorological sensors of this dataset are mounted at 47 m, well above the mean canopy height of about 30 m (Etzold et al. 2011; Shekhar et al. 2024).

title: Site information
text:
The bedrock is limestone, marl and sandstone, with transition zones between them (Swiss FluxNet site page). Soils are rendzic leptosols (rendzinas) and haplic cambisols in the World Reference Base classification (Etzold et al. 2011). The litter layer is thin: leaf litter decomposes nearly completely within one year (Swiss FluxNet site page).



Table 6: Soil properties reported by Etzold et al. (2011).





property
value




soil pH
4.0-7.5


soil carbon stock, 0-20 cm
8.4-9.6 kg m-2






The LWF plot page classifies the same soils in the WSL scheme as calcareous brown soil, chromic luvisol and mixed rendzina. The luvisol is not named in the World Reference Base pair above.
The pH range is wide because the two soil types differ: rendzinas over limestone are near-neutral to alkaline, the cambisols acidic. Soil moisture and soil temperature measured at the forest floor are documented under Soil water content and Soil temperature.

title: Site information
text:
The forest is a high forest, and the two halves of the flux footprint are managed differently. The southern part has been managed under Forest Stewardship Council certification since 1998. The northern part is a nature reserve in which tree harvesting stopped around the late 1990s. Footprint modelling indicates that the eddy covariance fluxes come from both parts in roughly equal proportion (Etzold et al. 2011).
The fluxes therefore describe an approximately even mixture of a managed and an unmanaged stand, not a single management regime. The dataset holds no record of management events.

title: Site information
text:
The site belongs to several programmes besides Swiss FluxNet, which is why more than one measurement record exists at the same location:

Swiss FluxNet, operated by the Grassland Sciences Group, ETH Zurich, which runs the eddy covariance system this dataset is built from (Shekhar et al. 2024).
NABEL, the Swiss national air pollution monitoring network, operated by EMPA, which runs its own meteorological sensors on the same tower (Etzold et al. 2011). The NABEL air temperature and radiation measurements at 49 m are used as co-located references in the meteorological products. WSL gives the NABEL presence as running through 2017. In the data used here, the NABEL series ceases to be independent in mid-2018; the meteorological products use this date, because it is taken from the measurements rather than from a report.
LWF, the long-term forest ecosystem research programme of WSL (Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research), which runs the 1.34 ha inventory plot described above.
The University of Zurich (Soil Science and Biogeochemistry) and a second ETH Zurich group (Land-Climate Dynamics) also measure at the plot (LWF).
CarboEurope IP, the European carbon flux network the site joined at the start of the measurements (Swiss FluxNet site page).

The site is not an ICOS station. Shekhar et al. (2024) name ICOS Class 1 status for the subalpine site CH-Dav, which they treat alongside CH-LAE, not for CH-LAE itself.

title: Raw Data: Eddy Covariance
text:
The raw eddy covariance data are not part of FP2026.1. This page describes the data the fluxes were calculated from.



Height and rate. The sonic anemometer and the gas analysers are mounted at 47 m on the tower and sampled at 20 Hz. The sonic orientation is 209° (see Level 0).
Gas analysers.

IRGA72, the enclosed-path LI-7200, from 11 January 2016. The fluxes in FP2026.1 are calculated from this analyser.
IRGA75, the open-path LI-7500, from 2004 to 12 December 2017, and from 17 January to 20 March 2019 as a stand-in for the defective LI-7200. Its fluxes are in progress for FP2026.2 and are not part of FP2026.1.

Both analysers measured in parallel from 11 January 2016 to 12 December 2017. Models, serial numbers and exchanges of all instruments are listed on Instrumentation.




The raw data are stored as binary files, each typically covering 6 hours. The file name gives the start of the file: 2013070615.b02 starts on 6 July 2013 at 15:00.
The setup changes over time. Each change of hardware or configuration starts a new setup period, labelled by year and number (2016_2). The setup table on Yearly Notes lists every setup period with its first and last raw file, its instruments and their separations. Its numbered notes are explained on the SwissFluxNet page on the raw binary format.



The binary files are converted to ASCII with bico before the flux calculation. Two corrections are made in this step:

Wrong calibration gas. All IRGA72 CO2 concentrations from 14 December 2017 to 15 March 2019 were calibrated against the wrong reference gas. They are multiplied by 0.974 during the conversion, so every flux calculated from them is corrected.
File names in July 2013. The names of the files from 2013070615.b02 to 2013071214.b00 give a start time that is wrong by about 6 hours. The converted files are renamed after the conversion. This affects only the IRGA75 record.





No fluxes from 13 December 2021 to 7 February 2022. The raw data of setup periods 2021_2 and 2022_1 were logged in an unknown format, and the conversion fails on an unrecognised analyser record. The data may be corrupted.

title: Overview
text:
The CH-LAE flux product holds the half-hourly ecosystem fluxes and meteorological data of the mixed forest site CH-LAE (Site information). The current version is FP2026.1, released on 27 October 2026 and available on request from the Grassland Sciences group, ETH Zurich. Release details are in Dataset Versions.





Table 1: FP2026.1 at a glance.









period
1 January 2016 00:15 to 30 September 2026 23:45


time step
30 minutes


timestamp
TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE, the middle of each half-hour, in UTC+01:00 all year (no daylight saving)


size
188,448 half-hours, 548 variables


files
CH-LAE_FP2026.1_2016-2026.09 as parquet and CSV, and an _INFO.md file with the unit and description of every variable







Fluxes from the enclosed-path LI-7200 gas analyser (IRGA72), measured from 11 January 2016: NEE, LE, ET and H, quality-controlled and gap-filled, with the random, USTAR and joint uncertainty of NEE. The full Level-1 output of EddyPro is included as well.
Meteorological data: thirteen products, from radiation and air temperature at 47 m to soil water content and soil temperature at the forest floor. See Meteo Data.

The column names and units are listed on Variables. Use the columns gap-filled with XGBoost (_gfXG); the MDS columns (_gfMDS) are included for comparison only. MDS fills long gaps poorly: in April and May 2016, after the start-up period of the analyser was removed, it gives an NEE of -235 gC m-2 against -113 gC m-2 with XGBoost.




Raw data: the 20 Hz eddy covariance raw data, converted from binary to ASCII.
Level 0: preliminary flux runs, used to check the setup and to choose the time-lag ranges.
Level 1: final flux calculation with EddyPro, one run per setup period.
The post-processing chain: Level 2 quality flags, Level 3.1 storage term (NEE only), Level 3.2 outlier removal, Level 3.3 USTAR filtering (NEE only, three fixed thresholds) and Level 4.1 gap-filling. Level 4.2, the partitioning of NEE, is not part of FP2026.1.

The dataset file is cut from a collection of all fluxes and meteorological data from 2004: 10_FLUXES_and_METEO_2004-2026.09 and 20_CH-LAE_FP2026.1_2016-2026.09.




The fluxes of the open-path LI-7500 (IRGA75), 2004 to 12 December 2017 and 17 January to 20 March 2019. They are in progress for FP2026.2, which will extend the flux record back to 2004 and supersede FP2026.1.
PREC, SWC, TS, G, SW_OUT and LW_OUT for January to September 2026. These columns end on 31 December 2025.
The partitioning of NEE into GPP and RECO.
A correction of LE and H for the energy balance closure.





H is missing from 10 January to 20 March 2019, and the gap-filled H in that period is model output only.
H in 2024 is about a third lower than in the other years. This has not been checked yet.

title: Meteo: Air temperature (TA) (2005-2025)
text:
Integrity checks

# The overview describes the product, so it starts by checking that the product is what everything
# below assumes: one continuous 30MIN record, no duplicates, no gaps left in either value column,
# nothing outside the physical limits, and complete years. A silent violation here would be
# reported as a result.
_expected = pd.date_range(start=df.index[0], end=df.index[-1], freq='30min')
assert df.index.equals(_expected), "index is not continuous at 30MIN"
assert not df.index.duplicated().any(), "duplicate timestamps"
for _col in (varname, varname_measured):
    assert df[_col].notna().all(), f"{_col} is gap-filled and must not contain missing values"
    assert df[_col].between(*LIMITS).all(), (
        f"{_col} outside {LIMITS}: {df[_col].min()} to {df[_col].max()}")
assert df[flagname].isin(FLAG_LEGEND).all(), (
    f"unknown fill flag codes: {sorted(set(df[flagname].unique()) - set(FLAG_LEGEND))}")
assert df[sourcename].isin(FLAG_SOURCE_LEGEND).all(), (
    f"unknown source flag codes: {sorted(set(df[sourcename].unique()) - set(FLAG_SOURCE_LEGEND))}")

_records = df[varname].resample('YE').count()
_expected_records = [17568 if calendar.isleap(y) else 17520 for y in _records.index.year]
assert (_records.to_numpy() == _expected_records).all(), f"incomplete years:\n{_records}"

# The two value columns differ by two corrections, and what is checked here is that each acts only
# where it should. Before the sensor change the difference is a single positive constant - the
# zero-point error of the old analog chain. After it the difference is the radiation shield term:
# never positive, exactly zero wherever there is no sun to drive it, and not a constant. If it were
# a constant it would be a second offset rather than a correction to the shape of the day, and
# every daily statistic below would mean something different.
_delta = (df[varname] - df[varname_measured]).round(6)
_pre = _delta[df[sourcename] != 0]
_post = _delta[df[sourcename] == 0]

assert _pre.nunique() == 1, f"the pre-2016 offset is not a single constant: {sorted(_pre.unique())}"
OFFSET = float(_pre.iloc[0])
assert OFFSET > 0, f"the pre-2016 correction is {OFFSET:+.4f} {units} and does not raise that era"

assert (_post <= 0).all(), (
    f"the shield term warms the later era by up to {_post.max():+.4f} {units} somewhere - it "
    f"removes a warm bias and can only ever cool")
assert (_post == 0).any(), \
    "the shield term is nowhere zero, so it is not acting only where there is radiation"
assert _post.nunique() > 100, (
    f"the post-2016 correction takes only {_post.nunique()} distinct values - it is behaving like "
    f"a second constant rather than a term that follows the radiation")
SHIELD_MAX = float(-_post.min())

print(f"Integrity checks passed for {FIRST_YEAR}-{LAST_YEAR}.")
print(f"Sensor change at: {df.index[df[sourcename] == 0][0]}")
print(f"Correction before it: a constant of {OFFSET:+.4f} {units} on every record.")
print(f"Correction after it:  a shield term, 0 {units} in the dark to {-SHIELD_MAX:.4f} {units} "
      f"at most, mean {_post.mean():+.4f} {units} over the era.")

Correction before it: a constant of +1.3197 °C on every record.
Correction after it:  a shield term, 0 °C in the dark to -0.5877 °C at most, mean -0.1600 °C over the era.

# Two series that several sections need, derived once here.

# `series_measured` holds the measured records only and is what the extremes are read from; it has
# gaps by construction. `daily` carries the daily minimum, mean and maximum used by the threshold
# days, the growing season and the annual cycle, plus the gap-filled share of each day, so a daily
# value that mostly comes from the model can be recognised as such.
series_measured = series.where(df[flagname] == 0).rename(f"{varname}_MEASURED")

daily = series.resample('D').agg(['min', 'mean', 'max'])
daily['gap-filled (%)'] = df[flagname].gt(0).resample('D').mean() * 100

# Daily extremes of the measured records only, for the sections that report records. Reading them

daily_measured = series_measured.resample('D').agg(['min', 'max'])

print(f"Measured records: {series_measured.notna().sum():,} of {len(series):,} "
      f"({series_measured.notna().mean() * 100:.1f} %)")

section: Which instrument each year came from
text:
Which instrument each year came from
The fill flag says whether a record was measured; this says which sensor measured it. Codes 2 and 3 are records that no instrument stands behind — the January 2016 changeover, and the months before the tower record begins — and they are the rows to drop if provenance has to be certain.

# Share of each year by instrument era. A year split between two codes is a year that cannot be
# compared with an undivided one without the homogenisation.
_src = pd.crosstab(df.index.year, df[sourcename])
_src.columns = [FLAG_SOURCE_LEGEND[c] for c in _src.columns]
_src.index.name = 'YEAR'
_src_pct = (_src.div(_src.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100)

display(styled(_src_pct, caption=f"share of each year (%) by instrument era. The sensor changed on "
                                 f"21 January 2016, which is why {df.index[df[sourcename] == 0][0]:%Y} "
                                 f"is the one year drawing on both. Codes marking records no "
                                 f"instrument produced are listed beside them",
               fmt="{:.1f}", cmap="Blues"))

# Codes 2 and 3 mark records no sensor produced. Code 3 lies entirely in 2004, which this
# overview excludes, so only the January 2016 changeover survives the FIRST_YEAR cut.
_n_no_sensor = int(df[sourcename].isin([2, 3]).sum())
print(f"Records no instrument stands behind: {_n_no_sensor:,} "
      f"({100 * _n_no_sensor / len(df):.2f} % of {FIRST_YEAR}-{LAST_YEAR}).")
print(f"Source codes present in {FIRST_YEAR}-{LAST_YEAR}: {sorted(df[sourcename].unique())}. "
      f"Code 3 (before the tower record begins) falls entirely in 2004 and is outside this "
      f"overview.")

text:
Period means

# Means of the yearly means, on the same basis as the overall mean above. The record is split into
# the most recent N_RECENT_YEARS and everything before them, and the earlier period is the
# reference the recent one is compared against. The split follows the record, so it moves on as the
# dataset grows. Both boundary years are included.
_first_recent = ym.index.max() - N_RECENT_YEARS + 1
assert _first_recent > ym.index.min(), "not enough years before the recent period"
_early = (ym.index.min(), _first_recent - 1)
_recent = (_first_recent, ym.index.max())

_early_mean = ym.loc[_early[0]:_early[1]].mean()
_recent_mean = ym.loc[_recent[0]:_recent[1]].mean()
print(f"Average {var} {_early[0]}-{_early[1]}: {_early_mean:.1f} {units}")
print(f"Average {var} {_recent[0]}-{_recent[1]}: {_recent_mean:.1f} {units} "
      f"({_recent_mean - _early_mean:+.1f} {units} compared to {_early[0]}-{_early[1]})")

# The same difference on the measured column, to show how much of it is the sensor change.
_ym_meas = per_year(df[varname_measured], 'mean')
_early_meas = _ym_meas.loc[_early[0]:_early[1]].mean()
_recent_meas = _ym_meas.loc[_recent[0]:_recent[1]].mean()
print(f"\nOn the measured column the same difference is "
      f"{_recent_meas - _early_meas:+.1f} {units}. The gap between the two is the "
      f"instrument,\nnot the climate: see the homogenisation note at the top.")

text:
Mean annual cycle

# Mean annual cycle of the daily mean, with the spread across years behind it and the most recent
# year drawn on top. The bands are computed per day of year, so day 366 rests on the leap years
# only and is noisier than its neighbours.
_doy = daily['mean'].groupby(daily.index.dayofyear)
_x = _doy.mean().index

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 6), dpi=72, layout="constrained")
ax.fill_between(_x, _doy.min(), _doy.max(), color='#ECEFF1',
                label=f"daily minimum to maximum {FIRST_YEAR}-{LAST_YEAR}")
ax.fill_between(_x, _doy.quantile(0.1), _doy.quantile(0.9), color='#B0BEC5',
                label="10th to 90th percentile")
ax.plot(_x, _doy.mean(), color='#37474F', lw=2, label="mean")
_last_year = daily['mean'].loc[str(LAST_YEAR)]
ax.plot(_last_year.index.dayofyear, _last_year.to_numpy(), color='#F44336', lw=1, label=str(LAST_YEAR))
ax.set_xlabel("Day of year")
ax.set_ylabel(xlabel)
ax.set_title(f"Mean annual cycle of daily mean {var} ({FIRST_YEAR}-{LAST_YEAR})")
ax.set_xlim(1, 366)
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=9)
figcap(fig, f"mean annual cycle of daily mean {var}, with the spread across years behind it and the "
            f"most recent year drawn on top. The bands are computed per day of year, so day 366 rests "
            f"on the leap years alone and is noisier than its neighbours.")
fig.show()

section: Recent period against the earlier years, per month
text:
Recent period against the earlier years, per month

# The two periods of the period means, resolved by calendar month: which months carry the
# difference between them. A difference here is not a trend estimate, it is the distance between
# two averages; the trends are further below.
_split = monthly_avg.index.max() - N_RECENT_YEARS + 1
_early_label = f"{monthly_avg.index.min()}-{_split - 1} ({units})"
_recent_label = f"{_split}-{monthly_avg.index.max()} ({units})"
_difference_label = f"difference ({units})"

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    _early_label: monthly_avg.loc[:_split - 1].mean(),
    _recent_label: monthly_avg.loc[_split:].mean(),
})
comparison[_difference_label] = comparison[_recent_label] - comparison[_early_label]
comparison.index.name = "MONTH"

_styler = styled(comparison, caption=f"the two periods of the period means resolved by calendar month, with the "
                        f"difference between them. It shows which part of the year carries that "
                        f"difference; it is a distance between two averages, not a trend estimate",
                 subset=[_early_label, _recent_label])
display(anomaly_bars(_styler, _difference_label))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 7), dpi=72, layout="constrained")
_colors = plt.get_cmap('twilight_shifted')(np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, len(_diurnal.columns)))

    ax.plot(_diurnal.index, _diurnal[_month], color=_colors[_i], lw=2,
            label=calendar.month_abbr[_month])
ax.set_xlabel("Hour of day (local time, centre of the averaging window)")
ax.set_ylabel(xlabel)
ax.set_title(f"Mean diurnal cycle of {var} per month ({FIRST_YEAR}-{LAST_YEAR})")
ax.set_xticks(range(0, 25, 3))
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.legend(ncol=2, fontsize=9)
figcap(fig, f"mean diurnal cycle of {var} per calendar month. Both the level and the amplitude of the "
            f"daily course change through the year; the half-hourly heatmap further below shows the "
            f"same thing per date instead of per month.")
fig.show()

title: Meteo: Air temperature (TA) (2005-2025)
text:
Month by hour

# The same cycle as a surface, next to the departure of the most recent year from it. The right
# panel is centred on zero, so red and blue are equal distances from the long-term mean.
def _by_month_hour(s):
    """Mean of `s` per calendar month and hour, in the long form HeatmapXYZ expects."""
    frame = pd.DataFrame({'MONTH': s.index.month, 'HOUR': s.index.hour, 'z': s.to_numpy()})
    return frame.groupby(['MONTH', 'HOUR'], as_index=False)['z'].mean()


_clim_hm = _by_month_hour(series)
_last_hm = _by_month_hour(series.loc[str(LAST_YEAR)])
_anomaly_hm = _clim_hm.copy()
_anomaly_hm['z'] = _last_hm['z'].to_numpy() - _clim_hm['z'].to_numpy()
_absmax = _anomaly_hm['z'].abs().max()

fig, axs = plt.subplots(ncols=2, figsize=(17, 6), dpi=72, layout="constrained")
dv.plotting.HeatmapXYZ(x=_clim_hm['MONTH'], y=_clim_hm['HOUR'], z=_clim_hm['z']).plot(
    ax=axs[0], cb_digits_after_comma=0,
    xlabel="Month", ylabel="Hour of day", zlabel=f"{var} ({units})",
    format_style=dv.plotting.FormatStyle(title=f"Mean {var} by month and hour"))
dv.plotting.HeatmapXYZ(x=_anomaly_hm['MONTH'], y=_anomaly_hm['HOUR'], z=_anomaly_hm['z']).plot(
    ax=axs[1], cmap='RdBu_r', vmin=-_absmax, vmax=_absmax, cb_digits_after_comma=1,
    xlabel="Month", ylabel="Hour of day", zlabel=f"{LAST_YEAR} minus mean ({units})",
    format_style=dv.plotting.FormatStyle(title=f"{LAST_YEAR} departure from the mean"))
figcap(fig, f"left: mean {var} by calendar month and hour of day, the seasonal and the diurnal cycle "
            f"on one surface. Right: the departure of {LAST_YEAR} from that mean, centred on zero, so "
            f"it can be read for the time of day at which the year differed.")

# A gap-filled value outside the measured range would be quoted as a record by anyone reading the

          f"outside the measured range. Those values are model results.")

text:
Growing season

# Growing season and growing degree days per year, both on a 5 °C base. See `growing_season` for
# the definition; it is one convention among several and the numbers are only comparable to
# numbers computed the same way.
BASE = 5.0

_rows = {}
for _year, _daily_mean in daily['mean'].groupby(daily.index.year):
    _season = growing_season(_daily_mean, base=BASE)
    if _season is None:
        continue
    _rows[_year] = {"start": f"{_season['start']:%d %b}",
                    "end": f"{_season['end']:%d %b}",
                    "length (days)": _season['length'],
                    "start (day of year)": _season['start'].dayofyear,
                    "end (day of year)": _season['end'].dayofyear}
season = pd.DataFrame.from_dict(_rows, orient='index')
season.index.name = "YEAR"
season["growing degree days (°C d)"] = per_year((daily['mean'] - BASE).clip(lower=0), 'sum')

_fmt = "{:.0f}"
display(styled(season, caption=f"growing season per year on a {BASE:.0f} {units} base: start, end, length and "
                       f"growing degree days. The definition is the one in `growing_season` and "
                       f"the numbers only compare against numbers computed the same way", fmt=_fmt,
               subset=["length (days)", "growing degree days (°C d)"], cmap="YlGn"))

axs[0].bar(season.index, season["length (days)"], color='#66BB6A')
_fit = trend(season["length (days)"].astype(float))
axs[0].plot(_fit['fit'].index, _fit['fit'], color='#B71C1C', lw=2,
            label=f"Theil-Sen: {_fit['slope']:+.1f} days/decade (p={_fit['pvalue']:.3f})")
axs[0].set_title("Growing season length")
axs[0].set_ylabel("Days")
axs[0].legend(fontsize=9)
axs[1].plot(season.index, season["start (day of year)"], marker='o', color='#43A047',
            label="start")
axs[1].plot(season.index, season["end (day of year)"], marker='o', color='#EF6C00', label="end")
axs[1].set_title("Growing season start and end")
axs[1].set_ylabel("Day of year")
axs[1].legend(fontsize=9)
for _ax in axs:

title: Meteo: Air temperature (TA) (2005-2025)
text:
New records per year
Read forwards: a record is a record against what came before it, not against the whole dataset. Record highs are the statistic most exposed to whatever daytime inhomogeneity remains, so some part of their concentration in the later years may still be the change of sensor. Record lows rest on daily minima and are much less affected.

# Days that set a new record for the record so far, counted per year. The first year is left out:
# by construction almost every day of it sets a record, which would swamp the plot. Reading this
# forwards only is the point - a record is a record against what came before it, not against the
# whole dataset.
_running_high = daily_measured['max'].shift().cummax()
_running_low = daily_measured['min'].shift().cummin()
_new_high = daily_measured['max'] > _running_high
_new_low = daily_measured['min'] < _running_low

records = pd.DataFrame({
    "new record highs": per_year(_new_high.astype(float), 'sum'),
    "new record lows": per_year(_new_low.astype(float), 'sum'),
}).loc[FIRST_YEAR + 1:]

display(styled(records, caption=f"days that set a new record against everything measured before them, counted "
                       f"per year from {FIRST_YEAR + 1}. Records necessarily thin out as the "
                       f"record grows, so a late year holding several is the notable case",
               fmt="{:.0f}", cmap="RdYlBu_r"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 5), dpi=72, layout="constrained")
ax.bar(records.index - 0.2, records["new record highs"], width=0.4, color='#EF5350',
       label="new record highs")
ax.bar(records.index + 0.2, records["new record lows"], width=0.4, color='#42A5F5',
       label="new record lows")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("Days")
ax.set_title(f"Days setting a new daily record ({FIRST_YEAR + 1}-{LAST_YEAR})")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
figcap(fig, f"days setting a new daily record per year, highs against lows. The first year is left "
            f"out because by construction almost every day of it sets a record.")
fig.show()

# Quantiles of the half-hourly values per year. The ridgelines above show the shape of each year's
# distribution; this shows where its edges moved. A shift of the median with unchanged 5th and 95th
# percentiles is a different signal from a spread that widens at one end only.
QUANTILES = [0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95]
quantiles = series.groupby(series.index.year).quantile(QUANTILES).unstack()
quantiles.index.name = "YEAR"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 6), dpi=72, layout="constrained")
ax.fill_between(quantiles.index, quantiles[0.05], quantiles[0.95], color='#ECEFF1',
                label="5th to 95th percentile")
ax.fill_between(quantiles.index, quantiles[0.25], quantiles[0.75], color='#B0BEC5',
                label="25th to 75th percentile")
ax.plot(quantiles.index, quantiles[0.5], color='#37474F', lw=2, marker='o', label="median")
ax.plot(ym.index, ym, color='#F44336', lw=2, marker='o', label="mean")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel(xlabel)
ax.set_title(f"Distribution of half-hourly {var} per year")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
figcap(fig, f"percentile bands of half-hourly {var} per year, with the median and the mean. Bands "
            f"moving together is a shift of the whole distribution; one edge moving alone is a change "
            f"in the extremes only.")
fig.show()

_table = quantiles.copy()
_table.columns = [f"{int(q * 100)}th percentile ({units})" for q in _table.columns]
display(styled(_table, caption=f"percentiles of half-hourly {var} per year, the numbers behind the bands: "
                       f"whether a year moved as a whole or only at one end", axis=None))

fig, axs = plt.subplots(ncols=4, figsize=(21, 7), dpi=120, layout="constrained")

                          (axs[1], 'min', "monthly minimum"),

# The yearly anomalies as stripes: the same numbers as the bar plot above, in the form the figure
# is usually published in. One bar per year, no axis, colour is the whole message.
_anomaly = ym - ym.loc[REFERENCE_START_YEAR:REFERENCE_END_YEAR].mean()
_absmax = _anomaly.abs().max()
_cmap = plt.get_cmap('RdBu_r')
_norm = Normalize(vmin=-_absmax, vmax=_absmax)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 4), dpi=72, layout="constrained")
ax.bar(_anomaly.index, height=1.0, width=1.0, color=_cmap(_norm(_anomaly.to_numpy())))
ax.set_xlim(_anomaly.index.min() - 0.5, _anomaly.index.max() + 0.5)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_title(f"{var} anomaly per year against {REFERENCE_START_YEAR}-{REFERENCE_END_YEAR}")
fig.colorbar(plt.cm.ScalarMappable(norm=_norm, cmap=_cmap), ax=ax, label=f"anomaly ({units})")

            f"same numbers as the anomaly plot above, in the form the figure is usually published in.")

title: Meteo: Air temperature (TA) (2005-2025)
text:
Trend of the yearly means

# Trend of the yearly means. Theil-Sen for the slope and Kendall's tau for the significance, see
# the `trend` helper for why. The interval is the 95 % interval of the slope, not of the yearly
# values, and a trend over 21 years is a statement about this record, not a climate projection.
_fit = trend(ym)
print(f"Theil-Sen slope: {_fit['slope']:+.2f} {units} per decade "
      f"(95 % interval {_fit['low']:+.2f} to {_fit['high']:+.2f})")
print(f"Kendall tau:     {_fit['tau']:+.2f} (p = {_fit['pvalue']:.4f})")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 6), dpi=72, layout="constrained")
ax.plot(ym.index, ym, marker='o', color='#37474F', lw=1.5, label="yearly mean")
ax.plot(_fit['fit'].index, _fit['fit'], color='#F44336', lw=2,
        label=f"Theil-Sen: {_fit['slope']:+.2f} {units}/decade (p = {_fit['pvalue']:.4f})")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel(xlabel)
ax.set_title(f"Yearly mean {var} and its trend")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
figcap(fig, f"yearly mean {var} with its Theil-Sen trend; slope, interval and p are printed above the "
            f"figure. A trend over this record is a statement about these years, not a projection.")
fig.show()

# The same slope fitted to each calendar month separately: which part of the year carries the
# warming. Bars are drawn solid where Kendall's tau is significant at p < 0.05 and hollow where it
# is not; twelve tests on one record means a single significant month is weak evidence on its own.
_rows = {}
for _month in monthly_by_number.columns:
    _fit = trend(monthly_by_number[_month])
    _rows[calendar.month_abbr[_month]] = {
        f"trend ({units}/decade)": _fit['slope'],
        f"lower 95 % ({units}/decade)": _fit['low'],
        f"upper 95 % ({units}/decade)": _fit['high'],
        "p": _fit['pvalue'],

trends = pd.DataFrame.from_dict(_rows, orient='index')
trends.index.name = "MONTH"

_fmt = {c: "{:.2f}" for c in trends.columns}

    axs[0].plot(_r.index, _r.rolling(12, center=True).median(), color=_colour, lw=2,
                label=f"{_label}, 12-month rolling median")

axs[0].grid(alpha=0.3)

            f"monthly means with a 12-month rolling median, split into night and day. The night "
            f"residual passes through the sensor change unchanged, which is what the homogenisation "
            f"was derived to achieve; the day residual steps upwards, because the two sensors' "
            f"radiation shields differ and a constant offset cannot correct a daytime-only error. "

            f"record count.")

# The step, stated rather than left to the eye. Three complete years either side, so the January
# 2016 outage does not sit inside a compared window.
_yr = _break.year
_pre = (both.index.year >= _yr - 3) & (both.index.year <= _yr - 1)
_post = (both.index.year >= _yr + 1) & (both.index.year <= _yr + 3)
_rows = []
for _wname, _wmask in [('all hours', np.ones(len(both), bool)),
                       ('night', _is_night.to_numpy()), ('day', (~_is_night).to_numpy())]:

                      f'{_yr - 3}-{_yr - 1} ({units})': _r[_pre & _wmask].mean(),

})

The night column is close to flat across the whole record, which is what supports the homogenisation; the day column carries the shield difference and steps at the sensor change", fmt=_fmt,

section: What the correction does to the shape of the day
text:
What the correction does to the shape of the day
The residual above is a half-hourly average. The statistics this notebook is mostly built from are daily ones, and a correction that acts only in daylight moves a daily maximum and a daily minimum by different amounts. Those steps are measured here rather than described, because the warnings at the head of this notebook and above the extremes rest on them.
Each statistic is formed on the product and on the reference station for the same day, and the step is the change in their difference across the sensor change. Days are used only where the product was measured for at least 44 of its 48 records and the reference is as complete, so a daily maximum is a real one rather than the maximum of whatever survived.

_break_ts = df.index[df[sourcename] == 0][0]
_pre_years = list(range(_break_ts.year - 3, _break_ts.year))
_post_years = list(range(_break_ts.year, _break_ts.year + 3))
_full_pre = [_y for _y in sorted(set(df.index.year)) if _y < _break_ts.year]
_full_post = [_y for _y in sorted(set(df.index.year)) if _y >= _break_ts.year]

# Days that are essentially measured in the product and complete in the reference.
MIN_RECORDS_PER_DAY = 44
_ok = ((df[flagname].eq(0).resample('D').sum() >= MIN_RECORDS_PER_DAY)
       & (_reference.resample('D').count() >= MIN_RECORDS_PER_DAY))
assert _ok.sum() > 3000, f"only {_ok.sum()} days are complete enough to compare"

_stats = {'daily maximum': lambda s: s.resample('D').max(),
          'daily minimum': lambda s: s.resample('D').min(),
          'diurnal range': lambda s: s.resample('D').max() - s.resample('D').min()}

_rows = []
for _stat, _fn in _stats.items():
    _b = _fn(_reference)[_ok]
    for _label, _col in [('as measured', varname_measured), ('homogenised', varname)]:
        _r = (_fn(df[_col])[_ok] - _b).dropna()
        _row = {'statistic': _stat, 'column': _label}
        for _wlabel, _wa, _wb in [(f'{_pre_years[0]}-{_pre_years[-1]} against '
                                   f'{_post_years[0]}-{_post_years[-1]}', _pre_years, _post_years),
                                  ('full eras', _full_pre, _full_post)]:
            _row[f'step, {_wlabel} ({units})'] = (_r[_r.index.year.isin(_wb)].mean()
                                                  - _r[_r.index.year.isin(_wa)].mean())
        _row['days'] = len(_r)
        _rows.append(_row)
daily_shape_steps = pd.DataFrame(_rows).set_index(['statistic', 'column'])
_step_cols = [c for c in daily_shape_steps.columns if c.startswith('step')]
display(styled(daily_shape_steps, caption="the step across the sensor change in the daily "
                                          "statistics, against the MeteoSwiss station, before and "
                                          "after the correction. The homogenised rows are what "
                                          "this product carries; the measured rows are what it "
                                          "would carry without the correction",
               fmt="{:.2f}", subset=_step_cols, cmap='RdBu_r', center=True))

# The correction has to improve every one of these, on both windows. It corrects a daytime error,
# so the daily maximum is the one it was expected to move most; if any statistic came out worse
# the warnings below would have to be rewritten rather than relaxed.
for _stat in _stats:
    for _c in _step_cols:
        _before = abs(daily_shape_steps.loc[(_stat, 'as measured'), _c])
        _after = abs(daily_shape_steps.loc[(_stat, 'homogenised'), _c])
        assert _after < _before, (
            f"the correction makes the {_stat} step worse on '{_c}' ({_before:.2f} -> {_after:.2f} "
            f"{units}) - the warnings in this notebook must be re-derived, not relaxed")

_worst = max(abs(daily_shape_steps.loc[(_s, 'homogenised'), _c])
             for _s in _stats for _c in _step_cols)
print(f"Largest residual step over the three daily statistics and both windows: {_worst:.2f} {units}.")
print(f"The same statistics on the measured column step by up to "
      f"{max(abs(daily_shape_steps.loc[(_s, 'as measured'), _c]) for _s in _stats for _c in _step_cols):.2f} {units}.")

title: Release FP2026.1: CH-LAE fluxes and meteo, 2016-2026.09
text:
ℹ️ About this notebook
This notebook assembles the dataset of the release FP2026.1, CH-LAE_FP2026.1_2016-2026.09. It covers 1 January 2016 to 30 September 2026 and is cut from the collection 10_FLUXES_and_METEO_2004-2026.09, which holds all data available so far on one 30-minute timestamp from 2004 on.
The cut keeps the records of the release period and the variables that have at least one value in it. Variables whose record ends before 2016 are therefore not part of the release.
The dataset is written as parquet and as CSV. The last section lists every variable of the dataset with its unit, a short description, its source and its period. The units and descriptions come from variable_info.py in this folder.

title: Release FP2026.1: CH-LAE fluxes and meteo, 2016-2026.09

DATADIR = (r"<DATA_FOLDER>"

    'FPPC IRGA72': (rf"{DATADIR}\30_FLUX_POST-PROCESSING_CHAIN\IRGA72"
                    r"\99_FPPC_IRGA72_MERGED_2016-2026.09.parquet"),

title: C
text:
Get results

Results from the flux processing chain can be accessed using .get_data()
This returns a dataframe containing all input data and all newly generated variables, such as quality flags, quality-filtered fluxes and gap-filled fluxes


# results = fpc.get_data(verbose=1)
# results

title: C
text:
Model scores

Model scores and details on test data

# Show train/test details
print(fpc.report_traintest_model_scores())
print(fpc.report_traintest_details())
# fpc.report_traintest_model_scores(outpath=".")  # Save in current folder
# fpc.report_traintest_details(outpath=".")  # Save in current folder



Model scores on all data

fpc.report_gapfilling_model_scores()
# fpc.report_gapfilling_model_scores(outpath=".")  # Save in current folder

During long-term gap-filling, different years are pooled together to predict one central year, i.e., multiple models are used.
The used data pools can be display with:

fpc.report_gapfilling_poolyears()


fpc.report_gapfilling_feature_importances()  # Save in current folder
# fpc.report_gapfilling_feature_importances(outpath=".")  # Save in current folder

title: C
text:
Names of gap-filled variables

print("Used model, USTAR scenario, non-gapfilled variable and gap-filled variable:")
fpc.report_gapfilling_variables()


gapfilled_names = fpc.get_gapfilled_names()
gapfilled_names

Gap-filled data can also be accessed directly. To get all gap-filled variables and also the same variables before gap-filling in a dataframe, use .get_gapfilled_variables():

gapfilled_vars = fpc.get_gapfilled_variables()
gapfilled_vars.head(3)

The names of the flux that was gap-filled can be accessed like this:

nongapfilled_names = fpc.get_nongapfilled_names()
nongapfilled_names

title: C
text:
Plots

Heatmaps

fpc.showplot_gapfilled_heatmap()



Cumulatives per year

fpc.showplot_gapfilled_cumulative(gain=0.02161926, units=r'($\mathrm{gC\ m^{-2}}$)', per_year=True)



Cumulative across all data

fpc.showplot_gapfilled_cumulative(gain=0.02161926, units=r'($\mathrm{gC\ m^{-2}}$)', per_year=False)



ML Feature ranks per year (machine learning models only)

fpc.showplot_feature_ranks_per_year()



MDS gap-filling qualities (MDS only, otherwise skipped)

fpc.showplot_mds_gapfilling_qualities()

title: 00 BEST A
text:
Flux variable
FLUXVAR is the name of the flux variable in the data files. In the EddyPro _fluxnet_ output files, the flux variables we primarily use are: - FC … CO2 flux, becomes NEE after storage correction (Level-3.1) - LE … Latent heat flux (water) - H … Sensible heat flux - FN2O … Nitrous oxide flux - FCH4 … Methane flux
There are more flux variables in the output file, but we rarely need them: - FH2O … H2O flux, very important but it is the same as ET and LE but with different units - ET … Evapotranspiration, very important but it is the same as FH2O and LE but with different units. We can easily calculate ET from LE later, e.g. in diive as shown in the notebook Calculate ET from LE. - TAU … Momentum flux, a measure of the turbulent transfer of momentum between the land surface and the atmosphere
Set the name of the flux variable in the output file(s), must use the FLUXNET naming convention, e.g. FC, FH2O, LE, ET, H, FN2O, FCH4:

FLUXVAR = "FC"  # FC corrected for self-heating

title: 00 BEST A
text:
Site location

Latitude and longitude of the site where data were recorded. This info is mainly used to calculate potential radiation, which is then used to divide the dataset into daytime and nighttime data.
UTC offset of the timestamp used in the dataset, important for calculating potential radiation for this location with the correct timestamp.


SITE_LAT = 47.478333  # CH-LAE
SITE_LON = 8.364389  # CH-LAE
UTC_OFFSET = 1  # Time stamp offset in relation to UTC, e.g. 1 for UTC+01:00 (CET), important for the calculation of potential radiation for detecting daytime and nighttime

text:
Daytime/nighttime

Threshold for potential radiation in W m-2, records below threshold are considered nighttime


NIGHTTIME_THRESHOLD = 20

title: 00 BEST A
text:
Quality requirements

DAYTIME_ACCEPT_QCF_BELOW = 2 accepts high- (QCF=0) and medium-quality (QCF=1) fluxes for daytime, rejects low-quality (QCF=2) fluxes
NIGHTTIMETIME_ACCEPT_QCF_BELOW = 1 accepts high-quality (QCF=0) fluxes for nighttime, rejects medium-quality (QCF=1) and low-quality (QCF=2) fluxes
This strict quality-filtering removes a lot of data points during nighttime


DAYTIME_ACCEPT_QCF_BELOW = 2
NIGHTTIMETIME_ACCEPT_QCF_BELOW = 2

title: 00 BEST A
text:
User settings

A test for missing values is always included: flag calculated here from missing flux values in the EddyPro output file



SSITC tests (default: True)

Flag calculated in EddyPro
Combination of the two partial tests steady state test and developed turbulent conditions test
This notebook expects the SSITC flag to follow the flagging policy according to Mauder and Foken 2004:

0 for best quality fluxes
1 for fluxes suitable for general analysis such as annual budgets (although this is debatable for nighttime data)
2 for fluxes that should be discarded from the dataset

TEST_SSITC_SETFLAG_TIMEPERIOD can be used to specify time periods when the flag is set to given value, allowing for stricter SSITC filtering during certain time periods.

For example: Set flag 1 to value 2 between ‘2022-05-01’ and ‘2023-09-30’, and between ‘2024-04-02’ and ‘2024-04-19’ (dates inclusive): TEST_SSITC_SETFLAG_TIMEPERIOD = {2: [ [1, '2022-05-01', '2023-09-30'], [1, '2024-04-02', '2024-04-19'] ]}



TEST_SSITC = True  # True or False (default: True)
TEST_SSITC_SETFLAG_TIMEPERIOD = None
# TEST_SSITC_SETFLAG_TIMEPERIOD = {2: [[1, '2022-05-01', '2023-09-30']]}




Flux base variable completeness test (default: True)

Flag newly calculated here
Check completeness of the variable that was used to calculate the respective flux
Example: CO2 is the base variable that was used to calculate flux FC, the test is therefore run on CO2
Checks number of records of the relevant base variable available for each averaging Interval and calculates completeness flag as follows:

0 for files where >= 99% of base variable are available
1 for files where >= 97% and < 99% of base variable are available
2 for files where < 97% of base variable are available


List of flux base variables and the corresponding fluxes: - CO2: used to calculate FC - H2O: used to calculate FH2O - H2O: used to calculate LE - H2O: used to calculate ET - T_SONIC: used to calculate H - N2O: used to calculate FN2O - CH4: used to calculate FCH4

TEST_GAS_COMPLETENESS = False  # True or False (default: True)




Spectral correction factor test (default: True)

Flag calculated here from the gas SCF variable in EddyPro output file


TEST_SPECTRAL_CORRECTION_FACTOR = True  # True or False (default: True)




Signal strength test

Always recommended if flux was calculated using a gas analyzer.


Do not use for H (sensible heat flux). This test is only relevant for fluxes where the concentration/temperature was measured by a gas analyzer, e.g. FC, FH2O, LE, ET, N2O, CH4, etc …


Signal strength / AGC / window dirtiness test (if available)
Flag calculated here from the signal strength / AGC variable for the gas analyzer in EddyPro output file.
The original info for this flag comes from the IRGA diagnostics. If the flag was already considered during EddyPro processing (bad values already filtered out) then this flag does probably not need to be considered here.
SIGNAL_STRENGTH_COL: Name of the column storing the signal strength, e.g. CUSTOM_AGC_MEAN for LI-7500, CUSTOM_SIGNAL_STRENGTH_IRGA72_MEAN for LI-7200, or something similar.
SIGNAL_STRENGTH_THRESHOLD: Signal strength threshold, flux values where threshold is exceeded are flagged as rejected.
SIGNAL_STRENGTH_METHOD: discard above flags fluxes where signal strength > threshold, discard below where signal strength < threshold. FOr IRGAs such as LI-7200 high signal strength values mean good signal, low values bad signal. For the open-path IRGA LI-7500 it is the opposite: high values bad signal, low values good signal.


# Signal strength
TEST_SIGNAL_STRENGTH = True  # True or False (default: True)
TEST_SIGNAL_STRENGTH_COL = 'CUSTOM_AGC_IRGA75_MEAN'  # Variable name in fluxnet files
TEST_SIGNAL_STRENGTH_METHOD = 'discard below'  # 'discard above' or 'discard below'
TEST_SIGNAL_STRENGTH_THRESHOLD = 50


# TimeSeries(series=df_orig[SIGNAL_STRENGTH_COL]).plot_interactive()
TimeSeries(series=maindf[TEST_SIGNAL_STRENGTH_COL]).plot()











Raw data screening tests

Flags were calculated in EddyPro
See here for more details: Despiking and raw data statistical screening (EddyPro help)


TEST_RAWDATA = True  # Default True
TEST_RAWDATA_SPIKES = True  # Default True
TEST_RAWDATA_AMPLITUDE = False  # Default True
TEST_RAWDATA_DROPOUT = True  # Default True
TEST_RAWDATA_ABSLIM = False  # Default False
TEST_RAWDATA_SKEWKURT_HF = False  # Default False
TEST_RAWDATA_SKEWKURT_SF = False  # Default False
TEST_RAWDATA_DISCONT_HF = False  # Default False
TEST_RAWDATA_DISCONT_SF = False  # Default False




Angle-of-attack test (default: False)

This test calculates sample-wise Angle of Attacks throughout the current flux averaging period, and flags it if the percentage of angles of attack exceeding a user-defined range is beyond a (user-defined) threshold.
Source: EddyPro help (3 Jan 2024) - Flag was calculated in EddyPro - Flag can be useful during some time periods when the sonic anemometer had issues - Not used by default (similar to ICOS)


TEST_RAWDATA_ANGLE_OF_ATTACK = False  # Default False
TEST_RAWDATA_ANGLE_OF_ATTACK_APPLICATION_DATES = []
# TEST_RAWDATA_ANGLE_OF_ATTACK_APPLICATION_DATES = [['2008-01-01', '2010-01-01'],
#                                                   ['2016-03-01', '2016-05-01']]




Steadiness of horizontal wind test (default: False)

This test assesses whether the along-wind and crosswind components of the wind vector undergo a systematic reduction (or increase) throughout the file. If the quadratic combination of such systematic variations is beyond the user-selected limit, the flux averaging period is hard-flagged for instationary horizontal wind (Vickers and Mahrt, 1997, Par. 6g).
Source: EddyPro help (3 Jan 2024) - Flag was calculated in EddyPro


TEST_RAWDATA_STEADINESS_OF_HORIZONTAL_WIND = False  # Default False

title: 01_IRGA75_FluxProcessingChain_L3.2_NEE_QCF10_2005-2019
text:
Flux variable
FLUXVAR is the name of the flux variable in the data files. In the EddyPro _fluxnet_ output files, the flux variables we primarily use are: - FC … CO2 flux, becomes NEE after storage correction (Level-3.1) - LE … Latent heat flux (water) - H … Sensible heat flux - FN2O … Nitrous oxide flux - FCH4 … Methane flux
There are more flux variables in the output file, but we rarely need them: - FH2O … H2O flux, very important but it is the same as ET and LE but with different units - ET … Evapotranspiration, very important but it is the same as FH2O and LE but with different units. We can easily calculte ET later from LE, e.g. in ReddyProc. - TAU … Momentum flux, a measure of the turbulent transfer of momentum between the land surface and the atmosphere
Set the name of the flux variable in the output file(s), must use the FLUXNET naming convention, e.g. FC, FH2O, LE, ET, H, FN2O, FCH4:

FLUXVAR = "FC"

title: 01_IRGA75_FluxProcessingChain_L3.2_NEE_QCF10_2005-2019
text:
Site location

Latitude and longitude of the site where data were recorded. This info is mainly used to calculate potential radiation, which is then used to divide the dataset into daytime and nighttime data.
UTC offset of the timestamp used in the dataset, important for calculating potential radiation for this location with the correct timestamp.


SITE_LAT = 47.478333   # CH-LAE
SITE_LON = 8.364389  # CH-LAE
UTC_OFFSET = 1  # Time stamp offset in relation to UTC, e.g. 1 for UTC+01:00 (CET), important for the calculation of potential radiation for detecting daytime and nighttime

title: 01_IRGA75_FluxProcessingChain_L3.2_NEE_QCF10_2005-2019
text:
Daytime/nighttime

Threshold for potential radiation in W m-2, records below threshold are considered nighttime


NIGHTTIME_THRESHOLD = 20

title: 01_IRGA75_FluxProcessingChain_L3.2_NEE_QCF10_2005-2019
text:
Quality requirements

The default setting is to accept highest-quality and medium-quality fluxes for daytime (overall quality flag QCF = 0 or 1), and highest-quality fluxes only for nighttime (flag QCF = 0)
DAYTIME_ACCEPT_QCF_BELOW = 2 accepts high- (QCF=0) and medium-quality (QCF=1) fluxes for daytime, rejects low-quality (QCF=2) fluxes
NIGHTTIMETIME_ACCEPT_QCF_BELOW = 1 accepts high-quality (QCF=0) fluxes for nighttime, rejects medium-quality (QCF=1) and low-quality (QCF=2) fluxes
This strict quality-filtering removes a lot of data points during nighttime


DAYTIME_ACCEPT_QCF_BELOW = 2
NIGHTTIMETIME_ACCEPT_QCF_BELOW = 1

title: 01_IRGA75_FluxProcessingChain_L3.2_NEE_QCF10_2005-2019
text:
User settings

A test for missing values is always included: flag calculated here from missing flux values in the EddyPro output file



SSITC tests (default: True)

Flag calculated in EddyPro
Combination of the two partial tests steady state test and developed turbulent conditions test
This notebook expects the SSITC flag to follow the flagging policy according to Mauder and Foken 2004:

0 for best quality fluxes
1 for fluxes suitable for general analysis such as annual budgets (although this is debatable for nighttime data)
2 for fluxes that should be discarded from the dataset



TEST_SSITC = True  # Default True
TEST_SSITC_SETFLAG_TIMEPERIOD = False  # {2: [[1, '2022-05-01', '2023-09-30']]}




Flux base variable completeness test (default: True)

Flag newly calculated here
Check completeness of the variable that was used to calculate the respective flux
Example: CO2 is the base variable that was used to calculate flux FC, the test is therefore run on CO2
Checks number of records of the relevant base variable available for each averaging Interval and calculates completeness flag as follows:

0 for files where >= 99% of base variable are available
1 for files where >= 97% and < 99% of base variable are available
2 for files where < 97% of base variable are available


List of flux base variables and the corresponding fluxes: - CO2: used to calculate FC - H2O: used to calculate FH2O - H2O: used to calculate LE - H2O: used to calculate ET - T_SONIC: used to calculate H - N2O: used to calculate FN2O - CH4: used to calculate FCH4

TEST_GAS_COMPLETENESS = False  # Default True




Spectral correction factor test (default: True)

Flag calculated here from the gas SCF variable in EddyPro output file


TEST_SPECTRAL_CORRECTION_FACTOR = True  # Default True




Signal strength test

Always recommended if flux was calculated using a gas analyzer.


Do not use for H (sensible heat flux). This test is only relevant for fluxes where the concentration/temperature was measured by a gas analyzer, e.g. FC, FH2O, LE, ET, N2O, CH4, etc …


Signal strength / AGC / window dirtiness test (if available)
Flag calculated here from the signal strength / AGC variable for the gas analyzer in EddyPro output file
SIGNAL_STRENGTH_COL: Name of the column storing the signal strength, typically ‘CUSTOM_AGC_MEAN’ for LI-7500, ‘CUSTOM_SIGNAL_STRENGTH_IRGA72_MEAN’ for LI-7200, or something similar
SIGNAL_STRENGTH_THRESHOLD: Signal strength threshold, flux values where threshold is exceeded are flagged as rejected
SIGNAL_STRENGTH_METHOD: discard above flags fluxes where signal strength > threshold, discard below where signal strength < threshold


# Signal strength
TEST_SIGNAL_STRENGTH = True
TEST_SIGNAL_STRENGTH_COL = 'CUSTOM_AGC_IRGA75_MEAN'  # Typical variable name in fluxnet files
TEST_SIGNAL_STRENGTH_METHOD = 'discard above'
TEST_SIGNAL_STRENGTH_THRESHOLD = 90


# TimeSeries(series=df_orig[SIGNAL_STRENGTH_COL]).plot_interactive()
TimeSeries(series=maindf[TEST_SIGNAL_STRENGTH_COL]).plot()











Raw data screening tests

Flags were calculated in EddyPro
See here for more details: Despiking and raw data statistical screening (EddyPro help)


TEST_RAWDATA = True  # Default True
TEST_RAWDATA_SPIKES = True  # Default True
TEST_RAWDATA_AMPLITUDE = False  # Default True
TEST_RAWDATA_DROPOUT = True  # Default True
TEST_RAWDATA_ABSLIM = False  # Default False
TEST_RAWDATA_SKEWKURT_HF = False  # Default False
TEST_RAWDATA_SKEWKURT_SF = False  # Default False
TEST_RAWDATA_DISCONT_HF = False  # Default False
TEST_RAWDATA_DISCONT_SF = False  # Default False




Angle-of-attack test (default: False)

This test calculates sample-wise Angle of Attacks throughout the current flux averaging period, and flags it if the percentage of angles of attack exceeding a user-defined range is beyond a (user-defined) threshold.
Source: EddyPro help (3 Jan 2024) - Flag was calculated in EddyPro - Flag can be useful during some time periods when the sonic anemometer had issues - Not used by default (similar to ICOS)


TEST_RAWDATA_ANGLE_OF_ATTACK = False  # Default False
TEST_RAWDATA_ANGLE_OF_ATTACK_APPLICATION_DATES = []
# TEST_RAWDATA_ANGLE_OF_ATTACK_APPLICATION_DATES = [['2008-01-01', '2010-01-01'],
#                                                   ['2016-03-01', '2016-05-01'],
#                                                   ['2021-12-10', '2021-12-23']]




Steadiness of horizontal wind test (default: False)

This test assesses whether the along-wind and crosswind components of the wind vector undergo a systematic reduction (or increase) throughout the file. If the quadratic combination of such systematic variations is beyond the user-selected limit, the flux averaging period is hard-flagged for instationary horizontal wind (Vickers and Mahrt, 1997, Par. 6g).
Source: EddyPro help (3 Jan 2024) - Flag was calculated in EddyPro


TEST_RAWDATA_STEADINESS_OF_HORIZONTAL_WIND = False  # Default False

title: Calculate scaling factors for self-heating correction of open-path fluxes from parallel measurements (NEE)
text:
Here the scaling factors are calculated from parallel measurements
Scaling factors are determined in 20 classes of USTAR, separately for daytime and nighttime data
The scaling factors corresponds to the fraction of the (unscaled) flux correction term that is added to the measured open-path flux NEE


Imports

from datetime import datetime
import pandas as pd
from diive.core.io.files import save_parquet, load_parquet
from diive.pkgs.flux.selfheating import ScopPhysics, ScopOptimizer, ScopApplicator

title: 11_IRGA72_FPC_NEE-QCF11-L3.2_2016-2017
text:
Flux variable
FLUXVAR is the name of the flux variable in the data files. In the EddyPro _fluxnet_ output files, the flux variables we primarily use are: - FC … CO2 flux, becomes NEE after storage correction (Level-3.1) - LE … Latent heat flux (water) - H … Sensible heat flux - FN2O … Nitrous oxide flux - FCH4 … Methane flux
There are more flux variables in the output file, but we rarely need them: - FH2O … H2O flux, very important but it is the same as ET and LE but with different units - ET … Evapotranspiration, very important but it is the same as FH2O and LE but with different units. We can easily calculate ET from LE later, e.g. in diive as shown in the notebook Calculate ET from LE. - TAU … Momentum flux, a measure of the turbulent transfer of momentum between the land surface and the atmosphere
Set the name of the flux variable in the output file(s), must use the FLUXNET naming convention, e.g. FC, FH2O, LE, ET, H, FN2O, FCH4:

FLUXVAR = "FC"

title: 11_IRGA72_FPC_NEE-QCF11-L3.2_2016-2017
text:
Site location

Latitude and longitude of the site where data were recorded. This info is mainly used to calculate potential radiation, which is then used to divide the dataset into daytime and nighttime data.
UTC offset of the timestamp used in the dataset, important for calculating potential radiation for this location with the correct timestamp.


SITE_LAT = 47.478333  # CH-LAE
SITE_LON = 8.364389  # CH-LAE
UTC_OFFSET = 1  # Time stamp offset in relation to UTC, e.g. 1 for UTC+01:00 (CET), important for the calculation of potential radiation for detecting daytime and nighttime

text:
Quality requirements

DAYTIME_ACCEPT_QCF_BELOW = 2 accepts high- (QCF=0) and medium-quality (QCF=1) fluxes for daytime, rejects low-quality (QCF=2) fluxes
NIGHTTIMETIME_ACCEPT_QCF_BELOW = 1 accepts high-quality (QCF=0) fluxes for nighttime, rejects medium-quality (QCF=1) and low-quality (QCF=2) fluxes
This strict quality-filtering removes a lot of data points during nighttime
