The hand-drawn removal, and where its window comes from
REMOVE_DATES is the only thing in this notebook that deletes data because a person decided to. The screening notebook for TS_FF1_0.05_4 saw the anomaly at 1MIN and left it in as too ambiguous to judge there. At 30MIN against its own twin it is not ambiguous.
The window is located blind first. The scan below compares each channel’s daily amplitude with the median of its depth-mates, normalises by that channel’s own long-run ratio so a channel that is simply livelier than its neighbours is not flagged for it, and reports contiguous runs where the ratio departs by more than a factor of two. Only then is the fieldbook asked what happened there.

def daily_frames(df, channels, min_per_day=40):
    """Daily mean and daily amplitude, with part-days dropped rather than counted as small."""
    _day = {c: df[c].resample("1D") for c in channels}
    _mean = pd.concat({c: d.mean().where(d.count() >= min_per_day) for c, d in _day.items()}, axis=1)
    _amp = pd.concat({c: (d.max() - d.min()).where(d.count() >= min_per_day)
                      for c, d in _day.items()}, axis=1)
    return _mean, _amp


def amplitude_scan(amp: pd.DataFrame, depth_channels: dict, window=None, factor=None,
                   min_block=None):
    """Runs where a channel's daily amplitude departs from its depth-mates AND from its own history.

    Two normalisations, both necessary. Against the depth-mates, because the seasonal cycle of
    amplitude is common to the whole profile and would otherwise dominate. Against the channel's
    own median ratio, because these are not replicates - the Campbell 109 at 0.05 m really is 1.7x
    its neighbours all the time, and a fixed threshold would flag it for existing.

    The ratio is computed only where EVERY channel of the depth is reporting: a peer median that
    silently loses a member steps, and the step looks exactly like a fault in whoever is left.
    """
    window = AMP_SCAN_WINDOW if window is None else window
    factor = AMP_SCAN_FACTOR if factor is None else factor
    min_block = AMP_SCAN_MIN_BLOCK if min_block is None else min_block
    rows, blocks = [], {}
    for _d, _chans in depth_channels.items():
        if len(_chans) < 2:
            rows.append({"depth_m": float(_d), "channel": _chans[0] if _chans else "-",
                         "n_peers": 0, "median_ratio": np.nan, "n_days_off": np.nan,
                         "blocks": "no depth-mate - this scan cannot see this channel"})
            continue
        _complete = amp[_chans].notna().all(axis=1)
        for _c in _chans:
            _peers = [p for p in _chans if p != _c]
            _ratio = (amp[_c] / amp[_peers].median(axis=1)).where(_complete)
            _ratio = _ratio.rolling(window, min_periods=window // 2).median()
            _rel = _ratio / _ratio.median()
            _off = _rel[(_rel > factor) | (_rel < 1 / factor)].dropna()
            _grp = (_off.index.to_series().diff().dt.days.fillna(1) > 7).cumsum()
            _bl = [(g.index[0], g.index[-1], len(g)) for _, g in _off.groupby(_grp) if len(g) >= min_block]
            blocks[_c] = _bl
            rows.append({"depth_m": float(_d), "channel": _c, "n_peers": len(_peers),
                         "median_ratio": round(float(_ratio.median()), 2), "n_days_off": len(_off),
                         "blocks": "; ".join(f"{a:%Y-%m-%d} -> {b:%Y-%m-%d} ({n} d)"
                                             for a, b, n in _bl) or "-"})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["depth_m", "channel"]), blocks


DAILY_MEAN, DAILY_AMP = daily_frames(diive_, MODERN_ALL)
AMPSCAN, AMPBLOCKS = amplitude_scan(DAILY_AMP, MODERN)
print("Table: the blind amplitude scan: runs where a channel's daily amplitude departs from its "
      "depth-mates by more than a factor of two, found before the fieldbook was asked")
display(AMPSCAN)

FOUND = {c: b for c, b in AMPBLOCKS.items() if b}
print("Runs found blind, before any date was looked up:")
for _c, _bl in FOUND.items():
    for _a, _b, _n in _bl:
        print(f"   {_c:<16} {_a:%Y-%m-%d} -> {_b:%Y-%m-%d}  ({_n} days)")
print("\nThe fieldbook, asked afterwards about the longest of them:")
_worst = max((b for bl in FOUND.values() for b in bl), key=lambda t: t[2])
fieldbook_near(_worst[0] - pd.Timedelta(days=14), _worst[0], days=0)

print("\nNot every run above becomes a removal, and the short ones are why the scan reports rather\n"
      "than deletes. Two of them sit against a whole-station outage, where the surviving days at\n"
      "the edge of the window are few and their amplitudes unrepresentative; the amplitude ratio\n"
      "of a two-week winter period at 0.3 m, where every channel's daily range is one or two\n"
      "quantiser steps, is not evidence of anything either. Only the run whose ratio departs by a\n"
      "factor of several, for months, against an undisturbed twin at the same depth is removed -\n"
      "and it is audited below.")

Not every run above becomes a removal, and the short ones are why the scan reports rather
than deletes. Two of them sit against a whole-station outage, where the surviving days at
the edge of the window are few and their amplitudes unrepresentative; the amplitude ratio
of a two-week winter period at 0.3 m, where every channel's daily range is one or two
quantiser steps, is not evidence of anything either. Only the run whose ratio departs by a
factor of several, for months, against an undisturbed twin at the same depth is removed -

# Apply the windows. A removal is a value becoming NaN in the CHANNEL, before any combination -
# never a value being overwritten in a depth column, which would leave the flag saying a sensor
# measured something it did not.
diive_clean = diive_.copy()
_rows = []
for _c, _wins in REMOVE_DATES.items():
    for _a, _b, _why in _wins:
        _m = (diive_clean.index >= pd.Timestamp(_a)) & (diive_clean.index <= pd.Timestamp(_b))
        _rows.append({"channel": _c, "from": _a, "to": _b,
                      "n_removed": int(diive_clean.loc[_m, _c].notna().sum()), "reason": _why})
        diive_clean.loc[_m, _c] = np.nan
REMOVED = pd.DataFrame(_rows)
print("Table: what REMOVE_DATES actually deleted, per channel and window")

assert (REMOVED["n_removed"] > 0).all(), (

The audit of the removal window
CLAUDE.md reserves the full two-direction audit for a notebook whose REMOVE_DATES is not empty. So the window’s own justification is recomputed on every run, not quoted from the paragraph above:

Is what was removed genuinely bad? The blind scan must fire inside the window and not before it. If the anomaly predates the window, the window is mislabelled and the removal is deleting good data along with bad.
Is everything real still there? The channel’s agreement with its depth-mates outside the window must be unremarkable, and the depth column must lose nothing. This channel is a fill at 0.05 m, so the audit ends by counting how many records of the exported column actually changed.


for _c, _wins in REMOVE_DATES.items():
    for _a, _b, _why in _wins:
        _a, _b = pd.Timestamp(_a), pd.Timestamp(_b)
        _bl = AMPBLOCKS.get(_c, [])
        _inside = [t for t in _bl if t[0] >= _a - pd.Timedelta(days=AMP_SCAN_WINDOW) and t[1] <= _b]
        _before = [t for t in _bl if t[1] < _a - pd.Timedelta(days=AMP_SCAN_WINDOW)]
        print(f"{_c}  window {_a:%Y-%m-%d} -> {_b:%Y-%m-%d}")
        print(f"   blind detections inside it : {[(f'{x:%Y-%m-%d}', f'{y:%Y-%m-%d}', n) for x, y, n in _inside]}")
        print(f"   blind detections before it : {[(f'{x:%Y-%m-%d}', f'{y:%Y-%m-%d}', n) for x, y, n in _before]}")
        assert _inside, (f"{_c}: the blind scan finds nothing inside the removal window. The "
                         f"evidence for this removal no longer stands - re-derive it or drop it.")
        assert not _before, (f"{_c}: the blind scan also fires BEFORE the window, so the window "
                             f"starts too late and good data is being kept as bad, or bad data as good.")

        # Direction two: how the channel behaves in the years the window does NOT cover.
        _peers = [p for p in MODERN["0.05"] if p != _c]
        _ratio = (DAILY_AMP[_c] / DAILY_AMP[_peers].median(axis=1)).where(
            DAILY_AMP[MODERN["0.05"]].notna().all(axis=1))
        _out = _ratio[(_ratio.index < _a) | (_ratio.index > _b)].dropna()
        _in = _ratio[(_ratio.index >= _a) & (_ratio.index <= _b)].dropna()
        print(f"   amplitude ratio to its depth-mates: {_out.median():.2f} outside the window "
              f"({len(_out):,} days), {_in.median():.2f} inside it ({len(_in):,} days)")
        assert _in.median() > 2 * _out.median(), (
            "the window no longer stands out against the rest of the record - the justification "
            "written beside it is not what the data say")

        # Audit in proportion to what was removed. This channel is a FILL at its depth, so most of
        # what the window deletes was never going to reach the product: what matters is only the
        # records where every higher-priority channel of the same depth is also missing.
        _depth = next(d for d in DEPTHS if _c in MODERN[d])
        _above = MODERN[_depth][:MODERN[_depth].index(_c)]
        _win = (diive_.index >= _a) & (diive_.index <= _b)
        _would_have = int((diive_.loc[_win, _c].notna()
                           & diive_.loc[_win, _above].isna().all(axis=1)).sum())
        print(f"   records the window deletes: {int(diive_.loc[_win, _c].notna().sum()):,}")
        print(f"   of those, records that would have reached the {_depth} m column (every "
              f"higher-priority\n   channel of the depth also missing): {_would_have:,}")
        if _would_have == 0:
            print("   -> the removal changes no exported value at all. It is kept because a "
                  "channel\n      known to be faulty must not be standing by as a fill.")

Build the columns
The index runs from the first early record to the end of 2025 and is continuous throughout. Where nothing measured, the value is NaN and the flag is 0.
Order matters: modern first, in priority order, then the early era into whatever is still empty. The other way round would let a 2004-2021 early channel win the 348-day overlap and put the wrong sensor generation into a year of the modern record.

full_index = pd.date_range(f"{RECORD_START} 00:15:00", f"{RECORD_END} 23:45:00",
                           freq="30min", name="TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE")
ts = pd.DataFrame(index=full_index)
CONTRIB = []

for _d in DEPTHS:
    _combined = pd.Series(dtype=float)
    _flag = pd.Series(FLAG_NONE, index=full_index, dtype=int)

    for _rank, _c in enumerate(MODERN[_d]):
        _s = diive_clean[_c].dropna()
        if _s.empty:
            print(f"  (!) {_c} carries no data at all after the removals - skipped")
            continue
        _outside = _s.index.difference(full_index)
        assert _outside.empty, (f"{_c}: {len(_outside):,} records lie outside the exported index "
                                f"({_outside[0]} ... {_outside[-1]}) - widen RECORD_START/END")
        if _rank == 0:
            _off, _code = 0.0, FLAG_PRIMARY
        else:
            _off = OFFSETS[_d][_c]
            _code = FLAG_C109 if _c in C109 else FLAG_SECONDARY
        _new = _s.index.difference(_combined.index)
        _combined = pd.concat([_combined, (_s + _off).reindex(_new)]).sort_index()
        _flag.loc[_new] = _code
        CONTRIB.append({"depth_m": float(_d), "rank": _rank, "channel": _c,
                        "instrument": INSTRUMENT.get(_c, "-"),
                        "role": "primary" if _rank == 0 else "fill",
                        "flag": _code, "offset_K": round(_off, 3), "n_contributed": len(_new)})

    # The 0.3 m replacement probe gets its own code. Taken from the channel's own records after the
    # swap date, and only where that channel is what the column is carrying.
    if _d == SWAP_DEPTH and SWAP_CHANNEL in MODERN[_d]:
        _ix = diive_clean[SWAP_CHANNEL].dropna().index
        _ix = _ix[_ix >= pd.Timestamp(SENSOR_SWAP)].intersection(_flag.index[_flag == FLAG_PRIMARY])
        _flag.loc[_ix] = FLAG_REPLACEMENT
        CONTRIB.append({"depth_m": float(_d), "rank": 0, "channel": SWAP_CHANNEL,
                        "instrument": INSTRUMENT.get(SWAP_CHANNEL, "-"), "role": "replacement",
                        "flag": FLAG_REPLACEMENT, "offset_K": 0.0, "n_contributed": len(_ix)})

    for _c in EARLY[_d]:
        _s = mst[_c].dropna()
        _outside = _s.index.difference(full_index)
        assert _outside.empty, f"{_c}: records outside the exported index"
        _new = _s.index.difference(_combined.index)
        _combined = pd.concat([_combined, _s.reindex(_new)]).sort_index()
        _flag.loc[_new] = FLAG_EARLY
        CONTRIB.append({"depth_m": float(_d), "rank": 90, "channel": _c, "instrument": "early",
                        "role": "early", "flag": FLAG_EARLY, "offset_K": 0.0,
                        "n_contributed": len(_new)})

    ts[col(_d)] = _combined.reindex(full_index)
    ts[flagcol(_d)] = _flag

CONTRIBTAB = pd.DataFrame(CONTRIB).set_index(["depth_m", "rank"]).sort_index()

The combination is exact
Five ways it can go wrong, one assertion each: a value without provenance (or the reverse), a record invented or lost, a flag code outside the vocabulary, a fill that is doing more work than a fill should, and a value outside the physical band.

# 1) Value and flag agree everywhere, at every depth; every code is in the vocabulary.
for _d in DEPTHS:
    assert (ts[col(_d)].notna() == ts[flagcol(_d)].isin(MEASURED_FLAGS)).all(), \
        f"{col(_d)}: a record has a value without a flag, or a flag without a value"
    assert ts[flagcol(_d)].isin(FLAG_SOURCE_LEGEND).all(), f"{flagcol(_d)}: unknown code"

# 2) Nothing invented: every record in a depth column came from exactly one contributing channel.
for _d in DEPTHS:
    _expected = int(CONTRIBTAB.loc[float(_d)].query("role != 'replacement'")["n_contributed"].sum())
    _got = int(ts[col(_d)].notna().sum())
    assert _got == _expected, f"{col(_d)}: {_expected:,} records contributed but {_got:,} in the column"

# 3) Physical band. The screening already applied each channel's own limits, so this can only fire
#    on a wrong file or an offset applied in the wrong unit.
for _d in DEPTHS:
    _v = ts[col(_d)].dropna()
    _bad = _v[~_v.between(*TS_PLAUSIBLE_DEGC)]
    assert _bad.empty, (f"{col(_d)}: {len(_bad)} value(s) outside {TS_PLAUSIBLE_DEGC} degC, "
                        f"e.g. {_bad.iloc[0]:.2f} at {_bad.index[0]}")

# 4) The primary must dominate. A depth whose "primary" supplies less than this is not one sensor
#    extended, it is a blend, and the paragraph above it is then wrong.
MIN_PRIMARY_SHARE = 0.75
_share = {}
for _d in DEPTHS:
    if not MODERN[_d]:
        continue
    _modern = ts[flagcol(_d)].isin(MODERN_FLAGS)
    _prim = ts[flagcol(_d)].isin((FLAG_PRIMARY, FLAG_REPLACEMENT))
    _share[_d] = float(_prim.sum() / _modern.sum())
    assert _share[_d] >= MIN_PRIMARY_SHARE, (
        f"{col(_d)}: the primary supplies only {100 * _share[_d]:.0f} % of the modern era; this is "
        f"a blend of sensors, not one sensor extended")
print("share of the modern era supplied by the depth's own primary channel:")
print("   " + "   ".join(f"{_d} m: {100 * _v:.1f} %" for _d, _v in _share.items()))

# 5) Each era's block sits where the era does.
_rows = []
for _d in DEPTHS:
    for _code, _name in ERA_NAMES.items():
        _ix = ts.index[ts[flagcol(_d)] == _code]
        if len(_ix):
            _rows.append({"depth_m": float(_d), "flag": _code, "source": _name, "n": len(_ix),
                          "first": _ix[0], "last": _ix[-1]})
BLOCKS = pd.DataFrame(_rows).set_index(["depth_m", "flag"])
print("Table: the longest contiguous run of each source flag, per depth")
display(BLOCKS)
for (_d, _code), _r in BLOCKS.iterrows():
    if _code == FLAG_EARLY:
        continue
    assert _r["first"] >= MODERN_START, f"{_d} m: a modern flag before the modern record starts"

# What the order of operations cost, stated rather than left to be noticed: in the 348-day overlap
# the modern era wins, so the early channel's records there are read, used to measure the era
# offset, and then NOT exported. That is deliberate - the alternative is a column that switches
# back to the old sensor for a year after the new one is already running.
print()
for _d in DEPTHS:
    if not (MODERN[_d] and EARLY[_d]):
        continue
    _avail = sum(int(mst[_c].notna().sum()) for _c in EARLY[_d])
    _used = int((ts[flagcol(_d)] == FLAG_EARLY).sum())
    print(f"  {_d:>5} m  early records available {_avail:>7,}, exported {_used:>7,}, "
          f"superseded by the modern era in the overlap {_avail - _used:>6,}")

# The April 2024 SDI-12 bus failure is the one place a fill does real work, and it works because
# the two Campbell 109s are analogue and were not on the bus that failed.
_bus = ts.loc["2024-04-03":"2024-04-23"]
print(f"\nApril 2024, the SDI-12 bus failure: the 0.05 m column carries "
      f"{int((_bus[flagcol('0.05')] == FLAG_C109).sum()):,} records from a Campbell 109,\n"
      f"and every depth without an analogue channel has a gap there. That is the fill doing the "
      f"one job\nit exists for.")
print("\nCombination verified.")

title: Download and prepare TS for the FF1 soil profile (2004-2025)
section: ⚖️ From channels to one series per depth
text:
⚖️ From channels to one series per depth
Everything so far kept the individual channels apart, which is the first half of the export. This section builds the second half: one overall column per depth, in three steps.

Merge the modern replicates onto the depth’s primary channel (the level-matched fill already built into ts[col(_d)] above).
Homogenise the early era onto the modern level where an overlap let the offset be measured, so 0.05 and 0.1 m only.
Gap-fill every remaining hole from the other depths, by a regression fitted separately for each sensor generation.

A METHOD flag on every record says which step produced it, so the measured series stays recoverable by filtering the flag.

Step 2 first: homogenise where the eras overlap
09 had to homogenise soil moisture across a break that nothing measured through, using climatology alone. Here the two generations reported side by side for 348 days at 0.05 m and 0.1 m, so the offset is a measurement of two thermometers in the same weather.
At 0.3 and 0.5 m the eras do not overlap (the early probes died in March 2010, the modern ones began in April 2020), so their offset cannot be measured and is not invented. Those depths still get an overall column, but their early era sits at its own level, METHOD says so (code 2), and a trend drawn across 2020 there still carries the sensor change.

ERA_OFFSET, ERA_MONTHLY = {}, {}
_rows = []
for _d in DEPTHS:
    if not (MODERN[_d] and EARLY[_d]):
        _rows.append({"depth_m": float(_d), "verdict": "single era - nothing to homogenise",
                      "n_overlap": 0, "offset_K": np.nan})
        continue
    _early = pd.concat([mst[_c].dropna() for _c in EARLY[_d]]).sort_index()
    _modern = ts[col(_d)].where(ts[flagcol(_d)].isin(MODERN_FLAGS)).dropna()
    _ix = _early.index.intersection(_modern.index)
    if len(_ix) < 2000:
        _rows.append({"depth_m": float(_d),
                      "verdict": "eras do not overlap - NO homogenised column, on purpose",
                      "n_overlap": len(_ix), "offset_K": np.nan})
        continue
    _diff = (_modern.reindex(_ix) - _early.reindex(_ix)).dropna()
    ERA_OFFSET[_d] = float(_diff.median())
    ERA_MONTHLY[_d] = _diff.groupby(_diff.index.month).median()
    _rows.append({"depth_m": float(_d), "verdict": "measured on the overlap",
                  "n_overlap": len(_ix), "offset_K": round(float(_diff.median()), 3),
                  "sd_K": round(float(_diff.std()), 3),
                  "first": _ix[0], "last": _ix[-1],
                  "monthly_min_K": round(float(ERA_MONTHLY[_d].min()), 2),
                  "monthly_max_K": round(float(ERA_MONTHLY[_d].max()), 2)})
ERATAB = pd.DataFrame(_rows).set_index("depth_m")
print("Table: the measured early-to-modern offset at 0.05 and 0.1 m, the two depths whose eras "
      "overlap")
display(ERATAB)

Step 3: fill the gaps from the other depths
Coverage is very uneven: 0.05/0.1 m are near-complete, 0.2/0.6 m only start in 2020, 0.3/0.5 m carry a ten-year hole. But the depths of one profile are the same wave, damped and delayed, so a missing depth can be predicted from the ones that are present.
What predicts what. The fill is an era-split ordinary least squares over every available depth at once, each contributing its concurrent value and its thermal memory: rolling means over 3 h, 1 d, 10 d, 30 d and 120 d, plus a day-of-year harmonic. The memory is the part that matters. A deep temperature is a lagged, damped integral of the shallow history, not a function of the instantaneous shallow value, which is precisely what a single-depth instantaneous regression cannot express. Measured held-out, it takes the 0.5 m deep-hole error from 0.55 K to 0.22 K.






NoteThis is still a linear model, and that was the finding rather than the assumption



TS_FF1_GAPFILL_ML_COMPARISON.ipynb tested this against multi-depth-without-memory, sklearn’s histogram gradient boosting and XGBoost, on these same held-out tests. Once every method was fitted era-split, the linear model won. The gain is in the features, not the model class, so it costs no new dependency, no hyperparameters and no seed.
It also keeps the one property a decade-long hole needs: a tree cannot predict outside the range of its training targets, so it clamps the extremes exactly where a long fill is used. A linear model extrapolates linearly, which for near-linear heat conduction is the right shape.


Ragged availability is the hard part, and it is handled explicitly. The depths start and stop at different times, so there is no single feature vector present everywhere: a naive “use all other depths” matrix has an all-NaN column over any window predating or postdating one of them, and a row-wise dropna() then empties the very windows the fill exists for. So the gaps are grouped by which depths they actually have, and each group gets its own fit, richest pattern first. The table printed below says which predictor set produced which records. Patterns too rare to fit fall through to the single-depth fill this replaced, which still rescues about 14,000 records.
Four rules constrain it, unchanged from before:

Era-split. A separate fit per sensor generation, applied only within its own era, so a fill can never carry one generation’s level onto the other.
The distance to the nearest contributing depth is flagged (METHOD 3 or 4). Read it as provenance, not as a quality ranking: with every depth in the model, a 4 at 0.5 m is now more accurate than some 3s.
Measured predictors only, so error cannot compound down a chain of holes. The fill is a pure function of the measured snapshot and does not mutate it, which is what the negative control above checks.
Within the measured span only, in time and in value. In time, a depth is filled only between its own first and last real measurement, never carried back before its sensor existed (0.2/0.6 m) or forward after it died (0.15 m). In value, a filled point is clipped to the min..max that depth measured in the same era. The clip costs a measured 0.003-0.010 K and is kept: it is what stops a damped deep depth being overshot from a swingy shallow one.

So the fill closes the 0.3/0.5 m ten-year hole and the outages inside a depth’s span. What stays empty: outages where every sensor was dead at once, and everything outside a depth’s own measured span. That boundary is the line between reconstructing a measurement and inventing one.

%%time
# The measured frame the fill reads from: one series per depth, gaps as NaN, on the homogenised
# level. The fill predicts a target depth from the OTHER columns of this frame.
DEPTH_OF = {_d: float(_d) for _d in DEPTHS}
_measured = overall.copy()   # measured-only snapshot; the fill never reads its own output back
IS_MODERN = pd.Series(full_index >= ERA_BOUNDARY_MID, index=full_index)

# The profile's feature frame, built ONCE and sliced per target inside the fill: each depth, its
# thermal memory (3 h / 1 d / 10 d / 30 d / 120 d rolling means) and a day-of-year harmonic.
FEATURES = memory_features(_measured)
print(f"feature frame: {FEATURES.shape[1]} columns over {len(FEATURES):,} records")

# (!) Checked PER ERA and inside the 2010-2020 hole, never on the total. A 120-day rolling mean
#     needs half its window present, so a whole-record availability figure can read healthy while
#     the era the fill actually works in has degenerated - the trap the SWC notebooks document.
#     A depth is usable at a timestamp only where its WHOLE block is present.
_avail_windows = {
    "early_%": _measured.index < EARLY_DEEP_END,
    "in_the_2010-2020_hole_%": ((_measured.index >= EARLY_DEEP_END)
                                & (_measured.index < ERA_BOUNDARY_MID)),
    "modern_%": _measured.index >= ERA_BOUNDARY_MID}
FEATAVAIL = pd.DataFrame([
    {"depth_m": float(_d),
     **{_lbl: round(100 * float(FEATURES[[_d] + [f"{_d}_m{_w}" for _w in MEMORY_WINDOWS]]
                                .notna().all(axis=1)[_m].mean()), 1)
        for _lbl, _m in _avail_windows.items()}}
    for _d in DEPTHS]).set_index("depth_m")
print("\nTable: feature-block availability, by era. The shallow depths are what fills the hole, so their\n"
      "middle column is the number that matters:")
display(FEATAVAIL)

FILL_STATS, FILL_PATTERNS = [], []
for _d in DEPTHS:
    _filled, _fm = cross_depth_fill_mm(_measured, _d, DEPTH_OF, IS_MODERN,
                                       min_n=FILL_MIN_N_PER_MONTH, adjacent_m=FILL_ADJACENT_M,
                                       features=FEATURES, patterns_out=FILL_PATTERNS)
    # (!) Interpolate WITHIN this depth's own measured span; never extrapolate beyond it. A gap-fill
    #     fills holes between measurements - it does not invent a record before the sensor was
    #     installed or after it died. Without this, 0.15 m (last measured 2021-03) would be carried
    #     to 2025 from neighbours, fabricating 3.5 years from a dead channel - exactly the fabrication
    #     refused for 0.2/0.6 m before 2020. The span is closed on both ends here, symmetrically.
    # (a) TIME span: interpolate within the measured span, never extrapolate beyond either end.
    _first = _measured[_d].first_valid_index()
    _last = _measured[_d].last_valid_index()
    _in_span = (full_index >= _first) & (full_index <= _last)
    _extrapolated = int((_filled.notna() & overall[_d].isna() & ~_in_span).sum())
    _filled = _filled.where(_in_span)

    # (b) VALUE span: a fill is an interpolation in value too, so clip it to the min..max this depth
    #     actually measured - within the SAME era, to match the era-split fit. Predicting a damped
    #     deep depth from a swingy shallow one can otherwise overshoot past the deepest sensor's real
    #     range (0.3 m ran ~0.7 K above its warmest measurement before this). The clip is to a
    #     temperature the sensor genuinely reached, never a fabricated extreme.
    _clipped = 0
    for _era in (True, False):
        _mera = _measured[_d].where(IS_MODERN == _era).dropna()
        if _mera.empty:
            continue
        _sel = _filled.notna() & (IS_MODERN == _era)
        _before = _filled[_sel].copy()
        _filled.loc[_sel] = _filled[_sel].clip(float(_mera.min()), float(_mera.max()))
        _clipped += int((_filled[_sel] != _before).sum())

    # Only the gaps are overwritten; measured records keep their value and their 1/2 method code.
    _gap = overall[_d].isna()
    overall.loc[_gap, _d] = _filled[_gap]
    method.loc[_gap & (_fm == METHOD_FILL_NEAR) & _in_span, _d] = METHOD_FILL_NEAR
    method.loc[_gap & (_fm == METHOD_FILL_FAR) & _in_span, _d] = METHOD_FILL_FAR
    FILL_STATS.append({
        "depth_m": float(_d),
        "measured_span": f"{_first:%Y-%m-%d} -> {_last:%Y-%m-%d}",
        "measured_range_degC": f"{_measured[_d].min():.1f} .. {_measured[_d].max():.1f}",
        "measured_%": round(100 * float(_measured[_d].notna().mean()), 1),
        "filled_near": int(((method[_d] == METHOD_FILL_NEAR)).sum()),
        "filled_far": int(((method[_d] == METHOD_FILL_FAR)).sum()),
        "not_extrapolated": _extrapolated,
        "clipped_to_range": _clipped,
        "overall_%": round(100 * float(overall[_d].notna().mean()), 1)})
FILLTAB = pd.DataFrame(FILL_STATS).set_index("depth_m")
print("Table: what the fill did at each depth: measured coverage, records filled near and far, "
      "records held back from extrapolation, records clipped to the era's measured range")
display(FILLTAB)

# Which predictor set actually filled what. This is the main new thing a reader has to be able to
# audit: the fill is no longer "the nearest depth", it is one OLS per (available depths, era), and
# this table says which fit produced which records. `method` -1 marks the single-depth fallback.
PATTAB = (pd.DataFrame(FILL_PATTERNS).set_index(["depth_m", "era", "predictors"])
          .sort_index() if FILL_PATTERNS else pd.DataFrame())
print("\nTable: which predictor set filled which records (richest pattern first, per depth and era):")
display(PATTAB)

# The value-span rule, asserted: no filled value lies outside the range that depth measured in its
# own era. This is the range analog of the time-span rule above, and it is checked, not trusted.
for _d in DEPTHS:
    for _era in (True, False):
        _mera = overall[_d].where(method[_d].isin(METHOD_MEASURED) & (IS_MODERN == _era)).dropna()
        _fera = overall[_d].where(method[_d].isin(METHOD_MODELLED) & (IS_MODERN == _era)).dropna()
        if _mera.empty or _fera.empty:
            continue
        assert _fera.min() >= _mera.min() - 1e-9 and _fera.max() <= _mera.max() + 1e-9, \
            f"{_d} m: a filled value fell outside the era's measured range {_mera.min():.2f}.."\
            f"{_mera.max():.2f} ({_fera.min():.2f}..{_fera.max():.2f})"

# The rule, asserted: every filled value lies inside its depth's measured span. This is the line
# between interpolation (allowed) and extrapolation (refused), and it is checked, not trusted.
for _d in DEPTHS:
    _m = overall[_d].where(method[_d].isin(METHOD_MEASURED))
    _lo, _hi = _m.first_valid_index(), _m.last_valid_index()
    _outside = overall[_d].notna() & ((overall[_d].index < _lo) | (overall[_d].index > _hi))
    assert not _outside.any(), \
        f"{_d} m: {int(_outside.sum())} filled value(s) lie outside the measured span {_lo}..{_hi}"
if FILLTAB["not_extrapolated"].sum():
    print(f"held back from extrapolation beyond a depth's measured span: "
          f"{FILLTAB['not_extrapolated'].sum():,} records "
          f"(mostly 0.15 m after its 2021 death) - filled would have been fabrication, not fill")

# A fill cannot invent a value where every depth was missing, and cannot leave a value physically
# impossible. Both are asserted rather than hoped.
_allmiss = _measured.isna().all(axis=1)
for _d in DEPTHS:
    assert not (overall[_d].notna() & _allmiss).any(), \
        f"{_d} m: a value was invented at a timestamp where no depth measured anything"
    assert overall[_d].dropna().between(*TS_PLAUSIBLE_DEGC).all(), \
        f"{_d} m: a modelled value left the plausible band {TS_PLAUSIBLE_DEGC}"
    assert (overall[_d].notna() == method[_d].isin((METHOD_MODERN, METHOD_EARLY,
            METHOD_FILL_NEAR, METHOD_FILL_FAR))).all(), f"{_d} m: value and METHOD flag disagree"
print(f"\nOverall coverage now {FILLTAB['overall_%'].min():.1f}-{FILLTAB['overall_%'].max():.1f} % "
      f"per depth. Unfillable whole-station outages remaining: {int(_allmiss.sum()):,} "
      f"({100 * _allmiss.mean():.1f} %).")

Does the fill predict what it claims? Two held-out tests
Both fills are run, on identical code and identical timestamps, and shown side by side with the change: the upgraded multi-depth fill and the single-depth one it replaced. Showing the replaced fill is the point. It makes the upgrade auditable from this notebook rather than from the experiment that motivated it, and it is what the no-regression assert at the end is computed on.
Two tests, the second the one that matters: hide whole years and predict them from all other depths (the easy case, where a neighbour is usually present), then hide every deep depth at once and predict them from the shallow ones alone, which is the exact shape of the 2010-2020 hole this fill exists to close.
Test 2 is scored with the product’s value-span clip applied, so the numbers are the error of the values actually exported rather than of the raw model output. What the clip itself costs is printed separately.

def _held_out(target, hide_mask, allowed=None, fill_fn=None, clip=False,
              return_pairs=False):
    """Hide something, fill it back, score it. `fill_fn` selects which fill is under test, so the
    upgraded fill and the single-depth one it replaces are measured by identical code.

    `clip` applies the product's own per-era value-span rule before scoring. The comparison
    notebook's numbers are unclipped, and the clip is a product decision that costs a little
    accuracy in exchange for never reporting a temperature the sensor at that depth did not reach -
    so it is measured here rather than assumed negligible.
    """
    fill_fn = cross_depth_fill_mm if fill_fn is None else fill_fn
    _tf = _measured.copy()
    if allowed is None:
        _tf.loc[hide_mask, target] = np.nan
    else:
        _tf.loc[hide_mask, [c for c in DEPTHS if c not in allowed]] = np.nan
    _pred, _ = fill_fn(_tf, target, DEPTH_OF, IS_MODERN,
                       min_n=FILL_MIN_N_PER_MONTH, adjacent_m=FILL_ADJACENT_M)
    if clip:
        for _era in (True, False):
            _mera = _tf[target].where(IS_MODERN == _era).dropna()
            if _mera.empty:
                continue
            _sel = _pred.notna() & (IS_MODERN == _era)
            _pred.loc[_sel] = _pred[_sel].clip(float(_mera.min()), float(_mera.max()))
    _truth = _measured[target].where(hide_mask).dropna()
    _p = _pred.reindex(_truth.index).dropna()
    _truth = _truth.reindex(_p.index)
    _e = (_p - _truth).to_numpy()
    if len(_e) == 0:
        return (None, None, None) if return_pairs else None
    _stats = {"n": len(_e), "bias_K": round(float(_e.mean()), 2),
              "rmse_K": round(float(np.sqrt((_e ** 2).mean())), 2),
              "p95_K": round(float(np.percentile(np.abs(_e), 95)), 2)}
    return (_stats, _truth, _p) if return_pairs else _stats


def _side_by_side(rows_old, rows_new, keys):
    """One table, both fills, and the change. The point of showing the replaced fill is that the
    upgrade is auditable from this notebook alone rather than from the experiment it came from."""
    _o = pd.DataFrame(rows_old).set_index(keys)[["n", "rmse_K"]].rename(
        columns={"rmse_K": "rmse_single_depth"})
    _n = pd.DataFrame(rows_new).set_index(keys)[["rmse_K", "bias_K", "p95_K"]].rename(
        columns={"rmse_K": "rmse_multi_memory"})
    _t = _o.join(_n)
    _t["change_%"] = (100 * (_t["rmse_multi_memory"] - _t["rmse_single_depth"])
                      / _t["rmse_single_depth"]).round(0)
    return _t


print("TEST 1 - hide a whole year, predict from all other depths:")
_r_old, _r_new = [], []
for _d in DEPTHS:

    columns={"rmse_K": "rmse_unclipped"}).join(_t2[["rmse_multi_memory"]])
_t2c["cost_of_the_clip_K"] = (_t2c["rmse_multi_memory"] - _t2c["rmse_unclipped"]).round(3)

The upgraded fill is no worse than the single-depth fill it replaces at any depth on either test (tolerance 0.02 K), and closes the deep hole to 0.26 K RMSE at worst. The fills are still MODELLED, and flagged as such.




Does the fill step at the era boundary?
At 0.3 and 0.5 m the two sensor generations never overlap, so everything before April 2020 is modelled from the early profile and everything after is measured on the modern one. If the fill were biased, the two would sit apart by that bias and a user crossing April 2020 would read it as climate.
The offset is real, and it is not the fill’s doing. Those depths were genuinely measured until March 2010, and over that period the early sensors themselves sat well above the modern relationship. The honest requirement is therefore not “no step” but “no step the sensors did not themselves record”: the modelled era must not invent a larger offset than the measured early record shows, nor flip its sign. That is what is asserted below.
Worth knowing when reading the fill’s history: the single-depth fill this replaced returned about +0.29 K at 0.3 m and −0.03 K at 0.5 m, i.e. it flattened the era difference toward the modern relationship. Being a weaker model made the product appear more continuous across 2020 than the instruments themselves were.

# Season-matched, because the gradient between two depths reverses sign twice a year: a raw
# before/after mean over the boundary compares Dec-Apr with Apr-Aug and reports the season as a
# step. Everything below is a day-of-year climatology.
# (!) EARLY_DEEP_END is a claim about when the early deep channels stopped, and the window this
#     whole check runs in depends on it. So it is re-derived here rather than believed: if a
#     re-ingest extends or truncates those channels, this fails instead of silently comparing
#     climatologies built over the wrong years.
for _d in ("0.3", "0.5"):
    _last_early = _measured[_d].where(method[_d] == METHOD_EARLY).last_valid_index()
    assert abs((_last_early - pd.Timestamp(EARLY_DEEP_END)).days) <= 7, (
        f"{_d} m: the early channel's last record is {_last_early:%Y-%m-%d}, not within a week of "
        f"EARLY_DEEP_END = {EARLY_DEEP_END}. Update the setting before trusting the table below")
print(f"early deep channels end within a week of EARLY_DEEP_END ({EARLY_DEEP_END}), as assumed.\n")

_ref = overall["0.1"]
_rows = []
for _d in ("0.3", "0.5"):
    _diff = overall[_d] - _ref
    _modelled = _diff.where(method[_d].isin(METHOD_MODELLED)
                            & (_diff.index < ERA_BOUNDARY_MID)).dropna()
    _measured_modern = _diff.where(method[_d] == METHOD_MODERN).dropna()
    # What the early INSTRUMENTS said, over the years both this depth and 0.1 m were measured.
    _early_meas = (_measured[_d] - _measured["0.1"]).where(
        _measured[_d].notna() & (_diff.index < EARLY_DEEP_END)).dropna()

    def _clim(s):
        return s.groupby(s.index.dayofyear).mean()

    _cm, _cs, _ce = _clim(_modelled), _clim(_measured_modern), _clim(_early_meas)
    _fill_off = float((_cm - _cs).dropna().mean())
    _meas_off = float((_ce - _cs).dropna().mean())
    _rows.append({"depth_m": float(_d),
                  "fill_offset_K": round(_fill_off, 3),
                  "measured_early_offset_K": round(_meas_off, 3),
                  "fraction_of_the_real_offset": round(_fill_off / _meas_off, 2)})
STEPTAB = pd.DataFrame(_rows).set_index("depth_m")
print("Table: the era step at the two depths whose generations never overlap, against the offset "
      "the early sensors themselves measured. The fill may reproduce it, never exceed it")
display(STEPTAB)

# (!) The fill may reproduce the era difference the instruments recorded; it may not exceed it or
#     reverse it. Both directions matter: overshooting fabricates a step, and a negative value
#     would mean the modelled early era had been pushed to the wrong side of the modern one.
for _d, _r in STEPTAB.iterrows():
    assert _r["measured_early_offset_K"] > 0, (
        f"{_d} m: the early sensors did not sit above the modern relationship, so the premise of "
        f"this check no longer holds - re-derive it before trusting the assert below")
    assert 0.0 <= _r["fill_offset_K"] <= _r["measured_early_offset_K"] + 0.1, (
        f"{_d} m: the modelled early era sits {_r['fill_offset_K']:+.2f} K from the modern one "
        f"while the early sensors measured {_r['measured_early_offset_K']:+.2f} K. The fill is "
        f"inventing an era step rather than reproducing one")
for _line in [
    "The modelled early era reproduces part of the era difference the early sensors themselves",
    "recorded, and never exceeds it. The remainder is regression shrinkage towards the modern",
    "relationship, which biases the filled early era slightly TOWARDS the modern level - the",
    "conservative direction. The step that survives is hardware, is flagged (METHOD 2 vs 1), and",
    "is why the closing notes tell you not to draw a trend across April 2020 at these depths.",
]:
    print(_line)

title: Download and prepare TS for the FF1 soil profile (2004-2025)
text:
🔍 Cross-checks across the profile
Four checks, in order of how much they can prove.

Is the exported profile still a profile? Amplitude must damp monotonically with depth and the daily maximum must lag, separately in each era. The only check that can fail because of something this notebook did: a wrong channel in a depth column shows up as an inversion. The lag is asserted end to end, not step by step, because below 0.3 m the daily wave is one or two quantiser steps; 0.6 m comes out marginally ahead of 0.5 m, which is quantisation, not heat flowing upwards.
Did any channel quietly stop being coupled? Screening and the band check catch the loud failure. The quiet one is a sensor still returning smooth, in-range, plausible values that no longer respond to the soil: invisible to any test on one series, visible as a drop in agreement with everything else.
Is the early profile internally consistent? The same question asked of the early era, where it needs a different null and where the answer is no. The largest finding in the notebook.
Does the profile agree with the air above it? 02’s air temperature cannot validate a depth, but it would catch a whole-profile error: a wrong file, a wrong unit, a shifted year.


Is the exported profile still a profile?
Amplitude must damp with depth and the daily maximum must lag, checked separately in each era.

_rows = []
for _d in DEPTHS:
    for _era, _mask in [("modern", ts[flagcol(_d)].isin(MODERN_FLAGS)),
                        ("early", ts[flagcol(_d)] == FLAG_EARLY)]:
        _s = ts[col(_d)].where(_mask).dropna()
        if len(_s) < 20000:
            continue
        _r = thermal_diagnostics(_s, col(_d))
        _r.update({"era": _era, "depth_m": float(_d)})
        _rows.append(_r)
ORDERING = pd.DataFrame(_rows).set_index(["era", "depth_m"]).sort_index()
print("Table: the exported profile checked as a profile: amplitude must damp with depth and the "
      "daily maximum must lag, separately in each era")
display(ORDERING[["n", "amp_JJA", "amp_DJF", "hour_max_JJA", "annual_range", "mean"]].round(3))

for _era in ORDERING.index.get_level_values("era").unique():
    _sub = ORDERING.loc[_era].sort_index()
    assert _sub["annual_range"].is_monotonic_decreasing, (
        f"{_era} era: the annual range does not damp monotonically with depth\n{_sub['annual_range']}")
    assert _sub["amp_JJA"].is_monotonic_decreasing, (
        f"{_era} era: the summer daily amplitude does not damp monotonically with depth\n"
        f"{_sub['amp_JJA']}")
    print(f"{_era:<7} annual range damps monotonically: "
          f"{' > '.join(f'{v:.1f}' for v in _sub['annual_range'])} K "
          f"over {_sub.index.min()} - {_sub.index.max()} m")

# The phase has to lag with depth too, and it is the check the quantiser cannot fake: a channel
# placed at the wrong depth by a level error would still damp correctly, but not lag correctly.
# Compared against the shallowest depth of the same era, wrapped, because 0.5 m peaks after
# midnight and 23.9 h is 0.2 h later than 23.7, not 23.7 h earlier.
for _era in ORDERING.index.get_level_values("era").unique():

    _lag = ((_sub["hour_max_JJA"] - _sub["hour_max_JJA"].iloc[0] + 12) % 24) - 12
    print(f"{_era:<7} lag of the daily maximum against the shallowest depth [h]: "
          f"{_lag.round(1).to_dict()}")
    assert _lag.iloc[-1] > _lag.iloc[0], f"{_era}: the daily maximum does not lag with depth"

Did any channel stop being coupled?
Each channel’s 3-day change of the daily mean is correlated with the median of the same quantity over the whole modern profile, in a rolling 60-day window. A sensor measuring the soil moves with the profile; one that has come loose or is reporting its own enclosure does not. Three details decide whether this works at all.

3-day changes, not daily ones. At 0.5 m and 0.6 m a one-day change is a few hundredths of a kelvin, below the 0.1 K grid, so a daily-increment correlation there compares two quantisation patterns and reads about 0.5 all the time.
Each channel against its own baseline. The deepest channels sit lower for the same reason, so a fixed cut-off would flag TS_FF1_0.6_1 permanently. A channel is flagged where its agreement falls DECOUPLE_DROP below its own median; below DECOUPLE_MIN_BASELINE the scan says it cannot resolve the channel.
A correlation across a gap is not a low correlation, it is no correlation. TS_FF1_0.05_4 is missing for ten weeks in early 2022, and the windows straddling that hole came back with r ≈ 0.6 on a handful of surviving pairs, indistinguishable from a sensor that had come loose. Every window must now hold at least DECOUPLE_MIN_COVERAGE of its days as valid pairs.


def decoupling_scan(mean: pd.DataFrame, channels, step=None, window=None, drop=None):
    """Rolling agreement of each channel's N-day change with the profile's, against its own baseline."""
    step = INC_STEP_DAYS if step is None else step
    window = DECOUPLE_WINDOW if window is None else window
    drop = DECOUPLE_DROP if drop is None else drop
    _inc = mean.diff(step)
    _prof = _inc[channels].median(axis=1)
    rows, runs = [], {}
    for _c in channels:
        _r = _inc[_c].rolling(window, min_periods=window // 2).corr(_prof)
        # A window straddling a gap in this channel returns a correlation of a handful of pairs,
        # and it looks exactly like a decoupled sensor. Refuse it rather than report it.
        _n_valid = (_inc[_c].notna() & _prof.notna()).rolling(window).sum()
        _r = _r.where(_n_valid >= DECOUPLE_MIN_COVERAGE * window)
        _base = float(_r.median())
        _resolvable = _base >= DECOUPLE_MIN_BASELINE
        _low = _r[_r < _base - drop].dropna() if _resolvable else pd.Series(dtype=float)
        _grp = (_low.index.to_series().diff().dt.days.fillna(1) > 14).cumsum() if len(_low) else None
        _runs = ([(g.index[0], g.index[-1], len(g)) for _, g in _low.groupby(_grp)
                  if len(g) >= DECOUPLE_MIN_RUN] if len(_low) else [])
        runs[_c] = _runs
        rows.append({"channel": _c, "instrument": INSTRUMENT.get(_c, "-"),
                     "median_|change| [K]": round(float(_inc[_c].abs().median()), 3),
                     "baseline_r": round(_base, 3),
                     "windows_dropped_for_coverage": int(_r.isna().sum() - _inc[_c].isna().sum()),
                     "resolvable": _resolvable,
                     "n_windows_low": len(_low),
                     "runs": "; ".join(f"{a:%Y-%m-%d} -> {b:%Y-%m-%d} ({n} d)"
                                       for a, b, n in _runs) or "-"})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("channel"), runs

Is the early profile internally consistent? No, and this is the largest finding here
The early era needs its own scan and a different null. Its channels are on a continuous scale, so the quantiser is not the problem, but the gradient between two depths reverses sign twice a year, so a fixed tolerance on a raw depth difference fires every November on physics alone. Each channel is therefore compared with the mean of the other two, and that deviation measured against its own day-of-year climatology.
Between January 2009 and May 2012 the three early channels disagree by 1.5 to 3.5 K beyond their own seasonal norm, for months at a time, in mirror-image pairs, TS_PRF_FF1_0.05_1 running warm while _0.15_1 runs cold. Across the other thirteen years they agree to a few tenths of a kelvin. The period brackets the years when the forest-floor logger was repeatedly losing power (the 2009, 2010 and 2011 whole-station gaps above, two of them named in the legacy fieldbook as a dead logger and a fuse that slipped out) and ends around the 2012-04-25 logger program “with corrected multipliers and offset”, which 09 calls the only candidate gain change in the early era, and which names no channels.






WarningThis is reported, not repaired



Three channels disagreeing does not say which is wrong: the leave-one-out deviation of a three-member profile moves all three when any one moves, and there is no fourth soil sensor and no external reference to break the tie. So the affected records stay in the product, flagged as measured, and carry FLAG_TS_FF1_<d>_SUSPECT. The period is re-derived on every run; only the coarse window it must fall inside is a setting.

Does the profile agree with the air above it?
02’s gap-filled air temperature is 47 m up a tower over a forest, so it cannot validate a depth. It can catch a whole-profile error: a wrong file, a wrong unit, a shifted year. The one statement with teeth is that agreement with the air has to weaken with depth, because that is what a thermal lag does.
It is also the only check here that can see a shift common to every channel, which is what makes the column choice matter. TA_COL is 02’s homogenised column: the measured one carries a 1.32 °C step at the January 2016 acquisition change, and since the early era runs 2004-2020 that step lands on about two thirds of it. Read with the measured column, this table reports the early era about 0.8 K warmer than the air at every depth and the two eras looking as though they disagree about their installation — an artefact of the reference, not a property of the soil. This notebook used the measured column until version 3.

# The air temperature above the profile. Not a validation of a depth - it is 47 m up a tower over a
# forest - but a whole-profile error would show here and nowhere else.
_rows = []
for _d in DEPTHS:
    for _era, _mask in [("modern", ts[flagcol(_d)].isin(MODERN_FLAGS)),
                        ("early", ts[flagcol(_d)] == FLAG_EARLY)]:
        _s = ts[col(_d)].where(_mask).dropna()
        if len(_s) < 20000:
            continue
        _both = pd.DataFrame({"ts": _s, "ta": ta.reindex(_s.index)}).dropna()
        _ann = _both.resample("YS").mean()[_both["ts"].resample("YS").count() > 14000]
        _rows.append({"era": _era, "depth_m": float(_d), "n_years": len(_ann),
                      "mean_TS_minus_TA_K": round(float((_ann["ts"] - _ann["ta"]).mean()), 2),
                      "sd_over_years_K": round(float((_ann["ts"] - _ann["ta"]).std()), 2),
                      "r_daily": round(float(_both["ts"].resample("1D").mean()
                                             .corr(_both["ta"].resample("1D").mean())), 3)})
TATAB = pd.DataFrame(_rows).set_index(["era", "depth_m"]).sort_index()
print("Table: every depth against the air temperature 47 m up the tower. The test is not the "
      "offset but that agreement weakens monotonically with depth, as a thermal lag requires")
display(TATAB)

assert TATAB["mean_TS_minus_TA_K"].abs().max() < 3.0, (
    "a depth's annual mean differs from the air by more than 3 K - that is not a forest floor, "

assert (TATAB["r_daily"] > 0.70).all(), (
    "a depth column no longer follows the air temperature at the daily scale - a timestamp or a "

# The stronger statement, and the one a wrong channel in a depth column would break: agreement

for _era in TATAB.index.get_level_values("era").unique():
    _sub = TATAB.loc[_era].sort_index()
    assert _sub["r_daily"].is_monotonic_decreasing, (

cannot tell 0.2 m from 0.3 m. Both eras sit within a few tenths of a kelvin of the air
and mostly a little below it, which is only visible because TA's own January 2016 step is
removed first: read with `02`'s MEASURED column instead of its homogenised one, the early
era comes out about 0.8 K warmer at every depth and the two eras appear to disagree about
their installation. That apparent disagreement is a property of the air-temperature
record, not of the soil.

largest early-minus-modern difference in TS-TA at a shared depth: 0.29 K




📊 Plot: the depth columns against the air temperature
Top, the measured part of every overall column against TA, with the modern profile’s start and the 0.3 m probe swap marked. Bottom, annual means of the gap-filled columns.

fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows=2, figsize=(15, 8), dpi=100, layout="constrained", sharex=True)
_colors = plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0.05, 0.9, len(DEPTHS)))
for _c, _d in zip(_colors, DEPTHS):
    # The MEASURED part of the overall column, so the top panel shows only what a thermometer read.
    _daily = overall[_d].where(method[_d].isin(METHOD_MEASURED)).resample("1D").mean()
    axs[0].plot(_daily.index, _daily.values, lw=0.6, color=_c, label=f"{_d} m")
axs[0].plot(ta.resample("1D").mean().index, ta.resample("1D").mean().values,
            lw=0.4, color="#B0BEC5", alpha=.8, zorder=0, label="TA, 47 m")
axs[0].axvline(MODERN_START, color="#F44336", ls="--", lw=1.2)
axs[0].axvline(pd.Timestamp(SENSOR_SWAP), color="#7B1FA2", ls=":", lw=1.2)
axs[0].set_ylabel("daily mean [°C]")
axs[0].set_title("The overall columns, MEASURED part only. Dashed = the modern profile starts, "
                 "dotted = the 0.3 m probe swap", fontsize=11)
axs[0].legend(fontsize=8, ncol=8)

for _c, _d in zip(_colors, DEPTHS):
    # The full gap-filled overall column: annual means are now defined at every depth every year.
    _ann = overall[_d].resample("YS").mean().where(overall[_d].resample("YS").count() > 14000)
    # (!) x is the timestamp index, NOT .index.year. This axis is shared with a datetime axis
    #     above, so an integer 2004 would be read as day 2004 of the epoch and land in 1975.
    axs[1].plot(_ann.index, _ann.values, marker="o", ms=4, color=_c, label=f"{_d} m")
axs[1].set_xlabel("year")
axs[1].set_ylabel("annual mean [°C]")
axs[1].set_title("Annual means of the gap-filled overall columns (every depth, every year now "
                 "defined)", fontsize=11)
axs[1].legend(fontsize=8, ncol=7)
plt.show()
print("Figure: top, the measured part of every overall column against TA; bottom, annual means of "
      "the gap-filled columns, where every depth is now defined in every year")

title: Download and prepare TS for the FF1 soil profile (2004-2025)
section: 🧭 Two dates, and what the forest-floor programs say
text:
🧭 Two dates, and what the forest-floor programs say
Three things this notebook had not done, all of them checks rather than corrections: it had never read the logger programs of its own station, never asked whether the January 2016 site renewal reached this profile, and never asked what happened at the forest-floor rewiring of 25 June 2015 where 09 measures a −3.9 % VWC step in soil moisture. Nothing here changes an exported value.
The programs turn out to answer a question the closing notes list as open, and the June 2015 date turns out to be the more useful of the two: soil temperature not moving there is what tells 09 that its soil-moisture step was confined to the soil-moisture wiring.

What the forest-floor programs say the early sensors were
The closing notes call the identity of the early profile open, on the strength of a fieldbook entry naming three Campbell 107 sensors trashed the day every early channel stops — and note that “three 107s replaced by two 109s does not balance”. The programs settle most of it.
Both surviving forest-floor programs, of September 2004 and May 2006, are identical in this respect and take eight Campbell 107 readings per scan, in two groups:

a five-sensor stick, whose storage locations the programs’ own label table names SoilT_05, SoilT_10, SoilT_15, SoilT_30, SoilT_50 — 5, 10, 15, 30 and 50 cm, which is exactly this product’s five early depths and in the same order;
separate probes SoilT_A, SoilT_B, SoilT_C and SoilT_D, whose comments place them with the soil heat-flux plates rather than in the profile pit.

Two consequences. The fieldbook’s three device numbers are not the station’s whole 107 inventory, so the arithmetic that looked wrong was never a constraint. And the three mst-era TS_FF1_0.05_* channels this notebook excludes as mislabelled — placed by the damping analysis at roughly 0.15, 0.22 and 0.31 m — are what heat-flux-plate probes would look like: three sensors, at three unrelated depths, not in the pit. That is the same explanation this notebook already accepts for the modern Campbell 109s, arrived at independently.
The conversion matters too. Every one of the eight readings uses Mult 1.0 and Offset 0.0: the Temp (107) instruction applies Campbell’s own polynomial internally and the program adds no site-specific scaling. So in the program’s form there is no soil-temperature multiplier to have been changed, which is a partial answer to the 2012-04-25 entry, “new Loggerprogramm with corrected multipliers and offset”, that both this notebook and 09 list as an open question. It is partial and not complete: no forest-floor program between May 2006 and the modern era survives, so what the 2012 program did cannot be read, only bounded by what came before it.

_rows = []
for _names, _text in ff_programs().items():
    _tab, _labels = ff_thermistor_channels(_text, _names)
    _rows.append({"program(s)": _names, "readings": int(_tab["reps"].sum()),
                  "instructions": len(_tab),
                  "multiplier": float(_tab["multiplier"].iloc[0]),
                  "offset": float(_tab["offset"].iloc[0]),
                  "channels": " | ".join(_tab["channels"])})
FF_T107 = pd.DataFrame(_rows).set_index("program(s)")
print("Table: every Campbell 107 reading each forest-floor program takes, resolved to the channel "
      "names in the program's own storage-location table. Both programs agree, and every reading "
      "applies the identical conversion")
display(FF_T107)

_consts = {(r.multiplier, r.offset) for r in FF_T107.itertuples()}
assert len(_consts) == 1, f"the programs disagree about the thermistor conversion: {_consts}"
T107_MULT, T107_OFFSET = next(iter(_consts))
assert (T107_MULT, T107_OFFSET) == (1.0, 0.0), (
    f"the thermistor conversion is {T107_MULT} / {T107_OFFSET:+}, not 1.0 / 0.0. The argument that "
    f"there is no site-applied soil-temperature scaling rests on it being 1.0 / 0.0")

# The stick, and the claim that it IS this product's early profile: five sensors whose names give
# depths in centimetres, matching the five depths that have an early channel, in the same order.
_, _labels = ff_thermistor_channels(next(iter(ff_programs().values())), "stick")
STICK = {_n: int(_n.split("_")[1]) / 100 for _n in _labels.values() if _n.split("_")[1].isdigit()}
PROBES = sorted(_n for _n in _labels.values() if not _n.split("_")[1].isdigit())
print(f"\nstick sensors, depth from the name: {STICK}")
print(f"separate probes (with the heat-flux plates): {PROBES}")

EARLY_DEPTHS_HERE = sorted(float(_d) for _d in DEPTHS if EARLY[_d])
print(f"depths of this product with an early channel: {EARLY_DEPTHS_HERE}")
assert sorted(STICK.values()) == EARLY_DEPTHS_HERE, (
    f"the program's stick is at {sorted(STICK.values())} m but this product's early depths are "
    f"{EARLY_DEPTHS_HERE} m. The identification of the stick with the early profile does not hold "
    f"- re-read the section before repeating it")
assert len(PROBES) >= len(DISPUTED_EARLY), (
    f"the program carries {len(PROBES)} separate probe(s) but this notebook excludes "
    f"{len(DISPUTED_EARLY)} mislabelled channel(s). The explanation offered for them - that they "
    f"are plate probes rather than stick sensors - needs at least as many probes as channels")
print(f"\nThe stick's five depths are exactly this product's five early depths, and the program "
      f"carries\n{len(PROBES)} further 107s beside the heat-flux plates - enough to account for the "
      f"{len(DISPUTED_EARLY)} mislabelled channels this notebook excludes ({DISPUTED_EARLY}).")

The January 2016 site renewal did not reach this profile
09 established this for soil moisture; the same question has to be asked here, because a renewal that moved TA by 1.32 °C, stepped RH and PA, and broke half of LW_IN five months later is not something to assume away.
The structural reason is the same: the renewal replaced the tower installation, and this profile is on the forest-floor logger. The tower program installed at the changeover contains no soil-temperature instruction of any kind. The data agree — no records lost while the tower logger was replaced, and no half-hour in the surrounding three weeks changing by more than the record’s own routine scatter.
One honest limit. The level test that could see a change common to all channels is the residual against air temperature, and it resolves about ±0.75 K. Within that, nothing happens at 2016. Anything smaller this notebook cannot see, and says so rather than claiming a null it has not earned.

# 1) the tower program takes no soil temperature at all
_tower_text = uncommented(Path(PROGRAM_TOWER_CR1000).read_text(encoding="latin-1"))
_tower_soil = re.findall(r"Temp \(107\)|SoilT|TS_|Teros|107\b", _tower_text)
_tower_sdi = re.findall(r"SDI12Recorder\s*\(\s*([A-Za-z_0-9]+)", _tower_text)
print(f"{Path(PROGRAM_TOWER_CR1000).name}")
print(f"  soil-temperature references in the live code: {len(_tower_soil)}")
print(f"  SDI-12 instructions:                         {_tower_sdi}")
assert len(_tower_soil) == 0, (
    "the tower program contains a soil-temperature reference. The argument that the January 2016 "
    "changeover cannot have touched this profile rests on it not doing so")

# 2) no records lost while the tower logger was replaced
_win = slice(pd.Timestamp(TOWER_ACQUISITION_CHANGE) - pd.Timedelta("2D"),
             pd.Timestamp(TOWER_ACQUISITION_CHANGE) + pd.Timedelta("4D"))
_poss = len(mst.loc[_win])
_cov = {_c: int(mst.loc[_win, _c].notna().sum()) for _c in EARLY_LONG}
print(f"\nrecords measured {TOWER_ACQUISITION_CHANGE} -2 d .. +4 d, of {_poss} possible: {_cov}")
assert all(_v == _poss for _v in _cov.values()), (
    f"this station lost records while the tower logger was replaced ({_cov} of {_poss})")

# 3) no half-hour in the surrounding three weeks stands out from the record's own scatter
_rows = []
for _c in EARLY_LONG:
    _all = mst[_c].diff().abs()
    _here = mst[_c].loc["2016-01-14":"2016-02-04"].diff().abs()
    _rows.append({"channel": _c, "max_abs_30min_change_K": float(_here.max()),
                  "when": _here.idxmax(), "record_p99.9_K": float(_all.quantile(0.999)),
                  "record_max_K": float(_all.max())})
JAN2016 = pd.DataFrame(_rows).set_index("channel")
print("Table: the largest 30-minute change in each early channel over the three weeks around the "
      "January 2016 tower changeover, against that channel's own distribution over seventeen years")
display(JAN2016.round(3))
assert (JAN2016["max_abs_30min_change_K"] < JAN2016["record_p99.9_K"]).all(), (
    "a half-hour around the January 2016 changeover changes by more than that channel's own p99.9")

# 4) the only test that can see a change common to every channel, with its resolution stated
_ta30 = ta.rolling(48 * 30, min_periods=48 * 20).mean()
_res = {}
for _c in EARLY_LONG:
    _r = (mst[_c] - _ta30).dropna()
    _g = _r.groupby(_r.index.to_period("M"))
    _res[_c] = _g.mean().where(_g.size() >= 500)
RESID = pd.DataFrame(_res)
_anom = RESID - RESID.groupby(RESID.index.month).transform("mean")
_prof = _anom.mean(axis=1)


def _resid_step(boundary, win=12):
    _b = pd.Period(boundary, "M")
    _pre = _prof.loc[(_prof.index < _b) & (_prof.index >= _b - win)].dropna()
    _post = _prof.loc[(_prof.index >= _b) & (_prof.index < _b + win)].dropna()
    return (_post.mean() - _pre.mean()) if (len(_pre) >= 8 and len(_post) >= 8) else np.nan


_cands = pd.period_range("2006-01", "2020-01", freq="M")
RESID_STEPS = pd.Series({str(_b): _resid_step(_b) for _b in _cands}).dropna()
RESID_RESOLUTION = float(RESID_STEPS.abs().quantile(0.90))
print(f"\nlevel residual against air temperature: {len(RESID_STEPS)} boundaries tested")
print(f"  median |step| {RESID_STEPS.abs().median():.3f} K   p90 {RESID_RESOLUTION:.3f} K "
      f"<- the resolution of this test")
for _b in ["2015-06", "2016-01", "2016-02"]:
    if _b in RESID_STEPS.index:
        print(f"  {_b}: {RESID_STEPS[_b]:+.3f} K")
assert abs(RESID_STEPS["2016-01"]) < RESID_RESOLUTION, (
    f"the residual moves {RESID_STEPS['2016-01']:+.3f} K at January 2016, beyond this test's own "
    f"p90 of {RESID_RESOLUTION:.3f} K. That is worth looking at before repeating the null")
print(f"\nJanuary 2016 moves the residual by {RESID_STEPS['2016-01']:+.3f} K, inside the test's own\n"
      f"resolution. Combined with no outage and no unusual half-hour, this profile did not\n"
      f"participate in the tower renewal.")

25 June 2015: soil moisture stepped and soil temperature did not
09 finds a −3.9 % VWC step at every soil-moisture depth in a single half-hour on the morning of 25 June 2015, when the fieldbook has the forest-floor logger being rewired, and attributes it to the soil-moisture probes’ own connectors — which an entry three weeks earlier reports finding loose. That attribution rested on the fieldbook alone. It can be tested here, because soil temperature is measured on the same station, through the same enclosure and the same power supply: a station-wide power or reference change would move both variables, and a change confined to the soil-moisture wiring would move only one.
Soil temperature does not move. The comparison needs care, because a departure at breakfast-time in June is not zero on an ordinary morning — the morning warming curve accelerates and a straight line fitted before it under-predicts what follows, by about +0.7 K at 0.05 m. So the same statistic is computed at the same clock time on every May-to-July morning of the record, and the date under test is placed in that distribution. The identical machinery is then run on 09’s soil moisture, so the two are not being judged by different standards.
The result is unambiguous, and it is the reason this section exists: at the same timestamp, on the same station, soil temperature sits at the middle of its own distribution and soil moisture sits in the extreme tail of its. The step was in the soil-moisture chain.

swc_prod = read_product(SWC_FILE)
print(f"`09`'s product: {swc_prod.shape[0]:,} records, {swc_prod.shape[1]} columns\n")

print(f"Departure at {FF_WIRING_BREAK}, against the same statistic on every May-July morning:\n")
print("  soil TEMPERATURE (K), this notebook's early channels")
TS_DEP = {}
for _c in EARLY_LONG:
    TS_DEP[_c] = departure_percentile(mst[_c], FF_WIRING_BREAK, _c)

print("\n  soil MOISTURE (% VWC), from `09`, identical machinery")
SWC_DEP = {}
for _d in ["0.05", "0.1", "0.2", "0.3"]:
    _v = f"SWC_FF1_{_d}_1"
    _s = swc_prod[_v].where(swc_prod[f"FLAG_{_v}_SOURCE"] == 1)
    SWC_DEP[_v] = departure_percentile(_s, FF_WIRING_BREAK, _v)

JUNE2015 = pd.DataFrame(
    [{"series": _k, "variable": "TS", "unit": "K", "departure": _v[0], "percentile": _v[1],
      "n_null": _v[2]} for _k, _v in TS_DEP.items()]
    + [{"series": _k, "variable": "SWC", "unit": "% VWC", "departure": _v[0], "percentile": _v[1],
        "n_null": _v[2]} for _k, _v in SWC_DEP.items()]).set_index(["variable", "series"])
print()
print("Table: the departure at the June 2015 rewiring and where it sits among comparable mornings. "
      "Soil temperature is ordinary for the hour at every depth; soil moisture is in the tail at "
      "every depth. Same station, same half-hour, same statistic")
display(JUNE2015.round(3))

_lo, _hi = DEPARTURE_ORDINARY_PCT
_ts_pct = [_v[1] for _v in TS_DEP.values()]
_swc_pct = [_v[1] for _v in SWC_DEP.values()]

    f"a soil-temperature channel is no longer ordinary for the hour at the June 2015 rewiring "
    f"(percentiles {[round(_p, 1) for _p in _ts_pct]}). If soil temperature moved too, the event "
    f"was station-wide and `09`'s attribution to the soil-moisture wiring needs re-reading")

    f"soil moisture is no longer in the tail at the June 2015 rewiring (percentiles "
    f"{[round(_p, 2) for _p in _swc_pct]}); the contrast this section rests on has gone")
print(f"\nsoil temperature percentiles: {[round(_p, 1) for _p in _ts_pct]} - the middle")
print(f"soil moisture percentiles:    {[round(_p, 2) for _p in _swc_pct]} - the tail")
print("\nThe 25 June 2015 event was confined to the soil-moisture chain. This profile needs no\n"
      "correction there, and `09`'s attribution now rests on an independent measurement rather\n"
      "than on the maintenance record alone.")

What the early-era consistency scan cannot see
Worth stating, because the scan above is the notebook’s strongest early-era check and its blind spot is structural rather than a matter of tolerance. It compares each channel with the mean of the other two, so it detects a channel moving relative to its neighbours. A shift common to all three cancels exactly and is invisible to it, at any size.
The only test here that can see a common-mode shift is the residual against air temperature, and it resolves about ±0.75 K — which is why the section above quotes that number rather than claiming a tighter null. Its largest boundaries are in 2013 and in 2007-2008, at up to about 1.2 K. Those are not reported as findings: since the inter-channel scan puts no channel-level disagreement there, they are common-mode by construction, and a common-mode residual against the air can as easily be soil-air coupling, the canopy, snow, or the air-temperature series itself as the thermistors. Naming a cause would be guessing.

# The blind spot, demonstrated rather than asserted: add the same offset to every early channel
# and the leave-one-out scan does not notice, while the air-temperature residual does.
_shift = 1.0
_daily_plain = pd.concat({_c: mst[_c].resample("1D").mean()
                          .where(mst[_c].resample("1D").count() >= 40) for _c in EARLY_LONG}, axis=1)
_daily_shift = _daily_plain.copy()
_daily_shift.loc["2014-01-01":] += _shift

_dev_plain = leave_one_out_deviation(_daily_plain, EARLY_LONG)
_dev_shift = leave_one_out_deviation(_daily_shift, EARLY_LONG)
_max_change = float((_dev_shift - _dev_plain).abs().max().max())
print(f"a {_shift:+.1f} K shift applied to ALL {len(EARLY_LONG)} early channels from 2014 changes "
      f"the leave-one-out\ndeviation by at most {_max_change:.2e} K - i.e. not at all.")
assert _max_change < 1e-9, (
    "a common-mode shift now changes the leave-one-out deviation, so the blind spot this section "
    "describes is not there - re-read it")

# ... and the residual against the air does see it, which is why that is the test quoted above.
_res_plain = (mst[EARLY_LONG[0]] - _ta30).loc["2012":"2016"].mean()
_res_shift = (mst[EARLY_LONG[0]] + _shift - _ta30).loc["2012":"2016"].mean()
print(f"the same shift moves the air-temperature residual by {_res_shift - _res_plain:+.2f} K, "
      f"which is\nwhy that test - at {RESID_RESOLUTION:.2f} K resolution - is the one the 2016 "
      f"question is settled with.")
assert abs((_res_shift - _res_plain) - _shift) < 0.01, \
    "the air-temperature residual does not track a common-mode shift one for one"

a +1.0 K shift applied to ALL 3 early channels from 2014 changes the leave-one-out
deviation by at most 5.33e-15 K - i.e. not at all.
the same shift moves the air-temperature residual by +1.00 K, which is
why that test - at 0.75 K resolution - is the one the 2016 question is settled with.

section: 🚫 What is left empty, and why
text:
🚫 What is left empty, and why
The overall columns of the depths measured on both sides of a gap are now filled to ~94 %, so the question turns around: what could not be filled?

Whole-station outages, every depth dead at once. No depth can predict another when none of them measured anything, so these stay empty in every overall column at once (~6 %). They are scanned for and matched to the fieldbook below.
Everything outside a depth’s own measured span, because the fill interpolates rather than extrapolates. 0.2 and 0.6 m have no fill before 2020, 0.15 m none after March 2021. These are the low-coverage rows below, and they are by design.

The table separates, per depth, what was measured from what the fill added, so coverage gained by modelling is never mistaken for coverage that was there all along. The individual channel columns are not filled: their gaps are the honest record of when each sensor was down.

_rows = []
for _d in DEPTHS:
    _meas = overall[_d].where(method[_d].isin(METHOD_MEASURED))
    _first, _last = _meas.first_valid_index(), _meas.last_valid_index()
    _rows.append({"depth_m": float(_d),
                  "measured_record": f"{_first:%Y-%m-%d} -> {_last:%Y-%m-%d}",
                  "n_measured": int(_meas.notna().sum()),
                  "n_filled": int(method[_d].isin(METHOD_MODELLED).sum()),
                  "n_still_empty": int((method[_d] == METHOD_NONE).sum()),
                  "overall_coverage_%": round(100 * float(overall[_d].notna().mean()), 1)})
GAPTAB = pd.DataFrame(_rows).set_index("depth_m")
print("Table: per depth, what was measured against what the fill added, with each depth's measured "
      "span, so coverage gained by modelling is not mistaken for coverage that was there")
display(GAPTAB)

print("The longest stretches that remain EMPTY in each overall column (whole-station outages only):\n")
for _d in DEPTHS:
    _blocks = sorted(missing_blocks(overall[_d].isna()), key=lambda t: -t[2])[:4]
    print(f"  {homogcol(_d)}")
    for _a, _b, _n in _blocks:
        print(f"     {_a:%Y-%m-%d} -> {_b:%Y-%m-%d}   {_n * 0.5 / 24:7.1f} d")

The whole-station gaps, and what caused them
Evidence first, fieldbook second. The cell below scans each era blind for periods where every channel of that era is missing at once, and only then asks the record what happened there. For the early era that means asking the legacy row, because all four of its long gaps fall in 2007-2011.
Two of the early gaps are the ones 09 SWC also found and named to the day, from remarks written a year or more after the fact: DOY 69-162 of 2009 (“No forest floor logger data recorded”) and 6 March to 28 May 2010 (a fuse had slipped out and the battery-run forest-floor logger sat without power). The other two, nine weeks in 2007 and four months in 2011, are found here for the first time.

STATION_GAPS = {}
for _era, _src, _cols, _lo, _hi in [
        ("modern", diive_clean, MODERN_ALL, MODERN_START, diive_.index[-1]),
        ("early", mst, EARLY_ALL, EARLY_START, pd.Timestamp("2021-03-24"))]:
    _allmiss = _src[_cols].isna().all(axis=1).loc[_lo:_hi]
    STATION_GAPS[_era] = [(a, b, n * 0.5 / 24) for a, b, n in missing_blocks(_allmiss)
                          if n * 0.5 / 24 > 0.5]
    print(f"{_era}: {len(STATION_GAPS[_era])} gaps longer than 12 h with EVERY channel of the era "
          f"missing, {_lo:%Y-%m-%d} -> {_hi:%Y-%m-%d}")
    for _a, _b, _dd in sorted(STATION_GAPS[_era], key=lambda t: -t[2])[:8]:
        print(f"   {_a:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M} -> {_b:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M}   {_dd:7.1f} d")

    "the shared gaps this section explains are not in the data - re-read it before quoting it"

EXPLAINED, UNEXPLAINED = [], []
_CAUSE = (r"Sicherung|fuse|Strom|power|Batterie|battery|logger|doy|Waldboden|forest floor|"
          r"Datenausfall|kein[e]? Daten")
for _a, _b, _dd in LONG_EARLY:
    print(f"\n--- {_a:%Y-%m-%d} -> {_b:%Y-%m-%d}   {_dd:.0f} days, every early channel missing")
    _near = legacy_near(_a, _b, days=30, limit=0)
    _cause = _near[_near["text"].str.contains(_CAUSE, case=False, na=False, regex=True)]
    if len(_cause):
        EXPLAINED.append((_a, _b, _dd))
        for _, _r in _cause.head(4).iterrows():
            print(f"   legacy {_r['date']:%Y-%m-%d}: {_r['text'][:380]}")
    else:
        UNEXPLAINED.append((_a, _b, _dd))
        print("   (nothing in the legacy record within +/-30 days)")

print(f"\nexplained by the legacy record: {len(EXPLAINED)} of {len(LONG_EARLY)}")
print(f"still unexplained: {[(f'{a:%Y-%m-%d}', f'{b:%Y-%m-%d}', f'{d:.0f} d') for a, b, d in UNEXPLAINED] or 'none'}")
assert len(EXPLAINED) >= 2, (
    "the legacy record no longer explains any whole-station gap; either the parse or the search "
    "pattern broke, and the closing notes must not repeat the claim that it does")

# The one quantitative claim the fieldbook makes that the data can falsify, checked rather than
# quoted. Only doy ranges that are ABOUT the forest-floor logger: the legacy record uses
# day-of-year for other instruments too, and those are not claims about this station.
_doy = LEGACY[LEGACY["text"].str.contains(r"doy\s*\d+\s*(?:to|bis|-|–)\s*\d+", case=False, regex=True)
              & LEGACY["text"].str.contains(r"forest floor|Waldboden|logger", case=False, regex=True)]
assert len(_doy) > 0, "the doy remark about the forest-floor logger is not in the parsed record"
_confirmed = 0
for _, _r in _doy.iterrows():
    _m = re.search(r"doy\s*(\d+)\s*(?:to|bis|-|–)\s*(\d+)", _r["text"], flags=re.I)
    _y = _r["date"].year
    _from = pd.Timestamp(year=_y, month=1, day=1) + pd.Timedelta(days=int(_m.group(1)) - 1)
    _to = pd.Timestamp(year=_y, month=1, day=1) + pd.Timedelta(days=int(_m.group(2)) - 1)
    _match = [(a, b, d) for a, b, d in STATION_GAPS["early"]
              if abs((a - _from).days) <= 3 and abs((b - _to).days) <= 3]
    print(f"\nlegacy {_r['date']:%Y-%m-%d}: doy {_m.group(1)}-{_m.group(2)} of {_y} "
          f"= {_from:%Y-%m-%d} -> {_to:%Y-%m-%d}")
    print(f"   whole-station gap found in the data: "
          f"{[(f'{a:%Y-%m-%d}', f'{b:%Y-%m-%d}', f'{d:.0f} d') for a, b, d in _match] or 'NONE'}")
    _confirmed += bool(_match)
assert _confirmed > 0, "no fieldbook claim about missing forest-floor data lines up with a gap"
