# The correction of code 6, against Laegern on measured records. The reference is the normal CS215
# (code 0) of HV_CS215_YEARS, homogenised as exported; code 6 is taken as measured. Code 6 covers a
# full year, so the two are matched month by month: per calendar month and class (night, and the
# Laegern shortwave bins by day), code 6 pooled over its months, the reference as the mean of its
# yearly means, averaged over the months used.
# The months used are those in which every class holds at least C6_MIN_RECORDS records in code 6
# and in each reference year. In the remaining months the sun does not reach the upper radiation
# bins, so the comparison of the day cannot be made in them; the full-calendar night value is
# printed beside the one used.
HV_TOLERANCE = 0.15     # degC, largest difference left after a correction (also used in step 12)
C6_MIN_RECORDS = 20     # records per calendar month, class and year


def radiation_class(frame):
    """'night', or the Laegern shortwave bin by day ('day, 0-200 W m-2', ...), per record."""
    _cls = pd.Series('unbinned', index=frame.index, dtype=object)
    _cls[frame['night']] = 'night'
    _day = ~frame['night']
    _bins = pd.cut(frame.loc[_day, 'sw_reference'], MAY_SW_BINS)
    _cls[_day] = [f"day, {int(_b.left)}-{int(_b.right)} W m-2" if pd.notna(_b) else 'unbinned'
                  for _b in _bins]
    return _cls


C6_CLASSES = ['night'] + [f"day, {_lo}-{_hi} W m-2" for _lo, _hi in zip(MAY_SW_BINS[:-1], MAY_SW_BINS[1:])]

c6_compare = pd.DataFrame({
    'tower': evidence['TA_T1_47_1'],
    'reference': evidence[REFCOL],
    'sw': swin_gf[SWIN_COL].reindex(evidence.index),
    'sw_reference': evidence[REFCOL_SW],
    'source': source_flag.reindex(evidence.index),
}).dropna(subset=['tower', 'reference', 'sw'])
c6_compare['night'] = NIGHT.reindex(c6_compare.index).fillna(False).astype(bool)
c6_compare['sample'] = np.select(
    [(c6_compare['source'] == SOURCE_CS215) & c6_compare.index.year.isin(HV_CS215_YEARS),
     c6_compare['source'] == SOURCE_CS215_MAY2025], ['CS215', 'code 6'], default='')
c6_compare = c6_compare[c6_compare['sample'] != '']
c6_compare['class'] = radiation_class(c6_compare)
c6_compare['year'] = c6_compare.index.year
c6_compare['month'] = c6_compare.index.month
c6_compare['residual'] = c6_compare['tower'] - c6_compare['reference']
assert (c6_compare.loc[c6_compare['sample'] == 'CS215', 'source'] == SOURCE_CS215).all(), \
    "the reference sample holds a record that is not the normal CS215"


def c6_monthly(frame, column):
    """Per (month, class): the reference as the mean of its yearly means, code 6 pooled, and counts."""
    _ref = frame[frame['sample'] == 'CS215'].groupby(['month', 'year', 'class'])[column].agg(['mean', 'count'])
    _c6 = frame[frame['sample'] == 'code 6'].groupby(['month', 'class'])[column].agg(['mean', 'count'])
    return _ref, _c6


def c6_months(frame, classes=C6_CLASSES):
    """The calendar months in which every class is populated in code 6 and in each reference year."""
    _ref, _c6 = c6_monthly(frame, 'residual')
    _ok_ref = (_ref['count'].unstack('class').reindex(columns=classes).fillna(0) >= C6_MIN_RECORDS)
    _ok_ref = _ok_ref.all(axis=1).unstack('year').reindex(columns=HV_CS215_YEARS).fillna(False).all(axis=1)
    _ok_c6 = (_c6['count'].unstack('class').reindex(columns=classes).fillna(0) >= C6_MIN_RECORDS).all(axis=1)
    _months = sorted(set(_ok_ref[_ok_ref].index) & set(_ok_c6[_ok_c6].index))
    if len(_months) < 3:
        raise ValueError(f"{len(_months)} calendar months hold every class, need three to match seasons")
    return _months


def c6_profile(frame, column_ref, column_c6, months, classes=C6_CLASSES):
    """Month-matched mean per class over `months`: reference, code 6, and code 6 minus reference."""
    _f = frame[frame['month'].isin(months)]
    _ref = _f[_f['sample'] == 'CS215'].groupby(['month', 'year', 'class'])[column_ref].mean()
    _ref = _ref.groupby(['month', 'class']).mean().unstack('class').reindex(columns=classes)
    _c6 = _f[_f['sample'] == 'code 6'].groupby(['month', 'class'])[column_c6].mean()
    _c6 = _c6.unstack('class').reindex(columns=classes)
    if _ref.isna().any().any() or _c6.isna().any().any():
        raise ValueError("a class is empty in one of the months used")
    return pd.DataFrame({'normal CS215 (degC)': _ref.mean(), 'code 6 (degC)': _c6.mean(),
                         'code 6 minus normal CS215 (degC)': (_c6 - _ref).mean()})


def c6_terms(frame, months):
    """The night term of code 6 over `months`, with the year-to-year scatter of the reference."""
    _night = c6_profile(frame, 'residual', 'residual', months, classes=['night'])
    _ref = frame[(frame['sample'] == 'CS215') & frame['month'].isin(months) & frame['night']]
    _ref = _ref.groupby(['month', 'year'])['residual'].mean().unstack('year')
    _scatter = max(abs((_ref[_y] - _ref.drop(columns=_y).mean(axis=1)).mean()) for _y in _ref.columns)
    return dict(night=float(_night.loc['night', 'code 6 minus normal CS215 (degC)']),
                night_scatter=float(_scatter), months=list(months))


C6_MONTHS = c6_months(c6_compare)
C6_TERMS = c6_terms(c6_compare, C6_MONTHS)
_by_month = c6_compare[c6_compare['night']].groupby(['month', 'sample', 'year'])['residual'].mean()
_by_month = _by_month.unstack(['sample', 'year'])
_by_month = _by_month[sorted(_by_month.columns, key=lambda _c: (_c[0] != 'CS215', _c[1]))]
_by_month.columns = [f"{_s} {_y}" for _s, _y in _by_month.columns]
_c6_cols = [_c for _c in _by_month.columns if _c.startswith('code 6')]
_ref_cols = [_c for _c in _by_month.columns if _c.startswith('CS215')]
_c6_pooled = c6_compare[c6_compare['night'] & (c6_compare['sample'] == 'code 6')].groupby('month')['residual'].mean()
_by_month['code 6 minus normal CS215'] = _c6_pooled - _by_month[_ref_cols].mean(axis=1)
_by_month['used'] = _by_month.index.isin(C6_MONTHS)
tabcap("the night residual against Laegern per calendar month and year, for the normal CS215 of "
       f"{HV_CS215_YEARS[0]}-{HV_CS215_YEARS[-1]} and for code 6, with the month-matched difference and "
       "the months in which every class is populated (degC)")

      f"CS215 night level over the same months {C6_TERMS['night_scatter']:.3f} degC (largest departure of "

Limitations of the May 2025 terms

Code 7 is under-corrected in sun by the amount in the last table: it receives the shield term of the normal CS215 and nothing more. Daytime values and daily maxima from its onset to 16 May 2025 are biased warm. Filter on the source flag where this matters.
The onset of code 7 is dated by a rule on a statistic over a centred window of a month. The excess grows gradually, so records shortly before the onset may already carry part of it.
The night term of code 6 is small against its uncertainty, the year-to-year scatter printed with it, and rests on one reference 2.5 km away. It is applied because the change is established, not because the night difference is resolved.

1️⃣2️⃣ The June 2026 probe change
On 5 June 2026 a Campbell HygroVUE10 (SN E6730, SDI-12) replaced the CS215 at 47 m. The field name TA_T1_47_1 and its database tags did not change. The change is dated by three independent observations:

The raw record. The 1-minute TA_T1_47_1 has a gap from 11:10 to 11:31 (local time, TIMESTAMP_END) that day. The first HygroVUE10 half-hour is therefore the one ending 12:00 (HV_START), and the half-hour 11:00 to 11:30 is a partial or mixed record (SWAP_RECORD, removed in Corrections, source code 5).
The fieldbook. It adds the HygroVUE10 at CH-LAE_T1_47 on 5 June, and on 11 June changes its SDI-12 configuration ID together with the logger program. It has no entry for the removal of the CS215, which GIN never registered at that location. The cell below asserts both dates.
The data. The residual against MeteoSwiss Lägern changes level from that day, most in sun (tables below).

Reference level. The HygroVUE10 era is brought onto the level of the normal CS215, and the shield term of step 🔟 is then applied to it as to that era, so all eras end on the same reference. The measured column keeps the HygroVUE10 values as measured.
Method. NABEL ended in 2018, so Lägern is the only reference that spans the change, and the transfer is fitted against it on two season-matched samples: the HygroVUE10 from 12 June to 30 September 2026 (5 to 11 June, before the configuration change, are transitional and enter no fit), and the normal CS215 (code 0) on the same calendar dates of 2022 to 2024. 2025 is not used: the CS215 was heated until 16 May that year and changed state after it (step 1️⃣1️⃣).

Radiation term. The residual (tower minus Lägern) of each sample is fitted against tower SW_IN with shield_basis, the basis of the shield term. hv_excess is the difference of the two curves with its zero-radiation part removed, so it is zero in the dark, and the driver is clipped to the range both samples cover.
Night term. A constant equal to the night difference between the samples. The probe change is established (fieldbook, raw-data gap, radiation-dependent step), so the night level is corrected as well. The year-to-year scatter of the CS215 night level (largest departure of one CS215 year from the mean of the other two) is reported as its uncertainty.
Scoring. With no second reference to score against, each month of 2026 is left out in turn, the transfer is refitted on the rest, and the month is predicted.

def fit_hv_transfer(frame):
    """Least-squares fit of the tower-minus-Laegern residual in tower SW_IN, on shield_basis.

    Raises on a sample too small to fit or too dark to constrain the radiation curve: a fit on a
    few days returns coefficients as confidently as one on a summer.
    """
    _sunny = int((frame['sw'] > 500).sum())
    if len(frame) < HV_MIN_RECORDS or _sunny < HV_MIN_SUNNY:
        raise ValueError(f"{len(frame)} records ({_sunny} above 500 W m-2), need {HV_MIN_RECORDS} "
                         f"({HV_MIN_SUNNY}) to fit a radiation response")
    _beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(shield_basis(frame['sw']), frame['residual'].to_numpy(), rcond=None)
    return _beta


def hv_terms(frame):
    """The HygroVUE10 transfer from one comparison frame: both fits, the clip and the night term.

    The night term is the night difference between the samples, applied as a constant: the probe
    change is established, so its night level is corrected as well as its radiation response. The
    CS215 year-to-year scatter of the same quantity (the largest departure of one CS215 year's night
    mean from the mean of the other years) is returned as the uncertainty of that term. The CS215
    night level is the mean of its yearly night means, so each year weighs the same as in the
    scatter.
    """
    _hv, _cs = frame[frame['sample'] == 'HygroVUE10'], frame[frame['sample'] == 'CS215']
    _beta_hv, _beta_cs = fit_hv_transfer(_hv), fit_hv_transfer(_cs)
    _cs_night = _cs[_cs['night']].groupby('year')['residual'].mean()
    if len(_cs_night) < 3:
        raise ValueError(f"{len(_cs_night)} CS215 years at night, need three to measure their scatter")
    _diff = _hv.loc[_hv['night'], 'residual'].mean() - _cs_night.mean()
    _scatter = max(abs(_cs_night[_y] - _cs_night.drop(_y).mean()) for _y in _cs_night.index)
    return dict(beta_hv=_beta_hv, beta_cs=_beta_cs,
                sw_max=float(min(_hv['sw'].quantile(0.999), _cs['sw'].quantile(0.999))),
                night_difference=float(_diff), night_scatter=float(_scatter),
                night=float(_diff))

def hv_profile(frame, column='residual'):

# The fit above is scored on the records it was fitted to, so its residual is small by
# construction. The hold-out removes that: each month of the HygroVUE10 sample is left out in turn,
# from both samples, the transfer is refitted on the rest, and the held-out month is predicted.
# The statistic is the month's mean HygroVUE10-minus-CS215 difference, the CS215 side being the
# mean of its yearly means for that month.
# The tolerance is the same statistic among the CS215 years: how far one year's month departs from
# the mean of the other years in that month. A held-out error inside it is as small as the
# difference between two summers of one sensor.

_months = sorted(hv_compare.loc[_is_hv].index.month.unique())
_rows, _cs_scatter = [], []
for _m in _months:
    _train = hv_compare[hv_compare.index.month != _m]
    _test = hv_compare[hv_compare.index.month == _m]
    _terms = hv_terms(_train)
    _hv_test = _test[_test['sample'] == 'HygroVUE10']
    _cs_years = _test[_test['sample'] == 'CS215'].groupby('year')['residual'].mean()
    _predicted = (_hv_test['residual'] - hv_excess(_hv_test['sw'], terms=_terms) - _terms['night'])
    _rows.append({'month': _m, 'HygroVUE10 records': len(_hv_test),
                  'as measured (degC)': _hv_test['residual'].mean() - _cs_years.mean(),
                  'held out, corrected (degC)': _predicted.mean() - _cs_years.mean(),
                  'night term of the refit (degC)': _terms['night']})
    _cs_scatter += [abs(_cs_years[_y] - _cs_years.drop(_y).mean()) for _y in _cs_years.index]
hv_holdout = pd.DataFrame(_rows).set_index('month')
HV_HOLDOUT_TOLERANCE = max(_cs_scatter)

Limitations of the HygroVUE10 term

One summer. The transfer is fitted on 12 June to 30 September 2026 and applied, as fitted, to every HygroVUE10 record, including 5 to 11 June. Its behaviour in winter, under snow or rime and at low sun is untested.
One reference. Lägern is 2.5 km away and about 100 m higher, and both the fit and the score use it. The month hold-out tests whether the transfer carries to data it was not fitted on, not whether it agrees with an independent instrument.
The CS215 level is a mean of three summers that differ among themselves at night by an amount comparable to the night term itself, so the night term is uncertain by that amount (printed above). The hold-out table shows how much it changes when one month is left out.
The reference level is unchanged. Like the CS215 era, the HygroVUE10 era ends on the shield behaviour of the MP101A, so the limitations of step 🔟 apply to it as well.

What the correction does not fix
The first item is measured in steps 9️⃣ and 🔟 against MeteoSwiss, which entered neither term. The three-year window and, for the constant, the full eras give the same result.

The shield error the two sensors share remains. Both eras carry the MP101A’s own error and read warm in sun and light wind throughout the record. Daily maxima and diurnal ranges are biased warm in every year, by a comparable amount on both sides of 2016. The step that survives is the shield row of the step table in step 🔟. Removing the shared error would require the aspirated scale, rejected above.
The radiative term depends on a gap-filled driver (SW_IN_T1_47_1_gfXG). Refitting on measured radiation alone changes it by hundredths of a degree, because the driver is almost complete over the CS215 era.
The records reconstructed from NABEL carry too little scatter. As values on a fitted line, those 1,530 records sit about 0.05 °C from NABEL, where a real measurement sits about 0.25 °C from it. Their means are sound; variance, extremes and other spread statistics over the periods they cover are understated. Most fall in January 2004; the export section gives the breakdown by month.
2004 has no measurement before 20 September. 72 % of that year is modelled, and January is reconstructed from NABEL rather than gap-filled, because MeteoSwiss begins on 1 February 2004. It carries source code 3 and is the least constrained year.
The mechanism of the zero-point error is inferred. The class of error is established; whether the 11 mV came from the probe’s zero trim or from a ground offset in the cabling is not.
The heated CS215 (code 7) stays too warm in sun. It is corrected as the normal CS215 only; step 1️⃣1️⃣ measures what remains. The night term of the CS215 after May 2025 (code 6) is smaller than its uncertainty. Both are listed at the end of step 1️⃣1️⃣.
The HygroVUE10 term rests on one summer and one reference. Its limitations are listed at the end of step 1️⃣2️⃣.

title: Download and prepare TA (2004-2026.09)
text:
🟪 Prepare dataframes
Split into five periods, gap-filled separately. The four boundaries have different causes:

The sensor change on 21 January 2016. A model trained across this 1.3 °C discontinuity produces values on neither era’s level. The boundary is what makes the homogenisation valid for filled records.
The end of NABEL, a change of drivers, with the same instrument.
The CS215 change on 16 May 2025 (step 1️⃣1️⃣) and the probe change on 5 June 2026 (CS215 to HygroVUE10, step 1️⃣2️⃣), for the same reason as the first. The probe half-hour before each belongs to the period before it.

The onset of the excess heating (code 7, autumn 2024) is not a boundary: the excess grew over weeks, so there is no record at which a model could be split, and the few gaps of code 7 are filled by the model of P3.
The January 2016 outage belongs to the first period, so the offset region and P1 cover the same span. The measured column then steps only at the sensor changes, and the homogenised column is continuous across them. The first two cut-offs are taken from the data; the other two are settings, checked against the data and the fieldbook in steps 1️⃣1️⃣ and 1️⃣2️⃣.

📋 Table: the five gap-filling periods

# Last year in which NABEL delivers a usable amount of data.
_nabel_per_year = ta_2004_2026['TA_NABEL_T1_49_1'].groupby(ta_2004_2026.index.year).count()
print("NABEL records per year:")
print(_nabel_per_year.to_string())
NABEL_LAST_YEAR = int(_nabel_per_year[_nabel_per_year > 0].index.max())
print(f"\nNABEL is used as driver up to and including {NABEL_LAST_YEAR}.")

# The five periods. P1 ends on the last record before the sensor change, so it carries the
# January 2016 outage: those records are modelled, and filling them with the earlier model puts
# them on the earlier era's level, which is what the offset below then corrects. P3 ends on the
# probe handling record of 16 May 2025 and holds code 7 as well; P3b is the CS215 after the
# handling (code 6) and ends on the probe swap record; P4 is the HygroVUE10 era.
_nabel_end = ta_2004_2026.loc[:f"{NABEL_LAST_YEAR}-12-31 23:59"].index[-1]
PERIODS = {
    'P1': dict(start=ta_2004_2026.index[0], stop=BREAK - pd.Timedelta('30min'), use_nabel=True,
               label=f'MP101A era, NABEL available (to {(BREAK - pd.Timedelta("30min")):%d %b %Y})'),
    'P2': dict(start=BREAK, stop=_nabel_end, use_nabel=True,
               label=f'CS215 era, NABEL available (to {_nabel_end:%d %b %Y})'),
    'P3': dict(start=_nabel_end + pd.Timedelta('30min'), stop=HANDLING_RECORD, use_nabel=False,
               label=f'CS215 era, NABEL has stopped (to {HANDLING_RECORD:%d %b %Y})'),
    'P3b': dict(start=RESET_START, stop=SWAP_RECORD, use_nabel=False,
                label=f'CS215 after the May 2025 change (to {SWAP_RECORD:%d %b %Y})'),
    'P4': dict(start=HV_START, stop=ta_2004_2026.index[-1], use_nabel=False,
               label='HygroVUE10 era, NABEL has stopped'),
}

_summary = []
for _k, _p in PERIODS.items():
    _slice = ta_2004_2026.loc[_p['start']:_p['stop']]
    _summary.append({'period': _k, 'label': _p['label'],
                     'from': _p['start'], 'to': _p['stop'], 'records': len(_slice),
                     'measured': int(_slice['TA_T1_47_1'].notna().sum()),
                     'NABEL as driver': _p['use_nabel']})
tabcap("the five gap-filling periods, their boundaries and the measured share of each. No model spans a sensor change")
display(pd.DataFrame(_summary).set_index('period'))

# The periods must tile the record exactly once, and none may span the sensor change - that is the
# whole point of the split, and it is cheap to assert.
_covered = pd.concat([pd.Series(True, index=ta_2004_2026.loc[_p['start']:_p['stop']].index)
                      for _p in PERIODS.values()])
assert len(_covered) == len(ta_2004_2026), \
    f"the periods cover {len(_covered)} of {len(ta_2004_2026)} records"
assert not _covered.index.duplicated().any(), "the periods overlap"
assert _covered.index.equals(ta_2004_2026.index), "the periods do not tile the record in order"
for _k, _p in PERIODS.items():
    assert not (_p['start'] < BREAK < _p['stop']), \
        f"period {_k} spans the sensor change - a model trained on it would learn both eras"
    # Each period lies wholly on one side of each sensor change. This form also catches a period
    # whose first or last record is the change itself.
    for _change, _at in [('the 2016 sensor change', BREAK), ('the May 2025 CS215 change', RESET_START),
                         ('the 2026 probe change', HV_START)]:
        assert _p['stop'] < _at or _p['start'] >= _at, \
            f"period {_k} spans {_change} - a model trained on it would learn both sensors"
assert PERIODS['P3']['start'] <= HANDLING_RECORD <= PERIODS['P3']['stop'], \
    "the probe handling record is not in the CS215 period before the May 2025 change"
assert PERIODS['P3b']['start'] <= SWAP_RECORD <= PERIODS['P3b']['stop'], \
    "the probe swap record is not in the CS215 period before the probe change"
assert PERIODS['P3b']['start'] == RESET_START, "P3b does not start at the May 2025 change"
# Code 7 is not a boundary: it lies wholly inside P3, whose model fills its gaps.
assert PERIODS['P3']['start'] <= EXCESS_START and HANDLING_RECORD <= PERIODS['P3']['stop'], \
    "code 7 does not lie inside P3"
_c7_gaps = int(ta_2004_2026.loc[EXCESS_START:HANDLING_RECORD - pd.Timedelta('30min'), 'TA_T1_47_1'].isna().sum())
print(f"code 7 gaps, filled by the P3 model: {_c7_gaps}")
assert PERIODS['P4']['start'] == HV_START, "the HygroVUE10 period does not start at the probe change"
# The HygroVUE10 period is one summer. It is fitted on its own rather than merged with P3, so it
# must hold enough measured records for a model; fewer would have to be said, not merged away.
for _k in ('P3b', 'P4'):
    _measured = int(ta_2004_2026.loc[PERIODS[_k]['start']:PERIODS[_k]['stop'], 'TA_T1_47_1'].notna().sum())
    assert _measured > 2_000, f"period {_k} holds only {_measured} measured records"
print("\nOK: five periods, tiling the record exactly once, none spanning a sensor change.")

title: Download and prepare TA (2004-2026.09)
text:
🟥 Gap-filling

Method
SWINGapFillerXGBoost (notebook 01) is specific to radiation: it zeroes nighttime gaps and negative predictions, removes a nighttime offset and interpolates the clearness index. None of this is valid for temperature; it would write 0 °C into every nighttime and frost gap. This notebook uses the general XGBoostTS with an explicit FeatureEngineer (what SWINGapFillerXGBoost wraps internally) and otherwise follows 01: drivers plus timestamp features, SHAP-based feature reduction, and interpolation of short gaps.

features_lag=[]. The model predicts only records with every feature present, so lagging a gappy driver would send more records to the weaker timestamp-only fallback.
SW_IN_POT is excluded from the rolling and EMA stages. It follows from the timestamp, so smoothed versions add features without adding information.
shap_max_rows=10_000. SHAP is the slowest step, computed four times per call (train, reduce, retrain, fill). Mean importances converge well before the full record, so rows are capped as in SWINGapFillerXGBoost. Only the importances and the feature reduction use the sample, which is reproducible through random_state; predictions and scores do not.
Hyperparameters are set explicitly, to the values SWINGapFillerXGBoost uses, because XGBoostTS ships no tuned defaults.

Short gaps (up to 1 h) are then filled by linear interpolation and flagged 4. The target is excluded from its own features, so the model cannot see a gap’s measured neighbours. Temperature is continuous across midnight, so the interpolation is not restricted to single days.

SHAP_MAX_ROWS = 10_000  # rows used for SHAP importances, see the note above


def short_gap_mask(series: pd.Series, limit: int) -> pd.Series:
    """True where `series` is missing AND its whole gap is at most `limit` records long.

    Whole runs are selected explicitly. Using pandas' `interpolate(limit=)` instead would fill
    the first `limit` records of a long gap as well, which is not wanted: those values would sit
    on a straight line spanning the entire gap.
    """
    missing = series.isna()
    run_length = missing.groupby((~missing).cumsum()).transform('sum')
    return missing & (run_length <= limit)


def gapfill_ta(target: pd.Series,
               drivers: pd.DataFrame,
               interpolate_limit: int = 2,
               reduce_features: bool = True,
               verbose: int = 1):
    """Gap-fill a temperature series with XGBoost, then interpolate the remaining short gaps.

    Returns (model, gapfilled, flag). `gapfilled` carries the `_gfXG` name, `flag` follows
    FLAG_LEGEND.
    """
    input_df = pd.concat([target, drivers], axis=1)

    engineer = dv.gapfilling.FeatureEngineer(
        target_col=target.name,
        features_lag=[],  # see the note above
        features_rolling=[4, 8, 24, 48],  # 2h, 4h, 12h, 24h on 30MIN data
        features_rolling_stats=['median'],
        features_rolling_exclude_cols=['SW_IN_POT'],  # deterministic, see the note above
        features_ema=[6, 24],  # 3h, 12h
        features_ema_exclude_cols=['SW_IN_POT'],
        vectorize_timestamps=True,
        add_continuous_record_number=True,
        verbose=0,
    )
    features_df = engineer.fit_transform(input_df)
    print(f"Features: {features_df.shape[1] - 1} over {len(features_df):,} records")

    model = dv.gapfilling.XGBoostTS(
        input_df=features_df,
        target_col=target.name,
        verbose=verbose,
        shap_max_rows=SHAP_MAX_ROWS,
        n_estimators=3000,
        max_depth=6,
        early_stopping_rounds=20,
        random_state=42,
        n_jobs=-1,
    )
    model.trainmodel(showplot_scores=False, showplot_importance=False)
    if reduce_features:
        model.reduce_features()
        model.trainmodel(showplot_scores=False, showplot_importance=False)
    model.fillgaps(showplot_scores=False, showplot_importance=False)

    gapfilled = model.results.gapfilled.copy()
    flag = model.results.flag.copy()

    if interpolate_limit:
        short = short_gap_mask(target, interpolate_limit)
        interp = target.interpolate(method='time', limit_area='inside')
        fill_locs = short & interp.notna()
        gapfilled[fill_locs] = interp[fill_locs]
        flag[fill_locs] = 4
        print(f"Short-gap interpolation: {int(fill_locs.sum())} records")

    gapfilled = gapfilled.rename(f"{target.name}_gfXG")
    flag = flag.rename(f"FLAG_{target.name}_ISFILLED")
    return model, gapfilled, flag




🟥 Gap-filling, one model per period
Each period is fitted separately, so no model sees more than one sensor era. P1 and P2 use measured NABEL (TA_NABEL_T1_49_1, 49 m, same tower) with its gaps, MeteoSwiss Lägern (TA_LAE_MS), gap-filled SW_IN and SW_IN_POT. Lägern carries the signal where NABEL is missing. NABEL is no longer gap-filled from the tower first, which had let the tower partly predict itself. P3, P3b and P4 have no NABEL.

%%time

TARGET = "TA_T1_47_1"

# One fit per period. Keeping the fitted objects lets the scores, the feature importances and the
# heatmaps below be shown per period without refitting anything.
results = {}
for _key, _p in PERIODS.items():
    print(f"\n{'=' * 78}\n{_key}: {_p['label']}\n{'=' * 78}")
    _ta = ta_2004_2026.loc[_p['start']:_p['stop']].copy()
    _dr = drivers.loc[_p['start']:_p['stop']].copy()
    if _p['use_nabel']:
        # NABEL enters as measured (gappy); Laegern, already in drivers, covers its gaps.
        _dr = pd.concat([_ta[['TA_NABEL_T1_49_1']], _dr], axis=1)
    else:
        _ta = _ta.drop(columns='TA_NABEL_T1_49_1')
    _model, _gapfilled, _flag = gapfill_ta(target=_ta[TARGET], drivers=_dr)
    results[_key] = dict(model=_model, gapfilled=_gapfilled, flag=_flag, ta=_ta, **_p)

🩹 Records the gap-filler could only fill from the clock
XGBoost predicts only where every feature is present. Otherwise the record falls to the timestamp-only fallback (ISFILLED == 2), which follows the season but not the weather and writes one prediction per hour to both half-hours.
Most such records are in January 2004 (table below), before MeteoSwiss Lägern begins on 1 February 2004. NABEL, two metres above the target on the same tower, is complete that month. These records are therefore reconstructed from NABEL with a straight line (slope and offset) fitted on the measured records of the same sensor era, and re-coded ISFILLED == 5. Records where NABEL is missing as well keep code 2. The cell assigns values rather than adjusting them, so re-running it changes nothing.

📋 Table: tower-on-NABEL fit per sensor era

# Fallback records that NABEL can repair. The fit is per sensor era: the tower-to-NABEL
# relationship differs between the two by the offset this notebook exists to document.
_nabel = ta_2004_2026['TA_NABEL_T1_49_1'].reindex(export_df.index)
_fallback = export_df[FLAGCOL] == FILL_FALLBACK
_measured = export_df[FLAGCOL] == FILL_OBSERVED

_eras = {'MP101A': export_df.index < BREAK,
         'CS215': (export_df.index >= BREAK) & (export_df.index < RESET_START),
         'CS215 after May 2025': (export_df.index >= RESET_START) & (export_df.index < HV_START),
         'HygroVUE10': export_df.index >= HV_START}
_report = []
for _era_name, _era_mask in _eras.items():
    _fit = _measured & _era_mask & _nabel.notna()
    _fix = _fallback & _era_mask & _nabel.notna()
    if _fix.sum() == 0:
        _report.append({'era': _era_name, 'repairable': 0, 'slope': np.nan, 'intercept': np.nan,
                        'fitted on': int(_fit.sum())})
        continue
    assert _fit.sum() > 10_000, \
        f"{_era_name}: only {int(_fit.sum())} measured records with NABEL to fit on"
    _slope, _intercept = np.polyfit(_nabel[_fit].to_numpy(), export_df.loc[_fit, VALCOL].to_numpy(), 1)
    # A guard on the fit: the two sensors measure the same air, so the slope must be near one.
    assert 0.9 < _slope < 1.1, f"{_era_name}: tower-on-NABEL slope {_slope:.3f} is not near 1"
    # Assignment, not adjustment - re-running the cell reproduces the same values.
    export_df.loc[_fix, VALCOL] = _slope * _nabel[_fix] + _intercept
    export_df.loc[_fix, FLAGCOL] = FILL_FROM_NABEL
    _report.append({'era': _era_name, 'repairable': int(_fix.sum()), 'slope': _slope,
                    'intercept': _intercept, 'fitted on': int(_fit.sum())})
tabcap("the tower-on-NABEL fit used to reconstruct the timestamp-only fallback records, per sensor era, with the number repaired")
display(pd.DataFrame(_report).set_index('era').round(4))

# --- structural checks ------------------------------------------------------------------------
assert export_df[VALCOL].notna().all() and export_df[HOMOGCOL].notna().all(), \
    "a gap-filled column must not contain missing values"
assert export_df[FLAGCOL].isin(FLAG_LEGEND).all(), "unknown code in the fill flag"
assert export_df[SOURCECOL].isin(FLAG_SOURCE_LEGEND).all(), "unknown code in the source flag"
assert export_df.index[-1] == pd.Timestamp(PERIOD_END), (
    f"the export ends at {export_df.index[-1]}, not at PERIOD_END ({PERIOD_END})")

# --- the homogenisation is exactly what it claims to be ---------------------------------------
# Four eras by time: MP101A before the break, CS215 with the shield term from the break to the
# May 2025 change (codes 0 and 7 and the handling record), CS215 after it (code 6 and the swap
# record), HygroVUE10 after the probe change.
_delta = export_df[HOMOGCOL] - export_df[VALCOL]
_pre = export_df.index < BREAK
_post = (export_df.index >= BREAK) & (export_df.index < RESET_START)   # CS215 with the shield term
_c6 = (export_df.index >= RESET_START) & (export_df.index < HV_START)  # CS215 after May 2025
_hv = export_df.index >= HV_START                                      # the HygroVUE10 era
assert _pre.sum() + _post.sum() + _c6.sum() + _hv.sum() == len(export_df), \
    "the four eras do not cover the export"
assert np.allclose(_delta[_pre], OFFSET), \
    "the pre-break era was not shifted by exactly the derived offset"
assert np.allclose(_delta[_post], -radiative_excess(_sw_export[_post])), \
    "the CS215 era does not carry exactly the radiative excess derived in the break section"
# Code 7 is homogenised exactly as code 0, and code 6 by the night term alone: one constant, the
# same at night and by day, with no radiation dependence.
_c7 = (export_df[SOURCECOL] == SOURCE_CS215_HEATED).to_numpy()
assert _c7.sum() > 0 and np.allclose(_delta[_c7], -radiative_excess(_sw_export[_c7])), \
    "code 7 is not homogenised exactly as the normal CS215"
assert np.allclose(_delta[_c6], -C6_TERMS['night']), \
    "the CS215 after May 2025 does not carry exactly the night term of step 11"
_c6_night = _c6 & NIGHT.reindex(export_df.index).fillna(False).astype(bool).to_numpy()
assert _c6_night.sum() > 1_000 and np.allclose(_delta[_c6_night], -C6_TERMS['night']), \
    "a night record of the CS215 after May 2025 was not moved by exactly the night term"
_hv_term = hv_excess(_sw_export[_hv]) + HV_TERMS['night']
assert np.allclose(_delta[_hv], -radiative_excess(_sw_export[_hv]) - _hv_term), \
    "the HygroVUE10 era does not carry exactly its transfer of step 12 plus the radiative excess"
# The shield term acts in daylight only, so a CS215 record with no sun must be untouched. This is
# what keeps the night level of step 8 intact, and it is the first thing a wrong sign would break.
_dark = _post & (_sw_export <= 0)
assert _dark.sum() > 50_000, f"only {int(_dark.sum())} dark records in the CS215 era to check"
assert np.allclose(_delta[_dark], 0.0), \
    "a CS215 record with no incoming radiation was modified by the shield term"
# A HygroVUE10 record with no sun moves by the night term of step 12 only.
_hv_dark = _hv & (_sw_export <= 0)
assert _hv_dark.sum() > 1_000, f"only {int(_hv_dark.sum())} dark records in the HygroVUE10 era to check"
assert np.allclose(_delta[_hv_dark], -HV_TERMS['night']), \
    "a HygroVUE10 record with no incoming radiation was moved by more than the night term"
# The shield term can only ever cool, by a bounded amount: in the CS215 era it is the whole
# correction, in the HygroVUE10 era it is what remains after the transfer. The transfer itself
# warms in sun, because the HygroVUE10 reads cooler than the CS215 there.
assert (_delta[_post] <= 1e-9).all(), "the shield term warmed a record of the CS215 era"
assert _delta[_post].min() > -1.5, \
    f"the shield term removes up to {-_delta[_post].min():.2f} degC, far more than it was fitted to"
assert ((_delta[_hv] + _hv_term) <= 1e-9).all(), "the shield term warmed a record of the HygroVUE10 era"
assert _delta[_hv].abs().max() < 1.5, \
    f"the HygroVUE10 era moves by up to {_delta[_hv].abs().max():.2f} degC, far more than it was fitted to"
assert (export_df.loc[export_df.index < BREAK, SOURCECOL] != SOURCE_CS215).all(), \
    "a record before the break is flagged as the CS215 era"
_normal = _post & (export_df.index < EXCESS_START)
assert (export_df.loc[_normal, SOURCECOL] == SOURCE_CS215).all(), \
    "a record of the normal CS215 era is not flagged as code 0"
assert (export_df.loc[_post & ~_normal & (export_df.index != HANDLING_RECORD), SOURCECOL]
        == SOURCE_CS215_HEATED).all(), "a record of the heated CS215 is not flagged as code 7"
assert (export_df.loc[_c6 & (export_df.index != SWAP_RECORD), SOURCECOL] == SOURCE_CS215_MAY2025).all(), \
    "a record of the CS215 after May 2025 is not flagged as code 6"
assert (export_df.loc[_hv, SOURCECOL] == SOURCE_HYGROVUE).all(), \
    "a record after the probe change is not flagged as the HygroVUE10 era"
# The two probe half-hours: modelled, flagged as such, and homogenised with the period that
# modelled them - the handling record as the CS215 before it, the swap record as code 6.
assert (export_df[SOURCECOL] == SOURCE_SWAP).sum() == 2 and \
    (export_df.loc[[HANDLING_RECORD, SWAP_RECORD], SOURCECOL] == SOURCE_SWAP).all(), \
    "the probe half-hours are not the only records flagged as code 5"
assert (export_df.loc[[HANDLING_RECORD, SWAP_RECORD], FLAGCOL] != FILL_OBSERVED).all(), \
    "a probe half-hour is flagged as measured"
assert np.isclose(_delta[HANDLING_RECORD], -radiative_excess([_sw_export[HANDLING_RECORD]])[0]), \
    "the probe handling record is not homogenised as the CS215 before the change"
assert np.isclose(_delta[SWAP_RECORD], -C6_TERMS['night']), \
    "the probe swap record is not homogenised as the CS215 after May 2025"

# --- the break year is corrected like any other ------------------------------------------------
# The whole-record checks above would pass on a product that treated the break year specially,
# since that year is a fraction of a percent of the record, so it is checked on both sides of the
# changeover. Its first three weeks are the outage: modelled on the MP101A level, they carry the
# constant (source code 2 means era undetermined, not uncorrected). From the changeover on, the
# year is CS215 and carries the shield term.
_bk_before = (export_df.index.year == BREAK.year) & (export_df.index < BREAK)
_bk_after = (export_df.index.year == BREAK.year) & (export_df.index >= BREAK)
assert _bk_before.sum() > 0 and _bk_after.sum() > 0, \
    "the break year does not straddle the break, so it cannot be checked on both sides"
assert np.allclose(_delta[_bk_before], OFFSET), \
    "the part of the break year before the changeover did not receive the constant"
assert np.allclose(_delta[_bk_after], -radiative_excess(_sw_export[_bk_after])), \
    "the part of the break year after the changeover does not carry exactly the shield term"
assert (export_df.loc[_bk_before, SOURCECOL] == SOURCE_CHANGEOVER).all(), \
    "the break year before the changeover is not flagged as the changeover"
assert np.allclose(_delta[export_df[SOURCECOL] == SOURCE_CHANGEOVER], OFFSET), \
    "a changeover record did not receive the constant - the outage that contains the sensor swap " \
    "is modelled on the MP101A level and must be corrected onto the CS215 level like the rest of " \
    "that era"

# --- the correction removes the step it was derived to remove ---------------------------------
# Re-derived here from the exported column against NABEL, not carried over from the section above,
# so that a change anywhere between the two is caught.
_audit = pd.concat([export_df[HOMOGCOL], export_df[VALCOL],
                    ta_2004_2026['TA_NABEL_T1_49_1']], axis=1).dropna()
_audit = _audit[NIGHT.reindex(_audit.index).fillna(False)]
_before = _audit.loc[:LAST_BEFORE]
_after = _audit.loc[BREAK:'2018']
for _col, _label in [(VALCOL, 'measured   '), (HOMOGCOL, 'homogenised')]:
    _step = ((_after[_col] - _after['TA_NABEL_T1_49_1']).mean()
             - (_before[_col] - _before['TA_NABEL_T1_49_1']).mean())
    print(f"\nNight-time step against NABEL, {_label}: {_step:+.3f} degC")
    if _col == HOMOGCOL:
        assert abs(_step) < 0.15, (
            f"the homogenised column still steps by {_step:+.3f} degC at the break - the "
            f"correction did not do what it was derived to do")

Does the reconstruction method work? A month where the answer is known
The level and spread tests below cannot fail for the reconstructed records, because these were fitted to NABEL. The method is tested instead: the line is refitted without January and predicts the measured Januaries of the same era. The residual is a real error estimate, compared with the scatter between the two co-located sensors, the floor no reconstruction can beat.


📋 Table: January hold-out of the NABEL reconstruction

# Refit without January, predict the measured Januaries of the MP101A era.
_m = (export_df[FLAGCOL] == FILL_OBSERVED) & (export_df.index < BREAK) & _nabel.notna()
_jan = _m & (export_df.index.month == 1)
_rest = _m & (export_df.index.month != 1)
assert _jan.sum() > 5_000, f"only {int(_jan.sum())} measured January records to test on"

_s_ho, _i_ho = np.polyfit(_nabel[_rest].to_numpy(), export_df.loc[_rest, VALCOL].to_numpy(), 1)
_resid = export_df.loc[_jan, VALCOL] - (_s_ho * _nabel[_jan] + _i_ho)
_floor = (export_df.loc[_m, VALCOL] - _nabel[_m]).std()   # sensor-to-sensor scatter, all hours

print(f"fitted without January on {int(_rest.sum()):,} records: "
      f"slope {_s_ho:.4f}, intercept {_i_ho:+.4f}")
print(f"predicting {int(_jan.sum()):,} measured January records "
      f"({export_df.index[_jan].year.min()}-{export_df.index[_jan].year.max()}):")
print(f"  bias {_resid.mean():+.3f} degC | RMSE {np.sqrt((_resid ** 2).mean()):.3f} degC")
print(f"  scatter between the two sensors anyway (the floor): {_floor:.3f} degC")
tabcap("hold-out test of the NABEL reconstruction: a fit made without January predicts the measured Januaries, per year")
display(_resid.groupby(_resid.index.year).agg(records='count', bias='mean').round(3))

# The reconstruction line is fitted over all hours and applied to a whole month, so the daytime
# has to be checked as well: the two sensors' shields differ, and that difference is a daytime one.
for _when, _mask in [('night', NIGHT.reindex(_resid.index).fillna(False)),
                     ('day  ', ~NIGHT.reindex(_resid.index).fillna(False))]:
    _r = _resid[_mask]
    print(f"  {_when}: bias {_r.mean():+.3f} degC | RMSE {np.sqrt((_r ** 2).mean()):.3f} degC "
          f"(n={len(_r):,})")

assert abs(_resid.mean()) < 0.25, (
    f"reconstructing a January from NABEL is biased by {_resid.mean():+.3f} degC - the line fitted "
    f"on the rest of the year does not transfer to winter")
assert np.sqrt((_resid ** 2).mean()) < 2 * _floor, (
    f"reconstruction RMSE {np.sqrt((_resid ** 2).mean()):.3f} degC is more than twice the "
    f"{_floor:.3f} degC the two sensors differ by anyway")

Every modelled record sits on the era it belongs to, and varies like it
The offset is added to every pre-break record, which is valid only if modelled values share the measured era’s level. Two night-time tests against NABEL:
Level, per year and per fill method. A yearly average can hide opposite errors that cancel: an earlier version passed a per-year check while holding 11,150 records 1.1 °C too cold and 1,495 records 5.5 °C too warm.
Spread, the stronger test. A timestamp-only climatology can have the right mean, but it scatters against NABEL several degrees more widely than a measurement.
Neither test is evidence for the records reconstructed from NABEL. Fitted to NABEL, they match its level and scatter less than a measurement. They rest on the slope guard of the fit and on the held-out January test above.

# Night bias against NABEL for everything before the break, by year and fill method.

_chk['bias'] = _chk[VALCOL] - _chk['TA_NABEL_T1_49_1']
_chk['YEAR'] = _chk.index.year

_ref = _chk[_chk[FLAGCOL] == FILL_OBSERVED]['bias']
LEVEL, SPREAD = _ref.mean(), _ref.std()
print(f"measured MP101A era at night: level {LEVEL:+.3f} degC, spread (SD) {SPREAD:.3f} degC "
      f"(n={len(_ref):,})")

_tab = (_chk.groupby(['YEAR', FLAGCOL])['bias']
        .agg(records='count', level='mean', spread='std'))
_tab['level departure'] = (_tab['level'] - LEVEL).abs()
_tab['spread ratio'] = _tab['spread'] / SPREAD
_tab = _tab.rename(index=FLAG_LEGEND, level=1)
tabcap("night bias against NABEL before the break, by year and fill method. Each population is tested on its own")
display(_tab.round(2))

# Assert per (year, fill method) group that is large enough for its statistics to mean anything.
TOLERANCE, SPREAD_RATIO_MAX, MIN_NIGHTS = 0.5, 5.0, 100
_tested = []
for (_yr, _flag), _row in _tab.iterrows():
    if _row['records'] < MIN_NIGHTS or _flag == FLAG_LEGEND[FILL_OBSERVED]:
        continue
    _tested.append((_yr, _flag.split(' = ')[0]))
    assert _row['level departure'] < TOLERANCE, (
        f"{_yr}, fill method {_flag!r}: sits {_row['level departure']:.2f} degC from the measured "
        f"level of its era. The homogenisation offset is not valid for those records.")
    assert _row['spread ratio'] < SPREAD_RATIO_MAX, (
        f"{_yr}, fill method {_flag!r}: scatters {_row['spread ratio']:.1f}x more widely against "
        f"NABEL than the measurements do. Those values carry a season but not the weather.")
_first_year = int(_chk['YEAR'].min())
assert any(_y == _first_year for _y, _ in _tested), (
    f"{_first_year} was not tested: no modelled group reached {MIN_NIGHTS} night records. That is "
    f"the year with most of the record's fills, so a check that skips it is not checking the "
    f"thing it exists for.")
print(f"OK: {len(_tested)} (year, fill method) groups tested - {_tested}")

The same figures from the finished columns
The break section computes these figures from measured records only. A user following the note below computes them from the exported columns, which include the modelled share, and gets slightly different numbers, so both are shown. Measured-only values are free of the model but seasonally biased where a year’s gaps cluster; the complete columns are free of that bias but include the model. Their difference shows how much the gap-filling moves these statistics.


📋 Table: headline figures, measured only and from the export

_yp = export_df[[VALCOL, HOMOGCOL]].resample('YE').mean()
_yp.index = _yp.index.year
_yp = _yp.loc[2005:LAST_FULL_YEAR]  # 2026 is partial
_e, _r = _yp.index < BREAK.year, _yp.index > BREAK.year

_rows = []
for _col, _name in [(VALCOL, 'as measured'), (HOMOGCOL, 'homogenised')]:
    _s = _yp[_col]
    _slope, _, _lo, _hi = theilslopes(_s.to_numpy(float), _s.index.to_numpy(float), alpha=0.95)
    _tau, _p = kendalltau(_s.index.to_numpy(float), _s.to_numpy(float))
    _rows.append({'series': _name,
                  f'{_yp.index.min()}-{BREAK.year - 1} (degC)': _s[_e].mean(),
                  f'{BREAK.year + 1}-{_yp.index.max()} (degC)': _s[_r].mean(),
                  'difference (degC)': _s[_r].mean() - _s[_e].mean(),
                  'Theil-Sen (degC/decade)': _slope * 10,
                  'lower 95 %': _lo * 10, 'upper 95 %': _hi * 10,
                  'Kendall tau': _tau, 'p': _p})
headline_product = pd.DataFrame(_rows).set_index('series')

_both = pd.concat([headline_measured.assign(computed_from='measured records only'),
                   headline_product.assign(computed_from='the exported columns')])

           - headline_measured.loc['homogenised', 'difference (degC)'])
print(f"The two ways of computing the homogenised period difference disagree by {_gap:.3f} degC, "
      f"which is\nthe influence of the {100 * (export_df[FLAGCOL] > 0).mean():.1f} % of the "
      f"product that is modelled. Both are reported; neither is\nsuppressed.")
assert _gap < 0.5, (

title: Download and prepare TA (2004-2026.09)
text:
📘 Note for downstream users
Which column to use.

Within one sensor era: TA_T1_47_1_gfXG, the values the instrument reported.
Across 21 January 2016, 16 May 2025 or 5 June 2026 (period means, trends, rankings of years, anomalies against a multi-year reference): TA_T1_47_1_HOMOGENIZED_gfXG. The measured column steps by about 1.3 °C at the first date for instrumental reasons, more than the climate signal over this record; it reads too warm in sun from autumn 2024 to 16 May 2025 and without the usual shield excess after it; and its HygroVUE10 era reads cooler in sun than the CS215.
The homogenised column differs from the measured one in every era: by a constant before 2016; in the CS215 era (codes 0 and 7) by a radiation-dependent amount that is zero at night and largest in strong sun; in the CS215 after May 2025 (code 6) by the constant night term of step 1️⃣1️⃣; and in the HygroVUE10 era by the radiation-dependent amount and the HygroVUE10 transfer of step 1️⃣2️⃣, which raises it in sun, plus the constant night term of step 1️⃣2️⃣. The difference between the two columns is therefore not a constant.

Which flag to filter on.

FLAG_TA_T1_47_1_ISFILLED == 0 selects measured records; all others are modelled. Code 5 marks records reconstructed from NABEL on the same tower, code 2 the few filled from the clock only.
FLAG_TA_T1_47_1_SOURCE: 1 Rotronic MP101A era, 0 Campbell CS215 era, 7 the heated CS215 (autumn 2024 to 16 May 2025), 6 the CS215 after its change of 16 May 2025, 4 Campbell HygroVUE10 era from 5 June 2026, 2 the 988 records of the January 2016 outage (neither era), 3 the months before the tower record begins in September 2004, 5 the probe handling and probe swap half-hours. Codes 2, 3 and 5 are everything no instrument stands behind; drop them where provenance must be certain. Drop code 7 for daytime statistics (daily maxima, diurnal ranges): it stays too warm in sun after homogenisation.

Both value columns share both flags: the homogenisation changes values, not provenance.
Known limitations. The homogenised column puts the later era onto the earlier era’s radiation shield, so the shield error both sensors share remains: both read warm in sun and light wind relative to an aspirated measurement. Daily maxima and diurnal ranges are biased warm, by a comparable amount on both sides of 2016. The residual step is measured on every run in What the correction does not fix above. That section also details two limitations the homogenisation does not address: records reconstructed from NABEL carry too little scatter, so spread statistics over their periods are understated, and 2004 has no measurement before 20 September. Code 7 is under-corrected in sun, and the night term of code 6 is smaller than its uncertainty (step 1️⃣1️⃣). The HygroVUE10 transfer is fitted on one summer against one reference and applied as fitted to the whole HygroVUE10 era (step 1️⃣2️⃣). The record ends on 30 September 2026, so the 2026 annual mean covers January to September only.
The evidence is re-derived on every run in The 2016 acquisition break, including its steps 1️⃣1️⃣ and 1️⃣2️⃣ for the May 2025 change and the June 2026 probe change.

Verify the written file
Reading the parquet back and checking it directly, rather than trusting the in-memory frame.

📋 Table: yearly means and measured share, from the written file

_written = dv.load_parquet(filepath=str(Path(OUTPATH) / f"{OUTNAME}.parquet"))

print(f"columns:   {list(_written.columns)}")
print(f"index:     {_written.index[0]} -> {_written.index[-1]}  ({len(_written):,} records)")
print(f"measured:  {int((_written[FLAGCOL] == FILL_OBSERVED).sum()):,} "
      f"({100 * (_written[FLAGCOL] == FILL_OBSERVED).mean():.2f}%)")
for _c in (VALCOL, HOMOGCOL):
    print(f"{_c}: median {float(_written[_c].median()):.3f} degC, "
          f"min / max {float(_written[_c].min()):.2f} / {float(_written[_c].max()):.2f} degC")

assert list(_written.columns) == [VALCOL, FLAGCOL, HOMOGCOL, SOURCECOL], (
    "unexpected columns in the written file")
assert len(_written) == len(export_df), "record count changed on write"
assert _written.index.equals(export_df.index), "index changed on write"
# Both value columns are documented as complete, and the plausible range is checked here on the
# file itself rather than on the frame that was handed to the writer.
for _c in (VALCOL, HOMOGCOL):
    assert _written[_c].notna().all(), f"{_c} has gaps in the written file, but it is exported complete"
    assert -40 < float(_written[_c].min()) and float(_written[_c].max()) < 45, (
        f"{_c} is outside the plausible range for this site in the written file")
assert (set(_written[FLAGCOL].unique()) <= set(FLAG_LEGEND)), (
    "the written file carries a fill code that FLAG_LEGEND does not document")
assert (set(_written[SOURCECOL].unique()) <= set(FLAG_SOURCE_LEGEND)), (
    "the written file carries a source code that FLAG_SOURCE_LEGEND does not document")
# The homogenisation is the reason this product has a second value column, so the read-back reports
# what it did on each side of the break rather than only that the column arrived. The correction is
# two terms, so the later era takes a range of values rather than a single one.
_diff = _written[HOMOGCOL] - _written[VALCOL]
_before = _diff[_written.index < BREAK]
_after = _diff[(_written.index >= BREAK) & (_written.index < RESET_START)]
_c6_after = _diff[(_written.index >= RESET_START) & (_written.index < HV_START)]
_hv_after = _diff[_written.index >= HV_START]
print()
print(f"homogenised - measured: before the break {_before.min():+.4f} to {_before.max():+.4f} degC "
      f"({_before.round(4).nunique():,} distinct), CS215 era {_after.min():+.4f} to {_after.max():+.4f} "

title: MeteoScreening TS_FF1_0.6_1 (2020-2025) from database (influxdb)
text:
ℹ️ About this notebook
Download raw soil temperature from the InfluxDB database, remove the worst outliers on the high-resolution data, resample to 30MIN, and upload the result back to the database. Screening uses StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb from diive (diive/preprocessing/qaqc/meteoscreening.py); download and upload use diive’s in-house InfluxDB engine (InfluxIO, in diive/core/io/db/influx).
Flow: download (InfluxIO) → screen on high-res data (diive) → resample to 30MIN → upload.
Scope is deliberately narrow. The raw record is millions of rows, so anything done here is expensive. This notebook only takes out what is unambiguously wrong at high resolution — the April 2024 SDI-12 decode garbage (absolute limits) and the seven December 2025 logger-artefact minutes (manual removal) — and hands over a clean 30MIN series. Everything else (sensor comparisons, level/offset questions, gap handling, homogenisation across sensor generations) is settled later in 30_PRODUCTS/, on the half-hourly data, where it costs a fraction as much.
Outlier detection is stepwise: run a test, inspect its preview plot, then commit it with mscr.addflag(). Re-run with different parameters as often as you like before committing. Run only the tests a variable actually needs. At the end all committed flags are aggregated into one overall quality flag QCF.

Which sensor this is. In this profile the replicate suffix names the sensor family, not the depth: _1 = the water-potential sensors of the 19 Mar 2020 install (MPS-2 at 0.05/0.1/0.6 m, TEROS 21 at 0.2/0.3/0.5 m), _2 = the TEROS 12 probes that also report SWC_FF1_<depth>_1, _3/_4 = Campbell 109 thermistors added at the March 2021 logger rebuild. This one is a METER MPS-2 water-potential sensor, temperature channel.


Database access needs the influxdb-client package, which this project pulls in via the diive[db] extra (declared in pyproject.toml). diive also ships a db dependency group, but dependency groups are local to the project that declares them — uv sync --group db only works inside the diive repo, not from here.

title: MeteoScreening TS_FF1_0.6_1 (2020-2025) from database (influxdb)
text:
⏱️ Timestamp convention (important)
The database stores every timestamp in UTC and as TIMESTAMP_END (the stamp marks the end of the averaging interval). Getting this right is the one thing that must not go wrong: the value written back to the database depends on it, and so does every window in REMOVE_DATES.
The single knob is TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS (set in User settings). It is applied identically on download and on upload:









Stage
Timezone
Convention
Done by




Database
UTC
TIMESTAMP_END
InfluxDB


After dbc.download(..., timezone_offset_to_utc_hours=N)
local (UTC+N)
TIMESTAMP_END
InfluxIO


During screening
local
TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (converted internally)
StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb


After mscr.resample()
local
back to TIMESTAMP_END
diive


After dbc.upload_singlevar(..., timezone_offset_to_utc_hours=N)

TIMESTAMP_END
InfluxIO



One place where this bites. REMOVE_DATES is matched against TIMESTAMP_MID, not TIMESTAMP_END: StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb hands the series to ManualRemoval after the internal conversion, so the record whose TIMESTAMP_END is 10:39:00 carries the label 10:38:30 inside the test. A bare '2025-12-19 10:39:00' would therefore match nothing and the removal would silently do nothing. It only matters when removing individual records: a window spanning days has edges far larger than the half-record offset.

title: MeteoScreening TS_FF1_0.6_1 (2020-2025) from database (influxdb)
text:
✏️ User settings (please adjust)
Adjust these before running. What each setting means:
Site - SITE, SITE_LAT, SITE_LON: site ID and coordinates. The coordinates set the day/night split used during screening — not used here, see Outlier detection.
Variable to screen - PROFILE, DEPTH, REPL: the sensor’s position tags. FIELD is assembled from them and is the InfluxDB _field. REPL changes the sensor family, not just the probe. - MEASUREMENT: exactly one measurement grouping the variables — TS for soil temperature.
Time range to screen - START: first timestamp to screen — is included. - STOP: upper bound — is not included.
Data settings - TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS: the critical timestamp knob — see Timestamp convention. Must match how the raw data was logged (1 for CET winter time) and must be the same value everywhere. - DATA_VERSION: the source data version in the database (raw). - DIRCONF: local folder holding the database connection config.
Resampling - RESAMPLING_FREQ / RESAMPLING_AGG: soil temperature is a state, so 'mean' — never 'sum'.
Physical range - TS_MIN, TS_MAX: the absolute-limits test, justified from this sensor’s own measured extremes.
Parameter help - SHOW_PARAM_HELP: True prints the full docstring of each screening method right before it runs.

# --- Site ---
SITE = 'ch-lae'
SITE_LAT = 47.478333  # CH-LAE
SITE_LON = 8.364389  # CH-LAE

# --- Variable to screen ---
# (!) REPL, not DEPTH, is what names the sensor family in this profile:
#       _1  the water-potential sensors of the 19 Mar 2020 install - MPS-2 at 0.05/0.1/0.6 m,
#           TEROS 21 at 0.2/0.3/0.5 m. Six channels.
#       _2  METER TEROS 12, the same probes that report SWC_FF1_<depth>_1. Five channels.
#       _3/_4  Campbell 109 thermistors at 0.05 m, added at the March 2021 logger rebuild.
# This notebook screens: METER MPS-2 water-potential sensor, temperature channel.
PROFILE = 'FF1'  # horizontal position (soil profile)
DEPTH = '0.6'
REPL = '1'  # <-- the sensor family, see above
FIELD = f'TS_{PROFILE}_{DEPTH}_{REPL}'
FIELDS = [FIELD]  # StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb expects a list
MEASUREMENT = 'TS'

# --- Time range to screen ---
# Raw resolution is 10MIN until the March 2021 logger rebuild and 1MIN after, so this
# range is ~2.5 million records. The record starts 2020-04-10 15:00; asking for
# 2020-01-01 simply starts at the first record.
START = '2020-01-01 00:00:01'  # included
STOP = '2026-01-01 00:00:01'  # not included

# --- Data settings ---
DATA_VERSION = 'raw'
TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS = 1  # UTC+01:00 (CET, winter time). Must match how the raw data was logged.
DIRCONF = r'<LOCAL>\poet\configs'
# DIRCONF = r'P:\Flux\RDS_calculations\_scripts\_configs\configs'

# --- Resampling ---
RESAMPLING_FREQ = '30min'  # screened high-res data is resampled to this frequency
RESAMPLING_AGG = 'mean'  # (!) soil temperature is a state variable, never summed

# --- Physical range of soil temperature at this site, in degC ---
# This channel holds the WIDEST raw range in the whole profile: 0.00 to 307.56 degC over
# 2020-2025. Both ends are artefacts rather than soil - 0.00 is the failed-SDI-12-read sentinel
# and 307.56 degC is April 2024 decode garbage (the profile-wide total for that failure is 41
# records between 40.5 and 307.56 degC, and the top of that range is this channel's).
# So the limits test is a workhorse here, unlike on the TEROS 21 channels at 0.3 and 0.5 m
# where the raw maximum is a real soil temperature and this test flags nothing.
# At 0.6 m the soil is the most heavily buffered in the profile: roughly 5-16 degC over the
# year, daily amplitude about 0.10 K. The limits below cannot fire on a measurement.
TS_MIN, TS_MAX = -5, 30

# --- Parameter help ---
SHOW_PARAM_HELP = False

title: MeteoScreening TS_FF1_0.6_1 (2020-2025) from database (influxdb)
text:
🔍 Outlier detection
Run a test → inspect its preview → commit with mscr.addflag(). Only the committed flag of the most recent test is added. Skip any test a variable does not need.
What is committed here: the December 2025 logger-artefact minutes (manual removal), the April 2024 SDI-12 decode garbage (absolute limits), and the missing-values flag. Why the rest are off:

Never split day and night. Soil temperature does have a diurnal cycle, but at this depth it is damped and lagged relative to the surface, so a solar-geometry split does not line up with it — it would only halve the sample behind every threshold. Every test below runs with separate_daytime_nighttime=False.
Distribution-wide tests measure the season, not a fault. A z-score over the whole record asks how far a value sits from the multi-year mean; January at 2 °C and July at 19 °C are both correct.
Differencing-based tests are degenerate on this record. The 10MIN era (to March 2021) is back-filled onto the 1MIN grid by diive, so nine of every ten increments are zero by construction; the 1MIN era is quantised to exactly 0.05 °C and the soil moves a few tenths of a kelvin a day, so ~97 % of minute-to-minute increments are genuinely zero. The rolling MAD a Hampel filter scales its band by is then zero, and raising n_sigma cannot help.


mscr.start_outlier_detection()

  > Starting step-wise outlier detection for variable TS_FF1_0.6_1 ...



Plot the current cleaned data at any point during detection:

for key, val in mscr.outlier_detection.items():
    val.showplot_cleaned(interactive=False)









Manual removal
Flag specific timestamps or time ranges for removal - known sensor failures, maintenance windows, logger artefacts. Give [start, stop] pairs and/or single timestamps.
Why this variable needs one. On 18-19 December 2025 two remote logger-program uploads corrupted the SDI-12 scale: in seven individual minutes all eleven SDI-12 channels of the profile depart from their own local median at once, by exactly the same factor — 0.00 × on four minutes and 0.50 × on three — while the two analogue Campbell 109 thermistors on a different port read a steady 4.8-5.7 °C throughout. Eleven probes between 5 and 60 cm cannot go to zero, or halve, in the same minute for any physical reason. No automatic test reaches them: 0.00 °C and 3.10 °C are both plausible December soil temperatures at 0.6 m, so absolute limits cannot see them, and the differencing tests are degenerate here.

The windows are written as [T − 1 min, T], and that is deliberate — see Timestamp convention. ManualRemoval matches against TIMESTAMP_MID, so the closed interval ['2025-12-19 10:38:00', '2025-12-19 10:39:00'] selects exactly the one record whose TIMESTAMP_END is 10:39:00, and a bare timestamp would select nothing. Asserted below.


⚠️ These windows are a bus event, not a property of this probe. They are shared with every SDI-12 channel — which is why they appear identically in the _1 notebook. Verify them on the preview plot rather than trusting the copy: REMOVE_DATES belongs to a sensor.


if SHOW_PARAM_HELP:
    help(dv.outliers.ManualRemoval)


REMOVE_DATES = [
    ['2025-12-18 17:44:00', '2025-12-18 17:45:00'],  # reads 0.00 on all eleven SDI-12 channels
    ['2025-12-19 09:48:00', '2025-12-19 09:49:00'],  # reads exactly half the true value
    ['2025-12-19 09:50:00', '2025-12-19 09:51:00'],  # reads exactly half the true value
    ['2025-12-19 09:56:00', '2025-12-19 09:57:00'],  # reads 0.00 on all eleven SDI-12 channels
    ['2025-12-19 10:30:00', '2025-12-19 10:31:00'],  # reads 0.00 on all eleven SDI-12 channels
    ['2025-12-19 10:35:00', '2025-12-19 10:36:00'],  # reads exactly half the true value
    ['2025-12-19 10:38:00', '2025-12-19 10:39:00'],  # reads 0.00 on all eleven SDI-12 channels
    # (!) THIS CHANNEL HAS AN EIGHTH WINDOW THE OTHER TWELVE DO NOT.
    # 2024-04-05 01:23 is a 0.00 reading on THIS channel alone, during the April 2024 SDI-12
    # bus failure - the other ten SDI-12 channels read normally that minute. It is the fifth
    # of the five profile-wide 0.00 timestamps, and the only one that is not shared. Because
    # 0.00 degC sits inside [-5, 30], the absolute-limits test cannot reach it; only a named
    # removal can. Verify it on the preview plot below: unlike the seven shared windows, this
    # one rests on a single channel, so it is the one most worth looking at.
    ['2024-04-05 01:22:00', '2024-04-05 01:23:00'],  # reads 0.00 on this channel only
]

# A window that brackets no middle stamp removes nothing at all, silently - so check the shape.
for _w in REMOVE_DATES:
    _s, _e = pd.Timestamp(_w[0]), pd.Timestamp(_w[1])
    assert _e - _s == pd.Timedelta('1min'), (
        f'(!) window {_w} is not the one-minute bracket the TIMESTAMP_MID convention needs')

if REMOVE_DATES:
    mscr.flag_manualremoval_test(remove_dates=REMOVE_DATES, showplot=True, verbose=True)
else:
    print('No manual removal windows for this sensor - skip the addflag cell below.')

  > running ManualRemoval ...











if REMOVE_DATES:
    mscr.addflag()

  > ++Added flag column FLAG_TS_FF1_0.6_1_OUTLIER_MANUAL_TEST to flag data





Absolute limits
Flags values outside a fixed physical range [minval, maxval]. This is the workhorse test for this channel: the only artefact that is not the December 2025 logger trouble is the April 2024 SDI-12 decode garbage, and every one of those records lands far outside anything the soil can do — this channel’s raw maximum is 80.00 °C.

⬆️ Upload data to database
Re-uploading overwrites the same variant - safe to re-run. With delete_from_db_before_upload=True (below), the upload first deletes, then writes. The delete is scoped to the exact match _measurement + varname + data_version (meteoscreening_diive) over the uploaded time range, so re-screening a period replaces only its previous screened result. It never touches the raw data (different data_version, and a different _raw bucket), other variables, or other data versions. The delete-first step (rather than a plain overwrite) matters because InfluxDB keys a point by its full tag set: if a tag changed between runs (e.g. units, gain, offset), a plain write would leave the old point as a duplicate - the delete removes it regardless of tags.

📝 Notes for this variable

Mean, not sum. RESAMPLING_AGG = 'mean' - soil temperature is a state, not a flux.
Units are °C, filegroup 12_meteo_forestfloor.
Sensor identity, and the trap in it. The temperature channel of a METER MPS-2 water-potential sensor installed 19 Mar 2020 at 0.6 m, first logged 2020-04-10 15:00. The family jumps back here. _1 is an MPS-2 at 0.05, 0.1 and 0.6 m but a TEROS 21 at 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5 m — so this channel is the same make as TS_FF1_0.05_1, not as TS_FF1_0.5_1 directly above it. Anyone copying a notebook down the profile will name the wrong instrument here unless they check.
The only channel with no same-depth partner, because no TEROS 12 was installed at 0.6 m. That is also one of the four measurements establishing the _1/_2 mapping: _2 exists at five depths, _1 at six — five and six, matching the eleven SDI-12 devices installed on 19 Mar 2020. It has consequences downstream: every other depth can be checked against a different make of sensor in the same soil, and this one cannot. Its nearest references are the 0.5 m pair above it and its own seasonal signal.
Coverage 2 507 048 records, 99.12 % — the most complete channel in the profile, tied with TS_FF1_0.1_1. The five shared power and logger outages only; no fault of its own.
Raw range 0.00 … 307.56 °C — the widest anywhere in the profile. Both ends artefacts: 0.00 is the failed-read sentinel, 307.56 is April 2024 decode garbage. The limits test is a workhorse here.
An eighth removal window, unique to this channel. Besides the seven shared bus-artefact minutes of 18-19 Dec 2025, this channel alone reads 0.00 °C at 2024-04-05 01:23, inside the April 2024 bus failure, while the other ten SDI-12 channels read normally. It sits inside the physical limits, so only a named removal reaches it.
The diurnal diagnostics are dead at this depth, and reporting them anyway would be misleading. Median daily amplitude is 0.10 K — exactly two steps of the 0.05 °C quantiser. A rolling correlation of daily increments against anything measures rounding, not soil: on the channels at this depth it runs at a median of 0.41-0.58 with several hundred days below 0.5, spread evenly across every season rather than clustered on any fault. A future reader who takes that at face value would delete several hundred good days. Do not compute it here, and do not carry the 0.05 m version of the diagnostic down.
What still works is the seasonal signal. The annual wave at 0.6 m has an amplitude of several kelvin — two orders of magnitude above the quantiser — and lags the surface by weeks. Its amplitude and phase are the diagnostics that discriminate at this depth, and they belong in 30_PRODUCTS/ on the 30MIN data. The diurnal maximum, for the record, arrives around 4 a.m. here: a solar-geometry day/night split would be actively wrong, which is why screening never uses one.
Long runs of identical values are correct behaviour, not a stuck sensor. With a daily signal of two quantiser steps, this channel spends hours — sometimes days in winter — reporting one value. Over the whole record it can only ever produce about 220 distinct values (a 5-16 °C span at a 0.05 °C step). Never enable a flat-run or stuck-value test at this depth; it would fire on the entire winter.
Two raw time resolutions, 10MIN until the March 2021 logger rebuild and 1MIN after; diive upsamples the coarser era onto the finest grid before screening.
A failed sensor read is a number, not a gap — a failed SDI-12 read arrives as the true value times a wrong scale factor (0 × or 0.5 ×), so notna() does not mean “measured”, and neither does “inside the physical range”.
Deferred to 30_PRODUCTS/, on the 30MIN data: the comparison against the rest of the FF1 profile and against air temperature, the placement and offset questions, and any gap handling. This notebook exports gaps where the station was down and does not fill them.



♻️ Sibling notebooks
This is the thirteenth and last channel of the FF1 soil-temperature profile, so there is nothing further to copy this to. What it is worth reading for is the two ways it breaks the pattern the twelve above it establish:

The sensor family jumps back to MPS-2. Depth does not name the family; the replicate suffix does, and not monotonically. Never infer the instrument from the notebook directly above.
Its REMOVE_DATES has an eighth window nobody else has. The seven shared ones are a bus event; the eighth is this channel alone. That is the whole reason this folder insists a removal window belongs to a sensor rather than to a variable — copying the seven down from a sibling would have silently left this channel’s own artefact in the record.

With no same-depth partner, 30_PRODUCTS/ has to lean on the 0.5 m pair and on the seasonal signal to check it. Say so there rather than quietly reporting a cross-check that has no counterpart.
The standing rule for all of them: REMOVE_DATES belongs to a sensor, not to a variable. These notebooks are copies of each other with a few settings changed, and carrying a window across a copy deletes good data under a justification written about a different probe.

title: MeteoScreening TS_FF1_0.5_1 (2020-2025) from database (influxdb)
text:
ℹ️ About this notebook
Download raw soil temperature from the InfluxDB database, remove the worst outliers on the high-resolution data, resample to 30MIN, and upload the result back to the database. Screening uses StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb from diive (diive/preprocessing/qaqc/meteoscreening.py); download and upload use diive’s in-house InfluxDB engine (InfluxIO, in diive/core/io/db/influx).
Flow: download (InfluxIO) → screen on high-res data (diive) → resample to 30MIN → upload.
Scope is deliberately narrow. The raw record is millions of rows, so anything done here is expensive. This notebook only takes out what is unambiguously wrong at high resolution — the April 2024 SDI-12 decode garbage (absolute limits) and the seven December 2025 logger-artefact minutes (manual removal) — and hands over a clean 30MIN series. Everything else (sensor comparisons, level/offset questions, gap handling, homogenisation across sensor generations) is settled later in 30_PRODUCTS/, on the half-hourly data, where it costs a fraction as much.
Outlier detection is stepwise: run a test, inspect its preview plot, then commit it with mscr.addflag(). Re-run with different parameters as often as you like before committing. Run only the tests a variable actually needs. At the end all committed flags are aggregated into one overall quality flag QCF.

Which sensor this is. In this profile the replicate suffix names the sensor family, not the depth: _1 = the water-potential sensors of the 19 Mar 2020 install (MPS-2 at 0.05/0.1/0.6 m, TEROS 21 at 0.2/0.3/0.5 m), _2 = the TEROS 12 probes that also report SWC_FF1_<depth>_1, _3/_4 = Campbell 109 thermistors added at the March 2021 logger rebuild. This one is a METER TEROS 21 water-potential sensor, temperature channel.


Database access needs the influxdb-client package, which this project pulls in via the diive[db] extra (declared in pyproject.toml). diive also ships a db dependency group, but dependency groups are local to the project that declares them — uv sync --group db only works inside the diive repo, not from here.

title: MeteoScreening TS_FF1_0.5_1 (2020-2025) from database (influxdb)
text:
⏱️ Timestamp convention (important)
The database stores every timestamp in UTC and as TIMESTAMP_END (the stamp marks the end of the averaging interval). Getting this right is the one thing that must not go wrong: the value written back to the database depends on it, and so does every window in REMOVE_DATES.
The single knob is TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS (set in User settings). It is applied identically on download and on upload:









Stage
Timezone

One place where this bites. REMOVE_DATES is matched against TIMESTAMP_MID, not TIMESTAMP_END: StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb hands the series to ManualRemoval after the internal conversion, so the record whose TIMESTAMP_END is 10:39:00 carries the label 10:38:30 inside the test. A bare '2025-12-19 10:39:00' would therefore match nothing and the removal would silently do nothing. It only matters when removing individual records: a window spanning days has edges far larger than the half-record offset.

title: MeteoScreening TS_FF1_0.5_1 (2020-2025) from database (influxdb)
text:
✏️ User settings (please adjust)
Adjust these before running. What each setting means:
Site - SITE, SITE_LAT, SITE_LON: site ID and coordinates. The coordinates set the day/night split used during screening — not used here, see Outlier detection.
Variable to screen - PROFILE, DEPTH, REPL: the sensor’s position tags. FIELD is assembled from them and is the InfluxDB _field. REPL changes the sensor family, not just the probe. - MEASUREMENT: exactly one measurement grouping the variables — TS for soil temperature.
Time range to screen - START: first timestamp to screen — is included. - STOP: upper bound — is not included.
Data settings - TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS: the critical timestamp knob — see Timestamp convention. Must match how the raw data was logged (1 for CET winter time) and must be the same value everywhere. - DATA_VERSION: the source data version in the database (raw). - DIRCONF: local folder holding the database connection config.
Resampling - RESAMPLING_FREQ / RESAMPLING_AGG: soil temperature is a state, so 'mean' — never 'sum'.
Physical range - TS_MIN, TS_MAX: the absolute-limits test, justified from this sensor’s own measured extremes.
Parameter help - SHOW_PARAM_HELP: True prints the full docstring of each screening method right before it runs.

# --- Site ---
SITE = 'ch-lae'

#       _1  the water-potential sensors of the 19 Mar 2020 install - MPS-2 at 0.05/0.1/0.6 m,
#           TEROS 21 at 0.2/0.3/0.5 m. Six channels.
#       _2  METER TEROS 12, the same probes that report SWC_FF1_<depth>_1. Five channels.
#       _3/_4  Campbell 109 thermistors at 0.05 m, added at the March 2021 logger rebuild.
# This notebook screens: METER TEROS 21 water-potential sensor, temperature channel.

DEPTH = '0.5'
REPL = '1'  # <-- the sensor family, see above
FIELD = f'TS_{PROFILE}_{DEPTH}_{REPL}'

# --- Time range to screen ---
# Raw resolution is 10MIN until the March 2021 logger rebuild and 1MIN after, so this
# range is ~2.5 million records. The record starts 2020-04-10 15:00; asking for
# 2020-01-01 simply starts at the first record.
START = '2020-01-01 00:00:01'  # included
STOP = '2026-01-01 00:00:01'  # not included

# --- Resampling ---
RESAMPLING_FREQ = '30min'  # screened high-res data is resampled to this frequency
RESAMPLING_AGG = 'mean'  # (!) soil temperature is a state variable, never summed

# --- Physical range of soil temperature at this site, in degC ---
# (!) On THIS channel the limits test is a backstop that will almost certainly flag nothing.
# Measured over 2020-2025 the raw record spans 0.00 to 17.15 degC, and the upper end is NOT
# decode garbage - 17.15 degC is a real late-summer soil temperature at this depth. (Its
# same-depth partner TS_FF1_0.5_2 reaches 277.00 degC, which IS decode garbage; the April 2024
# bus failure did not corrupt every channel equally, so do not assume from one what the other
# holds.) The lower end, 0.00, is the failed-SDI-12-read sentinel and sits INSIDE the limits,
# so this test cannot catch it either - the manual removal below is what does.
# At 0.5 m the soil is heavily buffered: roughly 4-17 degC over the year, with a daily
# amplitude of about 0.10 K. The limits below cannot fire on a measurement.
TS_MIN, TS_MAX = -5, 30

# --- Parameter help ---
SHOW_PARAM_HELP = False
