title: MeteoScreening from database (influxdb)
text:
ℹ️ About this notebook
Download raw meteo data from the InfluxDB database, quality-screen and correct it on the high-resolution data, resample to 30MIN, and upload the result back to the database. Screening uses StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb from diive. Download and upload use diive’s InfluxDB engine (InfluxIO, in diive/core/io/db/influx), which needs uv sync --group db.
Flow: download (InfluxIO) → screen on high-res data (diive) → resample to 30MIN → upload.
Screening is stepwise. Run a test, look at its preview, then commit it with mscr.addflag(). Run only the methods your variable needs. At the end all committed flags are aggregated into one quality flag QCF.

title: MeteoScreening from database (influxdb)
text:
⏱️ Timestamp convention (important)
The database stores every timestamp in UTC and as TIMESTAMP_END. The stamp marks the end of the averaging interval. This has to be right, because the day/night split during screening and the value written back to the database both depend on it.
The single knob is TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS, set in User settings. It is applied the same way on download and on upload:









Stage
Timezone
Convention
Done by




Database
UTC
TIMESTAMP_END
InfluxDB


After dbc.download(..., timezone_offset_to_utc_hours=N)
local (UTC+N)
TIMESTAMP_END
InfluxIO


During screening
local
TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (converted internally)
StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb


After mscr.resample()
local
back to TIMESTAMP_END
diive


After dbc.upload_singlevar(..., timezone_offset_to_utc_hours=N)
UTC
TIMESTAMP_END
InfluxIO



So screening runs on local middle-of-period timestamps, and the resampled value lands on the correct UTC end-of-period stamp. Set TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS to the timezone the raw data was logged in (for example 1 for CET winter time). The notebook prints the timestamps after the download and after the check download so you can confirm them.
This also affects manual removal. Removal is matched against TIMESTAMP_MID, so a single timestamp matches no record and removes nothing. Write a single record as a range that brackets it.

title: MeteoScreening from database (influxdb)
text:
✏️ User settings (please adjust)
Adjust these before running. What each setting means:
Site - SITE, SITE_LAT, SITE_LON: site ID and coordinates. The coordinates set the day/night split used during screening.
Variables to screen - FIELDS: variable name(s) exactly as stored in the database (the InfluxDB _field). Several are allowed. - MEASUREMENT: exactly one measurement that groups those variables.
Time range to screen - START: first timestamp to screen. It is included. - STOP: upper bound. It is not included.
Data settings - TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS: the timestamp knob, see Timestamp convention. It must match how the raw data was logged. - DATA_VERSION: the source data version in the database (raw). - DIRCONF: local folder holding the database connection config.
Resampling - RESAMPLING_FREQ: the screened high-res data is resampled to this frequency. - RESAMPLING_AGG: 'mean' or 'sum'. Use 'sum' only for variables that accumulate over the interval.

# --- Site ---
SITE = 'ch-lae'
SITE_LAT = 47.478333
SITE_LON = 8.364389

# --- Variables to screen ---
FIELDS = [
    'LW_OUT_T1_47_1',
]
MEASUREMENT = 'LW'

# --- Time range to screen ---
START = '2020-01-01 00:00:01'  # included
STOP = '2026-01-01 00:00:01'  # not included

# --- Data settings ---
DATA_VERSION = 'raw'
TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS = 1  # UTC+01:00 (CET, winter time)
DIRCONF = r'<LOCAL>\poet\configs'  # <-- set to your config folder
# DIRCONF = r'P:\Flux\RDS_calculations\_scripts\_configs\configs'

# --- Resampling ---
RESAMPLING_FREQ = '30min'
RESAMPLING_AGG = 'mean'  # 'mean' or 'sum'

text:
🔍 Outlier detection
Each method has a test cell and an mscr.addflag() cell. Run the test as often as you like with different settings and look at the preview. Only mscr.addflag() commits the flag, and it commits the most recent test. Run only the methods your variable needs.
separate_day_night=True uses separate thresholds for day and night. The boundary comes from the site coordinates given above.

mscr.start_outlier_detection()

  > Starting step-wise outlier detection for variable LW_OUT_T1_47_1 ...



Plot the current cleaned data at any point during detection. interactive=True opens a Bokeh plot in the browser instead, with hover and zoom. showplot_orig() and showplot_cleaned() take the same argument.

mscr.showplot_outlier_detection_cleaned(interactive=False)









Manual removal
Removes given timestamps or time ranges. Use it for known sensor failures and maintenance periods. A single timestamp matches nothing, so write a range that brackets the record (see Timestamp convention). For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.ManualRemoval).

REMOVE_DATES = [
    '2021-12-14 13:34:30',
]
mscr.flag_manualremoval_test(remove_dates=REMOVE_DATES, showplot=True, verbose=True)

  > running ManualRemoval ...











mscr.addflag()

  > ++Added flag column FLAG_LW_OUT_T1_47_1_OUTLIER_MANUAL_TEST to flag data





Hampel filter
Spike detection in a sliding window, using the median absolute deviation. It is a good general-purpose filter and is not thrown off by spikes already inside the window. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.Hampel).

mscr.flag_outliers_hampel_test(
    window_length=60 * 24 * 7,  # records per window
    n_sigma_daytime=5.5, n_sigma_nighttime=5.5,
    use_differencing=True, separate_day_night=True,
    repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Z-score
Flags values further from the mean than thres_zscore standard deviations. It uses the whole record, so it responds to the seasonal cycle as well as to faults. Some variables have valid values below zero or above a nominal maximum, and those are handled in Corrections, so check the preview before committing. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.zScore).

mscr.flag_outliers_zscore_test(
    thres_zscore=4.5, separate_day_night=True,
    repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Z-score (rolling window)
The same test in a moving window of winsize records. It follows slow drifts and flags only local spikes. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.zScoreRolling).

mscr.flag_outliers_zscore_rolling_test(
    thres_zscore=4.5, winsize=1440 * 7,
    repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Local standard deviation
Flags values further than n_sd standard deviations from a rolling window of winsize records. constant_sd=True uses one standard deviation for the whole record instead of one per window. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.LocalSD).

# mscr.flag_outliers_localsd_test(
#     separate_day_night=True, n_sd=5.5, winsize=60 * 24 * 7,
#     constant_sd=False, repeat=False, showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


mscr.addflag()



Increments z-score
Flags jumps between consecutive records that are too large. It catches spikes and steps that tests on the value itself miss. Differences are computed after missing records are dropped, so the records on either side of a gap are compared across it. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.zScoreIncrements).

mscr.flag_outliers_increments_zcore_test(thres_zscore=40, repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True)


mscr.addflag()



Local outlier factor
Density-based detection using nearest neighbours. Flags points that sit apart from their neighbours. Slow on high-resolution data, so use it on 30MIN or coarser. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.LocalOutlierFactor).

mscr.flag_outliers_lof_test(
    n_neighbors=30, contamination=0.01, separate_day_night=False,
    repeat=False, n_jobs=-1, showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Absolute limits
Flags values outside the fixed range [minval, maxval]. For separate day and night ranges set minval_daytime, maxval_daytime, minval_nighttime or maxval_nighttime. Setting any of those turns the day/night split on. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.AbsoluteLimits).

mscr.flag_outliers_abslim_test(minval=-200, maxval=550, showplot=True, verbose=True)

  > running AbsoluteLimits ...











mscr.addflag()

  > ++Added flag column FLAG_LW_OUT_T1_47_1_OUTLIER_ABSLIM_TEST to flag data





Trim low
Flags values below lower_limit, then flags the same number of the highest values, so the trim is symmetric. trim_daytime and trim_nighttime choose which period is trimmed. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.TrimLow).

mscr.flag_outliers_trim_low_test(
    trim_daytime=False, trim_nighttime=True, lower_limit=10,
    showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Missing values
Not an outlier test. It flags missing records so they are counted in QCF. There is no addflag() here.

mscr.flag_missingvals_test(verbose=True)

calculated from variable LW_OUT_T1_47_1, with flag 0 (good values) where LW_OUT_T1_47_1 is

Aggregate all committed flags into one flag QCF (0 = good, 1 = marginal, 2 = bad) and filter the series. Run this before corrections and resampling.

⬆️ Upload data to database
Re-uploading overwrites the same variant, so it is safe to re-run. With delete_from_db_before_upload=True the upload first deletes, then writes. The delete matches _measurement plus varname plus data_version (meteoscreening_diive) over the uploaded time range, so re-screening a period replaces only its own previous result. It does not touch the raw data, other variables, or other data versions.
The delete matters because InfluxDB keys a point by its full tag set. If a tag changed between runs, a plain overwrite would leave the old point in place as a duplicate. The delete removes the old point regardless of its tags.

text:
Check downloaded data

dbc downloads three variables:

data_simple: This is the simplest data download. It contains only the high-resolution variable(s) from the specified measurement. Each variable is in a separate column. Since different variables, can have different time resolutions, the highest time resolution across the variables is used as the index. This means that lower resolution variables will show gaps in the higher resolution timestamp.
data_detailed: This is the most important variable for the MeteoScreening from the database, because it contains not only the high-resolution time series of the variable(s), but also their tags. The tags are important when uploading data to the database. This is a very special format, because data for each variable are stored in a dictionary. A dictionary is a data structure that stores key-value pairs. The key is the variable name (e.g., TA_NABEL_T1_35_1) and the value is a complete dataframe that contains the time series of the respective variable and all tags.
assigned_measurements: An auxiliary variable that is useful to check whether the measurement of the variable(s) is correct. In case we are screening air temperatures, the measurement must be TA.

title: LW_IN_T1_47_1_2025
text:
Check for potential timestamp shifts
Compare radiation time series to potential radiation

Can be used for <b>SW_IN, SW_OUT, PPFD_IN, PPFD_OUT.</b>

This analysis generates a plot that shows the radiation time series in comparison to potential radiation. - The first (top) panel shows daily correlations - The second panel shows potential radiation and measured radiation on low correlation days all in one plot - The third panel (with 3 plots) shows potential radiation and measured radiation on the three days when their correlation was the lowest - The fourth (bottom) panel (with 3 plots) shows potential radiation and measured radiation on the three days when their correlation was the highest

title: MeteoScreening from database (influxdb)
text:
ℹ️ About this notebook
Download raw meteo data from the InfluxDB database, quality-screen and correct it on the high-resolution data, resample to 30MIN, and upload the result back to the database. Screening uses StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb from diive. Download and upload use diive’s InfluxDB engine (InfluxIO, in diive/core/io/db/influx), which needs uv sync --group db.
Flow: download (InfluxIO) → screen on high-res data (diive) → resample to 30MIN → upload.
Screening is stepwise. Run a test, look at its preview, then commit it with mscr.addflag(). Run only the methods your variable needs. At the end all committed flags are aggregated into one quality flag QCF.

title: MeteoScreening from database (influxdb)
text:
⏱️ Timestamp convention (important)
The database stores every timestamp in UTC and as TIMESTAMP_END. The stamp marks the end of the averaging interval. This has to be right, because the day/night split during screening and the value written back to the database both depend on it.
The single knob is TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS, set in User settings. It is applied the same way on download and on upload:









Stage
Timezone
Convention
Done by




Database
UTC
TIMESTAMP_END
InfluxDB


After dbc.download(..., timezone_offset_to_utc_hours=N)
local (UTC+N)
TIMESTAMP_END
InfluxIO


During screening
local
TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (converted internally)
StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb


After mscr.resample()
local
back to TIMESTAMP_END
diive


After dbc.upload_singlevar(..., timezone_offset_to_utc_hours=N)
UTC
TIMESTAMP_END
InfluxIO



So screening runs on local middle-of-period timestamps, and the resampled value lands on the correct UTC end-of-period stamp. Set TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS to the timezone the raw data was logged in (for example 1 for CET winter time). The notebook prints the timestamps after the download and after the check download so you can confirm them.
This also affects manual removal. Removal is matched against TIMESTAMP_MID, so a single timestamp matches no record and removes nothing. Write a single record as a range that brackets it.

title: MeteoScreening from database (influxdb)
text:
✏️ User settings (please adjust)
Adjust these before running. What each setting means:
Site - SITE, SITE_LAT, SITE_LON: site ID and coordinates. The coordinates set the day/night split used during screening.
Variables to screen - FIELDS: variable name(s) exactly as stored in the database (the InfluxDB _field). Several are allowed. - MEASUREMENT: exactly one measurement that groups those variables.
Time range to screen - START: first timestamp to screen. It is included. - STOP: upper bound. It is not included.
Data settings - TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS: the timestamp knob, see Timestamp convention. It must match how the raw data was logged. - DATA_VERSION: the source data version in the database (raw). - DIRCONF: local folder holding the database connection config.
Resampling - RESAMPLING_FREQ: the screened high-res data is resampled to this frequency. - RESAMPLING_AGG: 'mean' or 'sum'. Use 'sum' only for variables that accumulate over the interval.

# --- Site ---
SITE = 'ch-lae'
SITE_LAT = 47.478333
SITE_LON = 8.364389

# --- Variables to screen ---
FIELDS = [
    'G_FF1_0.05_2',
]
MEASUREMENT = 'G'

# --- Time range to screen ---
START = '2021-01-01 00:00:01'  # included
STOP = '2026-01-01 00:00:01'  # not included

# --- Data settings ---
DATA_VERSION = 'raw'
TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS = 1  # UTC+01:00 (CET, winter time)
DIRCONF = r'<LOCAL>\poet\configs'  # <-- set to your config folder
# DIRCONF = r'P:\Flux\RDS_calculations\_scripts\_configs\configs'

# --- Resampling ---
RESAMPLING_FREQ = '30min'
RESAMPLING_AGG = 'mean'  # 'mean' or 'sum'

title: MeteoScreening from database (influxdb)
text:
🔍 Outlier detection
Each method has a test cell and an mscr.addflag() cell. Run the test as often as you like with different settings and look at the preview. Only mscr.addflag() commits the flag, and it commits the most recent test. Run only the methods your variable needs.
separate_day_night=True uses separate thresholds for day and night. The boundary comes from the site coordinates given above.

mscr.start_outlier_detection()

  > Starting step-wise outlier detection for variable G_FF1_0.05_2 ...



Plot the current cleaned data at any point during detection. interactive=True opens a Bokeh plot in the browser instead, with hover and zoom. showplot_orig() and showplot_cleaned() take the same argument.

mscr.showplot_outlier_detection_cleaned(interactive=True)


Manual removal
Removes given timestamps or time ranges. Use it for known sensor failures and maintenance periods. A single timestamp matches nothing, so write a range that brackets the record (see Timestamp convention). For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.ManualRemoval).

REMOVE_DATES = [
    ['2021-01-01 00:15:00', '2021-12-31 23:45:00'],
]
mscr.flag_manualremoval_test(remove_dates=REMOVE_DATES, showplot=True, verbose=True)


mscr.addflag()



Hampel filter
Spike detection in a sliding window, using the median absolute deviation. It is a good general-purpose filter and is not thrown off by spikes already inside the window. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.Hampel).

mscr.flag_outliers_hampel_test(
    window_length=60 * 24 * 7,  # records per window
    n_sigma_daytime=5.5, n_sigma_nighttime=5.5,
    use_differencing=True, separate_day_night=True,
    repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Z-score
Flags values further from the mean than thres_zscore standard deviations. It uses the whole record, so it responds to the seasonal cycle as well as to faults. Some variables have valid values below zero or above a nominal maximum, and those are handled in Corrections, so check the preview before committing. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.zScore).

mscr.flag_outliers_zscore_test(
    thres_zscore=4.5, separate_day_night=True,
    repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Z-score (rolling window)
The same test in a moving window of winsize records. It follows slow drifts and flags only local spikes. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.zScoreRolling).

# mscr.flag_outliers_zscore_rolling_test(
#     thres_zscore=4.5, winsize=60 * 24 * 7,
#     repeat=False, showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


mscr.addflag()



Local standard deviation
Flags values further than n_sd standard deviations from a rolling window of winsize records. constant_sd=True uses one standard deviation for the whole record instead of one per window. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.LocalSD).

mscr.flag_outliers_localsd_test(
    separate_day_night=True, n_sd=5.5, winsize=60 * 24 * 7,
    constant_sd=False, repeat=False, showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Increments z-score
Flags jumps between consecutive records that are too large. It catches spikes and steps that tests on the value itself miss. Differences are computed after missing records are dropped, so the records on either side of a gap are compared across it. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.zScoreIncrements).

mscr.flag_outliers_increments_zcore_test(thres_zscore=40, repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True)


mscr.addflag()



Local outlier factor
Density-based detection using nearest neighbours. Flags points that sit apart from their neighbours. Slow on high-resolution data, so use it on 30MIN or coarser. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.LocalOutlierFactor).

mscr.flag_outliers_lof_test(
    n_neighbors=30, contamination=0.01, separate_day_night=False,
    repeat=False, n_jobs=-1, showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Absolute limits
Flags values outside the fixed range [minval, maxval]. For separate day and night ranges set minval_daytime, maxval_daytime, minval_nighttime or maxval_nighttime. Setting any of those turns the day/night split on. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.AbsoluteLimits).

mscr.flag_outliers_abslim_test(minval=-25, maxval=999, showplot=True, verbose=True)

  > running AbsoluteLimits ...











mscr.addflag()

  > ++Added flag column FLAG_G_FF1_0.05_2_OUTLIER_ABSLIM_TEST to flag data





Trim low
Flags values below lower_limit, then flags the same number of the highest values, so the trim is symmetric. trim_daytime and trim_nighttime choose which period is trimmed. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.TrimLow).

mscr.flag_outliers_trim_low_test(
    trim_daytime=False, trim_nighttime=True, lower_limit=10,
    showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Missing values
Not an outlier test. It flags missing records so they are counted in QCF. There is no addflag() here.

mscr.flag_missingvals_test(verbose=True)

text:
🔧 Corrections
Applied to the high-res, QCF-filtered data. Run only what applies to your variable.
Every call below is commented out on purpose. Each one changes the data using example settings, so a top-to-bottom Run All would otherwise alter values that should not be touched. Edit the settings, then uncomment the call.

mscr.showplot_cleaned()


Remove radiation zero offset
For incoming and outgoing shortwave and PAR. Finds the nighttime offset per day, sets night to zero, and shifts daytime values by the interpolated offset.

# mscr.correction_remove_nighttime_zero_offset()



Remove relative humidity offset
Removes the offset so values do not exceed 100%.

# mscr.correction_remove_relativehumidity_offset()



Set to maximum or minimum threshold
Sets values above (or below) a threshold to the threshold itself. This replaces a bad value with a plausible one that nothing downstream can identify as false. Removing the value is usually better.

# mscr.correction_setto_max_threshold(threshold=30)
# mscr.correction_setto_min_threshold(threshold=-5)



Set a time range to a value
Sets all records in the given date ranges to one value.

DATES = [
    ['2022-04-01', '2022-04-05'],
]
# mscr.correction_setto_value(dates=DATES, value=3.7, verbose=1)
# mscr.showplot_cleaned(interactive=False)



Set exact values to missing

⬆️ Upload data to database
Re-uploading overwrites the same variant, so it is safe to re-run. With delete_from_db_before_upload=True the upload first deletes, then writes. The delete matches _measurement plus varname plus data_version (meteoscreening_diive) over the uploaded time range, so re-screening a period replaces only its own previous result. It does not touch the raw data, other variables, or other data versions.
The delete matters because InfluxDB keys a point by its full tag set. If a tag changed between runs, a plain overwrite would leave the old point in place as a duplicate. The delete removes the old point regardless of its tags.

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
ℹ️ About this notebook
Downloads raw meteo data from InfluxDB, screens and corrects them at high resolution, resamples them to RESAMPLING_FREQ and uploads the result to the database. Screening uses StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb. Download and upload use InfluxIO, which needs pip install "diive[all]".
Screening is stepwise. Run a test, check its preview, then commit it with mscr.addflag(). At the end, all committed flags are combined into one quality flag, QCF.
Run All applies no outlier test and no correction, because they are all commented out. It still resamples, and it uploads only with UPLOAD = True.

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
⏱️ Timestamp convention (important)
The database stores all timestamps in UTC as TIMESTAMP_END, the end of the averaging interval. TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS sets the local time frame of the notebook, e.g. 1 for UTC+01:00. START, STOP, typed dates, the day/night split and day boundaries all use this frame. The download converts from UTC to this frame, the upload converts back. With a sub-daily RESAMPLING_FREQ such as '30min' the stored values are therefore the same for any offset. With '1D' the day boundaries follow the offset, so the daily values depend on it.
The raw data in the database are already in UTC, whatever clock the logger used. Use one fixed offset for every month, e.g. 1 (CET) also in summer. Changing it shifts START, STOP and typed dates, which leaves a gap or an overlap between runs.

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
✏️ User settings (please adjust)
Adjust these before running.
Site - SITE, SITE_LAT, SITE_LON: site ID and coordinates. The coordinates set the day/night split.
Variables to screen - FIELDS: one or more variable names exactly as stored in the database (the InfluxDB _field). - MEASUREMENT: exactly one measurement that holds these variables.
Time range to screen - START, STOP: each one second after a RESAMPLING_FREQ boundary, e.g. '2026-03-01 00:00:01' and '2026-04-01 00:00:01' for March. Timestamps mark the END of each interval, so the record at 2026-03-01 00:00:00 belongs to February. These values cover the records ending after 2026-03-01 00:00 up to and including 2026-04-01 00:00. The upload deletes the same range before writing. Other values stop the notebook in Auto settings.
Data settings - TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS: local time frame of this run, one fixed offset without daylight saving time, see Timestamp convention. - DATA_VERSION: data version of the source data (raw). - DIRCONF: local folder with the database connection config.
Resampling - RESAMPLING_FREQ: target time resolution of the screened data. - RESAMPLING_AGG: 'mean' or 'sum'. Use 'sum' only for variables that accumulate over the interval.
Upload - UPLOAD: False runs everything except the upload. Set True only for the run that should write the result. The upload replaces the stored values between START and STOP.

# --- Site ---
SITE = 'ch-fru'
SITE_LAT = 47.115833
SITE_LON = 8.537778

# --- Variables to screen ---
FIELDS = [
    'RH_T1_2_1',
]
MEASUREMENT = 'RH'

# --- Time range to screen ---
# One second after a RESAMPLING_FREQ boundary, because stamps mark the END of each interval:
# these values cover the records ending after 2026-03-01 00:00 up to and including 2026-04-01 00:00.
START = '2026-01-01 00:00:01'
STOP = '2026-10-01 00:00:01'

# --- Data settings ---
DATA_VERSION = 'raw'
# Local time frame of this run. The database holds UTC. Use one fixed value for every month,
# e.g. 1 (CET) also in summer: changing it shifts START/STOP and typed dates.
TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS = 1  # UTC+01:00
DIRCONF = r'<LOCAL>\poet\configs'  # <-- must be set: folder with the database connection config
# DIRCONF = r'P:\Flux\RDS_calculations\_scripts\_configs'

# --- Resampling ---
RESAMPLING_FREQ = '30min'
RESAMPLING_AGG = 'mean'  # 'mean' or 'sum'

# --- Upload ---
UPLOAD = True  # True writes the result to the database, replacing stored values between START and STOP

🤖 Auto settings

Buckets and time range check (do not adjust)

import pandas as pd

BUCKET_RAW = f'{SITE}_raw'  # source bucket
BUCKET_PROCESSED = f'{SITE}_processed'  # destination bucket
print(f'Source bucket (raw data):       {BUCKET_RAW}')
print(f'Destination bucket (processed): {BUCKET_PROCESSED}')

# START and STOP must be one second after a RESAMPLING_FREQ boundary, see the user settings.
one_second = pd.Timedelta(seconds=1)
for name, value in (('START', START), ('STOP', STOP)):
    expected = pd.Timestamp(value).floor(RESAMPLING_FREQ) + one_second
    if pd.Timestamp(value) != expected:
        raise ValueError(f"{name} = '{value}' is not one second after a {RESAMPLING_FREQ} boundary. "
                         f"Stamps mark the END of each interval. Use e.g. '{expected}'.")
if pd.Timestamp(STOP) <= pd.Timestamp(START):
    raise ValueError(f"STOP ('{STOP}') must be after START ('{START}').")
print(f'Time range: records ending after {pd.Timestamp(START) - one_second} '
      f'up to and including {pd.Timestamp(STOP) - one_second}')

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
🔍 Outlier detection
Each method has a test cell and an mscr.addflag() cell. Rerun a test with other settings as often as needed: mscr.addflag() commits the latest run. Run only the methods your variable needs.
Day and night. With separate_day_night=True the statistic is computed separately for daytime and nighttime, split by the site coordinates. Some methods also take separate daytime and nighttime thresholds, see the docs.
Windows. Window sizes are time spans such as '7D' or record counts. A time span becomes a record count at the time resolution of the data, so one setting works for 1-minute and 10-minute data. The window counts the records present, so across gaps it covers more calendar days. Local SD with separate_day_night=True counts only daytime or only nighttime records, so its window covers even more days: at 47° N in January about 16-20 days for daytime and 10-13 days for nighttime with '7D'. Data that change resolution are tested per resolution period.
All tests are commented out, so Run All applies none. The example settings are only a starting point and can remove valid data. To use a test, check its settings and notes, uncomment the test and its mscr.addflag() cell, then check the preview.

mscr.start_outlier_detection()

  > Starting step-wise outlier detection for variable RH_T1_2_1 ...



Plot the cleaned data at any point. With interactive=True the plot opens in the browser (Bokeh, with hover and zoom). showplot_orig() and showplot_cleaned() take the same argument.

mscr.showplot_outlier_detection_cleaned()









Manual removal
Flags single timestamps or [start, end] ranges (both ends included), e.g. known sensor failures. Use timestamps as in the downloaded data: local time, end of the averaging interval. Docs: flag_manualremoval_test, ManualRemoval.

# REMOVE_DATES = [
#     # '2026-03-10 14:31:00',  # single record
#     # ['2026-03-12 08:00:00', '2026-03-12 11:30:00'],  # range, both ends included
# ]
# mscr.flag_manualremoval_test(remove_dates=REMOVE_DATES, showplot=True, verbose=True)


# mscr.addflag()



Hampel filter
Flags spikes far from the median of a sliding window, measured in median absolute deviations (MAD).
With use_differencing=True a single spike also removes both its neighbours at n_sigma 5.5. With repeat=True blocks of up to four bad values in a row are removed, also next to gaps and at the ends of the data. Of longer blocks only the outer values are removed. With separate_day_night=True daytime records are compared with the daytime records of the window, nighttime records with the nighttime ones. Records with up to 20 W m-2 potential radiation count as night, so twilight records are judged against the night statistics and can be removed. A sensor stuck at one value is not flagged, because the MAD is zero there. Use manual removal or Set exact values to missing for that. Docs: flag_outliers_hampel_test, Hampel.

# mscr.flag_outliers_hampel_test(
#     window_length='7D',  # converted to a record count, see above
#     n_sigma_daytime=5.5, n_sigma_nighttime=5.5,
#     use_differencing=True, separate_day_night=True,
#     repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


# mscr.addflag()



Z-score
Flags values more than thres_zscore standard deviations from the mean of the whole period.
Not for precipitation: most records are zero, so every rain record looks like an outlier. Not for radiation with separate_day_night=True: twilight records count as night and stand out against the zeros. Docs: flag_outliers_zscore_test, zScore.

# mscr.flag_outliers_zscore_test(
#     thres_zscore=4.5, separate_day_night=True,
#     repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


# mscr.addflag()



Z-score (rolling window)
Z-score in a moving window of length winsize: it follows slow changes and flags local spikes.
Not for precipitation, as for the z-score: rain records stand out against the zeros. Docs: flag_outliers_zscore_rolling_test, zScoreRolling.

# mscr.flag_outliers_zscore_rolling_test(
#     thres_zscore=3.5, winsize='13D',  # converted to a record count, see above
#     repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


# mscr.addflag()



Local standard deviation
Flags values more than n_sd standard deviations from the rolling median over winsize.
Not for precipitation: the rolling median is zero most of the time, so rain records are removed. Docs: flag_outliers_localsd_test, LocalSD.

# mscr.flag_outliers_localsd_test(
#     separate_day_night=True, n_sd=5.5, winsize='7D',  # record count, see above; day/night covers more days
#     constant_sd=False, repeat=False, showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


# mscr.addflag()



Increments z-score
Flags records with unusually large jumps to their neighbours, from the z-score of the differences between records. Records are not compared across gaps.
Jumps are judged against the typical jump of the whole period, so variables with sudden real changes (precipitation, radiation under broken clouds) can lose valid records. Check the preview. Docs: flag_outliers_increments_zcore_test, zScoreIncrements.

# mscr.flag_outliers_increments_zcore_test(thres_zscore=40, repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True)


# mscr.addflag()



Local outlier factor
Flags points that sit apart from their nearest neighbours. It always flags the contamination fraction of records, also in clean data, and is slow on high-res data.
Not for precipitation: rain records sit apart from the many zeros, so they are removed. Docs: flag_outliers_lof_test, LocalOutlierFactor.

# mscr.flag_outliers_lof_test(
#     n_neighbors=30, contamination=0.01, separate_day_night=False,
#     repeat=False, n_jobs=-1, showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


# mscr.addflag()



Absolute limits
Flags values outside [minval, maxval], optionally with separate daytime and nighttime limits. The example limits fit air temperature in °C only. Docs: flag_outliers_abslim_test, AbsoluteLimits.

mscr.flag_outliers_abslim_test(minval=20, maxval=999, showplot=True, verbose=True)









mscr.addflag()

  > ++Added flag column FLAG_RH_T1_2_1_OUTLIER_ABSLIM_TEST to flag data





Trim low
Flags values below lower_limit in the chosen period, plus the same number of the highest values. Set lower_limit for your variable and season: the example value 10 would remove most nighttime air temperatures of a cool month. Check the preview. Docs: flag_outliers_trim_low_test, TrimLow.

# mscr.flag_outliers_trim_low_test(
#     trim_daytime=False, trim_nighttime=True, lower_limit=10,
#     showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


# mscr.addflag()



Missing values
Not an outlier test. Flags missing records so that QCF counts them. Needs no addflag(). Docs: flag_missingvals_test.

mscr.flag_missingvals_test(verbose=True)

  > MISSING VALUES TEST: Generated new flag variable FLAG_RH_T1_2_1_MISSING_TEST, newly calculated 
from variable RH_T1_2_1, with flag 0 (good values) where RH_T1_2_1 is available, flag 2 (bad values)
where RH_T1_2_1 is missing.





Overall quality flag QCF
Combines all committed flags into QCF and filters the series. Here every test gives 0 (good) or 2 (bad), and finalize removes the records flagged 2. Run it before resampling: without it, resample() ignores the committed flags. It also works when no test was committed. Docs: finalize_outlier_detection.

mscr.finalize_outlier_detection()

  ! RH_T1_2_1: the most recent test (FLAG_RH_T1_2_1_OUTLIER_LOCALSD_TEST) was not added with 
addflag(), so the QCF does not use it.

text:
🔧 Corrections
Applied to the high-res data, filtered by QCF if outlier detection ran. Run only what applies to your variable.
All calls are commented out, because they change the data with example settings. Edit the settings, then uncomment the call.

mscr.showplot_cleaned()









Remove radiation zero offset
For shortwave radiation and PAR, which read below zero at night. The correction runs in this order: 1. Night: records with potential radiation below 0.001 W m-2. 2. Daily offset: the mean of the night values of each calendar day, i.e. the night before sunrise and the night after sunset of that date. All records of the day get this one value, there is no interpolation between days. Days without night values get the median offset of all days. 3. Subtract: the offset is subtracted from every record of the day, day and night. 4. Night to 0: night records are set to 0. 5. Clamp: values still below 0, e.g. daytime records at dawn and dusk, are set to 0. clamp_negatives=False keeps them.
The figure shows these steps with their counts, the daily offset, the diel cycle near zero after steps 3 and 5, the night values before and after subtracting the offset, and a summary. Docs: correction_remove_nighttime_zero_offset.

# mscr.correction_remove_nighttime_zero_offset()



Remove relative humidity offset
For relative humidity that reads above 100 %. The correction runs in this order: 1. Find > 100 %: the values above 100 %. 2. Daily offset: for each day with such values, their mean minus 100. All records of the day get this one value. 3. Other days: the offset is interpolated linearly, record by record, between the nearest days with values above 100 %, and carried before the first and after the last such day. Without any value above 100 % the offset is 0. 4. Subtract: the offset is subtracted from every record. 5. Cap at 100 %: values still above 100 % are set to 100 %.
A single day above 100 % lowers every record of the period, so the result depends on the period screened. The figure shows these steps with their counts, the offset, the values near 100 %, the daily maximum and a summary. A pile just below 100 % without values above it means the sensor or logger caps the readings, and the correction finds no offset. Docs: correction_remove_relativehumidity_offset.

mscr.correction_remove_relativehumidity_offset()










Set to maximum or minimum threshold
Sets values above or below a threshold to the threshold. The result looks plausible but was not measured, so removing the value is usually better. Docs: correction_setto_max_threshold, correction_setto_min_threshold.

text:
🔁 Resampling

Resample
Resamples the screened high-res series to RESAMPLING_FREQ, with TIMESTAMP_END timestamps ready for upload.
mincounts_perc sets how much of each target period the kept records must fill. Periods with less are missing. - 'mean': the share becomes a minimum number of records, rounded down. Below three, one record is enough, so 10-minute data resampled to 30 minutes need one record per half-hour. - 'sum': the kept records must cover that share of the period. For precipitation use 1 if partial sums are not wanted: a sum over a partly covered period is too low.
'mean' is an arithmetic mean and does not suit angles such as wind direction, which need a circular mean. This notebook does not compute one.
After changing the screened data, run this cell again, or the upload stops with an error. Docs: resample.

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
⬆️ Upload data to database
Existing screened data are overwritten. The upload writes to the processed bucket as data version meteoscreening_diive. With delete_from_db_before_upload=True it first deletes the stored values of each uploaded variable (same site, measurement, name and data version) between START and STOP, both included, then writes the new ones. Old values are removed also where the new data have no records, e.g. at the end of the period. Raw data, other variables and other data versions stay untouched.
The upload runs only with UPLOAD = True. It stops before deleting anything if: - SITE, MEASUREMENT, FIELDS, START, STOP or TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS differ from the values used for the download or the screening (mscr), e.g. after a new download without a new screening. The stored values would be shifted, or a neighbouring period deleted. Run the notebook again from Download. - a variable was resampled to a resolution other than RESAMPLING_FREQ, e.g. after an extra resample() call. Run Resample again.

upload_attempted = False  # read by the verify cells
if not UPLOAD:
    print('UPLOAD = False: nothing was uploaded. Set UPLOAD = True in the user settings to write the data.')
else:
    # Refuse before anything is deleted if the settings changed after the download or the screening:
    # a changed offset stores shifted values, a changed START or STOP deletes a neighbouring period,
    # and a download run again without a new screening would upload the old screening in its range.
    now = dict(site=SITE, measurement=MEASUREMENT, fields=list(FIELDS), start=START, stop=STOP,
               offset=TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS)
    used = {'download': DOWNLOAD_SETTINGS, 'screening': SCREENED_SETTINGS,
            'screening object': dict(site=mscr.site, fields=list(mscr.fields), offset=mscr.utc_offset),
            'resampled data': dict(fields=list(mscr.resampled_detailed.keys()))}

    def as_compared(k, v):
        return pd.Timestamp(v) if k in ('start', 'stop') else sorted(v) if k == 'fields' else v

    changed = {f'{k} ({name})': (s[k], now[k]) for name, s in used.items() for k in s
               if as_compared(k, s[k]) != as_compared(k, now[k])}
    if changed:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f'Nothing uploaded. Settings differ (used, now): {changed}. '
            f'Run the notebook again from the download.')
    # Refuse before anything is deleted: the stored values between START and STOP would be
    # replaced by data at another resolution. Compared as durations, so '24h' equals '1D'.
    target = pd.Timedelta(to_offset(RESAMPLING_FREQ).nanos, unit='ns')
    wrong_freq = {v: mscr.tags[v]['freq'] for v in mscr.resampled_detailed.keys()
                  if pd.Timedelta(to_offset(mscr.tags[v]['freq']).nanos, unit='ns') != target}
    if wrong_freq:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f'Nothing uploaded. Resampled to a resolution other than RESAMPLING_FREQ '
            f'({RESAMPLING_FREQ!r}): {wrong_freq}. Run the Resample cell again with RESAMPLING_FREQ.')
    print(f'Uploading to bucket {BUCKET_PROCESSED}')
    upload_attempted = True  # set before the writes, so the verify cells also report a failed write
    for v in mscr.resampled_detailed.keys():
        dbc.upload_singlevar(
            to_bucket=BUCKET_PROCESSED,
            to_measurement=assigned_measurements[v],
            var_df=mscr.resampled_detailed[v],
            timezone_offset_to_utc_hours=TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS,
            delete_from_db_before_upload=True,
            delete_start=START,
            delete_stop=STOP,
        )

title: MeteoSwiss reference precipitation — Ehrendingen (OED), 2004-2025
text:
ℹ️ About this notebook
Downloads precipitation from the MeteoSwiss open-data STAC API for station Ehrendingen (OED) and writes two reference products for comparison against the tower gauge PREC_TOT_T1_47_1.
This notebook does not touch the InfluxDB database and screens nothing. It only fetches an independent reference series and puts it on our time axis.
Why OED and not LAE. The Lägern SMN station (lae) is the obvious candidate — it is on the same ridge and its 10-min files go back to Feb 2004 — but it does not measure precipitation at all: rre150z0 is empty in every 10-min record and rre150d0 is empty across all 13,190 daily records from 1989 to 2025. OED, 3.8 km NNW of the tower, is the nearest MeteoSwiss gauge.
Why two resolutions. OED’s sub-daily data only begins 09 Sep 2014. Before that only daily values exist (they run back to 1975). So the reference is necessarily:








Period
Resolution
Source file




2004-01-01 → 2014-09-09
daily
ogd-smn-precip_oed_d_historical.csv


2014-09-10 → 2025-12-31
30MIN (aggregated from 10-min)
ogd-smn-precip_oed_t_historical_*.csv



The two are spliced at a MeteoSwiss precip-day boundary so they neither overlap nor leave a gap.

title: MeteoSwiss reference precipitation — Ehrendingen (OED), 2004-2025
text:
⏱️ Timestamp convention (important)
MeteoSwiss publishes all reference timestamps in UTC. Two separate conventions apply, and mixing them up silently shifts the reference against our data:
10-min values — reference_timestamp marks the end of the 10-minute interval, so a record at t covers (t-10min, t]. This matches our database’s TIMESTAMP_END, so the 30MIN product is simply shifted by TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS into local time and carries TIMESTAMP_END.
Daily values — the MeteoSwiss precipitation day runs 06 UTC → 06 UTC, and the value labelled day D covers [D 06:00 UTC, D+1 06:00 UTC). This is not a local-midnight day, so the daily product is left on its native MeteoSwiss day and not shifted. Do not compare it against a local-midnight daily sum of our tower data without re-aggregating ours the same way.
Both conventions were verified empirically rather than taken on trust — see Validation below.

text:
⏲️ 30MIN product (handover → 2025)
The decade files are concatenated, put on a gapless 10-min grid (missing records are absent rows in the source, not NaN rows — without the reindex they would vanish instead of being counted), then summed to 30MIN.
Binning: with end-labelled stamps the 30MIN period ending at T holds the records T-20, T-10, T — which is exactly closed='right', label='right'. min_count=3 makes any half-hour with a missing record NaN rather than a silent under-sum.

hires_files = sorted(k for k in assets if '_t_historical_' in k)
print(f'Concatenating: {hires_files}')
hires = pd.concat([read_ms_csv(assets[k], PARAM_HIRES) for k in hires_files]).sort_index()
hires = hires[~hires.index.duplicated(keep='first')]
print(f'10MIN raw: {len(hires)} records, {hires.index[0]} -> {hires.index[-1]} (UTC)')

hires = hires.reindex(pd.date_range(hires.index[0], hires.index[-1], freq='10min'))
print(f'On gapless grid: {len(hires)} records, {hires.isna().sum()} missing '
      f'({hires.isna().mean() * 100:.2f}%)')

closed/label are easy to get subtly wrong and the result still looks plausible. Assert that one hand-checked half-hour really is the sum of the three expected 10-min records.

      f'{[s.strftime("%H:%M") for s in _expected_stamps]} '

🔗 Splice the two products
The daily day D covers [D 06:00 UTC, D+1 06:00 UTC), so handing over at the first such boundary at or after the first complete 30MIN period gives a seam with no gap and no overlap.

first_complete = prec30.index[prec30['N_RECORDS'] == 3][0]
handover = first_complete.normalize() + pd.Timedelta(hours=MS_DAY_START_UTC)
if handover < first_complete:
    handover += pd.Timedelta(days=1)
last_daily_day = handover.normalize() - pd.Timedelta(days=1)

daily_out = daily_all[(daily_all.index >= START) & (daily_all.index <= last_daily_day)].copy()
hires_out = prec30[(prec30.index > handover) & (prec30.index < STOP)].copy()

print(f'First complete {TARGET_FREQ} period: {first_complete} UTC')
print(f'Handover boundary:              {handover} UTC\n')
print(f'DAILY : {daily_out.index[0].date()} -> {daily_out.index[-1].date()}  '
      f'({len(daily_out)} days, {daily_out.isna().sum()} NaN, {daily_out.sum():.1f} mm)')
print(f'30MIN : {hires_out.index[0]} -> {hires_out.index[-1]}  '
      f'({len(hires_out)} periods, {hires_out["PREC_OED_MS"].isna().sum()} NaN, '
      f'{hires_out["PREC_OED_MS"].sum():.1f} mm)')

Handover boundary:              2014-09-10 06:00:00 UTC

30MIN : 2014-09-10 06:30:00 -> 2025-12-31 23:30:00  (198275 periods, 262 NaN, 10598.7 mm)



Sanity checks

# 30MIN axis is continuous, unique and at the expected resolution.
assert hires_out.index.is_monotonic_increasing, '(!) index not sorted'
assert not hires_out.index.has_duplicates, '(!) duplicate timestamps'
assert pd.infer_freq(hires_out.index) == TARGET_FREQ, f'(!) not {TARGET_FREQ}'
# Precipitation is non-negative and finite.
assert (hires_out['PREC_OED_MS'].dropna() >= 0).all(), '(!) negative precipitation'
assert (daily_out.dropna() >= 0).all(), '(!) negative daily precipitation'
# The seam must not double-count or skip.
assert last_daily_day + pd.Timedelta(days=1) + pd.Timedelta(hours=MS_DAY_START_UTC) == handover
print('PASSED - continuous index, no duplicates, non-negative, seam is exact')

text:
✅ Validation
Re-aggregate the derived 30MIN series back to the MeteoSwiss precipitation day and compare against the published daily file. This is what pins down both timestamp conventions: it only lines up if the 10-min stamps are end-labelled and the daily window starts at 06 UTC.
Only gap-free days are compared — a day containing a NaN half-hour would under-sum and muddy the comparison.

_back = hires_out['PREC_OED_MS'].shift(freq=f'-{MS_DAY_START_UTC}h').resample('D').sum()
_ok = (hires_out['N_RECORDS'] == 3).shift(freq=f'-{MS_DAY_START_UTC}h').resample('D').sum()
cmp = pd.DataFrame({'daily_file': daily_all.reindex(_back.index),
                    'from_30min': _back,
                    'complete': _ok == 48}).dropna(subset=['daily_file']).iloc[1:-1]
cmp = cmp[cmp['complete']]
_d = (cmp['from_30min'] - cmp['daily_file']).abs()

print(f'Gap-free days compared: {len(cmp)}')
print(f'  correlation      : {cmp[["daily_file", "from_30min"]].corr().iloc[0, 1]:.5f}')
print(f'  mean |difference|: {_d.mean():.4f} mm')
print(f'  max  |difference|: {_d.max():.2f} mm')
print(f'  totals           : {cmp["from_30min"].sum():.1f} mm (derived) vs '
      f'{cmp["daily_file"].sum():.1f} mm (published) '
      f'-> {(cmp["from_30min"].sum() / cmp["daily_file"].sum() - 1) * 100:+.3f}%')
assert cmp[['daily_file', 'from_30min']].corr().iloc[0, 1] > 0.99, '(!) FAILED - conventions disagree'
print('PASSED - timestamp conventions confirmed')

The derived and published values agree in total but not day by day: dry days match almost always, wet days only ~50-80% of the time, with differences of a few hundredths of a mm (rarely up to ~3 mm). This comes from the 0.1 mm resolution of the published 10-min values accumulating over 48 half-hours. Treat the published daily file as authoritative for daily totals and the 30MIN series as a derived product for sub-daily timing.

text:
💾 Export

outdir = Path(OUTDIR)outdir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)# Years come from the UTC axis (set before the local shift), so the 30MIN file is# labelled by the data it holds, not by where the +1h shift lands the last stamp.daily_export = daily_out.to_frame('PREC_OED_MS_DAILY')exports = {f'{OUTNAME_DAILY}_{DAILY_YEARS}': daily_export,           f'{OUTNAME_HIRES}_{HIRES_YEARS}': hires_out}written = {}for stem, frame in exports.items():    for fmt in EXPORT_FORMATS:        path = outdir / f'{stem}.{fmt}'        if fmt == 'parquet':            frame.to_parquet(path)        elif fmt == 'csv':            # index=True keeps the timestamp; NaN stays empty so a gap cannot be            # mistaken for a dry (0 mm) record when the csv is read back elsewhere.            frame.to_csv(path, index=True, na_rep='')        else:            raise ValueError(f'unsupported export format: {fmt}')        written[(stem, fmt)] = path        print(f'Wrote {path.name:<45s} ({path.stat().st_size / 1024:>7.0f} KB)')print(f'\n  in {outdir}')d_path = written[(f'{OUTNAME_DAILY}_{DAILY_YEARS}', 'parquet')]h_path = written[(f'{OUTNAME_HIRES}_{HIRES_YEARS}', 'parquet')]


Read the written files back

d_back = pd.read_parquet(d_path)h_back = pd.read_parquet(h_path)assert len(d_back) == len(daily_out) and len(h_back) == len(hires_out), '(!) row count changed'assert abs(d_back['PREC_OED_MS_DAILY'].sum() - daily_out.sum()) < 1e-6, '(!) daily total changed'assert abs(h_back['PREC_OED_MS'].sum() - hires_out['PREC_OED_MS'].sum()) < 1e-6, '(!) 30MIN total changed'print('PASSED - parquet reads back identical')# The csv round-trip is the fragile one: timestamps become strings and empty fields# could come back as 0.0 instead of NaN, which would turn gaps into dry records.for (stem, fmt), path in written.items():    if fmt != 'csv':        continue    back = pd.read_csv(path, index_col=0, parse_dates=True)    ref = exports[stem]    col = back.columns[0]    assert len(back) == len(ref), f'(!) {path.name}: row count changed'    assert back.index.equals(ref.index), f'(!) {path.name}: index changed'    assert back[col].isna().sum() == ref[ref.columns[0]].isna().sum(), \        f'(!) {path.name}: NaN count changed - gaps may have become zeros'    assert abs(back[col].sum() - ref[ref.columns[0]].sum()) < 1e-6, f'(!) {path.name}: total changed'    print(f'PASSED - {path.name} round-trips identical '          f'({len(back)} rows, {back[col].isna().sum()} NaN preserved)')print(f'\nDAILY {d_back.index[0].date()} -> {d_back.index[-1].date()}, {d_back["PREC_OED_MS_DAILY"].sum():.1f} mm')print(f'30MIN {h_back.index[0]} -> {h_back.index[-1]}, {h_back["PREC_OED_MS"].sum():.1f} mm')h_back.tail()




📝 Notes for downstream users

Source: MeteoSwiss. Cite it in anything derived from these files.
Two different time axes. 30MIN is local TIMESTAMP_END (UTC+1) and lines up directly with our database series. DAILY is on the MeteoSwiss precipitation day (06 UTC → 06 UTC) and is not shifted — re-aggregate our tower data the same way before comparing, or the comparison is off by six hours.
This is a different location. OED is 3.8 km NNW of the tower and at a different elevation. Convective summer rain in particular will not agree half-hour by half-hour; use the reference for totals, timing and gross faults (a blocked funnel, a dead gauge), not as ground truth.
FLAG_INCOMPLETE / N_RECORDS. A 30MIN sum is only written when all three 10-min records are present; otherwise it is NaN with FLAG_INCOMPLETE = 1. Do not fill those with 0 — a missing record is not a dry record.
No sub-daily data before 09 Sep 2014. The daily product is the only reference available for 2004-2014; nothing can recover 30MIN there from this station.
Not a gap-filling source. These files are for comparison only. Nothing here is written back to the database.

title: Meteo Product Chain
text:
How the thirteen meteo product notebooks (10_METEO/30_PRODUCTS) turn screened measurements into the finished variables, and which of them depend on each other.
The numbering is a run order: a notebook reads only products with a lower number, so running 01 to 13 and then the merge 99 satisfies every dependency. Five of those reads change an exported value. 02 and 03 use 01’s gap-filled SW_IN as a gap-filling driver, 04 uses 02’s measured and homogenised TA for its homogenised RH, and 07 computes VPD from the measured and the homogenised columns of 02 and 04. All other reads are diagnostic: 06 reads 01 and 02; 08 reads 02, 05 and 06; 09 reads 02 and 08; 10 reads 02 and 09; 11 reads 09 and 10; 12 reads 01; 13 reads 02 and 06. A diagnostic read changes what a notebook concludes, not what it writes.
01 to 07 and 99 run to 30 September 2026. 08 to 13 still end on 31 December 2025.

Figure 1: Inputs, notebooks and products of stage 10_METEO/30_PRODUCTS. Solid arrows are reads that change the exported values; dashed arrows are diagnostic-only reads.







Blue products are gap-filled or reference-filled (SW_IN, TA, PPFD_IN, PREC, TS), green products ship as measured (RH, PA, LW_IN, SWC, G, SW_OUT, LW_OUT), and the orange product is computed from other products (VPD).

Two notebooks do not read the database. 07 reads two finished product files and applies a formula. 10 reads the screened TS channels through TS_FF1_SCREENED_30MIN_2004-2025, which downloads the 34 channels once. 09 reads the early half of that download as its witness for the June 2015 wiring break.
01 feeds the gap-filling of 02 and 03. Its gap-filled SW_IN_T1_47_1_gfXG is a driver in both models, so 01 must run first. It is also the diagnostic partner of 06 and 12, which describe the other channels of the same radiometer.
02 is read by seven notebooks, more than any other product, and two of those reads change a value: 04 and 07. Air temperature separates rain from snow in 08, excludes snowmelt in 09, and gives the Stefan-Boltzmann reference emission in 06 and 13. Diagnostic reads across January 2016 use the HOMOGENIZED column, because the measured one carries the step of that date. 07 reads both columns and computes a VPD from each.
08 (PREC) reads three reference files, for two purposes. The Ehrendingen (OED) record is daily to September 2014 and 30MIN after; the 30MIN part fills the gaps. The regional ensemble supplies the homogenisation factors: one nearby gauge can show that the tower changed in 2018, but only a dozen of them can show which side of that break is wrong. 09 reads the same ensemble so that its jump detector does not read a gap in the tower gauge as a dry spell.
05 reads the MeteoSwiss pressure as a diagnostic only. It checks the tower record but never writes a value into it. The NABEL hut barometer is also read as a diagnostic and is not exported.
Six products have no external reference, and a second channel takes its place. No weather service measures this plot’s soil, and no station near the site measures the radiation this canopy emits and reflects. 09 (SWC), 10 (TS) and 11 (G) are checked against the other depths and plates of their own profile. 06 (LW_IN) and 13 (LW_OUT) are checked against the Stefan-Boltzmann emission at 02’s air temperature, and 13 also against 06, the other pyrgeometer of the same instrument. 12 (SW_OUT) is checked against 01: SW_OUT / SW_IN is the surface albedo, and anything that scales both channels of one radiometer cancels in that ratio. These checks catch a whole-record error such as a wrong file, unit or year, but cannot validate a single measurement.




Notebook 99 joins the value and flag columns of all thirteen products into one half-hourly table, 99_METEO_MERGED_2004-2026.09, and checks the joined index. It holds 61 columns: 31 data series and 30 flag columns. Products 08 to 13 end on 31 December 2025, so their columns are NaN from January to September 2026 until their notebooks are extended.

TA, RH, VPD and PREC each contribute two value columns, the measured and the homogenised series, and two flags.
09 contributes five soil-moisture depths and the homogenised series of four of them.
10 and 11 contribute only their reconciled series: seven soil-temperature depths and the soil heat flux plate mean. The 18 soil-temperature channels and the three plates are one sensor each and stay in their product files.
12 contributes SW_OUT with two flags, one naming the instrument and one the screening.

Eight of the 31 series are complete over the whole period. For every series that may contain NaN, the merge records the reason and checks it; the reasons are listed in the information file 99_METEO_MERGED_2004-2026.09_INFO.md written beside the data.
Precipitation aggregates differently from the other variables: rainfall is summed, not averaged. Each entry in the merge registry names its aggregation. A daily mean of 30-minute rainfall (about 0.05 mm) is not an interpretable quantity; the daily total is.

title: Soil temperature at the forest floor
text:
Half-hourly soil temperature at seven depths of the FF1 profile at CH-LAE, 2004-2025. The file is 10_METEO_TS_FF1_2004-2025 (parquet and CSV): 373,728 records on a continuous 30-minute index, TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (middle of the half-hour), in local time (UTC+01:00, no daylight saving), from 2004-09-07 00:15 to 2025-12-31 23:45. Values are in °C. The index begins in September 2004 because the soil record begins then.
The series ends on 31 December 2025. It is part of FP2026.1 and of the merged meteo product, where it is NaN from 1 January 2026; the extension to 30 September 2026 is in progress. Both carry the seven overall columns and their flags, not the eighteen individual channels.
The interactive dashboards summarise one depth each (coverage, provenance, seasonality, distributions, extremes and trends). They are standalone files and work offline: 0.05 / 0.1 / 0.15 / 0.2 / 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.6 m. Each covers only the whole years its depth measured, so 0.15 m ends in 2020 and 0.2 m and 0.6 m begin in 2021.
Notebooks:

10_METEO_TS_FF1: builds the product. It reconciles the channels, splices the sensor generations, fills the gaps and tests the record for breaks.
TS_FF1_SCREENED_30MIN: downloads the screened channels the product is built from.
TS_FF1_GAPFILL_ML_COMPARISON: the comparison that chose the gap-filling method.
The thirteen screening notebooks of the current profile, one per channel, under 10_METEO/20_SCREENING/TS/ in the notebook index.
Meteo_Data_SWC: soil water content of the same profile. Its June 2015 break is attributed using this variable.
Meteo_Product_Chain: where this product sits in the chain.







ImportantWhich column to use



The file holds two kinds of column.

TS_FF1_<d>_HOMOGENIZED_GAPFILLED is the column to analyse: one reconciled, gap-filled series per depth, with the sensor-generation step removed where it could be measured.
The eighteen individual channels (TS_FF1_0.05_2, TS_PRF_FF1_0.05_1, …) are the screened measurements, one sensor each, with gaps where that sensor was down. Use them when you need the record of a single instrument.

Filter on FLAG_..._METHOD before analysis. At 0.3 m and 0.5 m about 47 % of the overall column is modelled, because those depths had no sensor between March 2010 and April 2020.
Do not compute a diurnal or seasonal amplitude across April 2020. The levels are reconciled, the amplitudes are not: they differ by a factor of three at 0.05 m.




Thirty-five columns: eighteen individual channels, seven overall columns, seven METHOD flags and three SUSPECT flags. <d> is one of 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.6.

The spans differ because the sensors did: 0.15 m exists only in the early profile, 0.2 m and 0.6 m only from 2020, and the other depths span the whole record.
Where one depth has no value, no depth has: 5.7 % of records are missing at every depth at once, during station outages of the early era. The four longest are 124 days from February 2011, 93 days from March 2009, 83 days from March 2010 and 63 days from May 2007. The site record names two of them: a failed logger, and a fuse that slipped out of the battery-powered forest-floor station.




The early profile was a five-sensor Campbell 107 probe stick. The forest-floor logger programs name its sensors at 5, 10, 15, 30 and 50 cm, which are the five depths with an early record. It was replaced in March 2020 by the current sensors, which began reporting on 10 April 2020.
Unlike soil water content, the two generations here overlap, for 347 days, until the old stick stopped at the March 2021 logger rebuild. The overlap measures the level difference: about 0.6 K at 0.05 m and 0.4 K at 0.1 m. HOMOGENIZED in the column name refers to its removal.






WarningLevels are reconciled, amplitudes are not



The early sensors were much more closely coupled to the surface than the current ones at the same nominal depth. At 0.05 m the median summer daily amplitude is 3.13 K in the early era and 0.90 K in the current one, and the median annual range 25.4 K against 18.0 K. At 0.1 m the daily amplitude is 1.27 K against 0.59 K.
A daily or seasonal amplitude computed across April 2020 is therefore dominated by the sensor change. Annual and daily means are comparable across it; amplitudes are not.


At 0.3 m and 0.5 m there is no homogenisation, because the generations do not overlap: the early sensors at those depths stopped on 2010-03-06, ten years before the new ones were installed. The early era there keeps its own level, and a trend across April 2020 includes the sensor change. The climatological offsets used for soil water content are not used here, so that measured and climatological offsets are not mixed in one product.



Between January 2009 and May 2012 the three early channels depart from their own seasonal norm by 1.5 to 3.5 K, for months at a time and in opposite pairs: one runs warm while another runs cold. In the other thirteen years they agree to within a few tenths of a kelvin.
The period covers the years in which the forest-floor logger repeatedly lost power, and it ends around a logger program of April 2012 described as having “corrected multipliers and offset”. Which channel is wrong is not determined: with three sensors, one that moves shifts the comparison for all three, and there is no fourth soil sensor and no external reference. The records are kept, flagged SUSPECT, and not corrected.



Gaps in the overall columns are filled from the other depths of the same profile, with a least-squares fit made separately for each sensor generation, so a fill does not introduce a sensor step. The fit uses every available depth, each with rolling means over 3 h to 120 d, and a day-of-year term. It was validated by holding out whole years and by predicting the deep depths from the shallow ones alone.
Each depth is filled only within its own measured span and is not extrapolated. This is why 0.2 m and 0.6 m have no values before 2020 and 0.15 m none after March 2021. Within a span, the only remaining gaps are the station outages. The individual channels are never filled.




Amplitudes are not comparable across April 2020. The early sensors were more closely coupled to the surface than the current ones at the same nominal depth, so the diurnal and seasonal amplitude changes with the hardware, by a factor of three at 0.05 m. No correction is applied to the amplitudes.
Records between January 2009 and May 2012 carry the SUSPECT flag. The three early channels differ from one another by 1.5 to 3.5 K over that period, and which of them is wrong cannot be established. Filter on the flag before using those years quantitatively.
The deep columns have no usable diurnal cycle. At 0.5 m and 0.6 m the sensors report in steps of 0.1 K, and the median summer daily amplitude at those depths is 0.10 K, one reporting step. A diurnal cycle in the deep columns reflects the instrument resolution, not the soil.
Nearly half of 0.3 m and 0.5 m is modelled. Both are 47 % modelled over the file, almost all of it in the ten years between March 2010 and April 2020 when no sensor existed at those depths. These values are estimates from the other depths.

January 2016. The tower renewal moved air temperature by 1.32 °C and stepped humidity and pressure. It did not reach this profile, which is on the forest-floor logger; the tower program takes no soil temperature. The record shows no outage, no unusual half-hour and no level change at the date. The level test for a change common to every channel resolves about ±0.75 K, and finds no change within that.

Soil temperature does not move: at every channel it lies in the middle of the distribution of comparable mornings. title: Soil temperature at the forest floor
text:
The early profile was a five-sensor Campbell 107 probe stick. The forest-floor logger programs name its sensors at 5, 10, 15, 30 and 50 cm, which are the five depths with an early record. It was replaced in March 2020 by the current sensors, which began reporting on 10 April 2020.
Unlike soil water content, the two generations here overlap, for 347 days, until the old stick stopped at the March 2021 logger rebuild. The overlap measures the level difference: about 0.6 K at 0.05 m and 0.4 K at 0.1 m. HOMOGENIZED in the column name refers to its removal.






WarningLevels are reconciled, amplitudes are not



The early sensors were much more closely coupled to the surface than the current ones at the same nominal depth. At 0.05 m the median summer daily amplitude is 3.13 K in the early era and 0.90 K in the current one, and the median annual range 25.4 K against 18.0 K. At 0.1 m the daily amplitude is 1.27 K against 0.59 K.
A daily or seasonal amplitude computed across April 2020 is therefore dominated by the sensor change. Annual and daily means are comparable across it; amplitudes are not.


At 0.3 m and 0.5 m there is no homogenisation, because the generations do not overlap: the early sensors at those depths stopped on 2010-03-06, ten years before the new ones were installed. The early era there keeps its own level, and a trend across April 2020 includes the sensor change. The climatological offsets used for soil water content are not used here, so that measured and climatological offsets are not mixed in one product.

title: Outgoing shortwave radiation at 47 m
text:
Half-hourly outgoing (reflected) shortwave radiation at 47 m on the CH-LAE tower, 2005-2025, exported as measured. The file is 12_METEO_SW_OUT_2005-2025 (parquet and CSV): 355,872 records on a continuous 30-minute index, TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (middle of the half-hour), in local time (UTC+01:00, no daylight saving), from 2005-09-14 00:15 to 2025-12-31 23:45. The first measurement is at 2005-09-14 11:15.
The series ends on 31 December 2025. It is part of FP2026.1 and of the merged meteo product, where it is NaN from 1 January 2026; the extension to 30 September 2026 is in progress.
The interactive dashboard summarises coverage, provenance, seasonality, distributions, extremes and trends. Its instrument card shows how much of each year came from the CNR1, the changeover window and the CNR4.
Notebooks:

12_METEO_SW_OUT: builds the product. It merges the two screenings and shows that they are on one scale, applies the 2012 corrections and the nighttime offset, and identifies the instrument and conversion constant behind each part of the record.
SW_OUT_T1_47_1: the screening of the current era.
01_METEO_SW_IN: the incoming channel of the same radiometer. SW_OUT / SW_IN is the surface albedo, which is the only diagnostic available for this product and the basis of every albedo figure below.
Meteo_Data_LW_OUT: the outgoing longwave channel of the same instrument, with the same December 2021 boundary.
Meteo_Product_Chain: where this product sits in the chain.







ImportantOne value column, and which flag matters



The file has two flags for one value column, because the record has two boundaries on different dates.

FLAG_SW_OUT_T1_47_1_INSTRUMENT marks a real break. The radiometer was replaced on 14 December 2021, and the two instruments convert this channel differently. Filter on this flag before comparing values across that date. Drop code 2, the weeks in which the new instrument was still read with the old instrument’s constant, before using December 2021 or early January



FLAG_SW_OUT_T1_47_1_SOURCE is provenance only. It names the screening that produced each value. The two screenings agree to 0.03 % on two years of simultaneous records, so trends and multi-year means may be taken across the boundary between them. For the same reason there is no _HOMOGENIZED column.

Nothing is gap-filled, so the value column contains NaN and every non-null record is a measurement. Nighttime values are exactly 0, which is a physical value, not a gap.




The values are upwelling shortwave irradiance above the canopy. The stand reflects roughly a tenth of the incoming shortwave, so the values are an order of magnitude smaller than SW_IN: the daylight median is 22.0 W m-2, the daylight mean 32.4 W m-2, and the largest half-hour 236.2 W m-2. Over the whole record, nights included, the median is 0.2 W m-2.
Dividing by SW_IN gives the surface albedo. Over the 157,444 half-hours with an incoming flux above 20 W m-2 and a measured reflected flux, the median ratio is 0.112. Thirty-five of them (0.022 %) give a ratio above 1.05. They occur at low incoming flux, and 28 fall between December and March, as expected from snow on the upward-facing sensor and a low sun.

Four years are below 98 % measured: 2012 at 92.7 %, 2016 at 94.3 %, 2019 at 95.7 % and 2009 at 96.9 %. The 2012 figure results from this product: 1,212 records were removed inside the two windows of documented logger-wide fault, as in notebooks 01 to 03 and 06.
Two corrections change values. The August 2012 clock error is corrected by the same +15.5 h shift as the other tower variables. Unlike LW_IN, this variable can confirm the shift, because reflected shortwave follows the sun and its correlation with potential radiation shows whether the block is on the solar clock. The nighttime zero offset is removed per day over the whole record, because only the newer screening had removed it; without this step the first sixteen years would carry an offset that the last four do not.




The two screenings read different inputs: the MeteoScreeningTool read delivered CSV files, the diive screening reads the raw record. They could therefore have converted the same voltages with different constants. They overlap for two full years on the same instrument, which allows a direct comparison.
On 14,542 well-illuminated half-hours that both report, spread over 24 calendar months, the factor between them is 0.99970 (0.03 %), and the ratio of their standard deviations is 0.99955. The smallest conversion difference known at this site is 3.5 %, 118 times larger. The two eras are therefore joined without rescaling, and no _HOMOGENIZED column is exported.



The tower logger was replaced in January 2016. In June 2016 a new logger program changed a radiometer calibration factor from 10.03 to 12.83 µV/W/m2; this is the change that notebook 06 finds in LW_IN. Had that factor reached the outgoing shortwave channel, the albedo would have stepped by about a fifth, because only one of the two constants in the ratio would have changed.
It did not. The season-controlled albedo moves by −1.0 % across both 2016 dates, compared with −5.3 % for a placebo pair of periods within the earlier era and −21.8 % expected from a factor change on this channel alone. The record is homogeneous across both dates. The product notebook asserts this, so a re-run that finds such a step fails instead of exporting it.



The CNR1 was replaced by a CNR4 on 14 December 2021, and the conversion changed with it. The CNR1 logger programs convert all four channels with a single constant, so at least three of the four were converted with a constant that is not their own. The two shortwave channels of the CNR4 each have their own constant, and these differ by 3.5 %.
The size of the resulting step cannot be determined from this product. The season-controlled albedo differs by 4.2 % between the two instruments, but the same statistic differs by 10.0 % between two periods of the CNR4 era in which nothing changed. The growing-season albedo of the stand varies from year to year by more than the instrument difference, so the CNR1’s channel mismatch cannot be separated from it with the years available. Nothing is corrected: that would require the CNR1’s two detector sensitivities, which were not recorded at this site.
Code 2 isolates the weeks between the installation of the CNR4 and the update of its constants in the logger program. Compared with MeteoSwiss Lägern, which measures the incoming channel independently, the changeover window is 8.3 % away from an ordinary winter. If the CNR1 constant had still been in force, it would be 38.5 % away; these are 2.1 and 7.5 interquartile widths of the between-winter scatter. This is evidence against the old constant having been in force, but not proof that the window is correct. Seven winters can rule out an error of tens of per cent, not a small one, and the test applies to the incoming channel, whose constant in the same program was a different number. The window keeps its own code either way.




The record is not homogeneous across 14 December 2021, and the size of the step is not known. Filter on FLAG_SW_OUT_T1_47_1_INSTRUMENT before comparing values or albedos across that date, and treat any trend across it as containing an unquantified instrument change.
The 24 days of the changeover have an unverified conversion. Code 2 marks them. The MeteoSwiss comparison argues against the old constant, but does not establish which constant was applied.
The CNR1 era carries an unquantified channel mismatch. All four channels were converted with one constant, although each detector has its own factory calibration. Because both shortwave channels were divided by the same number, it cancels in their ratio, so the CNR1-era albedo does not depend on the absolute scale. The real difference between the two detectors does not cancel: the reflected flux of that era, and its albedo, include the difference between the two sensitivities. It is a fixed scale error within the era, not a break, so comparisons within the era are not affected.
The series contains gaps and is not gap-filled. Code that assumes a complete series will fail or propagate NaN. Nothing else measures what this canopy reflects: MeteoSwiss Lägern and NABEL measure incoming shortwave only, and the site’s other outgoing shortwave sensor is below the canopy. If a complete series is needed, fill it downstream, and do not train one model across the December 2021 boundary.
There is no independent reference. Every quantitative statement above uses the ratio to the incoming channel of the same instrument. This ratio cancels anything that scaled both channels together (a supply voltage, a dirty dome), and therefore cannot detect it.
The 2012 windows were removed without evidence from this series. They rest on the documented logger-wide fault, as in 01 to 03 and 06. The albedo can detect a fault in the reflected channel alone, not one that moved both channels of the instrument together, as a power-supply problem does.
Coverage counts nighttime zeros as measurements. In the diive era the screening set every nighttime value to zero, including gaps. This is physically correct, but from 2020 a nighttime record is a known value rather than a delivered measurement, and the coverage of those years is not strictly comparable with that of the earlier era.
A candidate removal window in July 2024 is still in the data. The screening notebook lists 2024-07-14 to 2024-07-19 for removal, but the removal was not committed. The albedo over the window is 2.6 % below the surrounding weeks, which is within how those weeks differ among themselves, and the maintenance record names no fault in this channel. The window is neither removed nor flagged; it is to be settled in the screening notebook.
The October 2010 rebuild of the MeteoSwiss Lägern station changes nothing in this file, but it steps that station’s incoming shortwave by about 5 %. A comparison of this product with Lägern across that date includes the step. The changeover test above uses only winters well after it.
