They could therefore have converted the same voltages with different constants. They overlap for two full years on the same instrument, which allows a direct comparison.
On 14,542 well-illuminated half-hours that both report, spread over 24 calendar months, the factor between them is 0.99970 (0.03 %), and the ratio of their standard deviations is 0.99955. The smallest conversion difference known at this site is 3.5 %, 118 times larger. The two eras are therefore joined without rescaling, and no _HOMOGENIZED column is exported.

title: Outgoing shortwave radiation at 47 m
text:
The tower logger was replaced in January 2016. In June 2016 a new logger program changed a radiometer calibration factor from 10.03 to 12.83 µV/W/m2; this is the change that notebook 06 finds in LW_IN. Had that factor reached the outgoing shortwave channel, the albedo would have stepped by about a fifth, because only one of the two constants in the ratio would have changed.
It did not. The season-controlled albedo moves by −1.0 % across both 2016 dates, compared with −5.3 % for a placebo pair of periods within the earlier era and −21.8 % expected from a factor change on this channel alone. The record is homogeneous across both dates. The product notebook asserts this, so a re-run that finds such a step fails instead of exporting it.

title: Outgoing shortwave radiation at 47 m
text:
The CNR1 was replaced by a CNR4 on 14 December 2021, and the conversion changed with it. The CNR1 logger programs convert all four channels with a single constant, so at least three of the four were converted with a constant that is not their own. The two shortwave channels of the CNR4 each have their own constant, and these differ by 3.5 %.
The size of the resulting step cannot be determined from this product. The season-controlled albedo differs by 4.2 % between the two instruments, but the same statistic differs by 10.0 % between two periods of the CNR4 era in which nothing changed. The growing-season albedo of the stand varies from year to year by more than the instrument difference, so the CNR1’s channel mismatch cannot be separated from it with the years available. Nothing is corrected: that would require the CNR1’s two detector sensitivities, which were not recorded at this site.
Code 2 isolates the weeks between the installation of the CNR4 and the update of its constants in the logger program. Compared with MeteoSwiss Lägern, which measures the incoming channel independently, the changeover window is 8.3 % away from an ordinary winter. If the CNR1 constant had still been in force, it would be 38.5 % away; these are 2.1 and 7.5 interquartile widths of the between-winter scatter. This is evidence against the old constant having been in force, but not proof that the window is correct. Seven winters can rule out an error of tens of per cent, not a small one, and the test applies to the incoming channel, whose constant in the same program was a different number. The window keeps its own code either way.

title: Outgoing shortwave radiation at 47 m
text:
The record is not homogeneous across 14 December 2021, and the size of the step is not known. Filter on FLAG_SW_OUT_T1_47_1_INSTRUMENT before comparing values or albedos across that date, and treat any trend across it as containing an unquantified instrument change.
The 24 days of the changeover have an unverified conversion. Code 2 marks them. The MeteoSwiss comparison argues against the old constant, but does not establish which constant was applied.
The CNR1 era carries an unquantified channel mismatch. All four channels were converted with one constant, although each detector has its own factory calibration. Because both shortwave channels were divided by the same number, it cancels in their ratio, so the CNR1-era albedo does not depend on the absolute scale. The real difference between the two detectors does not cancel: the reflected flux of that era, and its albedo, include the difference between the two sensitivities. It is a fixed scale error within the era, not a break, so comparisons within the era are not affected.
The series contains gaps and is not gap-filled. Code that assumes a complete series will fail or propagate NaN. Nothing else measures what this canopy reflects: MeteoSwiss Lägern and NABEL measure incoming shortwave only, and the site’s other outgoing shortwave sensor is below the canopy. If a complete series is needed, fill it downstream, and do not train one model across the December 2021 boundary.
There is no independent reference. Every quantitative statement above uses the ratio to the incoming channel of the same instrument. This ratio cancels anything that scaled both channels together (a supply voltage, a dirty dome), and therefore cannot detect it.
The 2012 windows were removed without evidence from this series. They rest on the documented logger-wide fault, as in 01 to 03 and 06. The albedo can detect a fault in the reflected channel alone, not one that moved both channels of the instrument together, as a power-supply problem does.
Coverage counts nighttime zeros as measurements. In the diive era the screening set every nighttime value to zero, including gaps. This is physically correct, but from 2020 a nighttime record is a known value rather than a delivered measurement, and the coverage of those years is not strictly comparable with that of the earlier era.
A candidate removal window in July 2024 is still in the data. The screening notebook lists 2024-07-14 to 2024-07-19 for removal, but the removal was not committed. The albedo over the window is 2.6 % below the surrounding weeks, which is within how those weeks differ among themselves, and the maintenance record names no fault in this channel. The window is neither removed nor flagged; it is to be settled in the screening notebook.
The October 2010 rebuild of the MeteoSwiss Lägern station changes nothing in this file, but it steps that station’s incoming shortwave by about 5 %. A comparison of this product with Lägern across that date includes the step. The changeover test above uses only winters well after it.

title: Soil water content at the forest floor
text:
Half-hourly volumetric soil water content at five depths of the FF1 soil profile at CH-LAE, 2004-2025. The file is 09_METEO_SWC_FF1_2004-2025 (parquet and CSV): 373,728 records on a continuous 30-minute index, TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (middle of the half-hour), in local time (UTC+01:00, no daylight saving), from 2004-09-07 00:15 to 2025-12-31 23:45. Values are in % VWC. The index begins in September 2004 because the soil record begins then.
The series ends on 31 December 2025. It is part of FP2026.1 and of the merged meteo product, where it is NaN from 1 January 2026; the extension to 30 September 2026 is in progress.
The interactive dashboards summarise one depth each (coverage, provenance, seasonality, distributions, extremes and trends). They are standalone files and work offline: 0.05 / 0.1 / 0.2 / 0.3 / 0.5 m.
Notebooks:

09_METEO_SWC_FF1: builds the product, splices the sensor generations and tests the older era for internal breaks.
The screening notebooks of the current profile, one per depth, which screen the raw high-resolution record before this product reads it: 0.05 / 0.1 / 0.2 / 0.3 / 0.5 m, and the shared profile download they use as a cross-check reference.
Meteo_Product_Chain: where this product sits in the chain.







ImportantWhich column to use



No column is homogeneous across April 2020, when the whole soil profile was replaced. The step between the two profiles is +7.6 to +10.7 % VWC, depending on depth. It is an instrument change, not weather.

Within one profile, use SWC_FF1_<d>_1, which is what the probe recorded.
Across April 2020, use SWC_FF1_<d>_1_HOMOGENIZED. Read The 2020 profile replacement first: this column rests on climatology alone and is a derived estimate, not a measurement.
At 0.5 m there is no homogenised column, because that depth has only one profile.

Nothing in this product is gap-filled. Coverage over the full period ranges from 80.8 % at 0.05 m to 96.0 % at 0.2 m. A missing record is NaN, never 0.




Fourteen columns: per depth, one measured value, one homogenised column and one flag, except at 0.5 m, which has no homogenised column. The columns are grouped by depth. <d> is one of 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5.

Means and ranges mix the two profiles and are for orientation only. The three longest gaps are not station outages. At 0.1 m, 480 days pass between the old probe failing and the new profile starting; at 0.3 m, 328 days pass until the replacement probe of 2025. The 695 days at 0.05 m are unexplained (see Known limitations).




The five TEROS 12 probes of the current profile were installed on 19 March 2020 and began reporting on 10 April 2020. The EC-20 probes they replaced had failed one by one over the preceding year and a half, so the two generations do not overlap at any depth. The interval between them runs from 22 days at 0.2 m to 480 days at 0.1 m and is not filled.
No other measurement spans the break: there is no second profile and no weather-service reference, and all depths changed on the same day. The step therefore cannot be calibrated as the 2018 precipitation step was. The _HOMOGENIZED columns shift the older era onto the current level with additive calendar-month offsets fitted on climatology alone. This assumes the two periods had the same monthly soil-moisture climate. Use these columns for continuity and trend work that has to cross 2020. Do not read a homogenised pre-2020 value as an estimate of the water content at the time.
The homogenised columns are not on one common reference period. Each is shifted onto its own depth’s current-profile era, which at 0.3 m ends at the April 2024 probe failure and elsewhere runs to the end of 2025. Within a depth this has no effect; a difference between depths across 2020 includes it.



On 25 June 2015, between 08:15 and 09:15, all four depths of the older profile drop by about 3.9 % VWC at once and stay at the lower level. The maintenance record has work on the forest-floor logger’s wiring that morning. Three weeks earlier it records the replacement of the plot’s power supply and loose connectors on the soil-moisture probes. These probes were read as a voltage scaled by a fixed multiplier, so a poor connection shifts the reported level directly. Soil temperature on the same logger does not change at that time (see Meteo_Data_TS), which confines the event to the soil-moisture wiring.
The break is not corrected, because a larger problem lies underneath it. Through 2005-2015 both the wettest and the driest conditions of each year rise steadily at every depth, by +0.5 to +1.2 % VWC per year (5 to 9 % VWC in total), while precipitation over the same decade trends slightly downward. The driest half-hour of a year is set by the soil, so a dry end that nearly doubles points to the instruments, not to the weather. The site inventory flags three of the four old probes as defective. A drift has no date at which a correction could be applied and no reference to fit against, so it is documented and not removed, as for the tower pyranometer (SW_IN) and the PAR sensor (PPFD_IN).
A level comparison within the pre-2020 era across June 2015 is not a comparison of measurements, and a trend fitted through that era is dominated by instrument drift, not by climate.



The January 2016 tower renewal moved air temperature, relative humidity and air pressure, and a program change in June 2016 left much of the longwave record reading low. This profile is not affected. It is on the forest-floor datalogger, the tower program contains no soil-moisture instruction, the profile lost no records while the tower logger was replaced, and neither the level nor any single half-hour changes at the date. The notebook asserts all three.




Depths are not replicates. Each is a single probe at one point. The probes share a logger, a power supply and an SDI-12 bus, so they fail together, but they measure different soil, and differences between them are real.
0.3 m carries three sensor generations and steps twice. The 2020 probe stopped communicating in April 2024 and took the whole profile’s SDI-12 port down with it, which is why every depth has a gap in April 2024. Its last value is at 2024-04-09 16:45. The 328-day gap that follows ends with a replacement probe installed on 4 March 2025, 40 cm downslope in different soil, which reads about 3 % VWC high relative to the other depths. Code 3 marks it; the measured column keeps the step and the homogenised column removes it.
The pre-2020 era was screened once, with the deprecated MeteoScreeningTool, and never re-screened. Values outside the physical range are removed here. These are failed sensor reads, which this hardware stores as a fixed negative value instead of a gap. A probe that stopped responding to rain while still reporting plausible values would not be caught. The per-depth screening notebooks run that test for the current profile only.
The two largest gaps of the older era are power failures documented in the site record: 10 March to 11 June 2009, and 6 March to 28 May 2010, when a fuse slipped out and the battery-powered forest-floor logger lost power. There is no site record for the forest floor before 2006, so gaps in the first two years cannot be explained.
The nearly two-year gap at 0.05 m (July 2013 to June 2015) has no explanation in the site record and, unlike the 2009 and 2010 gaps, affects one depth only. It is why 0.05 m has the lowest coverage and the longest gap of the five depths.
Sub-daily timestamps in August 2012 are uncertain. A logger clock error that month is corrected in the tower products. Whether the forest-floor logger had the same error is not recorded, and soil moisture has no diurnal cycle to check it against. No shift is applied.
FLUXNET’s SWC_F_MDS_1..4 are not this product. They splice the same two profiles with the 2020 step passed through unchanged, and fill some periods with a constant value. Use the source flag to keep the generations apart.

title: Precipitation at 47 m
text:
Half-hourly precipitation from the rain gauge at 47 m on the CH-LAE tower, 2004-2025. The file is 08_METEO_PREC_GAPFILLED_2004-2025 (parquet and CSV): 385,728 records on a continuous 30-minute index, TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (middle of the half-hour), in local time (UTC+01:00, no daylight saving), from 2004-01-01 00:15 to 2025-12-31 23:45. Values are sums over each half-hour in mm, on the gauge’s 0.1 mm tipping-bucket grid. Divide by 0.5 h for a rate.
The series ends on 31 December 2025. It is part of FP2026.1 and of the merged meteo product, where it is NaN from 1 January 2026; the extension to 30 September 2026 is in progress.
The interactive dashboard summarises coverage, provenance, seasonality, distributions, extremes and trends. It is a standalone file and works offline.
Notebooks:

08_METEO_PREC: builds the product and tests every hardware boundary in the record.
MeteoSwiss_OED_PREC: the Ehrendingen gauge, used both as diagnostic and as fill source.
MeteoSwiss_REGIONAL_PREC: the thirteen stations within 21 km that show which gauge moved in 2018.
Meteo_Product_Chain: where this product sits in the chain.







ImportantWhich column to use



The measured column is not homogeneous across mid-2018, when the gauge moved from one acquisition system to another. Annual totals average 830 mm before the change and 1,003 mm after it.

Within one era, use PREC_TOT_T1_47_1, which is what the gauge recorded.
Across mid-2018, use PREC_TOT_T1_47_1_HOMOGENIZED. A total across the change taken from the measured column is dominated by the acquisition change, not by the weather.

Neither column is complete: 0.58 % of records are NaN, all of them before June 2014. A missing record is not a dry one.




Both value columns are NaN at the same records. The flags apply to both, because the homogenisation changes values and not provenance.

The 932 filled records add 56.4 mm, and only 96 of them are wet; 759 of them fill the 16-day outage of November 2019. The 2,224 unfilled records all lie before 2014-06-04 10:15, because Ehrendingen has no sub-daily data before September 2014.





One instrument measured throughout, a Lambrecht 15188H at 47 m. In mid-2018 it was moved from EMPA’s acquisition system to the ETH CR1000 logger, and the recorded amounts rise by about a fifth. The break is in the measurement chain, not in the instrument.
The later era is the one to trust. Against every MeteoSwiss precipitation station within 21 km, the early era reads low (ratios 0.74 to 0.91), while the later era agrees with the network (0.91 to 1.05). Against the elevation gradient of these stations, the early era is 25 % below what a gauge on this ridge should catch and the later era 10 % below. About 10 % is ordinary wind under-catch for an exposed ridge top.
PREC_TOT_T1_47_1_HOMOGENIZED lifts the early era onto the later one with one factor per calendar month, fitted against those stations. The factors run from 1.07 to 1.44, equivalent to 1.21 applied uniformly. They raise the mean annual total of the complete early years from 830 mm to 991 mm, against 1,003 mm for the later era. The later era is copied unchanged.



The January 2016 datalogger replacement moved three other tower variables, and a program change in June 2016 left more than half of the longwave record reading low. Precipitation is not affected: the gauge stayed on EMPA’s acquisition until 2018 and no surviving tower program records it. The 20.6-day outage that pressure and longwave show during the logger replacement is absent here; all 988 half-hours are measured. The catch ratio against the regional stations shows no step at either 2016 date, nor at any later boundary, including the change of screening tool in January 2020.




Neither column is absolutely calibrated, and both read low. Against the regional stations’ elevation gradient, the later era is about 10 % below what a gauge on this ridge should catch, which is ordinary wind under-catch for an exposed ridge top. The homogenisation lifts the early era onto the later one and stops there, so this 10 % remains in both columns. A total from this product is what the gauge caught, not what fell.
Winter totals are biased low, and the bias changes at 2018. The gauge misses snow as it falls and releases part of it days later on melt, so sub-daily timing in winter is unreliable in both eras. On days below 2 °C the catch ratio averages 0.62 before 2018 and 0.56 after, but individual winters vary by more than that. The maintenance record has the gauge heating disconnected on 8 August 2018 (the day the gauge was rewired), still inactive in January 2024, and a new transformer fitted in July 2024. None of the three dates is visible in the data, so nothing is corrected. A winter total across 2018 mixes the acquisition change with a change in snow catch, which is why the winter months have the largest factors.
The homogenisation leaves light rain unchanged. Homogenised values are rounded back onto the 0.1 mm grid, and a small amount multiplied by 1.07 to 1.44 often rounds back to itself. In the early era, 9,146 of the 20,801 wet half-hours are identical in both columns, carrying 11 % of the rainfall: every 0.1 mm record, 55 % of the 0.2 mm records, 28 % of the 0.3 mm records, and none above 1 mm. Counts of wet half-hours and light-rain intensity statistics are therefore not homogenised. The factor delivered overall is 1.19 rather than the fitted 1.21, which is part of why the homogenised early era ends 1.2 % below the later level.
Filled records are suitable for sums, not for timing. A filled value is the Ehrendingen measurement (3.8 km away, 260 m lower), rescaled. On synthetic gaps the summed rainfall is correct to within 2.2 % at every gap length, but the median error of one gap’s total is 14 % for a two-week gap and about 35 % for a one-hour gap, so short gaps are the least reliable. At half-hourly resolution the correlation is 0.7; about a quarter of the half-hours a fill marks wet were dry at the tower, and about 30 % of wet half-hours are missed.
GAPFILLED in the file name does not mean complete. Unlike SW_IN, TA and PPFD_IN, this product contains NaN. Code that assumes a complete series will fail or propagate NaN.
2008 is the only year with low coverage, 93.2 %. A 24.6-day outage in May and June falls in the period that cannot be filled; Ehrendingen recorded 58.5 mm over that window. Every other year has a value for at least 98.3 % of its records.
Zeros are data. 91.2 % of records with a value are exactly 0, the correct value for no rain, not a missing-value code. The largest half-hour in the record is 27.7 mm, on 2023-07-12.

title: Air pressure at 47 m
text:
Half-hourly atmospheric pressure at 47 m on the CH-LAE tower, September 2005 to September 2026, exported as measured. The file is 05_METEO_PA_2005-2026.09 (parquet and CSV): 369,552 records on a continuous 30-minute index TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (middle of the half-hour, UTC+01:00, no daylight saving), from 2005-09-02 00:15 to 2026-09-30 23:45.
The interactive dashboard summarises the product on one page.
Method, evidence and checks:

05_METEO_PA: builds the product: unit harmonisation of the two screenings, 2012 corrections, identification of the barometer from the logger programs, the check of the absolute level against the barometric formula, and the two hardware boundaries.
Meteo Product Chain: no other meteo product is computed from this one.







NoteOne column, no flag, gaps left in



This product is not gap-filled. There is one value column and no flag column. About 1 % of the record is missing: a non-null value is a measurement and a NaN is a real gap.
There is no _HOMOGENIZED column, although the record changes level by about 0.09 kPa at the January 2016 acquisition change. See Known limitations for what to do about it.







Table 1: Columns of 05_METEO_PA_2005-2026.09.










column
unit
description




PA_T1_47_1
kPa
Atmospheric pressure at 47 m, measured and corrected. Gaps are NaN.






The unit is kPa, the FLUXNET convention. The database stores the two screenings in different units, kPa before 2022 and Pa after, because the two loggers wrote different units. The notebook harmonises them from the magnitude of the data and stops if that result disagrees with the database unit tag. Measured values range from 89.45 to 95.54 kPa, with a median of 93.31 kPa.



365,542 of the 369,552 records carry a value, 98.9 %. The record begins on 2005-09-02, when the archive of this logger begins; the barometer was already in service, but no earlier data are held. There is no PA for 2004 and the first eight months of 2005, and none is reconstructed, so this product starts later than SW_IN, TA and PPFD_IN.
Of 415 gaps, 399 are one hour or shorter. The longest is the 20.6-day outage of January 2016, during which the tower logger was replaced.

In 2012 a logger clock error shifted one block of August by 15.5 hours and was corrected. A tower power-supply failure in late July and August and storm damage in late October and November left biased values, and those periods were removed. The removal windows come from this variable’s own disagreement with the independent hut barometer, so they do not coincide exactly with the windows of SW_IN, TA and PPFD_IN. Use each product’s own missing values rather than assuming the products exclude identical periods.



The instrument is a Vaisala PTB101B barometer. Every logger program that has measured it, the six CR10X programs of 2004-2006 and the CR1000 program installed in January 2016, converts its signal with the same multiplier and offset, spanning 600 to 1060 hPa, the range of that barometer. The maintenance record does not name the instrument in twenty-one years: as far as the record goes it was never replaced, calibrated or cleaned, and it is not in the device inventory.
Pressure is the one meteo variable here whose absolute level can be checked against physics, and it passes. The barometric formula, with nothing fitted to the tower data, predicts the difference between this barometer and each reference from that reference’s own pressure, temperature and humidity. It places the barometer within 5 m of its nominal elevation using MeteoSwiss Lägern (2.5 km away at 845 m, about 110 m above the barometer) and within 9 m using the NABEL barometer at the hut; the two references agree with each other to 4 m. It also reproduces the annual wave in the difference between two barometers at different heights (89 Pa measured, 79 Pa predicted, correlation 0.98). A unit error, a wrong offset or a lost factor of ten would fail this check by orders of magnitude.



It moved the level by about 0.09 kPa, the only hardware change in this record with a measurable effect.
The barometer and its conversion did not change. The logger did: the CR10X measured the sensor single-ended, the CR1000 measures it differentially. A single-ended measurement includes any offset between the sensor’s ground and the logger’s; a differential one does not.
Three barometers place the change on the tower. Both differences involving the tower move across 2016, by -0.0884 and -0.0888 kPa, while the difference between the two references moves by -0.0001 kPa. The barometric prediction shows which era is correct: averaged over 2016 to 2025, the later era agrees with the prediction against both references and the earlier era lies about 0.1 kPa above it. Year by year, the departure of the later era from the prediction against Lägern goes from about +0.02 kPa in 2016 to about -0.06 kPa in 2025 (the drift under Known limitations). The record before 21 January 2016 therefore reads approximately 0.09 kPa high.
The 20.6-day outage that ends on 21 January 2016 brackets the step, so it cannot be dated more precisely. The logger program on disk is dated 18 January 2016, and the maintenance record names the same program file.
The December 2021 change of screening software has no effect here: the difference against MeteoSwiss changes less across that boundary than in an ordinary year.




The record is not homogeneous across 21 January 2016, and is not corrected. Values before that date read approximately 0.09 kPa high. No homogenised column is provided: the step is one part in a thousand of the value (under ten metres of air), so air density and the flux quantities computed from it change by the same one part in a thousand; a rescaled column would change the set of columns this product and the merged product ship; and a residual drift of the same size (next point) would remain after any homogenisation. For one absolute level across the whole record, subtract 0.09 kPa from the records before 21 January 2016. Analyses within a year, or of pressure changes rather than levels, are unaffected.
A slow drift of about 0.1 kPa over twenty years cannot be attributed. Apart from the two dated events, the difference between this barometer and MeteoSwiss Lägern falls by approximately 0.1 kPa across the record. Slightly more than half of that falls after mid-2018, when the second barometer at the site stops, so no third instrument can show which of the two is moving. It develops over years, so there is no boundary for a correction, and the barometric formula cannot settle it because it is computed from Lägern’s own pressure. January to September 2026 continues the drift: the difference against Lägern lies 0.023 kPa below the same months of 2025, the largest year-on-year change since 2016, but below the 0.04 kPa at which the notebook counts an event.
The MeteoSwiss Lägern pressure changed level in October 2010. The rebuild of that station’s instrumentation that moved its radiation record also moved PA_LAE_MS, by approximately 0.06 to 0.07 kPa relative to both barometers at this site. This product never uses Lägern to correct a value, but do not read a difference between this product and MeteoSwiss Lägern as evidence about the tower across that date.
The NABEL hut barometer is not independent after July 2018. The database series PA_NABEL_H1_2_1 runs nominally to the end of 2018, but from 3 July 2018 its values repeat the tower series to five decimal places. The notebook truncates the reference there. Any other use of that series should do the same.
The record begins in September 2005. When joining this product to SW_IN, TA or PPFD_IN, whose index starts on 2004-01-01, expect a shorter series.

title: Incoming longwave radiation at 47 m
text:
Half-hourly incoming (downwelling) longwave radiation at 47 m on the CH-LAE tower, September 2005 to September 2026, exported as measured. The file is 06_METEO_LW_IN_2005-2026.09 (parquet and CSV): 368,976 records on a continuous 30-minute index TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (middle of the half-hour, UTC+01:00, no daylight saving), from 2005-09-14 00:15 to 2026-09-30 23:45. 2026 holds January to September only.
The interactive dashboard summarises the product on one page.
Method, evidence and checks:

06_METEO_LW_IN: builds the product: merge of the two screenings, 2012 corrections, identification of the instrument from the logger programs and the maintenance record, and the measurement of the calibration change described below.
01_METEO_SW_IN: the shortwave channel of the same radiometer. It establishes the instrument’s identity, dates its replacement, and shows what the January 2016 and December 2021 hardware changes did to the shortwave side.
02_METEO_TA: the air temperature product, the only diagnostic driver of notebook 06.
Meteo Product Chain: where this product sits in the chain.







ImportantThe record changes level on 7 June 2016



This series is not homogeneous. Until 7 June 2016 the pyrgeometer signal was converted with the calibration factor of the pyranometer in the same instrument, 10.03 instead of 12.83 µV/W/m². On that date the logger program was corrected. Everything recorded before it reads too low.
The error is proportional to the difference between the value and \(\sigma T_a^4\), so it is largest under a clear sky and close to zero under low overcast: about 8 W m-2 in the middle of the distribution and up to about 23 W m-2 on a clear, dry night (17 % of the nighttime difference before the change, at its median and at its 2nd percentile).
No correction and no homogenised column are provided (see Known limitations). Filter on FLAG_LW_IN_T1_47_1_SOURCE before comparing the two eras, and treat any trend across mid-2016 as containing this change.

The values are downwelling longwave irradiance, median 316.15 W m-2, range 135.45 to 441.78 W m-2. A pyrgeometer’s voltage measures the net exchange between the sky and the instrument body, roughly -50 W m-2 at this site; the downwelling flux is that net signal plus the instrument’s own emission. That term is already included in every value. Reading the raw converted voltage as the flux would be wrong by about 370 W m-2.

Code 3 marks the three weeks between the installation of the CNR4 and the arrival of its own constants in the logger program, during which the new instrument was read through the old instrument’s factor. Neither the maintenance record nor the data can assign this interval to either side.




The measurement begins on 2005-09-14 13:15, when the pyrgeometer channel was wired to the tower logger. There is no longwave record before that date and none is reconstructed. 364,073 of the 368,976 records carry a value (98.7 %).
Of 998 gaps, 977 are one hour or shorter and eight exceed a day. The longest, 20.6 days from 1 to 21 January 2016, is the site-wide outage during which the tower logger was replaced; PA has the same gap.



Table 3: Years in which measured coverage is below 95 %. Every other year of 2006-2025 is at least 95 % measured, and January to September 2026 is complete.

In 2012 a logger clock error shifted one block of August by 15.5 hours, and a tower power-supply failure in late July and August and storm damage in late October and November left records that were removed. LW_IN shows no sign of either fault in its own values, and it has no independent reference that could reveal a level error. The removal therefore rests on the documented logger-wide fault and is the conservative choice.




The record is not homogeneous across 7 June 2016. Values before that date read low by about 17 % of the difference between the value and \(\sigma T_a^4\), over about half the record. This is not corrected. Undoing it requires splitting each stored value into the instrument’s own emission and its net signal, which needs the radiometer body temperature. This product does not read that channel, and its treatment in the processing that produced the earlier values cannot be verified from the available files. Rescaling with air temperature as a proxy would put an unverified model into the exported numbers. The SOURCE flag marks the affected era instead.
The record also changes across December 2021, and the cause is not established. The radiometer was replaced (CNR1 to CNR4) on 14 December 2021, and the screening software changed from mst to diive at the turn of the year. The two cannot be separated, and there is no reference against which to test either. The clear-sky part of the signal changes by about 11 %, about half the size of the June 2016 change, which accounts for most of the 6.5 W m-2 between the two periods once their temperature difference is removed. This is equally consistent with a change of instrument, a change of screening, and a gradual change in the lower atmosphere, which moved the same statistic in the same direction from 2019 to 2024 and reversed through 2025 and the dry year 2026. Nothing is corrected. Allow for a change of this order across that date; the SOURCE flag separates the two instruments.
The January 2016 acquisition change did not move this series. It moved TA_T1_47_1 by 1.3 °C and is easily confused with the June date five months later. The logger program installed at the changeover applies the same conversion as the programs before it, and the four months between the two 2016 dates behave like an ordinary year.
The series contains gaps and is not gap-filled. Code that assumes a complete series will fail or propagate NaN.
There is no independent reference for this variable at the site. MeteoSwiss Lägern has no longwave channel, NABEL has no pyrgeometer, and the below-canopy sensor installed in 2024 measures a different quantity. Every statement above rests on the physical relation between longwave radiation and air temperature rather than on a second instrument, so the evidence is weaker than for SW_IN or TA. Where it does not identify a cause, notebook 06 says so.
Summer 2026 was unusually dry and clear. At MeteoSwiss Lägern, relative humidity was 95 % or higher in 0.7 to 5.5 % of the half-hours of July to September 2026, against 4 to 38 % in the same months of 2019-2025. With so few overcast nights, the overcast ceiling of nighttime apparent emissivity (its 95th percentile), one of the two checks in notebook 06, falls to 0.93 to 0.95 in those months, below the same months of every earlier year. It falls in the same way when computed with the Lägern air temperature, so it reflects the weather, not the sensor.
Absolute accuracy is limited by the applied calibration. Both CNR1 eras convert the pyrgeometer with a single factory constant and no correction for the dome. The two radiometer channels of the successor instrument differ by 28 % in sensitivity, the scale of the error removed in June 2016. What remains is the ordinary field uncertainty of an unventilated pyrgeometer, which is larger than for the shortwave channel of the same instrument.

Products 01 to 07 run to 30 September 2026; products 08 to 13 still end on 31 December 2025. This page covers what all products share. Each variable has its own page with its columns, units, coverage, flag codes and known limitations.


An entry without a working link is a page or dashboard not yet written, not a variable missing from the dataset.

A dashboard is one standalone page per exported series: coverage and provenance, seasonality, distributions, extremes, trends and, where one exists, the comparison against the reference station, with a table view behind every chart. It works offline. Where a product exports both a measured and a _HOMOGENIZED column, the dashboard uses the homogenised one and names it at the top.



Notebook 99 joins all thirteen products onto one half-hourly index. The file is 99_METEO_MERGED_2004-2026.09 (parquet and CSV): 398,832 records from 2004-01-01 00:15 to 2026-09-30 23:45, with 61 columns, 31 data series and 30 flag columns. The values are exactly what each product notebook exported; the merge computes and corrects nothing.

01 to 07 (SW_IN, TA, PPFD_IN, RH, PA, LW_IN, VPD) run to 30 September 2026.
08 to 13 (PREC, SWC, TS, G, SW_OUT, LW_OUT) still end on 31 December 2025. Their columns are NaN from January to September 2026 until their notebooks are extended.
For TS and G the merged file carries only the reconciled series, one per depth and one plate mean. The individual channels and plates stay in the product files.

The file 99_METEO_MERGED_2004-2026.09_INFO.md, written beside the data, lists every column with its unit, range and flag codes, and the reason each series has gaps. Read the column list there; this page does not repeat it.
FP2026.1 carries all 61 meteo columns of the merged file, cut to the FP2026.1 period, 1 January 2016 to 30 September 2026. The six products that end in 2025 are therefore empty in FP2026.1 for January to September 2026. See Dataset versions.



Every month of the record on one grid
One tile per month, coloured by the selected metric and marked with what was notable in that month. The grid is drawn at three resolutions: months, meteorological seasons, and single days. The daily raster is the only one of the three that does not split a spell at a boundary. Open a month for its statistics against the calendar-month normal, its rank among the same month of the other years, and a calendar of its days; open a day for its statistics, flags and diurnal course.
The explorer aggregates and compares the exported products and corrects nothing. A month with too few measured records carries no badge and is not ranked. The normal is a period average over the whole record, not a stationary climate, so the trend of each calendar month is shown with it, together with the estimator, the coverage rule and the significance test. The file is standalone and works offline.



Each product notebook writes one file per variable as parquet and CSV. The notebooks are numbered 01 to 13 in the order in which they may read one another: 02 and 03 read 01, 04 reads 02, and 07 reads 02 and 04. These numbers are used as shorthand throughout the documentation. In the repository the notebooks are in workflow/10_METEO/30_PRODUCTS/; on this site they are under Notebooks and are linked under How they are built.
Two conventions apply to every product.
Timestamps are TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE, local standard time (UTC+01:00), on a continuous 30-minute index with no daylight saving. The timestamp marks the middle of the averaging period, so 09:15 covers 09:00 to 09:30.
Apply the provenance flag before analysis. It says, record by record, whether a value was measured, corrected, reconstructed or modelled. PA is the only product without a flag. PA, LW_IN, SWC, G, SW_OUT and LW_OUT are not gap-filled, so their gaps are NaN.

Flag names are given by their suffix; the full column is FLAG_<variable>_<suffix>.


A _HOMOGENIZED or _GAPFILLED column sits beside the measured one rather than replacing it, so the measured record remains available.
_HOMOGENIZED removes a step that a hardware change left in the values, so the eras on either side can be compared. It does not make either era more accurate: it removes the change in the instrument’s bias, not the bias itself. TA and RH carry one because their probe and acquisition system were replaced together in January 2016 and the probe again in June 2026, and VPD because it is computed from them. PREC carries one because its acquisition system changed in 2018, and SWC one per depth because the soil profile was replaced in 2020. Most rescale the earlier era onto the level of the later one. TA also corrects the difference between the radiation shields of the probes, which acts only in daylight.
_GAPFILLED means a model produced some of the values. For TS the model is a regression on the other depths of the profile, and the METHOD flag says which values are measured and which are modelled.



The limitations of each product are on that variable’s page under Known limitations: the dates across which the record is not homogeneous, the columns that are estimates rather than measurements, and what a trend or period comparison over the series contains besides the weather. Table 1 links every page.
Two limitations belong to a reference rather than to a product and recur on several pages. The MeteoSwiss Lägern station changed level in October 2010, when its instrumentation was rebuilt. The NABEL series on the same tower stop being independent records in mid-2018. Neither changes a value in any file, but both change what a comparison against those series means.



Every product reads the quality-screened half-hourly record from the database, joins the older mst screening to the newer diive one, applies the site’s shared 2012 repairs where the variable was on the affected logger, and is checked before it is written. Independent references do the validation and, where a product is filled, much of the filling: MeteoSwiss Lägern 2.5 km away, NABEL at 49 m on the same tower until 2018, the MeteoSwiss gauge at Ehrendingen for rain, and for PREC every MeteoSwiss station within 21 km. The soil products have no external reference and are checked against the other depths of their own profile. Meteo Product Chain shows which product reads which.
Each notebook documents its own decisions and the evidence behind them: 01 SW_IN, 02 TA, 03 PPFD_IN, 04 RH, 05 PA, 06 LW_IN, 07 VPD, 08 PREC, 09 SWC, 10 TS, 11 G, 12 SW_OUT, 13 LW_OUT, and 99, the merge. Unnumbered notebooks beside them export nothing and each settle one question, such as RADIATION_SENSOR_CONTINUITY; the variable pages link the ones that bear on them.

_HOMOGENIZED removes a step that a hardware change left in the values, so the eras on either side can be compared. It does not make either era more accurate: it removes the change in the instrument’s bias, not the bias itself. TA and RH carry one because their probe and acquisition system were replaced together in January 2016 and the probe again in June 2026, and VPD because it is computed from them. PREC carries one because its acquisition system changed in 2018, and SWC one per depth because the soil profile was replaced in 2020. Most rescale the earlier era onto the level of the later one. TA also corrects the difference between the radiation shields of the probes, which acts only in daylight.
_GAPFILLED means a model produced some of the values. For TS the model is a regression on the other depths of the profile, and the METHOD flag says which values are measured and which are modelled.



The limitations of each product are on that variable’s page under Known limitations: the dates across which the record is not homogeneous, the columns that are estimates rather than measurements, and what a trend or period comparison over the series contains besides the weather. Table 1 links every page.
Two limitations belong to a reference rather than to a product and recur on several pages. The MeteoSwiss Lägern station changed level in October 2010, when its instrumentation was rebuilt. The NABEL series on the same tower stop being independent records in mid-2018. Neither changes a value in any file, but both change what a comparison against those series means.



Every product reads the quality-screened half-hourly record from the database, joins the older mst screening to the newer diive one, applies the site’s shared 2012 repairs where the variable was on the affected logger, and is checked before it is written. Independent references do the validation and, where a product is filled, much of the filling: MeteoSwiss Lägern 2.5 km away, NABEL at 49 m on the same tower until 2018, the MeteoSwiss gauge at Ehrendingen for rain, and for PREC every MeteoSwiss station within 21 km. The soil products have no external reference and are checked against the other depths of their own profile. Meteo Product Chain shows which product reads which.
Each notebook documents its own decisions and the evidence behind them: 01 SW_IN, 02 TA, 03 PPFD_IN, 04 RH, 05 PA, 06 LW_IN, 07 VPD, 08 PREC, 09 SWC, 10 TS, 11 G, 12 SW_OUT, 13 LW_OUT, and 99, the merge. Unnumbered notebooks beside them export nothing and each settle one question, such as RADIATION_SENSOR_CONTINUITY; the variable pages link the ones that bear on them.

title: Level-4.2: NEE partitioning
text:
Level-4.2: NEE partitioning
The partitioning of NEE into gross primary production (GPP) and ecosystem respiration (RECO) is not part of FP2026.1. It is switched off in 01_FPPC_IRGA72_NEE (RUN_PARTITIONING = False).
When switched on, the notebook partitions the NEE of each USTAR scenario, gap-filled with XGBoost, with the nighttime method (Reichstein et al. 2005) and the daytime method (Lasslop et al. 2010) as implemented in ONEFlux. ONEFlux itself partitions a flux gap-filled with MDS, so the results would differ from ONEFlux output. See diive: partitioning.




 Back to top

title: Level-3.3: USTAR filtering
text:
Level 3.3 flags the NEE records of low turbulence. A record with a friction velocity USTAR below the threshold gets flag 2, by day and by night; unlike ONEFlux, the first record above the threshold is kept. The filter is run at three constant thresholds, which give three USTAR scenarios: CUT_16, CUT_50 and CUT_84. The flags enter the overall quality flag (QCF) of each scenario.

title: Level-3.1: Storage correction
text:
The storage term is added to the CO2 flux of the enclosed-path LI-7200 (IRGA72): NEE_L3.1 is FC plus the single-point storage term SC_SINGLE from EddyPro. The storage term used is in SC_SINGLE_gfRMED_L3.1, and every record with a measured FC has one.
LE and H get no storage term, as in Pastorello et al. (2020). Their Level-3.1 columns LE_L3.1 and H_L3.1 keep the level in the name but equal LE and H.
Method, evidence and checks:

01_FPPC_IRGA72_NEE, Step 3: the screening and its check plot.
diive: storage term: how the screening works.



The single-point storage term is the change in the CO2 concentration at 47 m between two consecutive records, so errors in the concentration enter it directly. Two steps screen it before it is added; the values they remove are filled with a rolling median.

Next to gaps in the concentration. After a signal loss the LI-7200 can restart with readings far from the real concentration and return to it over hours, for example 695 ppm on 21 December 2017. The return entered the storage term as a large negative flux, while the jump at the restart fell into the gap and was never counted. Over 2016 to 2026 these one-sided changes summed to about −150 gC m-2. Next to each gap in CO2_MOLAR_DENSITY, the storage values are discarded until the concentration is back within 3 robust standard deviations of its median at the same time of day (±7 days).
Spikes. Isolated spikes, found with a Hampel filter on the double differences, are replaced together with one record on either side by the mean of that block. The block keeps its sum, so the storage term stays balanced.

After the screening the cumulative storage term at measured fluxes stays close to zero, except in December 2017 to January 2018 and in November 2020, when the analyser was failing. The fluxes of these periods are rejected by the signal strength test or removed by hand at Level 3.2, so their storage term does not enter the flux. The numbers of each run are in the notebook.










Column
Content




NEE_L3.1

SC_SINGLE_gfRMED_L3.1
Storage term used, µmol m-2 s-1


FLAG_SC_SINGLE_gfRMED_L3.1_ISFILLED
0 measured, 1 filled because missing, 2 spike block replaced by its mean, 3 discarded next to a gap and filled

title: Level-1: EddyPro settings

This page lists the settings of these runs, taken from their EddyPro project (.eddypro) and metadata (.metadata) files and checked against the EddyPro output. The runs and the merged record are described on Level-1; the setup periods on Yearly Notes.

title: Level-1.1: Self-heating correction
text:
NoteIn progress for FP2026.2



Level 1.1 applies only to the open-path LI-7500 (IRGA75). Its corrected fluxes are in progress for FP2026.2 and are not part of FP2026.1. The fluxes of FP2026.1 come from the enclosed-path LI-7200 (IRGA72), which needs no self-heating correction.








TipNotebooks




31_SelfHeatingCorrection_ScalingFactors_NEE: scaling factors from the parallel measurements of 2016-2017.
41_SelfHeatingCorrection_Application_IRGA75_NEE_2004-2019: the correction applied to the IRGA75 record.



The correction refines the self-heating correction for open-path analysers of earlier studies (Burba et al., 2006; Järvi et al., 2009; Kittler et al., 2017). It is implemented in the Python library diive and applies to the CO2 flux only. It has three steps: an unscaled flux correction term \(\text{FCT}_{\text{unsc}}\) from physical relations, a scaling factor \(\text{SF}\) derived against the enclosed-path analyser, and the application of the scaled term to the flux.


In sun, the sensor head of the open-path analyser heats up and warms the air in its sampling path. The open-path analyser measures the CO2 molar density (\(q_c\), mol m-3), so the warmer, less dense air lowers the measured concentration. The result is a negative flux bias, an apparent CO2 uptake.



The correction term is calculated from the heat transfer between the instrument surface and the air. Three methods are available: Järvi et al. (2009) (JAR09), Burba et al. (2006) (BUR06) and the multi-surface approach of Burba et al. (2008) (BUR08). For JAR09 and BUR06:
\[\text{FCT}_{\text{unsc}} = \frac{(T_s - T_a) q_c}{r_a T_a K} \left(1 + 1.6077 \frac{\rho_v}{\rho_d}\right)\]

\(T_s\), \(T_a\): instrument surface and ambient air temperature. \(T_s\) is estimated from \(T_a\) with the parameterisation of the chosen method.
\(q_c\): CO2 molar density (µmol m-3).
\(r_a\): aerodynamic resistance to heat transfer (s m-1), from wind speed \(u\) and friction velocity \(u_*\).
\(T_a K\): ambient air temperature in kelvin.
\(1 + 1.6077 \rho_v/\rho_d\): water vapour correction factor, analogous to the WPL correction.

Gaps in \(\text{FCT}_{\text{unsc}}\), where an auxiliary variable is missing, are filled with a machine-learning model (a random forest in the existing notebooks), so that the correction can be applied to every flux.



The physical term has to be tuned to the instrument and the site. The enclosed-path LI-7200 is not affected by self-heating and measured in parallel with the LI-7500 from January 2016 to December 2017, so its flux serves as the reference. The scaling factor \(\xi\) minimises the L1 norm of the difference between the cumulative sums of the corrected open-path flux and of the reference flux, taken at every time step:
\[\text{Minimize} \sum \left| \sum \left( \text{Flux}_{\text{OP, raw}} + \text{FCT}_{\text{unsc}} \cdot \xi \right) - \sum \text{Flux}_{\text{CP, ref}} \right|\]
Matching the cumulative sums makes the long-term CO2 budgets of the two analysers agree. The optimisation is done separately for daytime and nighttime and for classes of a variable such as \(u_*\), because self-heating depends on radiation and turbulence. Circular block bootstrapping resamples the time series while preserving its autocorrelation, and gives a median scaling factor with confidence intervals for each class.



Each half-hour receives the median scaling factor of its class and of day or night. The corrected flux is:
\[\text{FCT} = \text{FCT}_{\text{unsc\_gf}} \cdot \text{SF}\]
\[\text{Flux}_{\text{OP, corr}} = \text{Flux}_{\text{OP, raw}} + \text{FCT}\]

title: Known Issues
text:
Open points that affect users of FP2026.1. Limitations of a single meteorological variable are on that variable’s page under Meteorological data; release details are in Dataset versions. Planned work is tracked in the Issues of the repository.


There is no measured sensible heat flux between 10 January 2019 15:15 and 20 March 2019 18:45 (TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE), 3320 half-hours. The gap-filled series H_L3.1_L3.3_CUT_NONE_QCF_gfXG covers the period, so its values there come from the model alone; FLAG_H_L3.1_L3.3_CUT_NONE_QCF_gfXG_ISFILLED marks them.
The gap has two causes. Setup period 2019_2 (10 to 17 January 2019), in which both LI-7200 units were defective, has no Level-1 run, so its sonic data were not processed. In 2019_3 (17 January to 20 March 2019) the open-path LI-7500 stood in for the LI-7200; its run is processed with the other IRGA75 fluxes and is not part of FP2026.1. The same sonic was in operation throughout, so H could be computed for this period from these two setup periods. This is under review.
The gas fluxes FC, NEE and LE have the same gap, for the reasons above. See Level-4.1 for the other long gaps.



The annual mean of the measured H is 25.8 W m-2 in 2024, against 33.9 to 51.8 W m-2 in the other full years 2016 to 2025, about a third lower. Incoming shortwave radiation was also lower in 2024 than in the other years, but the cause has not been checked yet. Treat annual H in 2024 with caution until it is.



In spring 2016 the measurements of the start-up period were removed (1 March to 25 May 2016), and the gap includes the leaf-out. MDS fills this gap from records far away in time and gives a much larger uptake than XGBoost: the April-May sum of NEE (CUT_50) is -235 gC m-2 with MDS and -113 gC m-2 with XGBoost. In the other years the April-May sums of both methods lie between -30 and -195 gC m-2. XGBoost is the gap-filling method of this dataset, and MDS is included for comparison only. Use the XGBoost series (_gfXG). See Level-4.1.



FP2026.1 contains fluxes of the enclosed-path LI-7200 (IRGA72) only, from 11 January 2016. The fluxes of the open-path LI-7500 (IRGA75, 2004 to 12 December 2017 and 17 January to 20 March 2019), with the self-heating correction of Level-1.1, are in progress for FP2026.2. FP2026.2 will contain FP2026.1 in full and supersede it.



FLUXNET detects USTAR thresholds per year with the method of Pastorello et al. (2020). For CH-LAE, the thresholds it detects change markedly after 2015 (Figure 1). The cause is not known. The change coincides with a change of gas analyser:

until 11 January 2016, only the open-path LI-7500 was in operation;
from 11 January 2016 to 12 December 2017, the LI-7500 and the enclosed-path LI-7200 ran in parallel;
from 14 December 2017, only the LI-7200 was in operation, except from 17 January to 20 March 2019, when the LI-7500 stood in for it.

Before 2016, the threshold detection therefore used LI-7500 NEE, corrected for self-heating in a similar way to Kittler et al. (2017).
FP2026.1 does not use the FLUXNET thresholds. It filters NEE at three constant thresholds detected on the LI-7200 data of 2016 to 2024: 0.272 (CUT_16), 0.304 (CUT_50) and 0.340 m s-1 (CUT_84). These are kept on purpose although FLUXNET uses much higher thresholds for CH-LAE. See Level-3.3.






Figure 1: USTAR thresholds detected by FLUXNET, based on data 2004-2023, from the file FLX_CH-Lae_FLUXNET2015_AUXNEE_2004-2023_1-3.csv.









TipNotebook



Sonic anemometer data





The daily cycle of incoming shortwave radiation at 47 m (SW_IN_T1_47_1) lags behind potential radiation by a few minutes from 2022 onwards (Figure 2). No error was found in the processing, and the shift is already present in the raw data. Its cause is not known. The product page is Incoming shortwave radiation at 47 m.


The shift was detected by comparing the phase of the 24-hour component (FFT) of measured and potential radiation on clear days, selected as days on which the measured radiation reached at least 70 % of the potential. The 2016-2024 record has a median offset of +1.93 min; from 2022 the daily shifts are larger.



Each processing step was checked at the half-hour of 1 August 2022, 09:00 to 09:30, and by repeating the FFT analysis on data from different stages:

Resampling. The 1-minute raw values from 09:01 to 09:30, averaged by hand, give 654.8015067 W m-2. The meteo screening, which reads the database and resamples to 30 minutes, gives 654.801507 W m-2. Resampling introduces no shift.
Nighttime offset correction. With the correction of negative nighttime values (an offset of about -10 W m-2), the value is 665.219439 W m-2, the same in the screening output and in the screened data downloaded from the database. After all SW_IN sources are merged, the offset correction runs again on the merged record and gives 664.929319 W m-2.
Middle timestamp. When the record is loaded for gap-filling, its timestamp is converted to TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE. The value at 09:15 is 664.929319 W m-2, unchanged.
Gap-filling and merging. The value is unchanged after gap-filling and after the merge with the flux data. Air temperature at 09:15, averaged by hand from the 1-minute raw files, matches as well.
Database against raw files. The FFT analysis gives identical results on the 1-minute raw file of August 2022 and on the 1-minute data downloaded from the database, with a median shift of 6.39 min at 30-minute resolution and 5.90 min at 1-minute resolution. The same holds for July 2021, at both resolutions.







Figure 2: Time shift in incoming shortwave radiation, 2016-2024, from the phase of the 24-hour FFT component of measured against potential radiation, 30-minute data. Top: daily shifts with a 15-day rolling median, showing a lag from 2022. Middle: distribution of all shifts, median +1.93 min. Bottom: monthly distributions.

Pastorello, Gilberto, Carlo Trotta, Eleonora Canfora, et al. 2020. “The FLUXNET2015 Dataset and the ONEFlux Processing Pipeline for Eddy Covariance Data.” Scientific Data 7: 225. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-020-0534-3.

produced by Lukas Hörtnagl
Documentation and notebooks for the PI dataset of the mixed forest station CH-LAE (Laegeren). The site is part of Swiss FluxNet, operated by the Grassland Sciences Group, ETH Zurich. Group leader: Prof. Nina Buchmann.
The dataset holds ecosystem fluxes measured by eddy covariance (CO2, H2O and sensible heat) and meteorological data. FP2026.1 contains the fluxes of the enclosed-path LI-7200 gas analyser from January 2016 on. The fluxes of the open-path LI-7500, measured from 2004 to 2017, are being processed for FP2026.2.

Overview: what the dataset contains and how it was produced.
Variables: the main variables, their units and the column suffixes.
Meteorological data: one page per variable, with its columns, coverage, flags and known limitations, and an interactive dashboard for each.
Post-processing chain: how the fluxes were quality-controlled, filtered and gap-filled.

Recent changes to the documentation are in the commit history, planned updates in the Issues of the repository.

title: Data dashboards
text:
Interactive summaries of the meteorological products, one page per series. Each dashboard is a standalone HTML file with its own charts and styling. It opens without a server, works offline, and can be shared with someone who has neither this site nor the data.
The dashboards are built from the exported product files, not from the database, so they show the record as a user of the dataset receives it. They are rebuilt at every deploy of this site.






NoteThe dashboards end in December 2025



The dashboards are still built from the product versions that end on 31 December 2025. They do not yet show January to September 2026, although SW_IN, TA, PPFD_IN, RH, PA, LW_IN and VPD in FP2026.1 run to 30 September 2026. There are no dashboards for the fluxes yet.





Every month of the record on one grid
The years 2005 to 2025 by twelve months, one tile per month, coloured by the selected metric and marked with what was notable in that month. The same grid is drawn at three resolutions: months, meteorological seasons, and every day of the record. The daily raster is the only one of the three that never splits a spell at a boundary, so a heatwave or a drought that ran across a month end is visible as one event there and split in the other two.
The explorer currently reads only the meteorological products.




Each dashboard covers a single exported series year by year: coverage and provenance, seasonality, distributions, extremes, trends, and the comparison against an independent reference station where one exists. Every chart has a table of the same numbers below it.
The soil profiles have one dashboard per depth, because each depth has its own sensor history, gaps and limitations.

The daily raster is the only one of the three that never splits a spell at a boundary, so a heatwave or a drought that ran across a month end is visible as one event there and split in the other two.
The explorer currently reads only the meteorological products.

a correction for the energy balance closure.

title: Instrumentation
text:
The instruments that produced the measurements in this dataset, and the periods in which each was in place. Sensor identities come from three sources, in order of authority:

the datalogger programs, which name the channel, its sensor and its conversion constants, and are the only source for how a raw signal became a value;
the GIN fieldbook device columns (Device Name, Device Model), which name the physical unit and its serial number at a location;
Yearly Notes, whose Setup EC table is the authority for the eddy covariance setup periods, sensor separations and flux-run configuration.







WarningFieldbook dates are entry dates, not deployment dates



The GIN export records when an entry was written, not when a device was installed. Entries dated 1 January 2016 (and 2003, 2006) are backdated inventory imports made when GIN was introduced: a device whose earliest entry carries one of these dates was already at the site, and its installation date is not in the export. Only entries that describe an event (a replacement, a repair, a device marked defective) date anything.




Two gas analysers were operated at this level, and the fluxes are processed per analyser rather than per year. The fluxes in FP2026.1 come from the LI-7200 (IRGA72) only. The LI-7500 (IRGA75) fluxes are in progress for FP2026.2.

The LI-7500 was removed from the site on 12 December 2017 but continued to write empty values into the data stream until it was taken out of it on 31 January 2018, which is why the setup table lists it for two further periods with no flux run. IRGA72 spans two physical LI-7200 units, exchanged inside the 2019 gap; the second has a different column set in the raw stream. The analyser was moved on the boom in March 2023, which changed its separation from the sonic. The fieldbook also records a freshly calibrated LI-7200 installed on 2 December 2025. The dates per setup period are in the setup table of the Yearly Notes.
The fieldbook records the enclosed-path system at this level as an LI-7200RS head with an LI-7550 analyser unit and an LI-7200-101 flow module.

The 8 January 2016 date covers several of these rows because they were one visit: the boom was retracted that morning and the LI-7200 with its analyser and flow-module box, the replacement cup anemometer, both Kipp & Zonen PAR sensors and a new tower box were installed together. The LI-7200’s first raw binary is three days later, on 11 January 2016. A new reflected-PAR sensor had been fitted once before, at the end of June or beginning of July 2008; that entry is a remark added after the fact and dates the work only to within about a fortnight.
The temperature and humidity sensor is identified from the logger programs alone. The fieldbook records no temperature or humidity device at the 47 m level before June 2026; the first such entry is a Campbell HygroVUE10 added on 5 June 2026, which replaced the CS215 on the same channel (see Air temperature and Relative humidity). The MP101A and CS215 identifications, and the January 2016 date of the change, rest on the CR10X and CR1000 programs and on the step in the data. The step is quantified and corrected on the Air temperature page.
The radiometer change is dated by the fieldbook, the calibration by the logger programs. The CNR1 predates GIN and has no device entry of its own, but a 2008 entry recording a relay replacement for it on the tower’s CR10X meteo logger confirms that it was in service then. The CNR4 was installed on 14 December 2021. Neither instrument change moved the shortwave series measurably; the product notebook tests this (see Incoming shortwave radiation).
One constant for four detectors. A CNR1 head holds four sensors, each calibrated separately by the factory. The logger programs convert all four with a single factor, that of the pyranometer, so the longwave and outgoing channels were converted with a factor that is not their own. The CNR4 is converted with four separate sensitivities, so the two instruments cannot be compared channel by channel without allowing for that difference. Both outgoing products flag the instrument era for this reason.
Two dates are easily confused. The CNR1 instruction first appears in the logger program of 18 August 2005, which measures all four channels. The program of 14 September 2005 changed the relay, moving the outgoing channels onto different differential inputs; the archive’s record begins on the same day. The period column above gives the record, not the program.
The serial is not fully reconciled. The logger program comments and this table give the tower CNR1 as SN 020484. The fieldbook row recording the 14 December 2021 exchange names CNR1_020522, at a different location. This is most likely a bookkeeping artefact in GIN rather than a second instrument, but it has not been resolved.






WarningUnverified: 14 December 2021 to 7 January 2022



The CNR4 was installed on 14 December 2021, and the installing entry notes that the logger script still needed to be adapted to the new calibration constants. The logger program was updated on 7 January 2022, adding the four CNR4 sensitivities and new raw-voltage variables.
The two dates are 24 days apart, and the conversion the logger applied in between is not recorded. If the CNR4 was read with the CNR1’s multiplier, the values of that period are wrong by the ratio of the two sensitivities.
Two products have tested the window. Together they bound the error but do not identify the constant. Outgoing shortwave radiation compares the window against the MeteoSwiss Lägern station and finds the levels not consistent with the old constant still being in force, which argues against the worst case. Outgoing longwave radiation bounds any error there at about 1.6 W m⁻², roughly 0.5 % of the reported value, because a conversion error scales only the small net signal a pyrgeometer measures and not the large Stefan-Boltzmann term added to it.
The window is flagged, not corrected, in all four radiation products. A correction, if one is derived, has to be applied to all four channels together, since they share the head and the constant. The bound above limits the error; it does not show that there is none.





The soil sensors were replaced as a set on 19 March 2020. This is the main date for the soil variables: a change of sensor generation with no overlap, so the step across it cannot be calibrated away.

The soil heat flux row describes three sensors rather than one. The GIN device records list three HFP01 plates at this location. One of them was discarded at the logger-box rebuild of 24 March 2021 and the two survivors were kept, which is why the product exports three plate columns of which the third ends in 2021. The plates sit metres apart under a deciduous canopy, so they are not replicates: under leaf-off sunflecks one plate can read several times another, because the light reaches them differently.
The depth is the one declared in the archive, not a surveyed figure. The field names carry 0.05 m until the end of 2011, 0.025 m from 2012 to March 2021, and 0.05 m again afterwards. The product notebook tests from the size and timing of the daily cycle whether the plates were reburied shallower. The result matches neither a move nor an unchanged depth, so the question is open. See Soil heat flux.
The 0.5 m depth exists only in the TEROS 12 generation, which is why the soil-water-content product carries a homogenised second column at four depths and deliberately none at 0.5 m. A second profile, FF2, carries MPS-2 water potential sensors at 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2 and 0.3 m. Coverage, flags and the sensor-generation step are documented under Soil water content and Soil temperature.
The subcanopy station (M1_2) carries a CS215 temperature and humidity sensor, installed on 26 March 2021 to replace a Rotronic MP100, alongside an Apogee SQ-521 and a LI-COR LI-190SA quantum sensor, an Apogee SN-500-SS net radiometer and a W200P wind vane. Forest-floor acquisition is a CR1000 with an AM16/32B multiplexer until March 2021 and an ARK-1124C from October 2021.



A temperature, humidity and wind profile is operated on the tower and on satellite masts at the site (T1_17.5, T1_35, M2, M3, M4). Its temperature and humidity sensors are Rotronic units of several generations: MP101, MP400H and MP402H transmitters with HygroClip S2, S3 and HC2-S3 probes, with individual heads replaced repeatedly between 2015 and 2021. Its wind sensors are Gill WindSonics. None of these profile sensors contributes to this dataset, which takes its meteorology from the 47 m level and the forest floor. They are listed here only because published descriptions of the site sometimes name them.



Three sensor identities given in the literature do not match the fieldbook or the logger programs. They are listed here for readers who compare this dataset with those papers.
Shekhar et al. (2024) give the site’s temperature and humidity sensor as a Rotronic HygroClip HC2-S3. The fieldbook does hold HygroClip HC2-S3 units at CH-LAE, but on the profile masts (M3, M4, T1_35), never at the 47 m level that supplies this dataset, and the logger programs give the MP101A and CS215 above.
The same study gives soil moisture as a Decagon ECH2O EC-5. The string EC-5 does not occur anywhere in the fieldbook export; the CH-LAE profile is EC-20 and then TEROS 12, as above. The study assigns EC-20 to the subalpine site it compares against, so the two sites’ sensors appear to have been transposed.
The same study assigns the Delta-T BF2 radiation sensor, serial BF2116, to the subalpine site. That serial is registered in the fieldbook at CH-LAE at the 47 m level.
These differences do not affect the values in either dataset, only the attribution of the instruments.





Shekhar, Ankit, Lukas Hörtnagl, Eugénie Paul-Limoges, et al. 2024. “Contrasting Impact of Extreme Soil and Atmospheric Dryness on the Functioning of Trees and Forests.” Science of The Total Environment 916: 169931. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2024.169931.

The LI-7500 was removed from the site on 12 December 2017 but continued to write empty values into the data stream until it was taken out of it on 31 January 2018, which is why the setup table lists it for two further periods with no flux run. IRGA72 spans two physical LI-7200 units, exchanged inside the 2019 gap; the second has a different column set in the raw stream. The analyser was moved on the boom in March 2023, which changed its separation from the sonic. The fieldbook also records a freshly calibrated LI-7200 installed on 2 December 2025. The dates per setup period are in the setup table of the Yearly Notes.
The fieldbook records the enclosed-path system at this level as an LI-7200RS head with an LI-7550 analyser unit and an LI-7200-101 flow module.

The 8 January 2016 date covers several of these rows because they were one visit: the boom was retracted that morning and the LI-7200 with its analyser and flow-module box, the replacement cup anemometer, both Kipp & Zonen PAR sensors and a new tower box were installed together. The LI-7200’s first raw binary is three days later, on 11 January 2016. A new reflected-PAR sensor had been fitted once before, at the end of June or beginning of July 2008; that entry is a remark added after the fact and dates the work only to within about a fortnight.
The temperature and humidity sensor is identified from the logger programs alone. The fieldbook records no temperature or humidity device at the 47 m level before June 2026; the first such entry is a Campbell HygroVUE10 added on 5 June 2026, which replaced the CS215 on the same channel (see Air temperature and Relative humidity). The MP101A and CS215 identifications, and the January 2016 date of the change, rest on the CR10X and CR1000 programs and on the step in the data. The step is quantified and corrected on the Air temperature page.
The radiometer change is dated by the fieldbook, the calibration by the logger programs. The CNR1 predates GIN and has no device entry of its own, but a 2008 entry recording a relay replacement for it on the tower’s CR10X meteo logger confirms that it was in service then. The CNR4 was installed on 14 December 2021. Neither instrument change moved the shortwave series measurably; the product notebook tests this (see Incoming shortwave radiation).
One constant for four detectors. A CNR1 head holds four sensors, each calibrated separately by the factory. The logger programs convert all four with a single factor, that of the pyranometer, so the longwave and outgoing channels were converted with a factor that is not their own. The CNR4 is converted with four separate sensitivities, so the two instruments cannot be compared channel by channel without allowing for that difference. Both outgoing products flag the instrument era for this reason.
Two dates are easily confused. The CNR1 instruction first appears in the logger program of 18 August 2005, which measures all four channels. The program of 14 September 2005 changed the relay, moving the outgoing channels onto different differential inputs; the archive’s record begins on the same day. The period column above gives the record, not the program.
The serial is not fully reconciled. The logger program comments and this table give the tower CNR1 as SN 020484. The fieldbook row recording the 14 December 2021 exchange names CNR1_020522, at a different location. This is most likely a bookkeeping artefact in GIN rather than a second instrument, but it has not been resolved.






WarningUnverified: 14 December 2021 to 7 January 2022



The CNR4 was installed on 14 December 2021, and the installing entry notes that the logger script still needed to be adapted to the new calibration constants. The logger program was updated on 7 January 2022, adding the four CNR4 sensitivities and new raw-voltage variables.
The two dates are 24 days apart, and the conversion the logger applied in between is not recorded. If the CNR4 was read with the CNR1’s multiplier, the values of that period are wrong by the ratio of the two sensitivities.
Two products have tested the window. Together they bound the error but do not identify the constant. Outgoing shortwave radiation compares the window against the MeteoSwiss Lägern station and finds the levels not consistent with the old constant still being in force, which argues against the worst case. Outgoing longwave radiation bounds any error there at about 1.6 W m⁻², roughly 0.5 % of the reported value, because a conversion error scales only the small net signal a pyrgeometer measures and not the large Stefan-Boltzmann term added to it.
The window is flagged, not corrected, in all four radiation products. A correction, if one is derived, has to be applied to all four channels together, since they share the head and the constant. The bound above limits the error; it does not show that there is none.
