The soil heat flux row describes three sensors rather than one. The GIN device records list three HFP01 plates at this location. One of them was discarded at the logger-box rebuild of 24 March 2021 and the two survivors were kept, which is why the product exports three plate columns of which the third ends in 2021. The plates sit metres apart under a deciduous canopy, so they are not replicates: under leaf-off sunflecks one plate can read several times another, because the light reaches them differently.
The depth is the one declared in the archive, not a surveyed figure. The field names carry 0.05 m until the end of 2011, 0.025 m from 2012 to March 2021, and 0.05 m again afterwards. The product notebook tests from the size and timing of the daily cycle whether the plates were reburied shallower. The result matches neither a move nor an unchanged depth, so the question is open. See Soil heat flux.
The 0.5 m depth exists only in the TEROS 12 generation, which is why the soil-water-content product carries a homogenised second column at four depths and deliberately none at 0.5 m. A second profile, FF2, carries MPS-2 water potential sensors at 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2 and 0.3 m. Coverage, flags and the sensor-generation step are documented under Soil water content and Soil temperature.
The subcanopy station (M1_2) carries a CS215 temperature and humidity sensor, installed on 26 March 2021 to replace a Rotronic MP100, alongside an Apogee SQ-521 and a LI-COR LI-190SA quantum sensor, an Apogee SN-500-SS net radiometer and a W200P wind vane. Forest-floor acquisition is a CR1000 with an AM16/32B multiplexer until March 2021 and an ARK-1124C from October 2021.

title: Instrumentation
text: A temperature, humidity and wind profile is operated on the tower and on satellite masts at the site (T1_17.5, T1_35, M2, M3, M4). Its temperature and humidity sensors are Rotronic units of several generations: MP101, MP400H and MP402H transmitters with HygroClip S2, S3 and HC2-S3 probes, with individual heads replaced repeatedly between 2015 and 2021. Its wind sensors are Gill WindSonics. None of these profile sensors contributes to this dataset, which takes its meteorology from the 47 m level and the forest floor. They are listed here only because published descriptions of the site sometimes name them.

title: Instrumentation
text:
Three sensor identities given in the literature do not match the fieldbook or the logger programs. They are listed here for readers who compare this dataset with those papers.
Shekhar et al. (2024) give the site’s temperature and humidity sensor as a Rotronic HygroClip HC2-S3. The fieldbook does hold HygroClip HC2-S3 units at CH-LAE, but on the profile masts (M3, M4, T1_35), never at the 47 m level that supplies this dataset, and the logger programs give the MP101A and CS215 above.
The same study gives soil moisture as a Decagon ECH2O EC-5. The string EC-5 does not occur anywhere in the fieldbook export; the CH-LAE profile is EC-20 and then TEROS 12, as above. The study assigns EC-20 to the subalpine site it compares against, so the two sites’ sensors appear to have been transposed.
The same study assigns the Delta-T BF2 radiation sensor, serial BF2116, to the subalpine site. That serial is registered in the fieldbook at CH-LAE at the 47 m level.
These differences do not affect the values in either dataset, only the attribution of the instruments.

title: Instrumentation
text: Shekhar, Ankit, Lukas Hörtnagl, Eugénie Paul-Limoges, et al. 2024. “Contrasting Impact of Extreme Soil and Atmospheric Dryness on the Functioning of Trees and Forests.” Science of The Total Environment 916: 169931. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2024.169931.

title: Level-0: Preliminary flux calculations
text:
Level 0 is a preliminary flux calculation with relaxed settings. Its results are not part of the dataset. They are used to choose the settings of the final calculation (Level 1):

to check that the flux processing works,
to check the wind direction across years,
to choose the time-lag windows for the final runs.

The Level-0 output of all EddyPro runs is merged into one record per gas analyser, and the checks below read that record. The method is described in the Swiss FluxNet flux processing chain.






NoteIRGA75 in progress



FP2026.1 contains the fluxes of the enclosed-path LI-7200 (IRGA72) only. The Level-0 results of the open-path LI-7500 (IRGA75) are shown here because they set up its final runs, which are in progress for FP2026.2. The IRGA75 fluxes are not part of FP2026.1.

The lag between the turbulent fluctuations of the vertical wind and of the gas was first searched in a wide time window (OPENLAG). For each setup period, the peak of the histogram of the lags found became the nominal (default) lag, and a window as narrow as possible around it became the lag search window of the final runs.



The OPENLAG window was -1 s to +10 s from 2016 to 2018 and -1 s to +20 s from 2019 on. The wider window was needed because an artificial lag of about 8 s was introduced in 2019.

title: Level-1: Final flux calculations
text:
Level 1 is the final flux calculation with EddyPro, run with fluxrun, one run per setup period. Its FLUXNET output is the input of the post-processing chain. FP2026.1 contains it in full: 329 columns, listed in the section “L1 fluxes IRGA72” of the _INFO.md file.
The Level-1 fluxes are not quality-filtered, and FC carries no storage term. For analyses, use the columns of the post-processing chain (see QCF and Level 4.1).
Notebook: 99_IRGA72_L1_MERGED_2016-2026.09 merges the runs and checks the merged record.

title: Level-2: Quality flag expansion
text:
Level 2 turns the quality information of the EddyPro output into one flag per test, FLAG_L2_FC_<TEST>_TEST (0 passed, 1 warning, 2 rejected), and combines them into the overall flag FLAG_L2_FC_QCF (see QCF). The tests are the same as in the 2016-2024 processing.
Notebook: 01_FPPC_IRGA72_NEE, Step 2.



Table 1: Level-2 tests of FC.










Flag
Test
Setting




SSITC
Steady state and developed turbulence (EddyPro)
Flag as reported


SCF
Size of the spectral correction factor
Warning from 2, rejected from 4


SIGNAL_STRENGTH
Signal strength of the LI-7200 (CUSTOM_SIGNAL_STRENGTH_IRGA72_MEAN)
Rejected below 60


CO2_VM97_SPIKE_HF
Spikes in the raw data (Vickers and Mahrt 1997)
Hard flag


CO2_VM97_DROPOUT_HF
Dropouts in the raw data (Vickers and Mahrt 1997)
Hard flag






Gas completeness, angle of attack and steadiness of the horizontal wind are not tested. In practice the SSITC test rejects nearly all records that Level 2 removes.


Notebooks: 11_FPPC_IRGA72_LE, 15_FPPC_IRGA72_H.

LE uses the same tests, with its own SSITC and spectral correction flags and the raw-data tests of H2O.
H comes from the sonic anemometer alone, so the tests of the gas analyser (signal strength, raw-data tests of CO2 and H2O) do not apply. The raw-data tests are those of the sonic temperature (T_SONIC_VM97_TEST): spikes, dropouts and absolute limits. The absolute-limits test is added for H, because a sonic temperature outside its plausible range indicates water or ice on the transducers.

title: Level-3.2: Outlier flagging
text:
Five tests remove outliers from NEE_L3.1. Each writes a flag column FLAG_L3.2_NEE_L3.1_QCF_OUTLIER_<TEST>_TEST (0 kept, 2 removed); a record counts for the first test that removed it.
Method, evidence and checks:

01_FPPC_IRGA72_NEE, Step 4: one plot per test and an overview of all removals.
diive: outlier tests: how the tests work.











Flag
Test
Settings




MANUAL
Periods removed by hand, see below
Whole days, both ends included


ABSLIM
Absolute limits
±50 µmol m-2 s-1


HAMPEL
Hampel filter on double differences: single spikes
13 days, 5.5 sigma, day and night separately


HAMPEL_2
Hampel filter on the values per time of day: values wrong for their time of day
13 days, 5.5 sigma, the half-hour and one on either side, at least 10 values


NEGNIGHT
Nighttime values clearly below zero
Below −4 times the robust spread of all nighttime values within ±15 days



The nighttime test uses the spread of all nighttime values rather than the uncertainty of each record. The per-record uncertainty grows with bad values in a noisy stretch: on 12 December 2021, while the LI-7200 was failing, night values of −41, −20 and −13 µmol m-2 s-1 passed a test based on it. High nighttime values are real respiration and are not tested.
Compared with the 2016-2024 processing, the absolute limits are kept, and the trimming of low values and the local standard deviation test are replaced by the two Hampel filters and the nighttime test.




Start-up of the LI-7200 in 2016. During the installation (11 to 22 January) and a period with too low a flow rate (1 March to 25 May), water in the filter lowered the fluxes. Both periods are removed by hand.
19 May to 7 June 2018. There is no FC: the flow module of the analyser had failed, so this period was processed with the sonic anemometer only.
30 December 2018 to 10 January 2019. The LI-7200 (IRGA72-B) was failing: low signal strength from December, an iced inlet filter, error codes and repeated stops of the data acquisition. It was replaced on 11 January 2019. Removed by hand.
8 November to 6 December 2020. A fault of the gas analyser: the scatter of the flux rose to many times its usual level, with half-hourly values from −190 to +190 µmol m-2 s-1, while the flow rate and the sonic stayed normal. The signal strength fell from 100 to about 60 on 12 November and recovered after the LI-7200 was replaced on 10 December. 8 to 27 November and 4 to 6 December are removed by hand; the days between them are within the usual scatter.
15 January to 4 February 2026. The nighttime scatter was about twice its seasonal level, also after the outlier tests, with winter daytime values above 20 µmol m-2 s-1. The signal strength fell from 93 to 87; the scatter ended when the LI-7200 was cleaned on 4 February. Removed by hand.
Wrong calibration gas, 14 December 2017 to 15 March 2019. The CO2 concentrations of this period were calibrated against the wrong reference gas. The correction, a factor of 0.974 on the concentration, was applied when the raw data were converted with bico, so FC is corrected.

The long gaps without any FC are listed on Level-4.1.



The notebooks 11_FPPC_IRGA72_LE and 15_FPPC_IRGA72_H run the first four tests. Negative nighttime values are not tested: LE can be negative at night (dew), and a negative H at night is physical.








Flux
Absolute limits
Why




LE
−50 to 800 W m-2
Above 800 W m-2 most values, and above 900 W m-2 all, exceed the incoming shortwave radiation of the same half-hour; below −50 W m-2, LE would mean condensation of more than 0.07 mm h-1.


H
−200 to 800 W m-2
The upper limit keeps the largest daytime values that agree with the incoming radiation, in spring before leaf-out; the lower limit lies below the nighttime values of summer and removes the large negative values of wet and freezing episodes in winter.



Periods removed by hand:

LE: the same windows as FC. The LI-7200 measures H2O and CO2 in the same cell, so its faults affect both fluxes; each window was checked in LE.
H comes from the sonic anemometer alone, so the faults of the gas analyser do not apply: H stays normal during the 2016 start-up and the November 2020 fault. Only 20 to 26 December 2018 is removed: after work at the LI-7200 the instrument boom was not fixed in its position, so the sonic could move with it.
Sonic electronics, 19 December 2019 to 10 January 2020. After the change from the HS-100 to the HS-50 (see Instrumentation) the electronics unit of the HS-100 stayed in use, so the fieldbook rates these data as possibly not entirely accurate. H of this period does not differ from the weeks around it and is kept.
Wet or freezing weather. The sonic can give H of several hundred W m-2 of either sign, while the sonic temperature falls several kelvin below its usual offset from the air temperature: water or ice on the transducers. These episodes occur every winter, most often in 2016 to 2019, before the sonic head was replaced. The absolute limits and the Hampel filters remove their values.

title: Level-4.1: Gap-filling
text:
The gaps of each USTAR scenario (CUT_16, CUT_50, CUT_84) are filled with XGBoost, the method of this dataset, and with MDS, the standard method of FLUXNET, for comparison only. Use the XGBoost series. The gap-filled series end in _gfXG and _gfMDS; their flags FLAG_..._ISFILLED are 0 where the flux was measured.
Method, evidence and checks:

01_FPPC_IRGA72_NEE, Steps 5 to 12: the records for gap-filling, the models and their scores, the comparison of the methods, the annual sums and the uncertainty.
11_FPPC_IRGA72_LE and 15_FPPC_IRGA72_H: the same for LE (with ET) and H.
diive: gap-filling with XGBoost, with MDS, uncertainty.



The gap-filling starts from the records that passed Levels 2 to 3.3 with a quality flag of 0 or 1, by day and by night (NEE_L3.1_L3.3_<scenario>_QCF, see QCF). The highest-quality records, flag 0, are in NEE_L3.1_L3.3_<scenario>_QCF0; use them for analyses that need measured values only.
The drivers are three complete meteo series at 47 m: air temperature (TA_T1_47_1_HOMOGENIZED_gfXG), vapour pressure deficit (VPD_T1_47_1_HOMOGENIZED) and incoming shortwave radiation (SW_IN_T1_47_1_gfXG). Temperature and VPD are the homogenised versions, which correct for the probe changes in 2016 and June 2026.



Each year has its own model for each scenario, trained on that year and its two neighbouring years, with features engineered from the drivers and selected with SHAP values. All scenarios use the same features. The number of trees is chosen once by cross-validation on held-out blocks of 14 days (up to 1000 tested) and used for every year: 110 trees for NEE, 130 for LE and 140 for H. The gaps are filled by a model refitted on all complete records. The 2016-2024 processing used a random forest.



MDS (mode='diive') fills every gap, also long ones, and uses only measured driver values as similar conditions. In long gaps it can rest on very few similar records, so a few unusual values near the edge of a gap set the fill for days. The notebook splits the difference between the sums of MDS and XGBoost by day and night, month and gap length.



The model fills these gaps without measurements nearby:

1 to 22 January 2016, before and during the installation of the LI-7200. With the start-up period removed by hand (1 March to 25 May), 2016 lacks about 108 days of measurements, including the leaf-out, so its annual sum rests largely on the model;
18 May to 7 June 2018, failed flow module;
10 January to 20 March 2019, both LI-7200 units defective, then the LI-7500 as a stand-in, whose fluxes are in progress for FP2026.2 and not part of FP2026.1;
18 December 2020 to 4 January 2021;
13 December 2021 to 7 February 2022, raw data that cannot be converted.

LE has the same gaps as FC, and the periods removed by hand add to them. H exists in several periods without FC (the 2016 start-up, 18 May to 7 June 2018, 6 to 10 January 2019, 18 December 2020 to 4 January 2021); its long gaps are 10 January to 20 March 2019 and 13 December 2021 to 7 February 2022. LE and H have no USTAR scenarios, no storage term and no uncertainty columns.



The uncertainty of the CUT_50 series of each method follows Pastorello et al. (2020), in µmol m-2 s-1 at 1 sigma:







Column
Content




_RANDUNC
Random uncertainty: spread of measured fluxes under similar conditions


_USTARUNC
USTAR uncertainty: half the difference between the CUT_84 and CUT_16 series


_JOINTUNC
Both combined: √(RANDUNC² + USTARUNC²)



For annual sums the random part adds in quadrature, the USTAR part as half the difference between the CUT_84 and CUT_16 sums. The difference between XGBoost and MDS is not part of the joint uncertainty; the notebook reports it beside it.




MDS in spring 2016. The data from 1 March to 25 May 2016 are removed (start-up of the LI-7200, see Level 3.2). MDS fills this gap from time windows with a median width of 70 days and gives far more uptake than XGBoost: April and May 2016 sum to -235 gC m-2 with MDS against -113 gC m-2 with XGBoost (CUT_50). In the other years, April and May range from -30 to -195 gC m-2 with either method. Use the XGBoost series.
H from 10 January to 20 March 2019 is model output only: there is no Level-1 H in this period (see Level 1).
H in 2024 is about a third lower than in the other years. This has not been checked yet.

title: Soil heat flux at the forest floor
text:
Half-hourly soil heat flux from the three Hukseflux HFP01 plates of the FF1 forest-floor station at CH-LAE, 2004-2025. The file is 11_METEO_G_FF1_2004-2025 (parquet and CSV): 373,728 records on a continuous 30-minute index, TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (middle of the half-hour), in local time (UTC+01:00, no daylight saving), from 2004-09-07 00:15 to 2025-12-31 23:45. Values are in W m-2, and positive means heat moving down into the soil. The index begins in September 2004 because the plate record begins then.
The series ends on 31 December 2025. It is part of FP2026.1 and of the merged meteo product, where it is NaN from 1 January 2026; the extension to 30 September 2026 is in progress. Both carry the reconciled column G_FF1_0.05_HOMOGENIZED and its NPLATES flag, not the three plate columns.
The interactive dashboard summarises the reconciled column (coverage, provenance, seasonality, distributions, extremes and trends). The three plate columns are shown in the notebook only.
Notebooks:

11_METEO_G_FF1: builds the product. It separates the acquisition changes from the field renames in the database, tests the declared depth, derives the scale correction and measures what the correction leaves.
The screening notebooks of the two plates still in use after the 2021 rebuild, plate 1 and plate 2, which apply each plate’s absolute limits to the raw record.
10_METEO_TS_FF1 and 09_METEO_SWC_FF1: soil temperature and soil water content of the same profile. They are used for the depth test and the storage-term estimate and contribute no values to this product.
Meteo_Product_Chain: where this product sits in the chain.







ImportantWhich column to use



The record spans three acquisition setups. Their boundaries are not the dates on which the fields were renamed in the database. The measurement changes at the March/April 2012 reconfiguration of the forest-floor logger and at the March 2021 logger-box rebuild. The field names change at the end of 2011 and at the 2021 rebuild.

Within one setup, use G_FF1_0.05_1, _2 or _3, which is what each plate recorded.
Across the 2012 or 2021 boundary, use G_FF1_0.05_HOMOGENIZED. Read The reconciled column first: it averages two plates after putting each earlier setup onto the scale and zero point of the current setup, and it is a derived estimate, not a measurement.
Exclude source flags 4 and 5 from any calculation. Flag 4 marks 519 records of the 2012 reconfiguration itself. Flag 5 marks 18,911 records in which a plate read with reversed sign. Neither is on the scale of any setup.

Nothing is gap-filled. A missing record is NaN, never 0; for a signed flux, 0 means that no heat crossed the plate. Heat storage in the soil above the plates is not added, so an energy-balance closure computed from these columns is a closure at 0.05 m, not at the surface.

The check reads each plate on its own. In the winter of 2004/2005 two of the three plates were reversed at the same time, so a comparison against the other plates would have marked plate 3, the correct one, as the outlier.
The periods are whole calendar months. Plate 2 actually reverses within one half-hour, on 2011-06-16 between 09:15 and 09:45, when it steps by −17 W m-2 while plate 1 does not move; the month of the change is excluded with the rest.
The values are not negated. Negated, these periods lie 5.0 to 10.8 W m-2 from the same plate’s readings in the same calendar months of the nearest unaffected years of the same setup. Over July to December 2011, for example, plate 2 as measured is at −8.4 W m-2, close to plate 1 at −9.0; negated it would be +8.4, while the plate normally reads about −4.8. A swapped wire negates cleanly; a wrong multiplier and offset in the logger program does not, and the maintenance record has those being corrected in 2012. Removing the offset as well would require fitting the plate to a neighbour without an independent reference. The records are therefore excluded from every fit, every per-setup statistic and the reconciled column. As a result, the reconciled column rests on plate 1 alone in the second half of 2011 and has no value in the winter of 2004/2005.



The database declares the plates at 0.025 m between 2012 and 2021, which would mean they were reburied at half the depth. A daily temperature wave weakens and is delayed with depth, so a plate moved to 0.025 m should show a daily amplitude about 1.28 times larger and a peak about 0.95 h earlier. Neither is seen. Across the two setups the mean amplitude ratio is 0.47 and the peak moves 2.8 h later. A change of depth cannot produce either sign, so the product treats the plates as at 0.05 m throughout. The cause of the 2012 change is not identified. The maintenance record points to the corrected multipliers in the new logger program; a plate disturbed while the wiring was redone is not ruled out.
The sign convention held across both boundaries. With the reversed periods set aside, every plate in every setup reads higher in the afternoon than before dawn, by 1.1 to 11.1 W m-2, so no plate was rewired backwards at a boundary.
The forest-floor rewiring of 25 June 2015, which stepped soil water content by about 3.9 % VWC, left no measurable trace here: the change in each plate’s spread across that date stays within what late June ordinarily shows. The comparison rests on twelve to seventeen years and is one-sided (a rewiring would raise the spread, not lower it), so the date is unremarkable rather than cleared.




G_FF1_0.05_HOMOGENIZED allows an analysis to cross the 2012 and 2021 boundaries. It is the mean of plates 1 and 2, after each of their earlier setups has been put onto the scale and the zero point of the diive setup. The diive setup is the reference because it is current and its annual means lie within a few tenths of a W m-2 of zero.
The correction has two terms, applied in this order.

A multiplicative gain per calendar month, fitted on the within-month spread, puts the amplitudes of the three setups onto one scale. The within-month spread of the original acquisition is 1.3 to 1.9 times that of the reference setup, and that of the reconfigured acquisition about 40 % of it. The gains run from 0.37 to 1.02 for the original and from 1.50 to 3.05 for the reconfigured acquisition.
One additive constant per plate and setup, fitted afterwards on the season-matched level of the gained series, sets the zero point. Over a full year the soil returns to about the temperature it started at, so the flux at a few centimetres must average near zero. The reconfigured and diive setups meet this to a few tenths of a W m-2; the original acquisition is 3.1 to 3.8 W m-2 below the reference at both plates. The constants are −1.48 and −1.67 W m-2 for the original and +0.13 and +1.17 W m-2 for the reconfigured acquisition. They are smaller than these level differences because the gain, applied first, also moves the mean.

Both terms are fitted on climatology alone. No service measures soil heat flux at this plot, the setups do not overlap by a single half-hour, and all three plates change together at both boundaries. Only the near-zero annual mean ties the additive term to something outside the record; the gain has no such anchor.
What remains. The season-matched level of the reconciled column steps by +0.47 W m-2 at 2012 and −0.03 W m-2 at 2021. The same statistic at 33 dates inside a single setup moves by 0.46 W m-2 in the median and up to 1.89 W m-2. Both boundaries are therefore within the ordinary variation, but a step smaller than 1.89 W m-2 cannot be detected by this test. With the gain alone, the 2012 boundary failed the same check.



A plate at 0.05 m measures the heat crossing that depth. The soil above it stores and releases heat that the plate does not see. This product exports the plate flux only. The storage term is estimated in the notebook, not added, from soil temperature and soil water content at 0.05 m (products 10 and 09) and a literature value for the dry heat capacity, because bulk density is not measured at this site. The notebook reports the estimate at that value and at 30 % above and below it.
In the reference setup the storage term has a spread of 2.36 W m-2 against 5.09 W m-2 for the measured flux, about 46 %. In the earlier setups it is 2.06 times the measured flux (reconfigured) and 3.44 times (original), but these ratios compare different instruments, because the plates’ own spread and the diurnal amplitude of the temperature reference both change at the setup boundaries. Use the value for the setup you work in, not an average of the three. The term averages near zero over a long record, so it changes the daily and seasonal course, not the level. Adding it properly would require a measured bulk density and a temperature above the plate, and neither is available at this site.




The plate columns are exported as recorded and step at the setup boundaries. The correction is only in G_FF1_0.05_HOMOGENIZED. A mean or trend across 2012 or 2021 from a plate column mixes three scales and three zero points.
Amplitudes are not comparable across 2011/2012 in any column. At the 2012 acquisition change the median daily amplitude of plates _1 and _2 falls by a factor of three to four, from 8.4 and 10.3 W m-2 in 2011 to 2.6 and 3.3 in 2012 and 1.2 and 1.8 in 2013. Plate _3 does not follow: 15.7, 12.1 and 10.8 over the same years. The change did not affect the three plates equally, and the monthly gains do not repair it: the reconciled column’s median daily amplitude is 4.8 in 2011, 5.7 in 2012, 3.4 in 2013 and 5.5 in 2014. Levels can be used with care, but do not use amplitudes, variances or trends through this period, and do not compare the early years with the later ones on any of these. The cause is not established. The daily-record panel of the dashboard shows the effect.
The gain includes an unknown amount of climate. Refitted on half the years of a setup and tested on the other half, the monthly gains miss by up to 69 %, most in winter, and within one setup they vary by up to a factor of two across the year. An instrument gain does not depend on the month, so part of what the factors remove is the difference between the years each setup covers, not between the electronics. The monthly form is kept because a single gain would fit each month less closely, and which error is smaller has not been measured. The additive constants behave as an instrument property should: held out the same way, they land within 0.42 W m-2 of the reference level.
A residual zero-point drift remains. After correction, the annual means of the corrected setups still drift by up to 0.35 W m-2 per year. Over the original acquisition the reconciled column’s annual means range from −1.07 to +0.96 W m-2, with a slope of −0.30 W m-2 per year. Interannual variability in the early years is a real signal plus this drift, and the product cannot separate them. A per-year offset was rejected, because it would force every year’s mean onto the reference and remove any interannual signal.
Plate 3 is not corrected and its zero point drifts most. It never reaches the reference setup, so no gain or offset can be fitted, and it is exported as measured. Its annual means fall steadily from −6.5 W m-2 in 2005 to −20.3 W m-2 in 2011, a trend of −1.76 W m-2 per year, which indicates a degrading plate or wiring, not a soil storing more heat each year. Do not use this column across the original acquisition. It is not part of the reconciled column.
Records with reversed sign are flagged, not repaired. Plates 1 and 2 from December 2004 to February 2005, and plate 2 from June to December 2011, carry source flag 5. They are exported with their values and excluded from every fit and from the reconciled column; filter the flag out. Do not negate them: the sign is only part of the fault (see Plates with reversed sign). The reconciled column has no value in the winter of 2004/2005, because both of its plates were affected. These three periods all fall in the first years, which is a further reason to treat the early record as less well characterised.
The plates are not replicates. They are metres apart under a deciduous canopy. When the leaves are off, a patch of sunlight can fall on one plate and not another, which then reads several times higher. Differences between them describe where the light fell.
Nothing is gap-filled. There is no soil heat flux reference near this plot to fill from, and the gaps are failed loggers, a flat battery and a rebuild, not weather.
The pre-2021 record was screened once, with the deprecated MeteoScreeningTool, and never re-screened. The two screening notebooks cover the current plates only. Where the raw 10-minute stream and the screened record overlap they are identical, so that screening changed no value there. A plate that stopped responding while still reporting plausible values would pass it; only the comparison between plates could reveal that.
The two current plates were screened with different absolute limits: −20 to 40 W m-2 for plate 1 and −25 to 999 W m-2 for plate 2. Neither limit was reached, so no value was removed by them, and the threefold difference between the two plates’ maxima is a property of the plates. The difference will matter for a future record, because the gains are fitted on the within-month spread, and a removed sunfleck lowers a spread just as a smaller flux would.
Sub-daily timestamps in August 2012 are uncertain. A logger clock error that month is corrected in the tower products. These plates are on the forest-floor logger, and whether it had the same error is not recorded. The daily cycle could only be aligned against a clock this station does not share, so no shift is applied.
The site record before 2011 is not found by a date filter, because it was pasted into the maintenance system as one entry, and there is no site record for 2004 and 2005. The product notebook parses that entry separately; statements about the first years still rest on less evidence than later ones.

Both terms are fitted on climatology alone. No service measures soil heat flux at this plot, the setups do not overlap by a single half-hour, and all three plates change together at both boundaries. Only the near-zero annual mean ties the additive term to something outside the record; the gain has no such anchor.
What remains. The season-matched level of the reconciled column steps by +0.47 W m-2 at 2012 and −0.03 W m-2 at 2021. The same statistic at 33 dates inside a single setup moves by 0.46 W m-2 in the median and up to 1.89 W m-2. Both boundaries are therefore within the ordinary variation, but a step smaller than 1.89 W m-2 cannot be detected by this test. With the gain alone, the 2012 boundary failed the same check.

title: Soil heat flux at the forest floor
text:
A plate at 0.05 m measures the heat crossing that depth. The soil above it stores and releases heat that the plate does not see. This product exports the plate flux only. The storage term is estimated in the notebook, not added, from soil temperature and soil water content at 0.05 m (products 10 and 09) and a literature value for the dry heat capacity, because bulk density is not measured at this site. The notebook reports the estimate at that value and at 30 % above and below it.
In the reference setup the storage term has a spread of 2.36 W m-2 against 5.09 W m-2 for the measured flux, about 46 %. In the earlier setups it is 2.06 times the measured flux (reconfigured) and 3.44 times (original), but these ratios compare different instruments, because the plates’ own spread and the diurnal amplitude of the temperature reference both change at the setup boundaries. Use the value for the setup you work in, not an average of the three. The term averages near zero over a long record, so it changes the daily and seasonal course, not the level. Adding it properly would require a measured bulk density and a temperature above the plate, and neither is available at this site.
crumbs: Soil heat flux at the forest floor

title: Soil heat flux at the forest floor
text:
The plate columns are exported as recorded and step at the setup boundaries. The correction is only in G_FF1_0.05_HOMOGENIZED. A mean or trend across 2012 or 2021 from a plate column mixes three scales and three zero points.
Amplitudes are not comparable across 2011/2012 in any column. At the 2012 acquisition change the median daily amplitude of plates _1 and _2 falls by a factor of three to four, from 8.4 and 10.3 W m-2 in 2011 to 2.6 and 3.3 in 2012 and 1.2 and 1.8 in 2013. Plate _3 does not follow: 15.7, 12.1 and 10.8 over the same years. The change did not affect the three plates equally, and the monthly gains do not repair it: the reconciled column’s median daily amplitude is 4.8 in 2011, 5.7 in 2012, 3.4 in 2013 and 5.5 in 2014. Levels can be used with care, but do not use amplitudes, variances or trends through this period, and do not compare the early years with the later ones on any of these. The cause is not established. The daily-record panel of the dashboard shows the effect.
The gain includes an unknown amount of climate. Refitted on half the years of a setup and tested on the other half, the monthly gains miss by up to 69 %, most in winter, and within one setup they vary by up to a factor of two across the year. An instrument gain does not depend on the month, so part of what the factors remove is the difference between the years each setup covers, not between the electronics. The monthly form is kept because a single gain would fit each month less closely, and which error is smaller has not been measured. The additive constants behave as an instrument property should: held out the same way, they land within 0.42 W m-2 of the reference level.
A residual zero-point drift remains. After correction, the annual means of the corrected setups still drift by up to 0.35 W m-2 per year. Over the original acquisition the reconciled column’s annual means range from −1.07 to +0.96 W m-2, with a slope of −0.30 W m-2 per year. Interannual variability in the early years is a real signal plus this drift, and the product cannot separate them. A per-year offset was rejected, because it would force every year’s mean onto the reference and remove any interannual signal.
Plate 3 is not corrected and its zero point drifts most. It never reaches the reference setup, so no gain or offset can be fitted, and it is exported as measured. Its annual means fall steadily from −6.5 W m-2 in 2005 to −20.3 W m-2 in 2011, a trend of −1.76 W m-2 per year, which indicates a degrading plate or wiring, not a soil storing more heat each year. Do not use this column across the original acquisition. It is not part of the reconciled column.
Records with reversed sign are flagged, not repaired. Plates 1 and 2 from December 2004 to February 2005, and plate 2 from June to December 2011, carry source flag 5. They are exported with their values and excluded from every fit and from the reconciled column; filter the flag out. Do not negate them: the sign is only part of the fault (see Plates with reversed sign). The reconciled column has no value in the winter of 2004/2005, because both of its plates were affected. These three periods all fall in the first years, which is a further reason to treat the early record as less well characterised.
The plates are not replicates. They are metres apart under a deciduous canopy. When the leaves are off, a patch of sunlight can fall on one plate and not another, which then reads several times higher. Differences between them describe where the light fell.
Nothing is gap-filled. There is no soil heat flux reference near this plot to fill from, and the gaps are failed loggers, a flat battery and a rebuild, not weather.
The pre-2021 record was screened once, with the deprecated MeteoScreeningTool, and never re-screened. The two screening notebooks cover the current plates only. Where the raw 10-minute stream and the screened record overlap they are identical, so that screening changed no value there. A plate that stopped responding while still reporting plausible values would pass it; only the comparison between plates could reveal that.
The two current plates were screened with different absolute limits: −20 to 40 W m-2 for plate 1 and −25 to 999 W m-2 for plate 2. Neither limit was reached, so no value was removed by them, and the threefold difference between the two plates’ maxima is a property of the plates. The difference will matter for a future record, because the gains are fitted on the within-month spread, and a removed sunfleck lowers a spread just as a smaller flux would.
Sub-daily timestamps in August 2012 are uncertain. A logger clock error that month is corrected in the tower products. These plates are on the forest-floor logger, and whether it had the same error is not recorded. The daily cycle could only be aligned against a clock this station does not share, so no shift is applied.
The site record before 2011 is not found by a date filter, because it was pasted into the maintenance system as one entry, and there is no site record for 2004 and 2005. The product notebook parses that entry separately; statements about the first years still rest on less evidence than later ones.

title: Outgoing longwave radiation at 47 m
text:
Half-hourly outgoing (upwelling) longwave radiation at 47 m on the CH-LAE tower, 2005-2025, exported as measured. The file is 13_METEO_LW_OUT_2005-2025 (parquet and CSV): 355,872 records on a continuous 30-minute index, TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (middle of the half-hour), in local time (UTC+01:00, no daylight saving), from 2005-09-14 00:15 to 2025-12-31 23:45. The first measurement is at 2005-09-14 13:15.
The series ends on 31 December 2025. It is part of FP2026.1 and of the merged meteo product, where it is NaN from 1 January 2026; the extension to 30 September 2026 is in progress.
The interactive dashboard summarises coverage, provenance, seasonality, distributions, extremes and trends. Read its trend together with the instrument card: the record steps in June 2016 and again in December 2021, neither step is corrected, and a trend over the whole record includes both.
Notebooks:

13_METEO_LW_OUT: builds the product. It compares the two screenings where they overlap, applies the 2012 corrections, removes the excursion during the radiometer exchange, and identifies the instrument and calibration factor behind each part of the record.
LW_OUT_T1_47_1: the screening of the current era, which dates the radiometer exchange to the minute.
06_METEO_LW_IN: the second pyrgeometer of the same instrument. Together the two give the net longwave exchange, but they are separate detectors with separate calibration factors, so each era question is tested again here.
02_METEO_TA: air temperature, which gives the Stefan-Boltzmann emission used in every check on this page. Its homogenised column is used, because the checks cross January 2016.
Meteo_Data_SW_OUT: the outgoing shortwave channel of the same instrument, with the same December 2021 boundary.
Meteo_Product_Chain: where this product sits in the chain.







ImportantThe record steps at the December 2021 radiometer exchange



The CNR1 was replaced by a CNR4 on 14 December 2021, and the series changes at that date by more than in any year without a change. The change of screening software falls close to the same date but is ruled out, because the two screenings give the same values where they overlap. The cause is the instrument.
The step is not corrected, and there is no homogenised column: its cause is known, its size is not, and a correction would need calibration data the site does not hold. Filter on FLAG_LW_OUT_T1_47_1_SOURCE before comparing the two eras, and drop code 3, the 24 days in which the new instrument was read with the old instrument’s constant.
Nothing is gap-filled, so the value column contains NaN and every non-null record is a measurement.




The values are upwelling longwave irradiance: the thermal emission of the canopy seen from 47 m, plus the small part of the downwelling flux that the canopy reflects. The median is 356.7 W m-2, the mean 359.1 W m-2, and the range 239.6 to 503.5 W m-2.
A pyrgeometer’s voltage measures only the net exchange between the viewed surface and the instrument body, so the instrument’s own emission is added to obtain the irradiance. Every value in this file includes it; the converted voltage alone would differ by some 300 to 400 W m-2.
A wrong calibration factor therefore scales only the net signal, not the added emission term. For a downward-facing pyrgeometer above a canopy the net signal is small: a few W m-2 in the median and a few tens at the extremes, against several hundred in the file. The factor error that costs LW_IN about 9 W m-2 in the middle of its distribution is worth much less here, which is why the checks below use percentiles of the net signal rather than the level.
Two physical checks pass. The ratio of the measured value to the Stefan-Boltzmann emission at air temperature has a nighttime median of 0.979 (5th to 95th percentile 0.963 to 0.996) and a daytime median of 0.990, as expected for a canopy radiating near air temperature. And the site loses longwave radiation in most half-hours: the median of LW_IN − LW_OUT is −46.4 W m-2, and 81 % of nighttime and 85 % of daytime half-hours are net losses. The second check would detect the two channels having been swapped anywhere between the logger and this file.

Here code 1 is the era from the June 2016 logger program, and all of 14 December 2021 carries the undetermined code, because the exchange happened during that day. The longest gap affects this channel only. The incoming channel of the same radiometer measured through those six weeks (99.0 % coverage in 2015), and SW_OUT has no gap there either. The cause is not known.
Five years are below 97 % measured: 2015 at 88.1 %, 2012 at 92.3 %, 2016 at 94.3 %, 2019 at 95.7 % and 2009 at 96.6 %. 2005 is a partial year, beginning in September.
This product removed three sets of records: 1,202 inside the two 2012 windows of documented logger-wide fault, as in notebooks 01 to 03 and 06; one record outside the physical range of 150 to 600 W m-2; and ten half-hours during the radiometer exchange that fell outside the range of the same time of day on the seven days either side, when the instrument was unmounted and no longer viewing the canopy. The August 2012 clock error is corrected by the same +15.5 h shift as the other tower variables. Unlike LW_IN, this variable can confirm the size of the shift, because the canopy heats in the sun and its emission follows.




The MeteoScreeningTool and the diive screening cover 35,032 of the same half-hours, and on those records they give the same series: median difference 0.000 W m-2, RMS difference 0.011 W m-2, largest single difference 2.06 W m-2, correlation 1.000. The join between them changes no value, and the change of screening is ruled out as the cause of the step at the turn of 2022. LW_IN has no such overlap.



On 7 June 2016 a new logger program changed a radiometer calibration factor from 10.03 to 12.83 µV/W/m2, the change that leaves more than half of LW_IN reading low. The maintenance record names one factor without saying which channels received it, so the question was tested in the data.
The statistic is the 2nd percentile of the nighttime net signal (measured value minus the Stefan-Boltzmann emission at air temperature), where a conversion error is largest. It moves from −15.9 W m-2 in 2006-2015 to −11.3 W m-2 in 2017-2021, a ratio of 0.721 that is the same at every percentile of the tail, as expected for a change of conversion. The documented factor change predicts 0.782; the two agree well within the year-to-year scatter of the statistic. Where the canopy is at air temperature and the net signal is near zero, no conversion factor can act, and the corresponding statistic moves by only 0.07 % across the date. A change in the canopy or the weather would not produce this pattern.
Effect on the values. Before 7 June 2016 the net signal is too large in magnitude by roughly a quarter. Values therefore read low at night, when the canopy is cooler than the instrument, and high during the day. Because the net signal is small, the error is a few W m-2 at most, compared with 9 W m-2 for the incoming channel. It is not corrected, because that would need the radiometer’s body temperature, which this product does not read. Code 2 marks the affected era, more than half the record.



Measured the same way, the first half of 2022 gives an envelope ratio of 0.710 against the three preceding years, outside the 0.808 to 1.050 that the statistic shows in years without a boundary. The record therefore steps at the exchange. The screenings agree, so the cause is the instrument or the weather, and the CNR1 was replaced by the CNR4 on that date. Nothing is corrected; the flag separates the two instruments.
From 14 December 2021 to 7 January 2022 the CNR4 was read by a logger program written for the CNR1, so its values were converted with the wrong sensitivity. Which of two candidate sensitivities was applied is not known: the program that set it does not survive, and the June 2016 entry does not say whether its new factor reached this channel. Both candidates were computed; neither is adopted. The error is small, because the constant scales the net signal, not the reported irradiance. Over the window the net signal has a median of −0.7 W m-2 and a 5th to 95th percentile range of −3.6 to +2.7 W m-2, so the worst case over both candidates is 1.6 W m-2 on a single half-hour, 0.5 % of the reported value. Code 3 marks the interval, so it can be dropped where an unambiguous calibration is needed.




The record is not homogeneous across December 2021. The step is measured and attributed to the instrument, but its size in W m-2 is not established. Filter on the source flag before comparing the two eras, and treat a trend across that date as containing the change.
More than half of the record was converted with the pyranometer’s factor. Everything before 7 June 2016 carries code 2 and reads low at night by roughly a quarter of the net signal, a few W m-2. It is not corrected, because that would need the radiometer’s body temperature.
The 24 days of the changeover have an unverified conversion, with an error of at most 1.6 W m-2 and the applied constant not identified. Code 3 marks them.
There is no independent reference at the site. MeteoSwiss Lägern measures no longwave, NABEL has no pyrgeometer, and the below-canopy sensor views a different surface. Every statement above rests either on the physics of the measurement, with the Stefan-Boltzmann emission at air temperature as the yardstick, or on the overlap between the two screenings. This is weaker evidence than a second instrument; where it does not suffice, the product notebook says so.
The physical checks use air temperature in place of two temperatures that are not measured: the canopy temperature and the radiometer body temperature. This is adequate to estimate the size of an effect, not to correct the data.
The January 2016 acquisition change did not move this series. It is listed because the same change moved TA_T1_47_1 by 1.3 °C and because it is easily confused with the June date five months later. Every surviving logger program applies the same conversion across it, and the data show no change.
The series contains gaps and is not gap-filled. Code that assumes a complete series will fail or propagate NaN. If a complete series is needed, for example for four-component net radiation or energy-balance closure, fill it downstream, and do not train one model across a calibration boundary.
The six-week gap of August and September 2015 has no known cause, and it makes 2015 the least complete year. No other channel of the same instrument shares it.
The 2012 windows were removed without evidence from this series, as in 06. They rest on a documented logger-wide fault, and this variable has no reference that could show a level error there.

title: Photosynthetic photon flux density at 47 m
text:
Half-hourly incoming photosynthetic photon flux density at 47 m on the CH-LAE tower, 2004 to September 2026, gap-filled to completeness. The file is 03_METEO_PPFD_IN_GAPFILLED_2004-2026.09 (parquet and CSV): 398,832 records on a continuous 30-minute index TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (middle of the half-hour, UTC+01:00, no daylight saving), from 2004-01-01 00:15 to 2026-09-30 23:45.
The interactive dashboard summarises the product on one page.
Method, evidence and checks:

03_METEO_PPFD_IN: builds the product (merge of the two screenings, 2012 corrections, nighttime offset, gap-filling), identifies the sensor and tests it at both hardware changes.
RADIATION_SENSOR_CONTINUITY: compares four radiation sensors and places the decline described below on this sensor rather than on either reference.
Meteo Product Chain: this product depends on SW_IN, which is built first.







ImportantThe sensor lost response between 2022 and 2024



Against both of its independent references the 47 m quantum sensor reads about 3 to 3.5 % lower in 2026 than in 2021, and about 6 to 7 % below its 2006-2010 level. The fall has not continued since 2024: 2025 and 2026 lie within 0.4 % of 2024.
The decline is not corrected (see Known limitations). A trend or period comparison that spans the last years of the record contains it. Comparisons within a year, and the use of single half-hours, are unaffected.


There is one value column and no _HOMOGENIZED column: one instrument over the whole record, read through the same conversion by two acquisition systems, with no step at either hardware boundary.


Every record carries a value, and the flag is defined at every record.

In 2012 a logger clock error shifted one block of August by 15.5 hours, and a tower power-supply failure in late July and August and storm damage in late October and November left records that could not be repaired. The clock error was corrected, the other two periods were removed, and all of it was gap-filled. The windows are the same as in SW_IN and TA, because the fault was in the logger and the power supply. The January 2016 outage runs from 1 January to 21 January 14:15, when the replacement logger came online.



Daytime gaps are filled by one XGBoost model over the whole record; unlike SW_IN and TA there is no period split, because all three drivers span the full record. The drivers are the gap-filled SW_IN from notebook 01, potential radiation computed from the site coordinates, and MeteoSwiss Lägern global radiation. The tower pyranometer is the strongest driver (same height, same mast, r2 0.99), but it is itself gap-filled, and PPFD_IN gaps tend to coincide with SW_IN gaps because both sensors are on the same logger. Lägern, 2.5 km away, covers that case with more scatter. Code 2 marks the few half-hours where neither radiation driver was available. Nighttime gaps are set to zero. A reference is used only as a driver and never replaces a measured value.




The sensor lost response between 2022 and 2024, and it has not recovered. It falls against the co-located tower pyranometer and against MeteoSwiss Lägern together, by 2.86 % and 3.45 % between 2021 and 2026, and reaches 5.63 % and 7.13 % below its 2006-2010 level in 2026. The change over the last year (+0.4 % and +0.3 %) is within the ordinary year-to-year change of these ratios (0.6 % and 0.7 %), so one stable season does not yet show that the response has settled. Both references moving together places the change on this instrument, and RADIATION_SENSOR_CONTINUITY reaches the same conclusion from four sensors. It is not corrected: it develops over years, so there is no boundary at which to apply a correction, and no maintenance record identifies a cause, so a correction would be a rescaling towards a reference. The likely cause is the sensor itself after twenty years in the field (soiling, or ageing of the diffuser and detector). Allow for several per cent in analyses that span the last years of the record, or use a reference-normalised quantity. Gap-filled records inherit the state of the sensor at the time and neither add nor remove the bias.
A comparison against SW_IN across 2013 shows that sensor’s drift, not this one’s. The 47 m pyranometer rises by about 3 % against its references from 2013 (see Incoming shortwave radiation at 47 m). Any ratio of the two products, such as a photon-to-energy ratio over the whole record, contains that change.
The MeteoSwiss gap-filling driver changed level in October 2010. SW_IN_LAE_MS steps by about 5 % on 6 October 2010, when that station’s radiation instrumentation was rebuilt. The fills are not affected, because a driver supplies the state of the sky. Do not read a difference between this product and MeteoSwiss Lägern as evidence about the tower across that date.
Nighttime values are exactly zero, not measurements. The sensor reads a small positive offset at night: about 4.2 µmol m-2 s-1 before the 2016 logger replacement and 2.5 µmol m-2 s-1 from then to the end of 2021. From 2022 the diive screening has already removed it. The offset was removed per day before gap-filling. For instrument noise or the offset itself, use the screened database series.
2004 is 72 % modelled. Everything before 2004-09-20 10:45 rests on the SW_IN product, which is itself reconstructed for that period. These records are a fill built on a fill and carry the uncertainty of both.




They did nothing measurable to this series. Two things happened that month: the tower logger was replaced, which moved TA_T1_47_1 by 1.3 °C, and the fieldbook records a new Kipp & Zonen PAR sensor installed on 8 January 2016.
That sensor is not this column. The CR1000 logger program reads two incoming-PAR instruments at 47 m and names both. PPFD_IN_T1_47_1, exported here, is a Delta-T sunshine sensor, whose signal is already scaled to µmol m-2 s-1 and is read at a multiplier of exactly 1. The Kipp & Zonen PAR LITE installed that January is PPFD_IN_T1_47_2, read at the reciprocal of its own sensitivity, and its record begins on 2016-01-21 14:15. The maintenance record alone cannot make this distinction, because it files both instruments under the same operation tag.
The Delta-T sensor was installed in August 2004 and appears in every surviving logger program since, at multiplier 1 and offset 0 in both the CR10X and the CR1000 era. The maintenance record shows no replacement and no calibration in twenty-two years, only two cleanings, in December 2016 and April 2021.
Across 2016 the ratio of this sensor to the tower pyranometer changes by +0.4 % and to MeteoSwiss Lägern by +0.5 %, both less than in an ordinary year. A change confined to the tower acquisition system could move both tower sensors and leave their ratio flat, but it could not move their ratio against a station 2.5 km away. Only the nighttime offset changed, and the per-day correction removes it on both sides of the date. The mst and diive screenings meet at the end of 2021 without a step either. Notebook 03 asserts all of this on every run.

title: Relative humidity at 47 m
text:
Half-hourly relative humidity at 47 m on the CH-LAE tower, 2004 to September 2026, complete. The file is 04_METEO_RH_CORRECTED_2004-2026.09 (parquet and CSV): 398,832 records on a continuous 30-minute index TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (middle of the half-hour, UTC+01:00, no daylight saving), from 2004-01-01 00:15 to 2026-09-30 23:45. 2026 is a partial year (January to September).
The interactive dashboard summarises the product on one page.
Method, evidence and checks:

04_METEO_RH: builds the product: merge of the two screenings, 2012 corrections, the RH > 100 % correction, the identification of the probes and their states, the 2016 and 2026 transfers, and the two reconstruction passes.
02_METEO_TA: the same probe delivers TA, and the dates of every probe change and probe state are derived there. Notebook 04 reads its product, so 02 runs first.
Meteo Product Chain: VPD is computed from this product.







ImportantWhich column to use



The 47 m record comes from three probes, and the second of them changed state twice before it was replaced (see Sensor history). The measured column steps up by 2.1 to 3.3 percentage points of RH at the 21 January 2016 probe change (3.9 to 4.1 on the half-hours away from saturation). At the 5 June 2026 probe change it becomes drier, increasingly so with the humidity.

Inside one probe state, use RH_T1_47_1, which is what the probe reported.
Across 21 January 2016 or 5 June 2026 (period means, trends, year rankings, anomalies) use RH_T1_47_1_HOMOGENIZED, which puts the other probes on the level of the CS215. It removes the steps at the probe changes, not the drift within each era (see Known limitations).
Where provenance has to be certain, select FLAG_RH_T1_47_1_SOURCE in {0, 1, 4, 6}. Codes 6 and 7 carry the probe’s heating in sun in both columns; exclude code 7 wherever the sun-dependent part of RH matters.





Every record carries a value, and both flags are defined at every record and describe both value columns.

In 2012 a logger clock error shifted one block of August by 15.5 hours, and a tower power-supply failure in late July and August and storm damage in late October and November left records that could not be repaired. The clock error was corrected, the other two periods were removed, and all of it was reconstructed from NABEL.



TA_T1_47_1 and RH_T1_47_1 arrive from one probe in one sensor call, so every date below is the same as in notebook 02, where most of them are derived. The field name and its database tags did not change at any of them.

Rotronic MP101A, to 31 December 2015 (code 1). Six CR10X programs of 2004-2006 name it and its analog conversion.
Campbell CS215, from 21 January 2016 (code 0). Named by the CR1000 program installed at the changeover, read over SDI-12.
The CS215 with excess daytime heating, 22 October 2024 to 16 May 2025 (code 7). Dated in notebook 02 from the daytime excess of the 47 m temperature over the 35 m sensor of the same tower, which grows in the weeks after intake tubing was attached at the 47 m sonic anemometer on 19 September 2024.
The CS215 after 16 May 2025 (code 6). The probe was handled during a site visit that day; the fieldbook records the heating connection of the tower inlet found melted and disconnected. See The May 2025 change.
Campbell HygroVUE10, from 5 June 2026 (code 4). The fieldbook adds it at this location that day. See The June 2026 probe change.

The fieldbook registers no temperature or humidity device at the 47 m location before the HygroVUE10, so the 2016 identification rests on the logger programs and on the data.

The probe and its acquisition system were replaced together: a Rotronic MP101A on a single-ended analog channel gave way to a Campbell CS215 over SDI-12. Air temperature and relative humidity come from that one probe, so the same date splits both variables.
The step is on the tower. Three humidity series span the changeover: the tower probe, a NABEL probe at 49 m on the same mast, and MeteoSwiss Lägern. Both comparisons that contain the tower probe step up at January 2016 by about ten times their ordinary year-to-year change, and the comparison between the two references does not move.



Table 6: The change in each pairwise difference across January 2016, in percentage points of RH, against the change of the same comparison between two ordinary years.

The 100 % ceiling hides part of the step. The measured series has a median of 82.8 % RH, and 11.1 % of its half-hours are at or above 99.9 %. Where both probes are at that bound the step cannot show, so the whole-record figure understates it: away from the ceiling the step is 1.2 to 1.8 times as large. Below 85 % RH it is 3.2 to 6.3 percentage points, above 95 % RH at most 1.1.
The replaced probe had drifted. 1,931 half-hours of the analog era (0.99 % of its 195,606 measured records) read above 100 % RH, the typical sign of an aged capacitive humidity element. Their share grows through that era to 3.6 % of 2015. The SDI-12 era has none.
The step is present at every hour, and is larger at night (+4.3 % RH against NABEL) than in daylight (+2.2 % RH). The radiation-shield difference that explains part of the TA step acts only in sunshine, so it does not explain this one.


Because the step depends on the humidity, a constant cannot remove it. The homogenised column raises the MP101A era by a transfer that varies with the humidity: per humidity bin, the difference between the eras is added to the earlier one.
Fitted on the era means, such a transfer is not stable. Both eras drift against Lägern, in opposite directions and by more over their own length than the step between them. In the 60 to 80 % RH band, over January to September of each year, the MP101A era drifts by -0.34 percentage points of RH per year (-3.44 over 2005-2015) and the CS215 era by +0.44 per year (+3.07 over 2017-2024): 6.51 in total, against a step of 5.46 between the era means. Estimates from the first and second half of each era differ by up to 4.93 % RH, the size of the correction, and summer and winter by up to 4.72 % RH.
Fitted at the break, it is stable. The transfer is fitted on tower minus NABEL, binned on the NABEL humidity: the MP101A over 2013-2015 against the CS215 from February 2016 to July 2018, the end of NABEL’s independent record. Close to the break the drift has had little time to act. Shorter windows change the result by less than the year-to-year noise of each bin plus a year of drift: from 40 % RH upwards by at most 1.27 % RH, never more than 0.95 of that bin’s tolerance. Each bin’s correction is attached to the MP101A’s own reading in that bin, interpolated between bins, and the result is capped at 100 %, so a saturated MP101A record stays saturated.
The transfer raises the MP101A era by 0 to 5.51 % RH, by 2.98 % RH on average over its measured records, most in the middle of the humidity range and close to zero near saturation. Scored against Lägern, which entered no fit, the mean step across the break falls from +4.21 to +0.83 % RH, within a tolerance of 1.81 % RH (Lägern’s own year-to-year change, 0.71, plus the drift contained in the fitting windows, 1.10). Every record before the changeover (codes 1, 2 and 3) receives the transfer, reconstructed records included, because their reconstruction offsets put them on the MP101A level.




The CS215 reports RH relative to its own temperature, so a probe that is too warm in sun reads a lower RH for the same amount of water vapour. Whether the change of 16 May 2025 is of that kind or a change of the humidity element is decided in vapour pressure, computed from each sensor’s own RH and TA: a temperature error moves RH and leaves vapour pressure unchanged.
Over the 30 days either side of the handling, against the same calendar dates of the normal CS215 summers 2022-2024, RH in sun rises by +4.43 % RH against Lägern, outside the range of the normal years (-3.07 to +1.13 % RH). The vapour pressure changes by +0.13 hPa, within theirs (+0.13 to +0.45 hPa), and the tower temperature in sun falls by 1.57 °C against Lägern. Against the normal years RH moves by +5.17 % RH, which at 17.9 °C corresponds to 1.06 hPa; the vapour pressure moves by -0.20 hPa, 19 % of that. The change is in the probe’s temperature, not in its humidity element.
RH_T1_47_1_HOMOGENIZED therefore leaves codes 6 and 7 as measured, like code 0. A correction of these records would be a correction of the probe temperature, which is the task of notebook 02. Against Lägern, RH in sun is +0.18 % RH under code 7 and +4.62 % RH under code 6, where the normal CS215 summers on the same dates give +0.18 to +3.37 and -0.20 to +3.12 % RH.



On 5 June 2026 a Campbell HygroVUE10 (SDI-12) replaced the CS215. A gap in the raw 1-minute record from 11:10 to 11:31 dates the swap; the half-hour 11:00 to 11:30 is removed and reconstructed (source code 5). In vapour pressure against Lägern the HygroVUE10 reads drier than the normal CS215, by 1.27 hPa over 12 June to 30 September, against a year-to-year scatter of 0.19 hPa among the CS215 summers. In RH as measured it lies 2.3 to 4.6 % RH below the CS215 summers between 30 and 90 % RH.
The HygroVUE10 also reads cooler than the CS215 in sun (notebook 02), so a transfer in % RH would mix the humidity elements with the temperature sensors. The transfer is therefore made in vapour pressure:

Vapour pressure e is computed from each sensor’s own RH and TA, on two season-matched samples: the HygroVUE10 from 12 June to 30 September 2026, after its configuration change of 11 June, and the normal CS215 (code 0) on the same calendar dates of 2022 to 2024.
The HygroVUE10-minus-CS215 difference Delta_e is fitted as a line in the Lägern vapour pressure (5,328 HygroVUE10 and 15,885 CS215 records). It runs from -0.90 hPa at 8 hPa to -1.66 hPa at 20 hPa. After the transfer the residual over all hours of the sample is -0.08 hPa, against -1.27 hPa before and a tolerance of 0.19 hPa, and no vapour pressure bin exceeds 0.09 hPa. In a month hold-out (each month predicted by fits without it) the residuals are -0.17 hPa in June, -0.32 hPa in July, -0.01 hPa in August and +0.19 hPa in September, all within a tolerance of 0.37 hPa pooled over the months.
RH_HOMOGENIZED = 100 * (e - Delta_e) / e_s(TA_HOMOGENIZED), where e_s is the saturation vapour pressure at the homogenised TA of notebook 02 for the same record, capped to [0, 100].

From June 2026 the homogenised RH refers to the homogenised temperature of notebook 02, not to the probe’s own temperature. That temperature carries no radiative excess, so in sun the homogenised RH lies above what a CS215 would read, and at night close to it. Against the CS215 summers it lies 0.74 % RH higher in sun, 0.30 % RH higher at night and 0.60 % RH higher over all hours; per Lägern humidity bin, 0.03 to 1.25 % RH higher between 30 and 90 % RH and 2.52 % RH higher above 90 %. On the HygroVUE10 records the homogenised column adds 3.92 % RH on average, at most 8.21 % RH.




The homogenised column removes the steps, not the drift. Against MeteoSwiss Lägern the MP101A era drifts down by 0.34 and the CS215 era up by 0.44 percentage points of RH per year, so each era moves further over its own length than the 2016 step (see The 2016 transfer). A trend from either column, or a comparison of years far from the break, still contains sensor movement. The drift is not corrected: it cannot be attributed to either station, and after the NABEL sensor stops in 2018 there is no third humidity series at the site to attribute it with. Correcting it towards MeteoSwiss would replace the measurement with the reference.
The 2016 transfer depends on the reference. Fitted against Lägern over the same windows instead of NABEL, it would raise the measured MP101A records of 2013-2015 by +3.36 instead of +2.82 % RH on average, 0.54 % RH more, and by up to 2.44 % RH more just below saturation (at a reading of 95 %), where NABEL finds almost no step and Lägern a large one. That difference is the uncertainty of the homogenised column across 2016, and it is largest in humid conditions. Shorter fitting windows give a correction smaller by 0.61 to 0.69 % RH on average between 40 and 85 % RH, so part of what the fitting windows attribute to the probes may be drift.
Codes 6 and 7 carry the probe’s heating in both value columns: in sun code 7 reads low and code 6 high against the normal CS215.
The HygroVUE10 transfer rests on one summer and one reference. It is fitted on June to September 2026 against Lägern and applied to the whole HygroVUE10 era, including the transitional week of 5 to 11 June. Its month hold-out residuals follow the season, from -0.32 hPa in July to +0.19 hPa in September, so the transfer leaves the early summer months slightly too dry and the late ones slightly too wet. Its behaviour outside the summer is untested, and it is to be refitted once the HygroVUE10 record includes a winter.
Which probe is correct is not settled. The homogenised column is on the level of the CS215; the evidence does not establish an absolute accuracy for any of the probes.
VPD inherits these properties. Notebook 07 computes VPD_T1_47_1 from the measured TA and RH and VPD_T1_47_1_HOMOGENIZED from the two homogenised columns. Use the homogenised VPD across 2016 or June 2026. See Vapour pressure deficit at 47 m.
Reconstructed records are estimates, not measurements. Code 3 carries about 3 % RH of uncertainty, against a sensor-to-sensor agreement of about 2 % RH in summer; code 4 more. January to September 2004 is reconstructed throughout and is the least constrained part of the record.
Values near 100 % are corrected, not restored. A drifting probe loses resolution close to saturation. Where the analog era read above 100 %, a daily offset was subtracted and the remainder clipped, which removes the impossible values but does not recover the information they stood for. Saturation frequency differs between the eras for this reason as well as because of the step.
The NABEL reference is not independent after July 2018. From August 2018 the ingested RH_NABEL_T1_49_1 column reproduces the tower column exactly. Nothing in this file is derived from those months, but a comparison of this product with that NABEL column over them compares the product with itself.
2026 is a partial year. A 2026 annual mean covers January to September only.

text:
The probe and its acquisition system were replaced together: a Rotronic MP101A on a single-ended analog channel gave way to a Campbell CS215 over SDI-12. Air temperature and relative humidity come from that one probe, so the same date splits both variables.
The step is on the tower. Three humidity series span the changeover: the tower probe, a NABEL probe at 49 m on the same mast, and MeteoSwiss Lägern. Both comparisons that contain the tower probe step up at January 2016 by about ten times their ordinary year-to-year change, and the comparison between the two references does not move.

The 100 % ceiling hides part of the step. The measured series has a median of 82.8 % RH, and 11.1 % of its half-hours are at or above 99.9 %. Where both probes are at that bound the step cannot show, so the whole-record figure understates it: away from the ceiling the step is 1.2 to 1.8 times as large. Below 85 % RH it is 3.2 to 6.3 percentage points, above 95 % RH at most 1.1.
The replaced probe had drifted. 1,931 half-hours of the analog era (0.99 % of its 195,606 measured records) read above 100 % RH, the typical sign of an aged capacitive humidity element. Their share grows through that era to 3.6 % of 2015. The SDI-12 era has none.
The step is present at every hour, and is larger at night (+4.3 % RH against NABEL) than in daylight (+2.2 % RH). The radiation-shield difference that explains part of the TA step acts only in sunshine, so it does not explain this one.


Because the step depends on the humidity, a constant cannot remove it. The homogenised column raises the MP101A era by a transfer that varies with the humidity: per humidity bin, the difference between the eras is added to the earlier one.
Fitted on the era means, such a transfer is not stable. Both eras drift against Lägern, in opposite directions and by more over their own length than the step between them. In the 60 to 80 % RH band, over January to September of each year, the MP101A era drifts by -0.34 percentage points of RH per year (-3.44 over 2005-2015) and the CS215 era by +0.44 per year (+3.07 over 2017-2024): 6.51 in total, against a step of 5.46 between the era means. Estimates from the first and second half of each era differ by up to 4.93 % RH, the size of the correction, and summer and winter by up to 4.72 % RH.
Fitted at the break, it is stable. The transfer is fitted on tower minus NABEL, binned on the NABEL humidity: the MP101A over 2013-2015 against the CS215 from February 2016 to July 2018, the end of NABEL’s independent record. Close to the break the drift has had little time to act. Shorter windows change the result by less than the year-to-year noise of each bin plus a year of drift: from 40 % RH upwards by at most 1.27 % RH, never more than 0.95 of that bin’s tolerance. Each bin’s correction is attached to the MP101A’s own reading in that bin, interpolated between bins, and the result is capped at 100 %, so a saturated MP101A record stays saturated.
The transfer raises the MP101A era by 0 to 5.51 % RH, by 2.98 % RH on average over its measured records, most in the middle of the humidity range and close to zero near saturation. Scored against Lägern, which entered no fit, the mean step across the break falls from +4.21 to +0.83 % RH, within a tolerance of 1.81 % RH (Lägern’s own year-to-year change, 0.71, plus the drift contained in the fitting windows, 1.10). Every record before the changeover (codes 1, 2 and 3) receives the transfer, reconstructed records included, because their reconstruction offsets put them on the MP101A level.

title: Relative humidity at 47 m
text:
The CS215 reports RH relative to its own temperature, so a probe that is too warm in sun reads a lower RH for the same amount of water vapour. Whether the change of 16 May 2025 is of that kind or a change of the humidity element is decided in vapour pressure, computed from each sensor’s own RH and TA: a temperature error moves RH and leaves vapour pressure unchanged.
Over the 30 days either side of the handling, against the same calendar dates of the normal CS215 summers 2022-2024, RH in sun rises by +4.43 % RH against Lägern, outside the range of the normal years (-3.07 to +1.13 % RH). The vapour pressure changes by +0.13 hPa, within theirs (+0.13 to +0.45 hPa), and the tower temperature in sun falls by 1.57 °C against Lägern. Against the normal years RH moves by +5.17 % RH, which at 17.9 °C corresponds to 1.06 hPa; the vapour pressure moves by -0.20 hPa, 19 % of that. The change is in the probe’s temperature, not in its humidity element.
RH_T1_47_1_HOMOGENIZED therefore leaves codes 6 and 7 as measured, like code 0. A correction of these records would be a correction of the probe temperature, which is the task of notebook 02. Against Lägern, RH in sun is +0.18 % RH under code 7 and +4.62 % RH under code 6, where the normal CS215 summers on the same dates give +0.18 to +3.37 and -0.20 to +3.12 % RH.

title: Incoming shortwave radiation at 47 m
text:
Half-hourly incoming shortwave radiation at 47 m on the CH-LAE tower, 2004 to September 2026, gap-filled to completeness. The file is 01_METEO_SW_IN_GAPFILLED_2004-2026.09 (parquet and CSV): 398,832 records on a continuous 30-minute index TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (middle of the half-hour, UTC+01:00, no daylight saving), from 2004-01-01 00:15 to 2026-09-30 23:45.
The interactive dashboard summarises the product on one page.
Method, evidence and checks:

01_METEO_SW_IN: builds the product (merge of the two screenings, 2012 corrections, nighttime offset, gap-filling) and shows that the record is homogeneous across both hardware changes.
RADIATION_SENSOR_CONTINUITY: compares four radiation sensors and attributes each level change in the record to one instrument.
Meteo Product Chain: TA and PPFD_IN use this product as a gap-filling driver.







NoteOne column, no homogenised variant



This series needs no homogenisation. The same sensor was read through the same calibration across the January 2016 acquisition change, and the December 2021 replacement of the radiometer did not move the level either. There is one value column and no _HOMOGENIZED column. A slow departure of the sensor from its references from 2013 is described under Known limitations.
