In 2012 a logger clock error shifted one block of August by 15.5 hours, and a tower power-supply failure in late July and August and storm damage in late October and November left records that could not be repaired. The clock error was corrected, the other two periods were removed, and all of it was gap-filled.



Daytime gaps are filled by an XGBoost model, trained separately for 2004-2018 and 2019-2026. The split is where the NABEL sensor at 49 m on the same tower ends, so that no model is trained on one driver set and applied to the other. Until 2018 the drivers are NABEL and MeteoSwiss Lägern (2.5 km away); from 2019 only Lägern remains, so the later fills rest on the more distant sensor. Code 2 marks the few half-hours where no driver was available. Drivers enter as measured, never gap-filled. Nighttime gaps are set to zero. A reference is used only as a driver and never replaces a measured value.




The sensor reads about 3 % high relative to its references from 2013. NABEL at 49 m, MeteoSwiss Lägern and the co-located PAR sensor all show it at once, which places the change on this radiometer. It develops over about three years rather than at a date, and the fieldbook records no maintenance or calibration of this radiometer between its installation in 2005 and its removal in 2021. The change is within the field uncertainty of a pyranometer of this class and is not corrected, because there is neither a boundary at which to apply a correction nor a known fault to justify one. Allow for a few per cent when comparing the middle of the record with its beginning.
The MeteoSwiss gap-filling driver changed level in October 2010. SW_IN_LAE_MS, the only driver after 2018, steps by about 5 % on 6 October 2010, when that station’s radiation instrumentation was rebuilt. Both tower radiation sensors and NABEL step against it together. The fills are not affected, because a driver supplies the state of the sky, which a scale change does not alter. Do not read a difference between this product and MeteoSwiss Lägern as evidence about the tower across that date.
Nighttime values are exactly zero, not measurements. The small drifting nighttime offset of the pyranometer was removed per day before gap-filling. For instrument noise or the offset itself, use the screened database series.
2004 and most of 2005 are entirely modelled. They precede the measurement and rest on MeteoSwiss Lägern alone, which itself begins on 1 February 2004. These are the least constrained parts of the record.




The January 2016 acquisition change did nothing measurable to this series. It is recorded here because the same changeover moved TA_T1_47_1 by 1.3 °C. For TA the sensor and its conversion changed; for shortwave radiation neither did. Every surviving logger program, three CR10X programs of 2005-2006 and the CR1000 program installed at the changeover, reads the same Kipp & Zonen CNR1 (serial number 020484) on a 25 mV differential channel at multiplier 99.7009 (the reciprocal of its sensitivity) and offset 0. Across 2016 every ratio among the three shortwave sensors changes by less than in an ordinary year. The largest change, 1.4 %, is in the pair that does not involve the tower. Notebook 01 asserts this on every run.
The December 2021 replacement of the radiometer did not move the level either. A CNR4 replaced the CNR1, with a sensitivity of 13.89 instead of 10.03 µV/W/m². The date coincides with the change of screening software, so the two possible causes of a step cannot be separated, but neither produces one.

In 2012 a logger clock error shifted one block of August by 15.5 hours, and a tower power-supply failure in late July and August and storm damage in late October and November left records that could not be repaired. The clock error was corrected, the other two periods were removed, and all of it was gap-filled.

title: Incoming shortwave radiation at 47 m
text: Daytime gaps are filled by an XGBoost model, trained separately for 2004-2018 and 2019-2026. The split is where the NABEL sensor at 49 m on the same tower ends, so that no model is trained on one driver set and applied to the other. Until 2018 the drivers are NABEL and MeteoSwiss Lägern (2.5 km away); from 2019 only Lägern remains, so the later fills rest on the more distant sensor. Code 2 marks the few half-hours where no driver was available. Drivers enter as measured, never gap-filled. Nighttime gaps are set to zero. A reference is used only as a driver and never replaces a measured value.

title: Incoming shortwave radiation at 47 m
text:
The sensor reads about 3 % high relative to its references from 2013. NABEL at 49 m, MeteoSwiss Lägern and the co-located PAR sensor all show it at once, which places the change on this radiometer. It develops over about three years rather than at a date, and the fieldbook records no maintenance or calibration of this radiometer between its installation in 2005 and its removal in 2021. The change is within the field uncertainty of a pyranometer of this class and is not corrected, because there is neither a boundary at which to apply a correction nor a known fault to justify one. Allow for a few per cent when comparing the middle of the record with its beginning.
The MeteoSwiss gap-filling driver changed level in October 2010. SW_IN_LAE_MS, the only driver after 2018, steps by about 5 % on 6 October 2010, when that station’s radiation instrumentation was rebuilt. Both tower radiation sensors and NABEL step against it together. The fills are not affected, because a driver supplies the state of the sky, which a scale change does not alter. Do not read a difference between this product and MeteoSwiss Lägern as evidence about the tower across that date.
Nighttime values are exactly zero, not measurements. The small drifting nighttime offset of the pyranometer was removed per day before gap-filling. For instrument noise or the offset itself, use the screened database series.
2004 and most of 2005 are entirely modelled. They precede the measurement and rest on MeteoSwiss Lägern alone, which itself begins on 1 February 2004. These are the least constrained parts of the record.

title: Incoming shortwave radiation at 47 m
text:
The January 2016 acquisition change did nothing measurable to this series. It is recorded here because the same changeover moved TA_T1_47_1 by 1.3 °C. For TA the sensor and its conversion changed; for shortwave radiation neither did. Every surviving logger program, three CR10X programs of 2005-2006 and the CR1000 program installed at the changeover, reads the same Kipp & Zonen CNR1 (serial number 020484) on a 25 mV differential channel at multiplier 99.7009 (the reciprocal of its sensitivity) and offset 0. Across 2016 every ratio among the three shortwave sensors changes by less than in an ordinary year. The largest change, 1.4 %, is in the pair that does not involve the tower. Notebook 01 asserts this on every run.
The December 2021 replacement of the radiometer did not move the level either. A CNR4 replaced the CNR1, with a sensitivity of 13.89 instead of 10.03 µV/W/m². The date coincides with the change of screening software, so the two possible causes of a step cannot be separated, but neither produces one.

title: Air temperature at 47 m
text:
Half-hourly air temperature at 47 m on the CH-LAE tower, 2004 to September 2026, gap-filled to completeness. The file is 02_METEO_TA_GAPFILLED_2004-2026.09 (parquet and CSV): 398,832 records on a continuous 30-minute index TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (middle of the half-hour, UTC+01:00, no daylight saving), from 2004-01-01 00:15 to 2026-09-30 23:45. 2026 is a partial year (January to September).
The interactive dashboard summarises the product on one page.
Method, evidence and checks:

On 21 January 2016 the Rotronic MP101A, read as an analog voltage, was replaced by a Campbell CS215 read over a digital line, together with the logger. Two things changed, and TA_T1_47_1_HOMOGENIZED_gfXG corrects both.
The old chain read too cold, day and night. A constant zero-point error of about -11 mV, at 10 mV per °C, left it reading about 1.1 °C below an aspirated reference on the same tower; the new probe reads about 0.2 °C above that reference. The difference between the two eras, +1.3197 °C, is added to every record before the changeover.
The two probes warm differently in sunshine. Both sit in passive radiation shields, which heat up in sun, and the newer one heats more. This part of the step occurs only in daylight, so a constant cannot remove it. It was measured against NABEL, an aspirated sensor at 49 m on the same tower, and subtracted from the later era. It is zero at night and 0.59 °C at most.
Both corrections were fitted against NABEL and scored against MeteoSwiss Lägern (2.5 km away), which entered neither fit.

The correction raises the earlier era by the constant and lowers the sunlit records of the later eras by the shield term (by 0.15 °C on average over the 2017-2025 annual means of measured records). Over the whole record it more than halves the apparent warming. From the complete columns, the difference between the 2005-2015 and 2017-2025 period means falls from +2.39 °C to +0.92 °C, and the Theil-Sen trend over annual means from +1.76 to +0.77 °C decade-1. From measured records only, the same figures are +2.47 °C and +1.00 °C, and +1.80 and +0.77 °C decade-1. Notebook 02 reports both.



On 16 May 2025 the raw 1-minute record of the 47 m probe jumps by about 5 °C between 09:32 and 09:42, while the 35 m sensor of the same tower does not change: the probe was handled. The fieldbook records a site visit that day, with the heating connection of the tower inlet found melted and disconnected. The half-hour 09:30 to 10:00 is removed and modelled (source code 5).
The change is placed on the 47 m probe by two comparisons. The 35 m sensor against MeteoSwiss Lägern, which contains no 47 m measurement, changes by an ordinary amount at the handling (-0.36 °C above 500 W m-2, 14 days after against 14 days before). The 47 m probe against the 35 m sensor changes in sun by -1.11 °C, more than on any other day of the surrounding half-year.

Code 7, the heated state from 22 October 2024, receives the shield term of the normal CS215 and nothing more. In strong sun it remains up to 0.92 °C too warm after homogenisation.
Code 6, from 16 May 2025, no longer has the daytime excess of the normal CS215 and receives no shield term. Its night level is compared with the normal CS215 of 2022-2024 against Lägern, month by month over March to September, and the difference, +0.058 °C, is removed as a constant. Its uncertainty is 0.22 °C, the year-to-year scatter of the same quantity among the reference years. After the correction, code 6 lies within 0.13 °C of the normal CS215 at night and in every radiation class. In a month hold-out (each month corrected with the term derived from the others) it departs from the normal CS215 by at most 0.215 °C, against up to 0.57 °C between one reference year and the others in the same month.




On 5 June 2026 a Campbell HygroVUE10 (SDI-12) replaced the CS215 at 47 m. The raw 1-minute record has a gap from 11:10 to 11:31 that day. The fieldbook adds the HygroVUE10 at this location on 5 June and records a change of its SDI-12 configuration with a new logger program on 11 June. The residual against MeteoSwiss Lägern changes level from that day, most in sun. The swap half-hour 11:00 to 11:30 is removed and modelled (source code 5).
NABEL ended in 2018, so Lägern is the only reference across this change. The transfer is fitted on two season-matched samples: the HygroVUE10 from 12 June to 30 September 2026 (5 to 11 June, before the configuration change, enter no fit) and the normal CS215 (code 0) on the same calendar dates of 2022 to 2024. It has two terms:

A radiation term, zero in the dark. In sun the HygroVUE10 reads cooler than the normal CS215 by an amount that grows with radiation, to 0.98 °C at 600 W m-2.
A night term, a constant. At night the HygroVUE10 reads 0.11 °C cooler than the mean of the CS215 summers, less than the scatter among those summers (0.19 °C).

After both terms the HygroVUE10 lies within 0.05 °C of the CS215 level at night and in every radiation class of the fitting sample. In a month hold-out (each month refitted without itself and predicted) the held-out months depart from the CS215 level by at most 0.18 °C, against up to 0.58 °C before the correction and up to 0.38 °C between one CS215 summer and the others in the same month. The shield term of the CS215 is then applied, so the HygroVUE10 era ends on the same reference level as the other eras.




A small difference in the shape of the day remains across 2016. The shield correction is fitted on the three years in which NABEL overlaps the CS215 (2016-2018) and applied until May 2025 and, through the transfer, to the HygroVUE10 era, so after 2018 it is an extrapolation. Against MeteoSwiss, 2013-2015 against 2016-2018, the homogenised column still carries a daily-maximum step of +0.21 °C, a diurnal-range step of +0.18 °C and a daily-minimum step of +0.03 °C; the measured column steps by up to +1.90 °C in the same statistics. Daily maxima and diurnal ranges are most affected by what remains.
The heated CS215 (code 7) is under-corrected in sun. Daytime values and daily maxima from 22 October 2024 to 16 May 2025 are biased warm, by up to 0.92 °C in strong sun. The excess grows gradually and its onset is dated by a rule over a month-long window, so records shortly before 22 October 2024 may already carry part of it.
The night term of code 6 is smaller than its uncertainty (+0.058 °C against 0.22 °C). It is applied because the change of probe state is established, not because the night difference is resolved, and it rests on one reference 2.5 km away.
The HygroVUE10 transfer rests on one summer and one reference. It is fitted on 12 June to 30 September 2026 against Lägern and applied as fitted to every HygroVUE10 record, including 5 to 11 June. Its behaviour in winter, under snow or rime and at low sun is untested. The CS215 level it is fitted to is a mean of three summers that differ among themselves at night by up to 0.19 °C, more than the night term of 0.11 °C. It is to be refitted once the HygroVUE10 record includes a winter.
The record is made self-consistent, not absolutely accurate. The later eras are standardised onto the shield behaviour of the MP101A, so its warm bias in sunshine (about +0.4 °C at strong radiation, relative to an aspirated sensor) remains in all of them.
Records reconstructed from NABEL have too little scatter. The 1,530 code-5 values come from a line fitted on NABEL, so they lie about 0.05 °C from it where a real measurement lies about 0.25 °C from it. Their means are sound; variance, extremes and other measures of spread over January 2004 are understated.
2004 is 72 % modelled. The tower record begins 2004-09-20 10:45. January 2004 is reconstructed from NABEL because the MeteoSwiss reference begins only on 1 February 2004. The first nine months of 2004 carry source code 3 and are the least constrained part of the record.
2026 is a partial year. A 2026 annual mean covers January to September only.

The excess grows gradually and its onset is dated by a rule over a month-long window, so records shortly before 22 October 2024 may already carry part of it.
The night term of code 6 is smaller than its uncertainty (+0.058 °C against 0.22 °C). It is applied because the change of probe state is established, not because the night difference is resolved, and it rests on one reference 2.5 km away.
The HygroVUE10 transfer rests on one summer and one reference. It is fitted on 12 June to 30 September 2026 against Lägern and applied as fitted to every HygroVUE10 record, including 5 to 11 June. Its behaviour in winter, under snow or rime and at low sun is untested. The CS215 level it is fitted to is a mean of three summers that differ among themselves at night by up to 0.19 °C, more than the night term of 0.11 °C. It is to be refitted once the HygroVUE10 record includes a winter.
The record is made self-consistent, not absolutely accurate. The later eras are standardised onto the shield behaviour of the MP101A, so its warm bias in sunshine (about +0.4 °C at strong radiation, relative to an aspirated sensor) remains in all of them.
Records reconstructed from NABEL have too little scatter. The 1,530 code-5 values come from a line fitted on NABEL, so they lie about 0.05 °C from it where a real measurement lies about 0.25 °C from it. Their means are sound; variance, extremes and other measures of spread over January 2004 are understated.
2004 is 72 % modelled. The tower record begins 2004-09-20 10:45. January 2004 is reconstructed from NABEL because the MeteoSwiss reference begins only on 1 February 2004. The first nine months of 2004 carry source code 3 and are the least constrained part of the record.
2026 is a partial year. A 2026 annual mean covers January to September only.

VPD is not measured. It is computed by formula from air temperature and relative humidity, so it inherits the properties of those two products.

title: Merge IRGA72 Level-0 output (2016-2026.09)
text:
ℹ️ About this notebook
Merges the EddyPro FLUXNET output files of the Level-0 (preliminary) flux calculations for the IRGA72 gas analyser into one continuous 30MIN dataframe and stores it in the external data folder, as parquet and as csv.
Its task is to bring the per-run output files onto one continuous timestamp index, so that the Level-0 check notebooks (03 fluxes, 04 wind direction, 05 time lags) all read the same file instead of each re-reading the raw output. No value is computed or corrected here. The only change to the incoming data is that the six biomet columns exported by mistake in the 2025 run are dropped, which is done here rather than in each reader so that the merged record has one column set over its whole length.

title: Merge IRGA72 Level-0 output (2016-2026.09)
text:
📇 Data sources
EddyPro FLUXNET output files (*_adv.csv), one per processing run, in the external data folder under 0_data/OPENLAG-IRGA72-Level-0_fluxnet_2016-2026.09/.
A run covers one or more setup periods, not a calendar year: 2016_2+3 is a single run over setup periods 2 and 3 of 2016, and a run boundary marks a hardware or configuration change. The merge therefore works on the timestamps inside the files, not on the file names. The setup periods, and the numbered notes that go with them, are documented in docs/Yearly_Notes.md and on the SwissFluxNet page it links to.
Three setup periods are missing from this folder, and none of them is an oversight:

2019_3 (17 Jan - 20 Mar 2019) was measured with the LI-7500 (IRGA75), which stood in for the defective LI-7200. It is processed with the other IRGA75 runs and stays in the IRGA75 source folder, which is what the +2019 in that folder’s name means.
2021_2 and 2022_1 (13 Dec 2021 - 7 Feb 2022) have no output at all: the raw data was logged in an unknown format and the conversion fails on an unrecognised record length, so it may be corrupted.

A fourth period is present but empty of gas fluxes: the LI-7200 was replaced on 11 January 2019 and both units were defective, so the 2019_2 file contributes no FC and no LE. It does contribute sensible heat flux, which comes from the sonic. Coverage below is therefore counted on FC, not on a flux that survives a gas-analyser fault.
The 2025 run additionally exported six biomet inputs (TA_1_1_1, RH_1_1_1, PA_1_1_1, SW_IN_1_1_1, LW_IN_1_1_1, PPFD_IN_1_1_1) that do not belong in the EC output and that no other run carries. They are dropped after the merge, so the merged record has one column set over its whole length; the meteo variables come from the 10_METEO products, not from the EddyPro output.

title: Merge IRGA72 Level-0 output (2016-2026.09)
text:
🕐 Timestamp convention
The EddyPro output carries TIMESTAMP_START and TIMESTAMP_END. MultiDataFileReader is called with output_middle_timestamp=True, so the merged record is indexed on TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE, the same convention the meteo products use. Timestamps are used as written by EddyPro; nothing is shifted here.

title: Merge IRGA72 Level-0 output (2016-2026.09)
text:
⚙️ Settings

# --- Source ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The Level-0 EddyPro FLUXNET output files. They live in the external (untracked) data folder and
# are addressed by absolute path, so the notebook does not depend on the working directory.
SOURCEDIR = (r"<DATA_FOLDER>"
             r"\workflow\0_data\OPENLAG-IRGA72-Level-0_fluxnet_2016-2026.09")
SOURCEPATTERN = "*_adv.csv"  # the FLUXNET output files; anything else in that folder is ignored
FILETYPE = 'EDDYPRO-FLUXNET-CSV-30MIN'

# --- Output ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Data files carry the same numeric prefix and the same relative path as the notebook producing
# them, in the external data folder. Same convention as the meteo notebooks.
OUTNAME = "01_OPENLAG_EDDYPRO_FLUXNET_OUTPUT_IRGA72_2016-2026.09"
OUTPATH = (r"<DATA_FOLDER>"
           r"\workflow\00_L0_CHECKS\IRGA72")

# --- Biomet columns exported by mistake ---------------------------------------------------------
# The 2025 run wrote its biomet inputs into the EC output. They belong to the meteo products in
# 10_METEO, not here, and only that one run carries them. Dropping them keeps the merged record on

title: Merge IRGA72 Level-0 output (2016-2026.09)
text:
🧹 Drop the biomet columns
The 2025 run exported the biomet inputs into the EC output by mistake. They are dropped here rather than in each reader, so that the merged record has one column set over its whole length and nobody downstream takes a meteo value from the EddyPro output instead of from the 10_METEO products.
The drop is guarded by reading the header of every source file, which tests the cause rather than a proxy for it. Guarding on the year does not work: a run begins at the last binary of the previous December (2025_1 starts at 2024123119.L00), so its records reach back into 31 December 2024 and the biomet columns legitimately hold data in two calendar years.

_present = [c for c in DROPCOLS if c in df.columns]

# Guard before the drop, on the cause rather than on a proxy for it: read the header of every
# source file and confirm that exactly one run carries these columns. Guarding on the year does not
# work here - a run starts at the last binary of the previous December (2025_1 starts at
# 2024123119.L00), so its records reach back into 31 December of the year before.
_files_with_biomet = []
for _f in sourcefiles:
    with open(_f, encoding='utf-8') as _fh:
        _header = _fh.readline().strip().split(',')
    if any(c in _header for c in DROPCOLS):
        _files_with_biomet.append(_f.name)

print("Source files carrying biomet columns:")
for _n in _files_with_biomet:
    print(f"  {_n}")
assert len(_files_with_biomet) == DROPCOLS_N_RUNS, \
    (f"{len(_files_with_biomet)} runs carry the biomet columns, expected {DROPCOLS_N_RUNS}. "
     f"Check whether the additional run really exported them by mistake before widening this.")

if _present:
    _biomet_records = df.index[df[_present].notna().any(axis=1)]
    print(f"\nColumns found: {_present}")
    print(f"Records holding data in them: {len(_biomet_records):,} "
          f"({_biomet_records[0]} -> {_biomet_records[-1]})")

df = df.drop(columns=_present)
print(f"\nDropped {len(_present)} column(s). {len(df.columns):,} columns remain.")

text:
🔍 Checks

# The merged index must be continuous 30MIN, unique and ascending. MultiDataFileReader reindexes
# to a continuous timestamp, so a failure here means the incoming files were not what was assumed.
assert df.index.is_monotonic_increasing, "timestamp index is not ascending"
assert not df.index.duplicated().any(), "duplicate timestamps in the merged record"
_steps = df.index.to_series().diff().dropna().unique()
assert len(_steps) == 1 and _steps[0] == pd.Timedelta(REQUIRED_TIME_RESOLUTION), \
    f"index is not continuous {REQUIRED_TIME_RESOLUTION}, found steps: {_steps}"

# A year can be present in the index and still be empty: the index is continuous, so a source file
# that was not exported shows up as a year full of NaN rather than as a gap in the index.
_available = df[CHECKCOL].groupby(df.index.year).count()
_missing = [y for y in EXPECTED_YEARS if _available.get(y, 0) == 0]
assert not _missing, f"no {CHECKCOL} data for {_missing}, source file missing?"

print(f"Available {CHECKCOL} records per year:")
display(_available.rename(f'{CHECKCOL} records'))

title: MeteoSwiss reference meteorology: Lägern (LAE), 2004 to September 2026
text:
ℹ️ About this notebook
Downloads the 10-minute record of the MeteoSwiss SMN station Lägern (lae) from the open-data STAC API, aggregates it to 30MIN and writes one multi-variable reference product. It does not use the InfluxDB database and applies no screening.
Why LAE. It is the MeteoSwiss station closest to the tower: 2.5 km away on the same ridge, at 845 m, above the tower top (689 m base + 47 m). Unlike the NABEL sensors, which end in 2018, it covers the whole record, and as a full weather station it provides references for TA, RH, PA and SW_IN in one download.
Parameters LAE does not measure (checked against the data, not the station description):








Variable

Precipitation

empty in every record; notebook 06 (LW_IN) has no reference here

empty

Coverage. The 10-min record begins on 2004-02-01, so January 2004 has no LAE reference. Diffuse radiation (ods000z0) begins in October 2010. Completeness per year and parameter is tabulated under Coverage per year.

title: MeteoSwiss reference meteorology: Lägern (LAE), 2004 to September 2026
text:
⏱️ Timestamp convention
MeteoSwiss timestamps are UTC. In the 10-min files reference_timestamp marks the end of the interval: a record at t covers (t-10min, t]. This matches the database’s TIMESTAMP_END, so the product is binned end-labelled and then shifted by TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS to local time. The convention is verified below against the published hourly file.
Means and spot values. gre000z0, ods000z0 and dkl010z0 are ten-minute means, so three of them average to a true half-hourly mean. tre200s0, ure200s0, tde200s0, pva200s0 and prestas0 are instantaneous values, so their 30MIN value is a three-sample estimate of the half-hourly mean. For smoothly varying quantities the difference is small but not zero.

✏️ Settings

# --- Reference station ---
STAC_COLLECTION = 'ch.meteoschweiz.ogd-smn'  # full automatic weather stations
STAC_STATION = 'lae'                         # Lägern, 47.481933 N / 8.397222 E, 845 m

# --- Time axis ---
TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS = 1  # UTC+01:00 (CET), as in the meteo notebooks
TARGET_FREQ = '30min'
RECORDS_PER_BIN = 3  # 10-min records in a complete 30MIN bin

# --- Period, local time (UTC+01:00) ---
START = '2004-01-01 00:00'  # start of the first period (data begin 2004-02-01)
END = '2026-10-01 00:00'    # TIMESTAMP_END of the last period, included (end of 30 Sep 2026)
YEARS = '2004-2026.09'      # period label in the file name, checked against the data before export

# --- Parameters to export: shortname -> (output column, aggregation) ---
# 'mean' for state variables and 10-min means, 'sum' for durations, 'max' for gusts,
# 'circmean' for wind direction.
PARAMS = {
    'tre200s0': ('TA_LAE_MS', 'mean'),          # air temperature 2 m [°C]
    'ure200s0': ('RH_LAE_MS', 'mean'),          # relative humidity 2 m [%]
    'tde200s0': ('TDEW_LAE_MS', 'mean'),        # dew point 2 m [°C]
    'pva200s0': ('VP_LAE_MS', 'mean'),          # vapour pressure 2 m [hPa]
    'prestas0': ('PA_LAE_MS', 'mean'),          # pressure at station altitude, QFE [hPa]
    'gre000z0': ('SW_IN_LAE_MS', 'mean'),       # global radiation [W m-2]
    'ods000z0': ('SW_IN_DIFF_LAE_MS', 'mean'),  # diffuse radiation [W m-2], from October 2010
    'sre000z0': ('SUNDUR_LAE_MS', 'sum'),       # sunshine duration [min]
    'fve010z0': ('WS_LAE_MS', 'mean'),          # wind speed, vectorial 10-min mean [m s-1]
    'fkl010z1': ('WS_GUST_LAE_MS', 'max'),      # gust peak, 1 s maximum [m s-1]
    'dkl010z0': ('WD_LAE_MS', 'circmean'),      # wind direction, 10-min mean [°]
}

text:
🔧 Helpers

STAC_ITEM_URL = f'https://data.geo.admin.ch/api/stac/v1/collections/{STAC_COLLECTION}/items/{STAC_STATION}'

# Period bounds in UTC, the time base of the MeteoSwiss files.
START_UTC = pd.Timestamp(START) - pd.Timedelta(hours=TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS)
END_UTC = pd.Timestamp(END) - pd.Timedelta(hours=TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS)


def stac_assets(url: str) -> dict:
    """Return {filename: href} for a STAC item. Raises if the item has no assets."""
    with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as r:
        item = json.load(r)
    assets = {k: v['href'] for k, v in item.get('assets', {}).items()}
    if not assets:
        raise ValueError(f'STAC item {url} exposes no assets - wrong collection or station?')
    return assets


def source_files(assets: dict, res: str) -> list:
    """Files of resolution *res* ('t' 10-min, 'h' hourly) covering the period.

    Returns the `historical_<decade>` files overlapping START..END, oldest first, followed by
    the `recent` file (current year). Raises unless both kinds are found.
    """
    hist = []
    for k in sorted(assets):
        m = re.search(rf'_{res}_historical_(\d{{4}})-(\d{{4}})\.csv$', k)
        if m and int(m[1]) <= END_UTC.year and int(m[2]) >= START_UTC.year:
            hist.append(k)
    recent = [k for k in assets if k.endswith(f'_{res}_recent.csv')]
    if not hist or len(recent) != 1:
        raise ValueError(f'expected historical files and one recent file for {res!r}: {hist}, {recent}')
    return hist + recent


def read_ms_csv(href: str, params: list) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read one MeteoSwiss CSV and return *params* as a UTC-indexed, sorted DataFrame."""
    with urllib.request.urlopen(href) as r:
        df = pd.read_csv(io.BytesIO(r.read()), sep=';')
    missing = [p for p in params if p not in df.columns]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f'{missing} not in {href} (has: {list(df.columns)})')
    df['TIMESTAMP'] = pd.to_datetime(df['reference_timestamp'], format='%d.%m.%Y %H:%M')
    return df.set_index('TIMESTAMP')[params].sort_index()


def circular_mean(deg: pd.Series, freq: str) -> pd.Series:
    """Resample a direction in degrees by averaging on the unit circle.

    A linear mean fails across the 0/360 wrap (350° and 10° give 180°, not 0°),
    so the sine and cosine components are averaged instead.
    """
    rad = np.deg2rad(deg)
    res_s = np.sin(rad).resample(freq, label='right', closed='right').mean()
    res_c = np.cos(rad).resample(freq, label='right', closed='right').mean()
    return (np.rad2deg(np.arctan2(res_s, res_c)) % 360).where(res_s.notna())


Negative control
Each helper that could silently return nothing is given bad input and must raise.

# Wrong collection: LAE is a full weather station, not a precip-only station.
try:
    stac_assets(f'https://data.geo.admin.ch/api/stac/v1/collections/'
                f'ch.meteoschweiz.ogd-smn-precip/items/{STAC_STATION}')
except Exception as e:
    print(f'OK, raised as expected: {type(e).__name__}')
else:
    raise AssertionError('expected a failure for the precip-only collection, got assets')

# Wrong parameter name must raise rather than return an empty frame.
try:
    read_ms_csv(stac_assets(STAC_ITEM_URL)['ogd-smn_lae_t_historical_2010-2019.csv'], ['nosuchparam'])
except ValueError as e:
    print(f'OK, raised as expected: {str(e)[:60]}...')
else:
    raise AssertionError('expected a ValueError for an unknown parameter')

# circular_mean must not return the linear mean across the 0/360 wrap.
_idx = pd.date_range('2020-01-01 00:00', periods=6, freq='10min')
_test = pd.Series([350.0, 10.0, 350.0, 10.0, 350.0, 10.0], index=_idx)
_got = circular_mean(_test, '30min').iloc[0]
assert _got > 340 or _got < 20, f'circular mean across the wrap is broken: got {_got}'
print(f'OK, circular mean of [350, 10, 350] = {_got:.1f}° (a linear mean would give 236.7°)')

📥 Download the 10-min record
MeteoSwiss splits each record into historical files, which end on 31 December of the previous year, and a recent file holding the current year up to the previous day. 2004-2025 come from the 10-min historical files and January to September 2026 from _t_recent; the _now file is not used. ⏲️ Aggregate to 30MIN
One rule per parameter, from PARAMS. N_RECORDS counts the 10-min values in each bin, so incomplete bins can be identified downstream.

def aggregate(df: pd.DataFrame, freq: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Aggregate 10-min (end-labelled) values to *freq*, one rule per parameter."""
    res = df.resample(freq, label='right', closed='right')
    out = {}
    for short, (name, how) in PARAMS.items():
        if how == 'mean':
            out[name] = res[short].mean()
        elif how == 'sum':
            out[name] = res[short].sum(min_count=1)  # min_count: all-NaN stays NaN, not 0
        elif how == 'max':
            out[name] = res[short].max()
        elif how == 'circmean':
            out[name] = circular_mean(df[short], freq)
        else:
            raise ValueError(f'unknown aggregation {how!r} for {short}')
    out['N_RECORDS'] = res['tre200s0'].count()
    return pd.DataFrame(out)

✅ Cross-check against the published hourly file
Rolling the 30MIN product up to hourly and comparing it with the published hourly product is an independent check of the timestamp convention. title: MeteoSwiss regional reference precipitation — station ensemble around CH-LAE, 2004-2025
text:
ℹ️ About this notebook
Downloads daily precipitation from the MeteoSwiss open-data STAC API for every station within MAX_DIST_KM of the tower that covers the whole 2004-2025 period, and writes them as one reference product.
This notebook does not touch the InfluxDB database and screens nothing. Like the other 10_REFERENCE notebooks it only fetches independent reference data and puts it on our time axis.






ImportantWhy an ensemble, when we already have OED



MeteoSwiss_OED_PREC_2004-2025.ipynb fetches the nearest gauge, Ehrendingen (OED), and that is the right tool for spotting when something changed at the tower: it is close, and it resolves accumulation faults over weeks.
It cannot answer a different question — which of two tower records is right. When the tower and one reference disagree, a single reference cannot say which of the two moved. The 2018 acquisition change at CH-LAE (see 30_PRODUCTS/08_METEO_PREC_2004-2025.ipynb) is exactly that situation: the tower’s catch ratio against OED steps by a factor of 1.3, and OED alone cannot rule out that OED is what changed.
An ensemble can. If the tower steps against thirteen independent stations at once, the tower moved. And because the stations span a range of elevations, they also give an elevation-precipitation gradient, which turns “the tower disagrees with its neighbours” into “the tower is N % away from what a station at 690 m should record”.
That is the whole purpose of this product. It is a diagnostic reference: nothing here is ever written into a tower series, and no value here is used to fill a gap. (Sub-daily gap-filling uses the OED 30MIN product, which is a different file.)

title: MeteoSwiss regional reference precipitation — station ensemble around CH-LAE, 2004-2025
text:
⏱️ Timestamp convention (important)
MeteoSwiss publishes all reference timestamps in UTC, and the precipitation day runs 06 UTC → 06 UTC: the value labelled day D covers [D 06:00 UTC, D+1 06:00 UTC). This is not a local-midnight day.
Like the OED daily product, this file is therefore left on its native MeteoSwiss precipitation day and is not shifted to local time. Anything comparing our own data against it must re-aggregate ours onto the same 06-UTC day first — notebook 30_PRODUCTS/08 does this with a to_ms_precip_day() helper. Comparing against a local-midnight daily sum is wrong by six hours and smears every rain event across two days.
Only the daily resolution is fetched here. Sub-daily data would be far heavier, most of these stations do not have it back to 2004, and the questions this product exists to answer — annual level, elevation gradient, era-to-era steps — are all daily-or-coarser questions.

series, info = {}, []
for _, r in near.iterrows():
    ab, coll = r['station_abbr'], r['collection']
    try:
        assets = stac_assets(coll, ab)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f'  {ab:<6} skipped: STAC lookup failed ({type(e).__name__})')
        continue
    files = sorted(k for k in assets if '_d_historical' in k)

    parts = []
    for k in files:

            parts.append(read_ms_csv(assets[k], PARAM_DAILY))

    if not parts:
        print(f'  {ab:<6} skipped: {PARAM_DAILY} absent (station measures no precipitation)')
        continue
    s = pd.concat(parts).sort_index()
    s = s[~s.index.duplicated(keep='first')].loc[START:STOP]

Characterising the ensemble

📝 Notes for downstream users

Source: MeteoSwiss. Cite it in anything derived from these files.
The index is the MeteoSwiss precipitation day (06 UTC → 06 UTC), not shifted to local time. Re-aggregate our own data onto the same day before comparing, or the comparison is off by six hours.
One column per station, named PREC_<ABBR>_MS_DAILY. PREC_MeteoSwiss_REGIONAL_STATIONS_*.csv carries each station’s elevation, distance and coordinates — you need the elevations to use this product for anything but a plain average.
Diagnostic only. Nothing here is written into a tower series and nothing here fills a gap. Sub-daily gap-filling in 30_PRODUCTS/08 uses the separate OED 30MIN product.
The ensemble is entirely below the tower. Stations span roughly 330-600 m against the tower’s 690 m, because the two local hilltop stations (Lägern, Uetliberg) publish no precipitation. Any elevation extrapolation to 690 m is therefore outside the fitted range — treat it as an order-of-magnitude expectation, not a calibration target.
Use the ensemble, not one station. The point of this product is that a disagreement with a single gauge is ambiguous, while a simultaneous disagreement with a dozen is not. For a regional index take the mean over days where every station reports.
Gaps are NaN, not 0. A missing day is not a dry day.

title: MeteoScreening from database (influxdb)
text:
ℹ️ About this notebook
Download raw meteo data from the InfluxDB database, quality-screen and correct it on the high-resolution data, resample to 30MIN, and upload the result back to the database. Screening uses StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb from diive. Download and upload use diive’s InfluxDB engine (InfluxIO, in diive/core/io/db/influx), which needs uv sync --group db.
Flow: download (InfluxIO) → screen on high-res data (diive) → resample to 30MIN → upload.
Screening is stepwise. Run a test, look at its preview, then commit it with mscr.addflag(). Run only the methods your variable needs. At the end all committed flags are aggregated into one quality flag QCF.

title: MeteoScreening from database (influxdb)
text:
⏱️ Timestamp convention (important)
The database stores every timestamp in UTC and as TIMESTAMP_END. The stamp marks the end of the averaging interval. This has to be right, because the day/night split during screening and the value written back to the database both depend on it.
The single knob is TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS, set in User settings. It is applied the same way on download and on upload:









Stage
Timezone
Convention
Done by




Database
UTC
TIMESTAMP_END
InfluxDB


After dbc.download(..., timezone_offset_to_utc_hours=N)
local (UTC+N)
TIMESTAMP_END
InfluxIO


During screening
local
TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE (converted internally)
StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb


After mscr.resample()
local
back to TIMESTAMP_END
diive


After dbc.upload_singlevar(..., timezone_offset_to_utc_hours=N)
UTC
TIMESTAMP_END
InfluxIO



So screening runs on local middle-of-period timestamps, and the resampled value lands on the correct UTC end-of-period stamp. Set TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS to the timezone the raw data was logged in (for example 1 for CET winter time). The notebook prints the timestamps after the download and after the check download so you can confirm them.
This also affects manual removal. Removal is matched against TIMESTAMP_MID, so a single timestamp matches no record and removes nothing. Write a single record as a range that brackets it.

title: MeteoScreening from database (influxdb)
text:
✏️ User settings (please adjust)
Adjust these before running. What each setting means:
Site - SITE, SITE_LAT, SITE_LON: site ID and coordinates. The coordinates set the day/night split used during screening.
Variables to screen - FIELDS: variable name(s) exactly as stored in the database (the InfluxDB _field). Several are allowed. - MEASUREMENT: exactly one measurement that groups those variables.
Time range to screen - START: first timestamp to screen. It is included. - STOP: upper bound. It is not included.
Data settings - TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS: the timestamp knob, see Timestamp convention. It must match how the raw data was logged. - DATA_VERSION: the source data version in the database (raw). - DIRCONF: local folder holding the database connection config.

title: MeteoScreening from database (influxdb)
text:
🔍 Outlier detection
Each method has a test cell and an mscr.addflag() cell. Run the test as often as you like with different settings and look at the preview. Only mscr.addflag() commits the flag, and it commits the most recent test. Run only the methods your variable needs.
separate_day_night=True uses separate thresholds for day and night. The boundary comes from the site coordinates given above.

mscr.start_outlier_detection()

  > Starting step-wise outlier detection for variable G_FF1_0.05_1 ...



Plot the current cleaned data at any point during detection. interactive=True opens a Bokeh plot in the browser instead, with hover and zoom. showplot_orig() and showplot_cleaned() take the same argument.

mscr.showplot_outlier_detection_cleaned()









Manual removal
Removes given timestamps or time ranges. Use it for known sensor failures and maintenance periods. A single timestamp matches nothing, so write a range that brackets the record (see Timestamp convention). For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.ManualRemoval).

REMOVE_DATES = [
    ['2024-07-14 07:15:00', '2024-07-19 00:00:15'],
]
mscr.flag_manualremoval_test(remove_dates=REMOVE_DATES, showplot=True, verbose=True)


mscr.addflag()



Hampel filter
Spike detection in a sliding window, using the median absolute deviation. It is a good general-purpose filter and is not thrown off by spikes already inside the window. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.Hampel).

mscr.flag_outliers_hampel_test(
    window_length=60 * 24 * 7,  # records per window
    n_sigma_daytime=5.5, n_sigma_nighttime=5.5,
    use_differencing=True, separate_day_night=True,
    repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Z-score
Flags values further from the mean than thres_zscore standard deviations. It uses the whole record, so it responds to the seasonal cycle as well as to faults. Some variables have valid values below zero or above a nominal maximum, and those are handled in Corrections, so check the preview before committing. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.zScore).

mscr.flag_outliers_zscore_test(
    thres_zscore=4.5, separate_day_night=True,
    repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Z-score (rolling window)
The same test in a moving window of winsize records. It follows slow drifts and flags only local spikes. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.zScoreRolling).

mscr.flag_outliers_zscore_rolling_test(
    thres_zscore=4.5, winsize=1440 * 7,
    repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Local standard deviation
Flags values further than n_sd standard deviations from a rolling window of winsize records. constant_sd=True uses one standard deviation for the whole record instead of one per window. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.LocalSD).

mscr.flag_outliers_localsd_test(
    separate_day_night=False, n_sd=5.5, winsize=60 * 24 * 3,
    constant_sd=False, repeat=False, showplot=True, verbose=True,
)

  > running LocalSD ...



  ITERATION#1 (global): Total found outliers: 4 values


















mscr.addflag()

  > ++Added flag column FLAG_G_FF1_0.05_1_OUTLIER_LOCALSD_TEST to flag data





Increments z-score
Flags jumps between consecutive records that are too large. It catches spikes and steps that tests on the value itself miss. Differences are computed after missing records are dropped, so the records on either side of a gap are compared across it. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.zScoreIncrements).

mscr.flag_outliers_increments_zcore_test(thres_zscore=40, repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True)


mscr.addflag()



Local outlier factor
Density-based detection using nearest neighbours. Flags points that sit apart from their neighbours. Slow on high-resolution data, so use it on 30MIN or coarser. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.LocalOutlierFactor).

mscr.flag_outliers_lof_test(
    n_neighbors=30, contamination=0.01, separate_day_night=False,
    repeat=False, n_jobs=-1, showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Absolute limits
Flags values outside the fixed range [minval, maxval]. For separate day and night ranges set minval_daytime, maxval_daytime, minval_nighttime or maxval_nighttime. Setting any of those turns the day/night split on. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.AbsoluteLimits).

mscr.flag_outliers_abslim_test(minval=-20, maxval=40, showplot=True, verbose=True)

  > running AbsoluteLimits ...











mscr.addflag()

  > ++Added flag column FLAG_G_FF1_0.05_1_OUTLIER_ABSLIM_TEST to flag data





Trim low
Flags values below lower_limit, then flags the same number of the highest values, so the trim is symmetric. trim_daytime and trim_nighttime choose which period is trimmed. For all parameters run help(dv.outliers.TrimLow).

mscr.flag_outliers_trim_low_test(
    trim_daytime=False, trim_nighttime=True, lower_limit=10,
    showplot=True, verbose=True,
)


mscr.addflag()



Missing values
Not an outlier test. It flags missing records so they are counted in QCF. There is no addflag() here.

mscr.flag_missingvals_test(verbose=True)

calculated from variable G_FF1_0.05_1, with flag 0 (good values) where G_FF1_0.05_1 is available, 
flag 2 (bad values) where G_FF1_0.05_1 is missing.





Overall quality flag QCF
Aggregate all committed flags into one flag QCF (0 = good, 1 = marginal, 2 = bad) and filter the series. Run this before corrections and resampling.

⬆️ Upload data to database
Re-uploading overwrites the same variant, so it is safe to re-run. With delete_from_db_before_upload=True the upload first deletes, then writes. The delete matches _measurement plus varname plus data_version (meteoscreening_diive) over the uploaded time range, so re-screening a period replaces only its own previous result. It does not touch the raw data, other variables, or other data versions.
The delete matters because InfluxDB keys a point by its full tag set. If a tag changed between runs, a plain overwrite would leave the old point in place as a duplicate. The delete removes the old point regardless of its tags.

text:
Check downloaded data

dbc downloads three variables:

data_simple: This is the simplest data download. It contains only the high-resolution variable(s) from the specified measurement. Each variable is in a separate column. Since different variables, can have different time resolutions, the highest time resolution across the variables is used as the index. This means that lower resolution variables will show gaps in the higher resolution timestamp.
data_detailed: This is the most important variable for the MeteoScreening from the database, because it contains not only the high-resolution time series of the variable(s), but also their tags. The tags are important when uploading data to the database. This is a very special format, because data for each variable are stored in a dictionary. A dictionary is a data structure that stores key-value pairs. The key is the variable name (e.g., TA_NABEL_T1_35_1) and the value is a complete dataframe that contains the time series of the respective variable and all tags.
assigned_measurements: An auxiliary variable that is useful to check whether the measurement of the variable(s) is correct. In case we are screening air temperatures, the measurement must be TA.

Simply contains the time series of the measured variable(s) in a nice-to-look-at dataframe.

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
ℹ️ About this notebook
Downloads raw meteo data from InfluxDB, screens and corrects them at high resolution, resamples them to RESAMPLING_FREQ and uploads the result to the database. Screening uses StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb. Download and upload use InfluxIO, which needs pip install "diive[all]".
Screening is stepwise. Run a test, check its preview, then commit it with mscr.addflag(). At the end, all committed flags are combined into one quality flag, QCF.
Run All applies no outlier test and no correction, because they are all commented out. It still resamples, and it uploads only with UPLOAD = True.

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
⏱️ Timestamp convention (important)
The database stores all timestamps in UTC as TIMESTAMP_END, the end of the averaging interval. TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS sets the local time frame of the notebook, e.g. 1 for UTC+01:00. START, STOP, typed dates, the day/night split and day boundaries all use this frame. The download converts from UTC to this frame, the upload converts back. With a sub-daily RESAMPLING_FREQ such as '30min' the stored values are therefore the same for any offset. With '1D' the day boundaries follow the offset, so the daily values depend on it.
The raw data in the database are already in UTC, whatever clock the logger used. Use one fixed offset for every month, e.g. 1 (CET) also in summer. Changing it shifts START, STOP and typed dates, which leaves a gap or an overlap between runs.
Timestamps at each stage:

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
✏️ User settings (please adjust)
Adjust these before running.
Site - SITE, SITE_LAT, SITE_LON: site ID and coordinates. The coordinates set the day/night split.
Variables to screen - FIELDS: one or more variable names exactly as stored in the database (the InfluxDB _field). - MEASUREMENT: exactly one measurement that holds these variables.
Time range to screen - START, STOP: each one second after a RESAMPLING_FREQ boundary, e.g. '2026-03-01 00:00:01' and '2026-04-01 00:00:01' for March. Timestamps mark the END of each interval, so the record at 2026-03-01 00:00:00 belongs to February. These values cover the records ending after 2026-03-01 00:00 up to and including 2026-04-01 00:00. The upload deletes the same range before writing. Other values stop the notebook in Auto settings.
Data settings - TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS: local time frame of this run, one fixed offset without daylight saving time, see Timestamp convention. - DATA_VERSION: data version of the source data (raw). - DIRCONF: local folder with the database connection config.
Resampling - RESAMPLING_FREQ: target time resolution of the screened data. - RESAMPLING_AGG: 'mean' or 'sum'. Use 'sum' only for variables that accumulate over the interval.
Upload - UPLOAD: False runs everything except the upload. Set True only for the run that should write the result. The upload replaces the stored values between START and STOP.

# --- Site ---
SITE = 'ch-lae'
SITE_LAT = 47.478333   # CH-LAE
SITE_LON = 8.364389  # CH-LAE

# --- Variables to screen ---
FIELDS = [
    'LW_IN_T1_47_1',
]
MEASUREMENT = 'LW'

# --- Time range to screen ---
# One second after a RESAMPLING_FREQ boundary, because stamps mark the END of each interval:
# these values cover the records ending after 2026-03-01 00:00 up to and including 2026-04-01 00:00.
START = '2026-01-01 00:00:01'
STOP = '2026-10-01 00:00:01'

# --- Data settings ---
DATA_VERSION = 'raw'
# Local time frame of this run. The database holds UTC. Use one fixed value for every month,
# e.g. 1 (CET) also in summer: changing it shifts START/STOP and typed dates.
TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS = 1  # UTC+01:00
DIRCONF = r'<LOCAL>\poet\configs'  # <-- must be set: folder with the database connection config
# DIRCONF = r'P:\Flux\RDS_calculations\_scripts\_configs'

# --- Resampling ---
RESAMPLING_FREQ = '30min'
RESAMPLING_AGG = 'mean'  # 'mean' or 'sum'

# --- Upload ---
UPLOAD = True  # True writes the result to the database, replacing stored values between START and STOP

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
🤖 Auto settings

Buckets and time range check (do not adjust)

import pandas as pd

BUCKET_RAW = f'{SITE}_raw'  # source bucket
BUCKET_PROCESSED = f'{SITE}_processed'  # destination bucket
print(f'Source bucket (raw data):       {BUCKET_RAW}')
print(f'Destination bucket (processed): {BUCKET_PROCESSED}')

# START and STOP must be one second after a RESAMPLING_FREQ boundary, see the user settings.
one_second = pd.Timedelta(seconds=1)
for name, value in (('START', START), ('STOP', STOP)):
    expected = pd.Timestamp(value).floor(RESAMPLING_FREQ) + one_second
    if pd.Timestamp(value) != expected:
        raise ValueError(f"{name} = '{value}' is not one second after a {RESAMPLING_FREQ} boundary. "
                         f"Stamps mark the END of each interval. Use e.g. '{expected}'.")
if pd.Timestamp(STOP) <= pd.Timestamp(START):
    raise ValueError(f"STOP ('{STOP}') must be after START ('{START}').")
print(f'Time range: records ending after {pd.Timestamp(START) - one_second} '
      f'up to and including {pd.Timestamp(STOP) - one_second}')

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
🔍 Outlier detection
Each method has a test cell and an mscr.addflag() cell. Rerun a test with other settings as often as needed: mscr.addflag() commits the latest run. Run only the methods your variable needs.
Day and night. With separate_day_night=True the statistic is computed separately for daytime and nighttime, split by the site coordinates. Some methods also take separate daytime and nighttime thresholds, see the docs.
Windows. Window sizes are time spans such as '7D' or record counts. A time span becomes a record count at the time resolution of the data, so one setting works for 1-minute and 10-minute data. The window counts the records present, so across gaps it covers more calendar days. Local SD with separate_day_night=True counts only daytime or only nighttime records, so its window covers even more days: at 47° N in January about 16-20 days for daytime and 10-13 days for nighttime with '7D'. Data that change resolution are tested per resolution period.
All tests are commented out, so Run All applies none. The example settings are only a starting point and can remove valid data. To use a test, check its settings and notes, uncomment the test and its mscr.addflag() cell, then check the preview.

mscr.start_outlier_detection()

Plot the cleaned data at any point. With interactive=True the plot opens in the browser (Bokeh, with hover and zoom). showplot_orig() and showplot_cleaned() take the same argument.

mscr.showplot_outlier_detection_cleaned()


Manual removal
Flags single timestamps or [start, end] ranges (both ends included), e.g. known sensor failures. Use timestamps as in the downloaded data: local time, end of the averaging interval. Docs: flag_manualremoval_test, ManualRemoval.

# REMOVE_DATES = [
#     # '2026-03-10 14:31:00',  # single record
#     # ['2026-03-12 08:00:00', '2026-03-12 11:30:00'],  # range, both ends included
# ]
# mscr.flag_manualremoval_test(remove_dates=REMOVE_DATES, showplot=True, verbose=True)


# mscr.addflag()



Hampel filter
Flags spikes far from the median of a sliding window, measured in median absolute deviations (MAD).
With use_differencing=True a single spike also removes both its neighbours at n_sigma 5.5. With repeat=True blocks of up to four bad values in a row are removed, also next to gaps and at the ends of the data. Of longer blocks only the outer values are removed. With separate_day_night=True daytime records are compared with the daytime records of the window, nighttime records with the nighttime ones. Records with up to 20 W m-2 potential radiation count as night, so twilight records are judged against the night statistics and can be removed. A sensor stuck at one value is not flagged, because the MAD is zero there. Use manual removal or Set exact values to missing for that. Docs: flag_outliers_hampel_test, Hampel.

# mscr.flag_outliers_hampel_test(
#     window_length='7D',  # converted to a record count, see above
#     n_sigma_daytime=5.5, n_sigma_nighttime=5.5,
#     use_differencing=True, separate_day_night=True,
#     repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


# mscr.addflag()



Z-score
Flags values more than thres_zscore standard deviations from the mean of the whole period.
Not for precipitation: most records are zero, so every rain record looks like an outlier. Not for radiation with separate_day_night=True: twilight records count as night and stand out against the zeros. Docs: flag_outliers_zscore_test, zScore.

# mscr.flag_outliers_zscore_test(
#     thres_zscore=4.5, separate_day_night=True,
#     repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


# mscr.addflag()



Z-score (rolling window)
Z-score in a moving window of length winsize: it follows slow changes and flags local spikes.
Not for precipitation, as for the z-score: rain records stand out against the zeros. Docs: flag_outliers_zscore_rolling_test, zScoreRolling.

# mscr.flag_outliers_zscore_rolling_test(
#     thres_zscore=3.5, winsize='13D',  # converted to a record count, see above
#     repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


# mscr.addflag()



Local standard deviation
Flags values more than n_sd standard deviations from the rolling median over winsize.
Not for precipitation: the rolling median is zero most of the time, so rain records are removed. Docs: flag_outliers_localsd_test, LocalSD.

# mscr.flag_outliers_localsd_test(
#     separate_day_night=True, n_sd=5.5, winsize='7D',  # record count, see above; day/night covers more days
#     constant_sd=False, repeat=False, showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


# mscr.addflag()



Increments z-score
Flags records with unusually large jumps to their neighbours, from the z-score of the differences between records. Records are not compared across gaps.
Jumps are judged against the typical jump of the whole period, so variables with sudden real changes (precipitation, radiation under broken clouds) can lose valid records. Check the preview. Docs: flag_outliers_increments_zcore_test, zScoreIncrements.

# mscr.flag_outliers_increments_zcore_test(thres_zscore=40, repeat=True, showplot=True, verbose=True)


# mscr.addflag()



Local outlier factor
Flags points that sit apart from their nearest neighbours. It always flags the contamination fraction of records, also in clean data, and is slow on high-res data.
Not for precipitation: rain records sit apart from the many zeros, so they are removed. Docs: flag_outliers_lof_test, LocalOutlierFactor.

# mscr.flag_outliers_lof_test(
#     n_neighbors=30, contamination=0.01, separate_day_night=False,
#     repeat=False, n_jobs=-1, showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


# mscr.addflag()



Absolute limits
Flags values outside [minval, maxval], optionally with separate daytime and nighttime limits. The example limits fit air temperature in °C only. Docs: flag_outliers_abslim_test, AbsoluteLimits.

mscr.flag_outliers_abslim_test(minval=20, maxval=999, showplot=True, verbose=True)


mscr.addflag()



Trim low
Flags values below lower_limit in the chosen period, plus the same number of the highest values. Set lower_limit for your variable and season: the example value 10 would remove most nighttime air temperatures of a cool month. Check the preview. Docs: flag_outliers_trim_low_test, TrimLow.

# mscr.flag_outliers_trim_low_test(
#     trim_daytime=False, trim_nighttime=True, lower_limit=10,
#     showplot=True, verbose=True,
# )


# mscr.addflag()



Missing values
Not an outlier test. Flags missing records so that QCF counts them. Needs no addflag(). Docs: flag_missingvals_test.

mscr.flag_missingvals_test(verbose=True)



Overall quality flag QCF
Combines all committed flags into QCF and filters the series. Here every test gives 0 (good) or 2 (bad), and finalize removes the records flagged 2. title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
🔧 Corrections
Applied to the high-res data, filtered by QCF if outlier detection ran. Run only what applies to your variable.
All calls are commented out, because they change the data with example settings. Edit the settings, then uncomment the call.

mscr.showplot_cleaned()


Remove radiation zero offset
For shortwave radiation and PAR, which read below zero at night. The correction runs in this order: 1. Night: records with potential radiation below 0.001 W m-2. 2. Daily offset: the mean of the night values of each calendar day, i.e. the night before sunrise and the night after sunset of that date. All records of the day get this one value, there is no interpolation between days. Days without night values get the median offset of all days. 3. Subtract: the offset is subtracted from every record of the day, day and night. 4. Night to 0: night records are set to 0. 5. Clamp: values still below 0, e.g. daytime records at dawn and dusk, are set to 0. clamp_negatives=False keeps them.
The figure shows these steps with their counts, the daily offset, the diel cycle near zero after steps 3 and 5, the night values before and after subtracting the offset, and a summary. Docs: correction_remove_nighttime_zero_offset.

mscr.correction_remove_nighttime_zero_offset()



Remove relative humidity offset
For relative humidity that reads above 100 %. The correction runs in this order: 1. Find > 100 %: the values above 100 %. 2. Daily offset: for each day with such values, their mean minus 100. All records of the day get this one value. 3. Other days: the offset is interpolated linearly, record by record, between the nearest days with values above 100 %, and carried before the first and after the last such day. Without any value above 100 % the offset is 0. 4. Subtract: the offset is subtracted from every record. 5. Cap at 100 %: values still above 100 % are set to 100 %.
A single day above 100 % lowers every record of the period, so the result depends on the period screened. The figure shows these steps with their counts, the offset, the values near 100 %, the daily maximum and a summary. A pile just below 100 % without values above it means the sensor or logger caps the readings, and the correction finds no offset. Docs: correction_remove_relativehumidity_offset.

# mscr.correction_remove_relativehumidity_offset()



Set to maximum or minimum threshold
Sets values above or below a threshold to the threshold. The result looks plausible but was not measured, so removing the value is usually better. Docs: correction_setto_max_threshold, correction_setto_min_threshold.

text:
🔁 Resampling

Resample
Resamples the screened high-res series to RESAMPLING_FREQ, with TIMESTAMP_END timestamps ready for upload.
mincounts_perc sets how much of each target period the kept records must fill. Periods with less are missing. - 'mean': the share becomes a minimum number of records, rounded down. Below three, one record is enough, so 10-minute data resampled to 30 minutes need one record per half-hour. - 'sum': the kept records must cover that share of the period. For precipitation use 1 if partial sums are not wanted: a sum over a partly covered period is too low.
'mean' is an arithmetic mean and does not suit angles such as wind direction, which need a circular mean. This notebook does not compute one.
After changing the screened data, run this cell again, or the upload stops with an error. Docs: resample.

mscr.resample(to_freqstr=RESAMPLING_FREQ, agg=RESAMPLING_AGG, mincounts_perc=.5)

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
⬆️ Upload data to database
Existing screened data are overwritten. The upload writes to the processed bucket as data version meteoscreening_diive. With delete_from_db_before_upload=True it first deletes the stored values of each uploaded variable (same site, measurement, name and data version) between START and STOP, both included, then writes the new ones. Old values are removed also where the new data have no records, e.g. at the end of the period. Raw data, other variables and other data versions stay untouched.
The upload runs only with UPLOAD = True. It stops before deleting anything if: - SITE, MEASUREMENT, FIELDS, START, STOP or TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS differ from the values used for the download or the screening (mscr), e.g. after a new download without a new screening. The stored values would be shifted, or a neighbouring period deleted. Run the notebook again from Download. - a variable was resampled to a resolution other than RESAMPLING_FREQ, e.g. after an extra resample() call. Run Resample again.

upload_attempted = False  # read by the verify cells
if not UPLOAD:
    print('UPLOAD = False: nothing was uploaded. Set UPLOAD = True in the user settings to write the data.')
else:
    # Refuse before anything is deleted if the settings changed after the download or the screening:
    # a changed offset stores shifted values, a changed START or STOP deletes a neighbouring period,
    # and a download run again without a new screening would upload the old screening in its range.
    now = dict(site=SITE, measurement=MEASUREMENT, fields=list(FIELDS), start=START, stop=STOP,
               offset=TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS)
    used = {'download': DOWNLOAD_SETTINGS, 'screening': SCREENED_SETTINGS,
            'screening object': dict(site=mscr.site, fields=list(mscr.fields), offset=mscr.utc_offset),
            'resampled data': dict(fields=list(mscr.resampled_detailed.keys()))}

    def as_compared(k, v):
        return pd.Timestamp(v) if k in ('start', 'stop') else sorted(v) if k == 'fields' else v

    changed = {f'{k} ({name})': (s[k], now[k]) for name, s in used.items() for k in s
               if as_compared(k, s[k]) != as_compared(k, now[k])}
    if changed:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f'Nothing uploaded. Settings differ (used, now): {changed}. '
            f'Run the notebook again from the download.')
    # Refuse before anything is deleted: the stored values between START and STOP would be
    # replaced by data at another resolution. Compared as durations, so '24h' equals '1D'.
    target = pd.Timedelta(to_offset(RESAMPLING_FREQ).nanos, unit='ns')
    wrong_freq = {v: mscr.tags[v]['freq'] for v in mscr.resampled_detailed.keys()
                  if pd.Timedelta(to_offset(mscr.tags[v]['freq']).nanos, unit='ns') != target}
    if wrong_freq:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f'Nothing uploaded. Resampled to a resolution other than RESAMPLING_FREQ '
            f'({RESAMPLING_FREQ!r}): {wrong_freq}. Run the Resample cell again with RESAMPLING_FREQ.')
    print(f'Uploading to bucket {BUCKET_PROCESSED}')
    upload_attempted = True  # set before the writes, so the verify cells also report a failed write
    for v in mscr.resampled_detailed.keys():
        dbc.upload_singlevar(
            to_bucket=BUCKET_PROCESSED,
            to_measurement=assigned_measurements[v],
            var_df=mscr.resampled_detailed[v],
            timezone_offset_to_utc_hours=TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS,
            delete_from_db_before_upload=True,
            delete_start=START,
            delete_stop=STOP,
        )

Check downloaded data

dbc downloads three variables:

data_simple: This is the simplest data download. It contains only the high-resolution variable(s) from the specified measurement. Each variable is in a separate column. data_detailed: This is the most important variable for the MeteoScreening from the database, because it contains not only the high-resolution time series of the variable(s), but also their tags. A dictionary is a data structure that stores key-value pairs. The key is the variable name (e.g., TA_NABEL_T1_35_1) and the value is a complete dataframe that contains the time series of the respective variable and all tags.
assigned_measurements: An auxiliary variable that is useful to check whether the measurement of the variable(s) is correct. In case we are screening air temperatures, the measurement must be TA.

text:
Check downloaded data

dbc downloads three variables:

data_simple: This is the simplest data download. It contains only the high-resolution variable(s) from the specified measurement. Each variable is in a separate column. Since different variables, can have different time resolutions, the highest time resolution across the variables is used as the index. This means that lower resolution variables will show gaps in the higher resolution timestamp.
data_detailed: This is the most important variable for the MeteoScreening from the database, because it contains not only the high-resolution time series of the variable(s), but also their tags. The tags are important when uploading data to the database. This is a very special format, because data for each variable are stored in a dictionary. A dictionary is a data structure that stores key-value pairs. The key is the variable name (e.g., TA_NABEL_T1_35_1) and the value is a complete dataframe that contains the time series of the respective variable and all tags.
assigned_measurements: An auxiliary variable that is useful to check whether the measurement of the variable(s) is correct. In case we are screening air temperatures, the measurement must be TA.

Simply contains the time series of the measured variable(s) in a nice-to-look-at dataframe.

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
ℹ️ About this notebook
Downloads raw meteo data from InfluxDB, screens and corrects them at high resolution, resamples them to RESAMPLING_FREQ and uploads the result to the database. Screening uses StepwiseMeteoScreeningDb. Download and upload use InfluxIO, which needs pip install "diive[all]".
Screening is stepwise. Run a test, check its preview, then commit it with mscr.addflag(). At the end, all committed flags are combined into one quality flag, QCF.
Run All applies no outlier test and no correction, because they are all commented out. It still resamples, and it uploads only with UPLOAD = True.

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
⏱️ Timestamp convention (important)
The database stores all timestamps in UTC as TIMESTAMP_END, the end of the averaging interval. TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS sets the local time frame of the notebook, e.g. 1 for UTC+01:00. START, STOP, typed dates, the day/night split and day boundaries all use this frame. The download converts from UTC to this frame, the upload converts back. With a sub-daily RESAMPLING_FREQ such as '30min' the stored values are therefore the same for any offset. With '1D' the day boundaries follow the offset, so the daily values depend on it.
The raw data in the database are already in UTC, whatever clock the logger used. Use one fixed offset for every month, e.g. 1 (CET) also in summer. Changing it shifts START, STOP and typed dates, which leaves a gap or an overlap between runs.

title: MeteoScreening from database (InfluxDB)
text:
✏️ User settings (please adjust)
Adjust these before running.
Site - SITE, SITE_LAT, SITE_LON: site ID and coordinates. The coordinates set the day/night split.
Variables to screen - FIELDS: one or more variable names exactly as stored in the database (the InfluxDB _field). - MEASUREMENT: exactly one measurement that holds these variables.
Time range to screen - START, STOP: each one second after a RESAMPLING_FREQ boundary, e.g. '2026-03-01 00:00:01' and '2026-04-01 00:00:01' for March. Timestamps mark the END of each interval, so the record at 2026-03-01 00:00:00 belongs to February. These values cover the records ending after 2026-03-01 00:00 up to and including 2026-04-01 00:00. The upload deletes the same range before writing. Other values stop the notebook in Auto settings.
Data settings - TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS: local time frame of this run, one fixed offset without daylight saving time, see Timestamp convention. - DATA_VERSION: data version of the source data (raw). - DIRCONF: local folder with the database connection config.
Resampling - RESAMPLING_FREQ: target time resolution of the screened data. - RESAMPLING_AGG: 'mean' or 'sum'. Use 'sum' only for variables that accumulate over the interval.
Upload - UPLOAD: False runs everything except the upload. Set True only for the run that should write the result. The upload replaces the stored values between START and STOP.

# --- Site ---
SITE = 'ch-lae'
SITE_LAT = 47.478333   # CH-LAE
SITE_LON = 8.364389  # CH-LAE

# --- Variables to screen ---
FIELDS = [
    'PA_T1_47_1',
]
MEASUREMENT = 'PA'

# --- Time range to screen ---
# One second after a RESAMPLING_FREQ boundary, because stamps mark the END of each interval:
# these values cover the records ending after 2026-03-01 00:00 up to and including 2026-04-01 00:00.
START = '2026-01-01 00:00:01'
STOP = '2026-10-01 00:00:01'

# --- Data settings ---
DATA_VERSION = 'raw'
# Local time frame of this run. The database holds UTC. Use one fixed value for every month,
# e.g. 1 (CET) also in summer: changing it shifts START/STOP and typed dates.
TIMEZONE_OFFSET_TO_UTC_HOURS = 1  # UTC+01:00
DIRCONF = r'<LOCAL>\poet\configs'  # <-- must be set: folder with the database connection config
# DIRCONF = r'P:\Flux\RDS_calculations\_scripts\_configs'

# --- Resampling ---
RESAMPLING_FREQ = '30min'
RESAMPLING_AGG = 'mean'  # 'mean' or 'sum'

# --- Upload ---
UPLOAD = True  # True writes the result to the database, replacing stored values between START and STOP

text:
🤖 Auto settings

Buckets and time range check (do not adjust)

import pandas as pd

BUCKET_RAW = f'{SITE}_raw'  # source bucket
BUCKET_PROCESSED = f'{SITE}_processed'  # destination bucket
print(f'Source bucket (raw data):       {BUCKET_RAW}')
print(f'Destination bucket (processed): {BUCKET_PROCESSED}')

# START and STOP must be one second after a RESAMPLING_FREQ boundary, see the user settings.
one_second = pd.Timedelta(seconds=1)
for name, value in (('START', START), ('STOP', STOP)):
    expected = pd.Timestamp(value).floor(RESAMPLING_FREQ) + one_second
    if pd.Timestamp(value) != expected:
        raise ValueError(f"{name} = '{value}' is not one second after a {RESAMPLING_FREQ} boundary. "
                         f"Stamps mark the END of each interval. Use e.g. '{expected}'.")
if pd.Timestamp(STOP) <= pd.Timestamp(START):
    raise ValueError(f"STOP ('{STOP}') must be after START ('{START}').")
print(f'Time range: records ending after {pd.Timestamp(START) - one_second} '
      f'up to and including {pd.Timestamp(STOP) - one_second}')
